MESSAGE from His Majesty, by Sir

Francis AJolyneux, Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this Honourable House to attend His Majesty, immediately, in the House of Peers.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to attend His Majesty.

And being returned;

Mr. Speaker acquainted the House, that, in pursuance of the Directions of an Act, passed in the Tenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, An Act to enable the Speaker of the House of Commons to issue his Warrants, to make out new Writs for the Choice of Members to serve in Parliament, " in the room of such Members as shall die during the " Recess of Parliament," he had issued his Warrants to the Clerk of the Crown, to make out new Writs for the Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the following Places; viz. for the Borough of mouth, in the County of Southampton, in the room of Maurice Suckling, Esquire; for the Borough of in the County of Carnival/,in the room' of Sir Charles Whitworth, Knight; and for the Town and County of the Town of Nottingham, in the room of Sir Charles Sedley, Baronet.

A Member present, and several Members returned upon new Writs, took the Oaths, and made and lub-feribed the Declaration, and took and lubscribed the Oath of Abjuration, according to the Laws made for those Purposes; and such of the said Members as are by Law required to deliver in to the Clerk of this House an Account of their Qualification, and to take and subscribe the Oath of Qualification, delivered in such Account, and took and lubscribed the said Oath, accordingly.

Vol. 37.

A Bill for the more effectual preventing Clandestine Outlawries, was read the First Time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second Time.

Mr. Speaker reported. That the House had attended His Majesty, in the House of Peers-, where His Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne, to both Houses of Parliament; of which, Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy; which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I have called you together in a Conjuncture which demands your most: serious Attention.

In the Time of profound Peace, without Pretence of Provocation, or Colour of Complaint, the Court of France hath not forborne to disturb the public Tranquil-'lity, in Violation of the Faith of Treaties, and the general Rights of Sovereigns; at first by the clandestine Supply of Arms and other Aid to My revolted Subjects in North America, afterwards by avowing openly their Support, and entering into formal Engagements with the Leaders of the Rebellion, and at length by committing open Iloftilities and Depredations on My faithful Subjects, and by an actual Invasion of My Dominions in America and the West Judies.

It is, I trust, unnecessary for Me to allure you, that the same Care and Concern for the Ilappinels of My People, which induced Me to endeavour to prevent the Calamities of War, will make Me desirous to fee a fte-storation of the Blcflings of Peace, whenever it can be effected with perfect Honour, and with Security to- the Rights of this Country.

In the mean Time, I have not neglecded to take the proper and necessary Measures for disappointing the malignant Designsof Our Enemies, and alto for making general Repril’als; and although My Efforts have not been attended with all the Succels, which the Justice of Our Caule and the Vigour of Our Exertions leemed to promise, yet the extensive Commerce of My Subjects has been protected in moll of its Branches, and large Reprisals have been made upon the injurious Aggrel-fors, by the Vigilance of My Fleets, and by the active and enterprising Spirit of My People,

Clandestine

Outlawries.

46" Novembris. A. 1778.

The great Armaments of other Powers, however friendly and sincere their Professions, however just and honourable their Purposes, must necedarily engage Our Attention.

It would have afforded Me very great Satisfaction to have informed you, that the conciliatory Measures, planned by the Wisdom and Temper of Parliament, had taken the desired Effect, and brought thq Troubles in North America to a happy Condufion.

In this Situation of Affairs, the national Honour and Security call so loudly upon Us for the most active Exertions, that I cannot doubt of your heartiest Concurrence and Support. From the Vigour of your Councils, and the Conduct and Intrepidity of My Officers and Forces by Sea and Land, I hope, under the Blessing of God, to derive the Means of vindicating and maintaining the Honour of My Crown, and the Interests of My People, against all Our Enemies.

Gentlemen of the Hause of Commons,

I will order the proper Efti mates for the Service of the ensuing Year to be laid before you; and when you consider the Importance of the Objects for which We are contending, you will, I doubt not, grant Me such Supplies as you shall judge necessary for the public Service, and adequate to the present Emergency.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I have, according to the Powers veiled in Me for that Purpose, called forth the Militia, to assist in the interior Defence of this Country; and I have, with the greatest and truest Satisfaction, been Myself a Witness of that public Spirit, that Heady Ardour, and that Love of their Country, which animate and unite all Ranks of My faithful Subjects, and which cannot fail of making Us safe at Home, and respected Abroad.

Addrefr A Motion was made, and the Question being pro-m ° h posed. That an humble Address be presented to His n*» peec . j^ajc^ tQ return His Majesty the Thanks of this House, for His most gracious Speech from the Throne;

To acknowledge His Majesty’s paternal Regard for the Happiness of His People, in His earnest and uniform Endeavours to preserve the public Tranquillity, and the good Faith and Uprightness of His Majesty’s Conduct to all Foreign Powers; and to assure His Majesty, that we have seen with Concern and Indignation that Tranquillity disturbed by the Court of France, without the least Pretence of Provocation, or Colour of Complaint; and that we have, with the warmest Emotions of Resentment, marked the Prog refs of their malignant Designs against this Country; first, by a clandestine Aid and Supply of Arms to His Majesty’s revolted Subjects in North; afterwards, in

Violation of the Faith of Treaties, and contrary to the Rights and common Interest of every Sovereign State in Europe possessed of Colonies and Dependencies, by entering into and avowing formal Engagements with the Leaders of the Rebellion; and, at length, by committing open Hostilities and Depredations, and by actually invading Part of His Majesty’s Dominions in America and the West Indies:

That we cannot but feel Concern and Regret, that the Measures taken by His Majesty, for disappointing these hostile and malignant Designs, have not been attended with all the Success which the Justice of the Cause, and tire Vigour of the Exertions, seemed to promise; yet we have at the same Time seen, with great Satisfaction, the extensive Commerce of His Majesty’s Subjects protected in most of its Branches, and large Reprisals made on the injurious Aggressors, by the Vigilance of His Majesty’s Fleets, and the active Spirit of the Nation:

That it would have given His faithful Commons the truest Happiness, to have received the Communication from His Majesty, that the just and humane Purposes of His Majesty, and His Parliament, for quieting the Minds of His revolted Subjects, had taken the desired Effect, and had brought the Troubles in North America to a happy Condufion.

To assure His Majesty, that His Majesty may rely on the hearty and zealous Occurrence ancf Assistance of His faithful Commons, in enabling His Majesty to liVflce -the most active and vigorous Exertions by Sea and Land, for vindicating and establishing the national Honour and Security ;g ' >0 declare our stedfast Resolution, and renew ou*triolemn Assurances, to His Maje%. that this House, convinced of the Importance of the ObjeCks for which we are contending, and impelled by every Motive of Duty and Interest that can animate the Hearts of Britons, will effectually assist His Majesty in the Profecurion of the present just and necessary War; and that they will, to the utmost of their Power, support His Majesty against all His Enemies;

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, -by.inferring after the Words " ,"

at the End of the Second Paragraph, these Words;

" To assure His Majesty, that with the truest Zeal for " the Honour of the Crown, and the warmest Affection for His Person and Family, we are ready to give " the most ample Support to such Measures as may " be thought necessary for the Defence of these Kingdoms, or for frustrating the Designs of that restless Power, which has so often disturbed the Peace of " Europe; but that we think it one of our most important Duties, in the present melancholy Posture " of Affairs, to inquire by what fatal Councils, or " unhappy Systems of Policy, this Country has been " reduced from that splendid Situation, which in the " early Part of His Majesty’s Reign made her the " Envy of all Europe, to such a dangerous State, as " that which has of late called forth our utmost Exertions, without any adequate Benefit."

And the Question being put. That those Words be there inserted;

The House divided.

That it would have given His faithful Commons the truest Happiness, to have received the Communication from His Majesty, that the just and humane Purposes of His Majesty and His Parliament, for quieting the Minds of His revolted Subjects, had taken the desired ElfcCt, and had brought the Troubles in North America to a happy Conclusion:

Ordered, That all Persons who will question any Returns of Members to serve in Parliament, do question the same within Fourteen Days next, and lo within Fourteen Days next after any new Return shall be brought in; and that all Members who are returned for Two or more Places do make their Election by this Day Three Weeks, for which of the Places they will serve, provided there be no Question upon the Return for that Place; and if any Thing shall come in Question touching the Return or Eletfion of any Member, he is to withdraw during the Time the Matter is in Debate; and that all Members returned upon Double Returns do withdraw till their Returns are determined.

Refqlved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That, where this House shall judge any Petition touching Elections to be frivolous and vexa-

tious the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned again!!.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath procured himself to be defied or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence, the same is declared to be a High Crime and Misdeameanour; and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath given false Evidence, in any Case, before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is a high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Resolved, That, in all Cases of controverted Elections for Counties in England and Wales, the Petitioners do, by themselves or by their Agents, within a convenient Time, to be appointed by the House, deliver to the Sitting Members, or their Agents, Lists of the Persons intended by the Petitioners to be objected to, who voted for the Sitting Members; giving, in the said Lifts, the several Heads of Objection, and distinguishing the same against-the Names of the Voters excepted to; and that the Sitting Members do, by themselves or by their Agents, within the same Time, deliver the like Lifts, on their Part, to the Petitioners, or their Agents.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from Time to Time, take into his Custody -any Stranger, or Strangers, that he shall see, or be informed of to be, in the House, or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is fitting; and that no Person, so taken into Custody, be difehavg-ed out of Custody, without the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That the Back Door of the Speaker’s Chamber be locked up every Morning at the Sitting of the House, and the Key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked up by him; and that he do not presume to deliver the same to any Person whatsoever, without Order of the House; and that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take Care to clear the Speaker’s Chamber every Day, before the Door is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger, or Strangers, into the House, or Gallery' thereof, while the House is fitting.

Ordered, That the Constables, and other Officers, of Middlesex and Westminster, do take Care, that, from Eleven of the Clock in the xVIorning till One in the Afternoon, and from Four till Six in the Afternoon, during the Session of Parliament, the Patfages through the Streets between Temple Bar and shall be kept free and open; and that no Obilructions be made, by Cars, Drays, Carts, or otherwise, to hinder the Passage of the Members to and from this House; and that the Seiyeant ax Arms attending this House do give Notice of this Order to the Officers aforesaid.

Mr. Grevillereported from the Committee, appointed

Yesterday to draw up an Address to be presented to His Majesty, That the Committee had drawn up an Address accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the Iloule; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, Your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, beg Leave to return Your Majesty the Thanks of this House, for Your most Gracious Speech from the Throne.

We acknowledge, with the utmost Gratitude, Your Majesty’s paternal Regard for the Happiness of Your People, in Your earned: and uniform Endeavours to preserve the public Tranquillity, and the good Faith and Uprightness of Yrour Majesty’s Conduct to all Foreign Powers: And we allure Your Majesty, that we have seen with Concern and Indignation, that Tranquillity disturbed by the Court of France, without the lead Pretence of Provocation, or Colour of Complaint; and we have, with the warmed Emotions of Resentment, marked the Progress of their malignant Designs against this Country; first by a clandestine Aid and Supply of Arms to Your Majesty’s revolted Subjects in North America; afterwards, in Violation of the Faith 0fT1eat.es, and contrary to the Rights and common Interest of every Sovereign State in Europe pof-leftfed of Colonies and Dependencies, by entering into and avowing formal Engagements with the Leaders of the Rebellion; and, at length, by committing open Hostilities and Depredations, and by actually invading

Part of Your Majesty's Dominions in America and the

West Indies.

We cannot but feel Concern and Regret, that the Measures taken by Your Majesty, for disappointing these hostile and malignant Designs, have not been attended with all the Success which the Justice of the Cause, and the Vigour of the Exertions, seemed to promise; yet we have at the same Time seen, with great Satisfaction, the extensive Commerce of Your Majesty’s Subjects protected in most of its Branches, and large Reprisals made on the injurious AggrelTors, by the Vigilence of Your Majesty’s Fleets, and the active Spirit of the Nation.

It would have given Your faithful Commons the truest Happiness, to have received the Communication from Your Majesty, that the just and humane Purposes of Your Majesty, and Your Parliament, for quieting the Minds of Your revolted Subjects, had taken the desired Effect, and had brought the Troubles in North America to a happy Conclusion.

Your faithful Commons do most heartily concur with Your Majesty, in the just Approbation You have been pleased to expressof the public Spirit which has lo con-fpicuously animated all Ranks of Y our Majesty’s faithful Subjects to Hand forth, at this Time of Danger, in the Service of the Militia, who, by their Discipline, and Heady Perseverance in their Duty, have enabled YTour Majesty to avail Yourself of that constitutional Force for the Defence of this Country.

Your Majesty may rely on the hearty and zealous Concurrence and Assistance of Your faithful Commons, in enabling Your Majesty to make the most active and vigorous Exertions by Sea and Land, for vindicating and establishing the national Honour and Security; and we beg Leave to declare our stedfast Resolution, and renew our solemn Assurances to Your Majesty, that this House, convinced of the Importance of the Ob-jests for which we are contending, and impelled by every Motive of Duty and Interest that can animate the Hearts of Britons, will effectually assist Your Majesty in the Prosecution of the present just and necessary War; and that we will, to the utmost of our Power, support Your Majesty against all Your Enemies.

The laid Address being read a Second Time;

Resolved, That the said Address be presented to His Majesty by the whole House.

Mr. Qrd, according to Order* reported From the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and arc as so:loweth, viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Seventy thousand Men be employed for the Sea-Service for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-nine, including Seventeen thousand Three hundred and Eighty-nine Marines.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Four Pounds per Man per Month, be allowed for maintaining the said Seventy thousand Men, for Thirteen Months, including Ordnance for Sea Service.

The laid Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Resolved, That this House will, Tomorrow Morning, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty.

A Petition of divers Merchants and Traders at chester, Arundel, Shoreham, i$c. in the County of Sussex, was presented to the House, and read; Set-

ting forth, That, by the Act of the Thirteenth of His present Majesty, to regulare the Importation and Exportation of Corn, the different Duties which arc payable on Corn imported have been made to depend entirely on the Pr ices thereof at the Places where the same may be imported, as they shall appear according to the Methods directed by the several Acts of Parliament for ascertaining the Rates and Prices of Corn and Grain imported; and that, in the Eastern District of the County of Sussex, the Prices of Corn have never been at all ascertained in order for Importation, although Application has been made to the Magift-ates for that Purpose; and that, in the Western District of the said County, it has not been done with that Accuracy which so important a Subject requires, neither have the proper Averages been always taken (as the Petitioners conceive) from the different Inland Market Towns, and the Returns have been sometimes made for feme particular Sorts of Corn only, and not for all Sorts, which several Omissions are, as the Petitioners also con-Voi. 37.

Decembris. 13

ccive, highly injurious, and render the above-mentioned most salutary Law's of little Effect: And therefore praying such Relief in the Premises, as the House shall fee expedient to grant.

A Petition of the Merchants and Traders of Port/- JLpojtatjoa mouth, Gosport, Emsworth, Havantthe Isle of Wight, 0 Corn*

and other Parts of the County of Southampton, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was also presented to the I louse, and read; Setting forth, That, by an Act of the Thirteenth of His present Majesty, to regulate the Importation and Exportation of Corn, it is enacted, that the Importation shall be regulated by the Prices of Corn at the Ports and Places where it shall be imported, as the feme shall appear, according to the Methods directed by the several Acts of Parliament for ascertaining the Rates and Prices of Corn and Grain imported; and that such Directions are found (with respect to the Out Ports) to be very vague, and inadequate to so important a Purpose, and liable to great Abuse from interested Persons; and that at the Sessions held in October last at Wine heft er, for the said County of Southampton, Returns most notoriously false were made of the Prices of Corn, whereby Wheat imported into the said County was rendered liable to the Payment of the high Duty, contrary to the Intention of the said Act of the Thirteenth of His present Majesty; and that the Petitioners are advised no adequate Remedy is at present provided by Law for Abuses of this Kind, and apprehend, that without some new and more effectual Regulations for ascertaining the Port Prices of Corn in order for Importation, the good and beneficial Purposes of the said Act are liable to be constantly interrupted and perverted: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and grant such Relief as shall seem meet.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

The House was moved. That the Manifesto and America* Proclamation Irom His Majesty’s Commissioners at New Commit..,wr* Fork, to the Members of the Congrels, the Members MauilelU*. of the General Assemblies, and to other Persons, Inhabitants of the Colonies ih America, contained in the printed Book presented to this House by Lord George Germain, on IVedmfday last, might be read.

And the same being read accordingly;

A Motion was made, and the Question being put.

That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, to express to His Majesty the Dilplealurc of this House, at a certain Manifesto and Proclamation, dared the 3d Day of October 1778, and published in America, under , the Hands and Seals of the Earl of Sir Henry

Clinton, Knight of the Bath, and William Eden, Esquire, Commissioners for restoring Peace to the Colonies, and countersigned by Adam Ferguson, Esquire, Sccreiary to the Commission; the said Manilelto containing a Declaration of the following Tenor:

" If there be any Persons who, diverted of mistaken Resentments, and uninfluenced by selfish Interests, really " think that it is for the Benefit of the Colonies to fe-

" parate

*9

jo Geo. III. 4* — c

parate themselves from Great and that, so

,u separated, they will find a Constitution more mild,

more free, and better calculated for their Prosperity, u than that which they heretofore enjoyed, and which '* we are impowered and disposed to renew and improve; with such Persons we will not dilpute a " Postion, which seems to be sufficiently contradicted " by the Experience they have had: But we think it " right to leave them fully aware of the Change which " the maintaining of such a Postion must make in the " whole Nature and future Couduft of thU War; more " especially, when to this Postion is added, the pretended Alliance with the Court of France. — The Policv, as well as the Benevolence, of Great Britain,

" have thus far checked the Extremes of War, when " they tended to distress a People dill considered as our " Fellow Subjects, and to desolate a Country thortly " to become again a Source of mutual Advantage;

" but when that Country ..rofeiles the unnatural Detign " not only rf eftrunging herself from us, but of m rtgaging herself, and her Resources, to our Enemies,

H the whole Contest is changed; and the Question is,

" How far Great Britain may, by every Means in her " Power, destroy, or render useless, a Connexion contrived for her Ruin, and for the Aggranduement of " France. Under such Circumstances, the Laws of " Self-Preservation mud direct the Conduct of Great Britain, and, if the British Colonies are to become

" an Accession to France, will direct her- to render that Accession of as little Avail as pofilble to her Enemy."

To acquaint His Majesty with the Sense of this House, that the said Coraraiifioners had no Authority whatsoever, under the Act of Parliament, in virtue of which they were appointed by His Majesty, to make the said Declaration, or to make any De> filiation to the same or to the like Purport; nor can this House be easily brought to believe, that the said Commissioners derived any such Authority from His Majesty’s Inductions.

Humbly to beseech His Majesty, that so much of the said Manifesto as contains the said Dec'aration, be forthwith publicly disavowed by His Majesty, as containing Matter inconsistent with the Humanity and generous Courage, which in all Times have distinguished the British Nation, subversive of the Maxims which

have been established among Christian and Civilized Communities, derogatory to the Dignity of the Crown of this Realm, tending to debase the Spirit, and to subvert the Difclpline, of His Majesty’s Armies; and to expose His Majesty’s innocent Subjects, in all Parts of His Dominions, to cruel and ruinuus Retaliations.

The House divided.

The Yeas went forth.

The Lord Clive reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the several Trustees whole Names 03 are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Trustees appointed to put in execution an Act of Parliament, passed in the Twenty-ninth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, "An Act for amending, widening,

" and keeping in Repair, several Roads leading from " The Market House, and elsewhere, in the Town of " Ludlow, in the County of Salop," was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, of the 25 th of April 17 74, relative to Turnpike Bills, had not been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followetk; viz.

Somerset Davis, Esquire, informed your Committee,

That the Reason why the Standing Orders had not been complied with was, that till after the Time limited for giving Notices required by those Orders, the Trustees had no Intention to apply in this Session of Parliament for enlarging the Term of the Act, as they conceived an Addition of Five Years was added to the Term of the said Act, by the General Law made in the Twenty-eighth Year of his said late Majesty, relating to the Turnpike Roads of this Kingdom.

Then, to prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said General Law, and the said Act, were read; by which it appeared, that the Term of the said Act did expire.at the End of the last Session of Parliament.

Then Mr. Davis informed your Committee, That the Trustees, imagining the Act to be in Force, had continued to receive the usual Tolls thereby granted: And he added, that a considerable Sum of Money had been borrowed, and is now due and owing upon the Credit of the said Act, which must be all loll to the Creditors, and the Roads become again in a ruinous Condition, unless the Term of the said Act is revived, and further continued.

A Member present confirmed Mr. Davis's Evidence.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That, in Consideration of the particular Circumstances mentioned in the said Report, Leave be granted, that Notices may be given, at the ensuing Christmas Quarter Sessions of the Peace, to be held for the Counties of Salop, Hereford, and Radnor, and

That the Lands and Grounds of the Petitioners, in the said Open and Common Fields, Common Pastures, Common Meadows, and other Commonable Lands and Grounds, lie intermixed and dispersed, and, in their present Situation,’ are incapable of any considerable Improvement; and it would be very advantageous to the Persons interested therein, if the said Fields, Lands, and Grounds, were: divided and inclosed, and specific Shares: thereof allotted to the several Proprietors, according to their respective Rights and Interests: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for dividing and inclosing the said Open and Common Fields, Common Pastures,

Mr. St. John reported from the Committee, to whom Whitstable the Petition of several of the Free Fishers and Dredgers, Oyster belonging to the Oyster Fishery, within the Manor and Filbrry. Royalty of Whitjlaole, in the County of Kent, in Behalf

io Geo. III. . p° Debembris. 3$

half of themselves, and alt other Free Fishers and Dredgers tl'.ere, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place j and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Tablet Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations’ of the said Petition, Mr. George Munk, being examined, laid, That there has

been, Time out of Mind, an Oyster Fishery within the Manor and Royalty of Wh, itt the East Part of the County of Kent, limited by Well kppwh Marks and Bounds, wherein’Certain People, regularly admitted Freemen, at a Court called Court of Dredging, held annually for that Purpose, have an executive Right of dredging and fishing for Oysters, or the Brood thereof. ’

Mr. Thomas Gann being examined, said, That he has known the Fishery or 45 Years, and that it has been greatly plundered for many Years past, by Strangers and Intruders fishing and dredging within the Limits thereof, and carrying off the Oysters, to the great Prejudice of the Free Fishermen, who are deprived of their immediate Property, and the Brood are destroyed by fishing in improper Seasons; and he further said, that this Fishery is so circumstanced, that they are ufiable to defend their Property as in the other contiguous Fisheries; that the said' Oyfler Ground, being great Part of it bounded to the open Sea, is. always accessible to Thieves, who can leave it again with any Wind; that the Boats of the Fishermen (having an exclusive Right to this Fishery) being moored in Shore, are left aground at Ebb Tides, which prevents all Possibility of following the Plunderers, whereas, the other Fisheries, being up Creeks, Persons attempting to rob them, have not such certain Means of escaping, and tnuft come at particular Times of the Tide, or there would not be sufficient Depth of Water at the Ebb for them to get out to Sea again, and not even then unless particular Winds to serve them j that the said Fishery, on former Occasions and lately, has been a Nursery for Seamen, and furnished many useful Men for the Service of the Public; that if the Fishery was protested from the Intrulion of Strangers, and properly secured to the Persons entitled to it as Freemen, whose Livelihood wholly depends thereupon, the same would not only be of great Advantage to them, but also to Numbers of the Inhabitants of the East Part of the County of Kent, and be of public Utility.

Mr. Augu/line Saver, who has known the Fishery 60 Years, and Mr. Stephen Qttaif 50 Years, confirmed the Evidence of the last Witnesss,

Mr. Ord, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had duelled him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as follow -eth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a N umber of Land Forces, including Three, thou-Vox- 37.

sand Two hundred and Thirteen Invalids, amounting to Thirty thousand Three hundred and Forty-six Effective Men, Commission and Non-commission Officers included, be employed for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-nine.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Eight hundred Thirty-three thousand Nine hundred and Eleven Pounds Eighteen Shillings and Sixpence, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Charge of Thirty thousand Three hundred and Forty-six Effective Men, for Guards, Garrisons, and other His Majesty's Land Forces, in Great , Jersey, and Guernsey, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-nine.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Thirty-seven thousand Two hundred and Six Pounds Eight Shillings and Sixpence Halfpenny, be granted to His Majesty, for the Pay of the General and General Staff Officers in Great Britain, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-nine.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One million One hundred Three Thousand One hundred and Eighteen Pounds and Eleven Shillings, be granted to His Majesty, for maintaining His Majesty’s Forces and Garrisons, in the Plantations, and AJrica, including those in Garrison at Minorca and Gibraltar, and for Provisions for the Forces in North America, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, Gibraltar, the Ceded Islands, and AJrica, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-nine.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Fifty-two thousand Nine hundred and Twenty-three Pounds One Shilling and Sixpence, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Charge of the Difference of Pay between the British and Irish Establishment of One Regiment of Light Dragoons and Six Regiments of Foot, serving in North America, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-nine.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion. of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Fifty-six thousand and Seventy-four Pounds Nineteen Shillings and Four Pence Halfpenny, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Charge of Five Hanoverian Battalions of Foot at Gibraltar and Minorca, and for Provisions for the Three Battalions of the said Troops at Gibraltar, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-nine.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Three hundred Sixty-seven thousand Two hundred and Three Pounds Nine Shillings and Ten Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Charge of Thirteen thousand Four hundred and Seventy-two Men, of the Troops of the Landgrave of HeJJe Cajjel, in the Pay of Great Britain, together with the Subsidy, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-nine, pursuant to Treaty.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Thirty-five thousand Four hundred Forty-one Pounds Nineteen Shillings and Nine Pence Halfpenny, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Charge of Two Regiments of Hanau, in the Pay of Great Britain, together with the Subsidy, pursuant to Treaty with the Hereditary Prince of Cajjel, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-nine.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Seventeen thousand Four hundred Ninety-eight Pounds Three Shillings and Two Pence Three Farthings, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Charge of a Regiment of Foot of Wal-deck, in the Pay of Great Britain, together with the Subsidy, pursuant to Treaty with the Reigning Prince of IValdeck, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-nine.

AMES S A G E, by Mr. Quarnie, Yeoman Ulher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

oral Assent The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s Commission lor declaring His Royal Assent to several Acts agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported. That the House, at the Desire of the Lords authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s Commission aforementioned, had been at the House of Peers} where a Commission under the Great Seal was read} giving, declaring, and notifying, the Royal Af-sent to the several Public Bills and One Private Bill therein mentioned} and allb impowering the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, the Lord President of the Council, the Lord Privy Seal, and several other Lords, to declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills} Vol. 37.

and that the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, the Earl of Sandzuich, and the Ix>rd named

allb in the said Commission, did accordingly declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills} which Bills are as followeth } viz.

An Act for granting Relief to the Captors of Prizes, with respect to bringing and landing certain French Prizes in this Kingdom;

An Act for granting further Time for allowing the Drawback upon the Exportation of certain Mullins, Callicoes, and Coffee:

An Act to authorize the Lord High Admiral, or the Commissioners for executing the Office of Lord High Admiral, for the Time being, to order any Court Martial, which may be appointed on the Charge of Vice Admiral Sir Hugh Palliser against the Honourable Admiral Augufius Keppel, to be holden on Shore:

An Act for making the Church, or Chapel, erected by Charles Roe, Esquire, in the Town of in the County Palatine of Chester, a perpetual Cure and Benefice-, and for endowing the lame, and veiling the Right of Nomination or Presentation thereof in the said Charles Roe, his Heirs and Assigns} and for other Purposes:

An Act for dividing and inclosing the Common or Waste Land, within the Parish of Bafiwick, in the County of Norfolk.

And then the House adjourned till fhurfday, the 14th Day of January next. Ten of the Clock in the Morning.

That the Trustees have proceeded in the Execution of the said Act*, and have borrowed a considerable Sum of Money on the Credit of the Tolls authorized to be collcded on such Part of the said Roads as leads from Stratford Bridge to Edghill, which still remains due; and that the Tolls collected upon the said Road from Stratford upon Avon to Edghill, together with the Money borrowed on the Credit thereof, have been applied towards the Re-pail's of the said ltoad, and great Progress hath been made therein; but the said Road cannot be effectually amended and kept in good Repair, and the Money borrowed repaid, unless the Term of the said Acts, so far as they relate to the said Road, be further continued, and some additional Powers granted to the Trustees for those Purposes; and that the Petitioners apprehend the said Road might be better amended and kept in Repair if the same was made a separate District, and put under the Care of separate Trustees, and if the several Clauses and Provisions necessary. for repairing the said Road, were reduced into and made One Act of Parliament: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for effecting the several Purposes aforesaid, by such Ways and Means, and in such Manner, as the House shall think proper.

(cJtw) \ Petition of Joseph Batin, Clerk, Vicar of the Pari 111 and Parish Church of Saint , in the City of Coventry, and of the several other Persons whole Names are thereunto subscribed, for and on Behalf of ' themselves, and the rest of the Inhabitants and Occupiers of Houses and other Tenements in the said Parish, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Right of Patronage of the above-named Benefice, or Vicarage, is vested in the King’s Majesty, in Right of His Crown; and the Tithes and Profits thereof do principally stand and depend upon a Statute of the Fourth and Fifth Year of the Reign of King Philip and Queen Mary, intituled, "An Act for the " Payment of Tithes in the City of Coventry;" and that the Rates and Assessments, made by virtue of the said Statute, have been much impaired from their true Value, and become not only arbitrary and unequal, but insufficient for the Maintenance and Support of the said Vicar; by reason whereof, several Suits and Differences have arisen about the Payment and Proportion of the said Tithes, to the great Prejudice and Impoverishment of the contending Parties; and that the Petitioners, in order to avoid all future Disputes relative to the said Tithes, have agreed, that a Pound Rate shall be laid upon the Inhabitants, and Occupiers of Houses and other Tenements, within the said Parish, and paid to the Vicar, for the Time being, instead of the Payments directed by the said Statute; such Rate to commence and be paid from Easier 1773, to be in lieu, and perpetual Discharge of, all Tithe*, and Ecclesiastical Dues and Demands what foe ver, payable to the Vicar of the said Parish: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to ascertain and establish the Payment of the said Pound Rate, in lieu of Tithes and Ecclesiastical Dues, within the said Parish of Saint Trinity, in Coventry.

And he concluded with laying. That it would be advantageous to both Districts, if the whole Roads were completely amended; but that the same cannot be done, and be kept in Repair for the future, and the Money borrowed be paid off, unless the Term of the said Act, which is near expiring, be continued, and the Powers are altered and enlarged.

A Petition of Thomas Jaques, of Leeds, in the County of York, Gentleman, was presented to the House, and read Setting forth. That the Petitioner- is informed Application is intended to be made to Parliament by Charles Brandling, Esquire, for Leave to bring in a Bill to amend an Act, passed in the Thirty-first Year of King George the Second, intituled, "An Act for establishing Agreements made between Charles " ling, Esquire, and other Persons, Proprietors of Lands,

" for laying down a Waggon Way, in order for the " better iiipplying the Town and Neighbourhood of " Leeds, in the County of York, with Coals;" and that, under the Authority of the said Act, or otherwise, the said Charles Brandling is obliged, or hath agreed, to supply the Inhabitants of Leeds aforesaid

with Twenty thousand Dozens of Corfs of Coals yearly, at the stipulated Price of Four Pence Three Farthings per Corf; and that the Petitioner is the Owner of the Inheritance of a Close called Cajjon Close, in the Town of Leeds aforesaid, now in Leate with other PremilTes to the said Charles Brandling, under a Yearly reserved Rent, for the Remainder of a Term granted to him by the Petitioner’s Uncle, John since deceased,

which Close is the only Coal Yard, or Repository, for the laying up, and Sale of, such Coals; and it is (amongst others) an express Condition in the said Lease, that, in case the said Charles Brandling, or other Owner and Proprietor of his Collieries or Coal Works therein mentioned, shall refuse or neglect, in any One Year during the said Lease, to bring or cause to be brought to the said Cajfon Close (the Repository or Coal Y ard aforesaid) the Quantities or Dozens of Corfs of Coals aforesaid, unless prevented by Fire, Water, or other inevitable Accident, or shall refuse to fell, or offer the same to Sale, when brought down to the said Coal Yard, for the Use and Consumption of the Inhabitants of the said Town of Leeds, at the Rate or Price aforesaid, as by them respectively should be required; in such Case, the Lessor, his Heirs, or Assigns, may enter upon the demised Premisses, and from thenceforth the Estate and Interest of the Lessee shall be void; and that the Petitioner is informed, the Object of the said Bill is to obtain Powers to bring double the present Quantity of Coals to the said Cajon Close, in order to be sold to the Inhabitants of Leeds aforesaid, or the Neighbourhood thereof, at the advanced Price of Five Pence Halfpenny per Corf; and to confirm the said Lease, notwithstanding the aforesaid Condition or Clause therein, without any additional Recompence or Benefit to the Petitioner on Account thereof, or of the Injury which he may sustain, although the Value of Lands in and about Leeds aforesaid, by the great Increase of Population and Trade, hath very considerably increased since the granting of the said Lease, and although such additional Price will bring in a large additional Income to the said Charles Brandling, besides the increased Benefit arising from a greater Sale; and that the Petitioner, not knowing the particular Terms on which the said Lease was granted, and being informed that the same would not be affected, nor his Property injured, by the said intended Bill, he was induced to sign, without due Consideration, a Consent to the passing of an Act, for an Amendment of the said Act of Parliament, (tipulating the said Charles Brandling to bring to the said Repository Ten thousand Dozens of Corfs ot Coals in each Quarter of the Year, provided Sale can be had for the fame, and to be allowed to sell the same there at Five Pence Halfpenny instead of Four Pence Three Farthings a Corf; but the Petitioner did not fee or peruse the said intended Bill, nor were any further Particulars of the Purport thereof explained to him; and that the Petitioner apprehends certain Parts of the said Bill will be prejudicial and injurious to his Estate and Interest: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant him such Relief as the Nature of his same requires, and particularly, that the Petitioner may be heard, by himself or Counsel, against such Parts of the said Bill as have a Tendency to affect his Interest.

A Petition of the President and Governors of the Hospital or Infirmary at Bath, was presented to the House, and read; reciting an Act of the Twelfth of King George the Second, for establishing and well-go* verning an Hospital or Infirmary in the City of Bath; and setting forth, That the said Hospital has been many Years completed, and great Numbers of poor Persons, who lived at great Distances from Bath, and from their indigent Circumstances incapable of using the Medicinal and Mineral Wateis of the said City, have been admitted Patients into the said Hospital for the Trial of the said Waters, many of whom have been perfectly restored to their Health, and others greatly relieved thereby, so that much public Good has been done by the said Hospital, which has been, and is, duly attended by able Physicians and Surgeons; and that the said Hospital has not yet realized or obtained anjvgreater Estate in Lands than £.24.0 a Year, toward* £. x,oooo a Year, which, by the said Act, they are enabled to obtain; and that the Personal Estate of the said Hospital consists wholly of £. 3,325 Three per . Bank Annuities, and £. 7,350 in Old South Sea Annul* ties, which produces a Yearly Income of about £. 320. 5J. to which, if the Yearly Rents of the said Lands are added, the whole Annual Income of the said Hospital will be about £. 560. 5 s.exclusive of voluntary Contributions and pecuniary Donations; and that the said Hospital is capable of holding about 113 Patients at a Time, but the present Annual Income thereof is not alone sufficient to support such a Number; and that many Persons have been, and may be, disposed to give Lands, Tenements, or Hereditaments, or (bme Interest therein, or to be derived thereout, or some Monies to be laid out in the Purchase of Lands, to* or in Tiuft: for, the charitable Ends of the said Hospital, whereby a Yearly Income in Lands of £. 1,000 a Year would be sooner obtained by the said Hospital, agreeable to the Intention, and for the Purposes of the said Act; but the Petitioners conceive they are incapable of taking and holding any Lands, Tenements, or Hereditaments, or any Monies that may be given and directed to be laid out in the Purchase of Lands, Tenements, or Hereditaments, that any Persons have been, or may be, disposed to give, by Will, or which have been, or may be, conveyed or limited, by any Deed or Conveyance, to or for the charitable Ends of the said Act, unless many Ceremonies and Requisites, not mentioned in the said Act, are complied with in such Deeds of Conveyance, which are wholly unknown to many Persons>. who have been, and may be, willing to promote the charitable Ends of the said Act, whereby the Donations and Gifts of many Persons to* or in Trust for, the charitable Ends of the said Hospital, have beetfc wholly frustrated, and the Hospital deprived of receiving and maintaining so large a Number of poor Persons therein as they otherwise would have been enabled to do, and many poor Persons, afflicted with Disorders to which the said Waters are applicable fof Relief, have been totally deprived of receiving any Relief therefrom; and the Petitioners conceive that, as. the said Act enables the Hospital to take and hold

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Thomas Barjlow, being examined, said. That he was present at a Meeting held at Leeds, pursuant to an Act-vertilement, for the Purpose of taking into Consideration a Bill now depending before the House, for rendering more beneficial an Act, made in the Thirty-first Year of the Reign of King George the Second, intituled,

" An Act for establishing Agreements, made between " Charles Brandling, Esquire, and other Persons, Proprietors of Lands, for laying down a Waggon Way,

" in order for the better supplying the Town and Neighbourhood of Leeds, in the County of York, with " Coals," by enabling the said Charles Brandling to supply, Annually, a larger Quantity of Coals to and for the Use of the said Town and Neighbourhood; that the Persons present at the said Meeting were unani-mously of Opinion, that the Prices for leading Coals should be ascertained by the Bill; and they then agreed upon the Prices for leading Coals from the Repository to the different Parts of the Borough of Leeds, and thought it would be of Advantage to the Town to have them inserted in the Bill, with a Power to the Quarter Sessions of the Borough to raise them, if necessary. And the Witness further said, That if Provision was made in the said Bill for delivering 1,000 Dozens of Corves of Coals, Part of the 40,000 Dozens of Corves mentioned in the said Bill, Quarterly, at any Place or Places within the said Borough of Leeds, short of the Repository at CaJJbn C.lose, it would be of great Convenience to the Town of Leeds, because . many Houses lie between the Coal Pits and he said Repository. And the Witness further added, 15

That this Provision was agreed upon at the said Meeting.

Mr. Joshua Green confirmed the above Evidence.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Committee, to whom the Bill for rendering more beneficial an Act, made in the Thirty-first Year of the Reign of King George the Second, intituled, "An Act for establishing Agreements, made between Charles Brandling, Esquire, and other Persons, Proprietors of " Lands, for laying down a Waggon Way, in order " for the better supplying the Town and Neighbourhood of Leeds, in the County of York, with Coals," by enabling the said Charles Brandling to supply, Annually, a larger Quantity of Coals to and for the Use of the said Town and Neighbourhood, is committed; That they have Power to make Provision in the said Bill for regulating the Prices of leading Coals from the Repository at Cajfon Close, within the Borough of Leeds, and for enabling the said Charles Brandling to deliver One thousand Dozens of Corves of Coals, Part of the Forty thousand Dozens mentioned in the said Bill, Quarterly, at any Place or Places within the said Borough of Leeds, short of the said Repository at Cajjon Close.

Mr. Duudasreported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the General Afilnibly of the Church of Scotland, under the Common Seal of the said Church of Scotland-, and also the Petition of the Reverend Doctor James Macknight, on Behalf of the Trustees for managing the Fund established by Two Acts, made in the Seventeenth and Twenty-second Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Serond, for establishing a Fund for a Provision for the Widows and Children of the Ministers of the Church of Scotland, were feve rally referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petitions; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petitions, the said Acts were read: And,

The Reverend Dr. Alexander Webjler being examined, laid. That the Fund established by virtue of the above-mentioned Acts has been found extremely beneficial; but that the Number of Annuitants has of late Years much increased, and is likely to continue augmenting, lb that the Fund is become inadequate to the Occasions of the Establishment, being limited to the Sum of £. 8o,oco. That, on an Average of Thirty Years past, Thirty Contributors to the Fund have died Annually', Twenty of whom have left Widows who have been entitled to Relief from the Fund. That there are at this Time Three hundred who want Assistance, and that the Number has amounted to Four hundred; and that a Capital of £. 100,000, together with the Annual Payments of the Contributors, i? not more thanlu/ficient to support that Number. And the Witness gave it as his Opinion, that permitting the Surplufcs, when any may arise, to accumulate till the Capital amounts to 100,000, will be the moll eligible Mode of increasing it to that Sum.

And being further examined, he said, That the granting of Loans to Contributors to the said Fund has been found very prejudicial, and should be discontinued. That it would be for the Benefit of the Fund, if Provision were made for allowing to every Widow marrying a Contributor, the Half of the Annuity she would be entitled to for Life if (he remained a Widow, while the Capital remains under £. 100,000, and the whole of the Annuity Ihc would be so entitled to, when the Capital shall amount to that Sum. That it would allb be beneficial to the Charity, if a Regulation were made, that whoever becomes a Contributor at the Age of Forty Years, shall pay the First Year, a Sum amounting to two Years and an Half Annuity of the Clals into which he shall be admitted. And he concluded with laying, That several other Amendments and Alterations in the said Abb are wanted, to render the same completely useful for the charitable Purposes thereby proposed.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the better railing and lecunng a Fund for a Provision for the Widows and Children of the Ministers of the Church of Scotland, and of the Heads, Principals, and Mailers, in the Universities of Saint Andrews, G/af-gozv, Edinburgh, and Aberdeen; and for repealing Two Atls, made in the Seventeenth and Twenty-second Y’ears of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, for those Purposes: And that Mr. Ditndas, Mr. Charles Dundas, and Mr. Ofivdo prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the several Persons whole Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the establishing a Manufactory, for making and printing Cotton and Linen Cloths upon a more extensive Plan than has hitherto been practised, would be of great Benefit to the Kingdom, and tend to increase the public Revenues arising from the Duties laid thereon; but such Manufacture cannot be established, and completely carried into Execution, without a very large Capital or Joint Stock; and that several Persons are willing to subscribe considerable Sums of Money for the Purpose of establishing and carrying on the said Manufactory, but are appre-hensive that Difficulties may arise, as well in recovering Debts which may grow due to the Proprietors of the said Manufactory, as also in defending Suits or Actions, which may be commenced by, or brought against them, for any Matter or Thing relative to the said Manufactory, as by Law all the several Proprietors, Subscribers to the said Manufactory, mult, in such Cases, sue and be ,sued, implead and be impleaded, by their several and distinct Names and Descriptions; and many Persons, who are not now liable to become Bankrupts within the Intent and Meaning of the Laws now in use concerning Bankrupts, are delirous to become Subscribers thereto, but are fearful they may thereby be liable to have Commissions of Bankruptcy issued against them as Traders, which Inconveniences cannot be completely removed without the Aid and Assistance of Parliament: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to form them, and every other Person and Persons who shall hereafter, either in their own Right, or as Executors, Administrators, or Assigns, in Right of any Persons become Proprietors of, or intereded in, any Part or Share of the said joint Capital Stock, or Fund, into a distinct and separate Body Politic and Corporate, with such Liberties and Privileges as shall be necessary for carrying the before-mentioned Plan into Execution, and subject to such Rules and Regulations as to the House shall appear proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the lame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

A, P E TITI O N. of several principal Landholders,. Importation l Merchants, and Traders in Corn, in the Isle of ^orn* Wight, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, by an Act, passed in the Thirteenth Year of His present Majesty, to regulate the Importation and Exportation, of Corn, it is enacted, that any Foreign Corn may be brought into, and landed at, the Ports of Bristol, Berwick, Beaumaris, Dover, Exeter, Fal-

mouth, Harwich, Hull, London, Lynn, Lancnjier, Liverpool, Milford, Newcastle, Newhaven, Poole, South amp-,

ton, Stockton, Whitehaven, Yarmouth, Aire, Leith, Glasgow, Aberdeen, and Kirkwall, at any Time when the Duties not repealed by the said Act shall be due, provided such. Corn be deposited in Warehouses, to be provided by the Importer, and secured under thejoinC Locks of His Majesty, and the Importer; and that such Corn shall not be delivered out of such Warehouses, to be confirmed in this Kingdom, but on Payment of such Duty as may be due thereon, or, if for Re-exportation, on giving Security to export the fame; and the Petitioners conceive, that, this Regulation has in View the Encouragement of Merchants, in laying up Stocks of Foreign Corn, to bring out on Emergencies of Scarcity and Dearth in this Kingdom, as well as supplying Foreign Countries therewith, a ’Branch of Trade hitherto enjoyed by the Dutch, who import Corn from the Baltic, which mult neceflai ily be brought

from that Sea the latter End of the Summer, whereas the Wants of this Kingdom, and of the Southern Parts of Europe, are seldom known till the Winter, or early in the Spring, when such a Store would be a Source for supplying their Wants; and that the general Good intended by the Regulations of the said Act is much circumscribed by the Limitation of that Privilege tQ the Ports above mentioned, which Experience has shewn are not sufficient nor the most convenient for fulfilling the intended Purposes; and that the principal Trade in the Isle of Wight is the Corn Trade, and the Traders therein, from their Connections and Dealings in the Exportation of British Corn, when the same is permitted, are consequently Dealers and Importers of Foreign Corn, when such is wanted for the Consumption of this Kingdom, in which Branch of Bufinel's they are much rcltrained, and exposed to many Inconveniences and Expences, from the Port of Cowes not being named and qualified by the said Act for storing Foreign Corn; and that the Port of Cowes is not only conveniently situated for storing such Foreign Corn, for the Consumption of this Kingdom, but is peculiarly so . for Re-exportation to Foreign Countries, having many Warehouses and Granaries situated on Wharfs at which Ships of Burthen can lay afloat to load and unload, and which were heretofore built for the Rice Trade from Carolina, a Branch of Business now in entire Stagnation, and therefore, if the Privilege of landing and storing Foreign Corn be extended to the said Port of Cowes, or made general, it would not only be advantageous to the Petitioners and others concerned in the Corn Trade, but also benefit, and tend to increase the general Trade and Navigation of this Kingdom; and representing to the House, that, when the Prices of Com exceed the Rate prescribed by Law for Exportation, the Articles of Corn, Flour, Bread, and Starch, become subject to the Laws relating to Goods prohibited to be exported, and of course not permitted to be carried Coastwise, without Bond being given, a Cocket taken out, and Certificate returned, which peculiarly affects the Petitioners, who, from their insular F f Situation,

Special Meeting, which was holden on the 26th of the same Month, the great Injury that would be sustained by the Petitioners, if the said Gate was continued, was very apparent, and' they having found, that by giving the said Gate to the said Lessee, they had vested in him not only a Power to col left the Highgate and Hampstead Road Toll, but also a Sunday Street Toll thereat (the said Lessee being also the Lessee of the Street Toll) than which nothing was farther from their Thoughts or Intentions, it was therefore resolved, by a Majority of more than Three Fourths of the Trustees present, that the said Gate should be removed, and an Advertisment printed in the Newspapers, to acquaint the Public of the said Resolution, and that the same stood for Confirmation at the next General Meeting; and that, at the said General Meeting, which was holden on the 1 ith of March following, Doubts having arisen, whether they had a Power to remove the said Gate after having given Possession thereof to the Lessee, and the said Lessee being called before the Board, and refilling to give up Pofllfllon of the said Gate, the said Trullees refeined the Resolution of their former Meeting, for removing the said Gate; and that loon after the Petitioners were informed, that by the said John Evans renting on Lease most of the Street and Turnpike Toll Gates in and about London, to the Annual Amount ot £.32,000, the Toll Gatherers, being appointed by him, behaved in the most atrocious Manner, and almolf daily insulted, and violently aliaulted, with Impunity, Persons of all Ranks passing through the several Gates,

A Petition of several Merchants and Traders engaged Kcwfoon<iia#J in the Fiftiery at Nezejoundland, and on the Banks there- ftlcry'

114 Februarii 1779,

Xiwfo> nHind 0f} on Behalf of themselves and others concerned in tiiuery. tj)e lai^ Fisher^', was prefen ted to the House, and read;

Setting forth, That an Act, made in the Fifteenth Year of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for " the Encouragement of the Fisheries carried on from " Great Britain, Ireland and the Dominions in

" Europe, and for securing a Return of the Fishermen,

" Sailors, and others, employed in the said Fisheries,

" to the Ports thereof, at the End of the Fishing Season," has been attended with many Hardships and Inconveniences, which the Petitioners apprehend were not foreleen at the Time of passing thereof, some of which they beg Leave to recommend to the Attention of the House, conceiving that they need only be pointed out in order to their being redressed; that, by the said Act, the Heirs and Assigns of the Petitioners are excluded from all Property in their Fishing Rooms or Habitations beyond the Expiration of One Season after the Decease of the Proprietor, if such Rooms or Habitations remain unoccupied during that Period; and the Petitioners beg Leave to observe, that it is sometimes absolutely impossible, and oftentimes highly inconvenient, for such Heirs or Assigns either to go themselves to Newfoundland, or to fend sufficient Power to others to act lor them within the Time prescribed, and apprehend the said Time should be enlarged, in order more effectually to secure such Property to the Heirs and Assigns of such'Proprietors; and that, by the said Act, the Hirer or Employer of any Seaman or Fishcrman is prohibited from paying to such Seaman or Fisherman, during the Time he shall be in his Service, mbre than One Half of the Wages that shall at any Time be due to him, under Pain of forfeiting £. to to any Person who shall inform or sue lor the lame, which Provision cannot be complied with without manifest. Inconvenience, as the Petitioners are under a Necessity of engaging a Variety of Men and Boys, to whom they give from £.5 to £. 30 for the Season; and if those who contract for the former Sum were to receive no more than Half of what may be due to them, after deducting what the Petitioners are compelled by the said Act to detain for their Passage Home, they could not possibly equip themselves with sufficient Cloathing, without which their Employers would be deprived of their Service; and should the Merchant furnish them with common NeceiTaries, or the Means of securing such NeceiTaries, he not only subjects himself to the Lois of the Overplus so advanced, but to the Penalty of £. 10, which the very Man, to whom he has generoully advanced this Overplus, may sue for and recover; and that, by the said Act, all Fish and Oil, which shall be taken and made by any Person who shall hire or employ Seamen or Fishermen, is subject and liable, in the First Place to the Payment of the Wages of every such Seaman or Fisherman, which Provision (in case of Insolvency) may subject the other Creditors of the Insolvent to very great Lois, while the Men, who may have occasioned this Insolvency by their Negligence or Disobedience, can claim and receive the whole Money due to them; and that the Petitioners apprehend the Penalty inflicted by the said Act on Seamen and Fishermen, for wilful Neglect of Duty, (being only a Forfeiture of Two Days Pay for every Day such Seaman or Fisherman shall wilfully neglect or refuse to work) affords Impunity to Offenders, instead of rellraining the Idle and Dissolute; and beg Leave to observe, that the Absence of a Boat’s Mailer for One Day, may probably occasion the Loss of Ten or Fifteen Pounds, while the only Recompence the Owner can obtain under this Act is no more than Six Shillings; and the Petitioners apprehend, that this Provision has produced Effects very different from the Intention of the Legislature, and has repeatedly proved prejudicial to the Interest of Individuals; and that the said Act has in other Particulars been found inconvenient, and the Petitioners apprehend, that, unlel's the 16

fame be repealed or amended, the said Trade will, in the Course of a very few Years, be inevitably ruined, to the great Loss of Individuals, and Detriment of the Commercial Interest of Great Britain: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant them such Relief as shall seem necessary.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Dealers in Teas and Spirits, re- Petition siding in the Towns of Southampton and Rcmfiy, and cotI,pk'n,ng the Villages adjacent thereto, was presented to the Smuggling. House, and read; Setting forth. That the pernicious and illicit Practice of Smuggling hath for Ten Years pall been carried on in so extensive a Manner throughout Hampshire, and the neighbouring Counties, that the Petitioners have suffered great Lolfes thereby; and that the Vessels, at present employed by Smugglers, are very numerous, and several of them of considerable Force, being equipped, both with respect to Men and Arms, as private Ships of War, and are lb peculiarly construded for fall failing, that the Persons on Board them arc able to refill or avoid any of the Cutters in the Government Service; and that Companies are formed for pure haling in France, Holland, and the Wands of Jersey, Guernsey, and Alderney, and transporting from thence into England, great Quantities of contraband Goods of every Denomination; and, in order to facilitate and secure the Landing of such Goods,

Signals are established and repeated on the Coasts by the Parties concerned therein -, and" upon the Arrival of the expected Cargoes on Shore, large Bodies of Smugglers alienable, receive, and divide the fame, and afterwards, with great Industry and Dispatch, convey it in a formidable Manner on Horseback into the interior Parts of the Country, in Defiance of the Laws, and to the Terror of the Community, by which Means a fraudulent Trade is openly carried on without Rilk or Opposition, to the Ruin of the fair Trader, and in Diminution of the Public Revenue; and that the said Goods being thus removed, are divided into smaller Parcels, for the Accommodation of an inferior Clals of Smugglers, called Hawkers and Duffers, who, disregarding all Penal Restraints, retail them from House to House, and even sometimes offer them for Sale in public Markets; and that the Sale of Tea, Spirits, and French Manufactures, is further promoted by the Afiiduity and Success of many itinerant Smugglers, who have established, and now maintain, a regular Correspondence throughout the Kingdom, and who solicit and take Orders for those Goods, which they agree to deliver safely into the Purchaser’s Possession, at their own Hazard, for a trifling Premium; and thus their deceitful Propofols, enforced with an Offer of felling those Commodities at the Price of Fifty per Cent, cheaper than the fair Trader can polfibly afford them, seldom fail to meet with Encouragement amongst all Ranks of People; and that the Amount of all Goods, clandestinely imported, is immediately paid for by a Remittance of the current Coin of this Nation, the greatest Part of which centers with our natural Enemies, and daily enriches them, by contributing to the very Efience and Support of their Commerce, whilst it lays a Foundation for the entire Lestruction of our own, a Circumstance, which, at this Conjuncture, is truly alarming, and mull justly raise the Indignation of every honest Tradesman, who, by the Pursuit of his lawful Business, advances the Public Revenue, and thereby, in feme Degree, adds to the Welfare and Security of the Kingdom; and that the Petitioners conceive, that the Reduction of the present Duties on Teas and Spirits will have an effectual Tendency towards preventing the fraudulent Practice of Smuggling, from the Consideration that, in all Cases, where the Temptation is lessened or abated, the Number of the tempted will Decrease in Proportion thereto:

And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to promote and enact such Bills for the immediate Relief of the Petitioners, and others who are concerned as legal Dealers in Teas and Spirits; and for restraining and preventing, by the most effectual Means, the dangerous Practice of Smuggling,

Mr. Allen reported from the Committee, to whom Bridgewater the Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and several of Market, Ac. the Burgesses, and other Inhabitants, of the Borough of Bridgewater, in the County of Somerset, and of the several other Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, residing in the Neighbourhood thereof, and often frequenting the said Borough, and the Market there held, as well on Behalf of themselves as others, was referral;

That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

James Bryant, being examined, said. That the Market of the said Town being held in the public Streets, the same has been found prejudicial to the Persons who attend there with Provisions and other Goods for Sale, and very inconvenient to Persons resorting thereto; for which Reasons a proper and commodious Market House is greatly wanted there j and that, in order to provide a convenient Situation for erecting such Market House, it will be necessary to purchase and take down several Houses and other Buildings now Handing in the said Borough.

And being further examined, he said, That the Streets, Lanes, and other public Passages within the said Borough, are very ill paved and cleansed — That they are rendered incommodious to Passengers, by Nuisances, Annoyances, and Obstructions; and that for Want of the same being properly lighted and watched, frequent Irregularities and Disorders are committed there — That it would tend greatly to the Safety and Convenience of the Inhabitants of the said Borough, and of all Persons resorting to or passing through the fame, if Powers were given to remedy the before-mentioned Inconveniences. And the Witness gave it as his Opinion, That in order to enable the Inhabitants of the said Borough to carry the aforesaid good Purposes into execution, the Expence of which would be very considerable, it would be proper to lay a ftnall Toll, to be taken on Sundays, and on the Days of the public Races, and on the Day before and Day after the fame.

Annually held near the said Borough, at the several Avenues leading into the said Town, and into the Race Ground; the Produce thereof to be applied towards defraying the Expences attending the several Works aforesaid.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for erecting a Market House, and regulating the Markets, within the Borough of Bridgewater, in the County of Somerset; and for paving, cleansing, lighting, and watching, the Streets, Lanes, and other public Passages and Places, within the said Borough: And that Mr. Allen and Mr. Poulett do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

ing of the undue Election and Return of George Stratton, Esquire, for the Borough of Callington, in the County of Cornwall, being come;

The House proceeded to the Appointment of a Stleft Committee, to try and determine the Merits of the said Petition.

The Serjeant at Arms was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to go with the Mace to the Places adjacent, and require the immediate Attendance of the Members on the Business of the House:

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and 106 Members being found to be present;

The Counsel and Agents on both Sides were called in to the Bar.

And the Door of the House being locked, the Clerk was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to read the Order of the Day for taking the said Petition into Consideration.

And the same being read accordingly;

The Names of all the Members of the House were, by the Clerk, taken out of the Box, which had been before prepared, and put into Six Glaftes; and were then drawn by the Clerk in the usual Manner, and read by Mr. Speaker to the House.

And the Names of Thirty-two Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of Alexander P opium, Esquire, be’>ng drawn, he was nominared to serve on the said Sclent Committee, by the Ccunfel for the Petitioner, and his Name was set aside.

And the N unes of Seventeen other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

Note, That, in the Course of drawing the said Names, the Names of Two other Members, then present, were drawn, and set aside with the Names of those who were absent from the House^ One, on Account of his being Sixty Years of Age or upwards, which he had before verified on Oath; and One, on Account of his Return to serve in Parliament not having been brought in Fourteen Days.

And the whole Number of Forty-nine Members so drawn as aforesaid, and not excused or set aside, being complete, the Counsel for the Sitting Member nominated James Adair, Esquire, to serve on the said Select Committee.

And Lists of the said Names were delivered, by the Clerk, to the said Counsel.

And the Door of the House being opened, the Counsel and Agents on both Sides withdrew.

Setting forth, That the Trade between this Kingdom and Turkey has, for a long Series of Years, been carried on by a Society of Merchants incorporated by Charters, and regulated by Acts of Parliament; and that, in order to carry on the said Trade with Safety, and to protect His Majesty’s Subjects in the Dominions, it has been found necessary that there should be an Ambassador lent from to reside

at Constantinople; and that there should be Consuls and Vice Consuls, and other Officers and Servants, in the other Parts of Turkey, where any British Subjects re-(ide, and where the English Merchants carry on Trade, the whole Expence whereof has been borne by the Turkey Company, which, together with many other necessary Expences incident to the carrying on of the said Trade, has of late Years amounted to near Ten thousand Pounds per Annum and that the Trade to and from Turkey, once so flourishing, is now, in Consequence of many unavoidable Events and concurring Circumstances, much reduced; and that the Assistance, which has been formerly granted to the Petitioners by Parliament, enabled them to pay off the Debt they had incurred, and to lower their Duties, which were (b high as to be a Burthen the Trade was not able to support and'that the Petitioners, having found themselves, by the former Bounty of Parliament, and by the Consequent Revival of their Trade, in a Situation to support their Expences during the last Three Years without Assistance, did not then make any Application, but they are fcnlible that they should not discharge the Duty incumbent upon them by their Charter, nor the Justice they owe to the Public, for whom they consider themselves as Trustees, if they did not declare their present Inability to support their necessary Expences, notwithstanding the y have found it expedient
