Turnpike Bills, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth j viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Acts were read: And,

Mr. Henry Bickerjiaff, being examined, said, That the Trustees have proceeded in the Execution of the said Acts, and borrowed the Sum of £. 1,000 011 the Credit of the Tolls arising upon the said Roads, which cannot be paid off, and the said Roads properly amended and kept in good Repair, unless the Term of the said Acts is further continued, and some additional Powers grantee) 1° the Trustees for those Purposes; thac the whole Roads included in the said Acts is about Twenty-six Miles, and that there is only One Toll taken upon the whole Roads in One D,ay. And being examined as to the Situation of the present Gates, he said. That the Places where the Gates are to be erected, are fixed in the Acts; that one is about Two Miles from Prejlonand the other about One Mile and an Half from And the Witness

added, that the Trustees have no Power to ered Gates at any other Places upon the Roads. And he further said, That Travellers, and Persons who live within the Two Gates, could make use of upwards of Twenty Miles of the Road*without paying any Toll; that is to say, Fourteen Miles upon one Branch, and Six or Eight Miles upon the other; and that a great Number of Carriages, belonging to Persons who live between the Two Gates, make use of the Road without being liable to pay any Toll for their Coals, Kennel, and ether Goods: And by the said Acts, Carts drawn with One Horse only are exempt from Toll; and that in Consequence of this Exemption, it is usual to bring Coals in Carts with narrow Wheels, and drawn with Three or Four Horses, for several Miles upon the Road, without going through any of the Turnpikes, and to leave those Coals at their own Houses, near the Turnpike Gates, and afterwards to carry such Coals through the Gates, in Carts drawn by One Horse only, and thereby evade the Payment of the Tolls for such Coals: He further said, That there were a very great Number of Carts out of the Field Country, with Wheels under the Breadth of Six Inches, which come over Preston Marfk, and over the new Bridge, and get upon the Turnpike Road within the Walton , and ' - *7

then travel several Miles upon the Road, for the Purpose of fetching their Coals and Kennel, without paying any Toll. And the Witness added. That the chief Damage done to the Road was, by the Carts of Persons who pay no Toll: And he said. That the said Acts require several Amendments and Alterations, and that the same might be better and more easily executed, if the several Clauses and Provisions necessary to continue in Force were reduced into One Act of Parliament.

Mr. 77 homersAddifon confirmed the above Evidence,

except with respect to the Money borrowed upon the Credit of the Tolls.

Owners or Proprietors of Lands lying in the North Level, Part of the said Great Level, and in the Manor of C-rozv-land, adjoining thereto, was referred; that the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, of the 25th of April 1774, relative to Bills of Drainage, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follower h; viz

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Fifteenth Year of the Reij>n of King Charles the Second, for settling the draining of the Great Level of the Fens, called Bedford Level, was read; whereby it appeared, that a Power was granted to lay Taxes on 95,000 Acres of Land, allotted as a Recompence for draining the said Great Level, in order to the Support, Maintenance, and Preservation of the said Great Level, and Works made and to be made for that Purpose, as by the said Act is set forth.

Then another Act, passed in the Twenty-seventh Year of King George the Second, intituled, "An Act " for discharging the Corporation of the Governor, " Bailiffs, and Commonalty, of the Company of Conservators of the Great Level of the Fens, commonly *5

" called Bedford Level, from a Debt due to the Duke " of Bedford and Earl of; and for enabling

the Proprietors of Lands in the North Level, Part " of the said Great Level, to raise Money to discharge " the Proportion of the said North Level in the Debts " of the said Corporation; and for ascertaining and " appropriating the Taxes to be laid on the said North " Level; and for the more effectual draining and preserving the said North Level, and divers Lands adjoining thereto, in the Manor of was

read; by which it appeared, that the several Parts of the said Great Level were distinguished by the Names of The North Level, The Middle Level, and The South Level, respectively: And it was thereby Enacted, That all the Taxes, Rents, and Revenues, of the said Corporation, arising from the said North Level, should be applied to raise, and keep in Repair, certain Works therein mentioned; and that the Lands and Grounds in the said North Level, and the Lands called sand, within the Manor of Crowland, intended to be drained under the Authority of the said Act, were divided into Five Districts, in Manner therein mentioned, and Commissioners were thereby appointed and directed to meet Annually, and assess and charge the Owners of the Lands within the said Districts, except as therein is excepted, with equal and proportionable yearly Rates and Taxes, not exceeding One Shilling per Acre Yearly during the First Four Years, and not more than Six Pence per Acre in any One Year after the Expiration of the said Four Years, payable to the said Commissioners; and they were thereby impowered to borrow, at Interest, £.14,000 on the Credit of the said Taxes, which, with the said Taxes, was directed to be applied in certain other Works for draining the said Five Districts, as therein mentioned. And,

Mr. John Wing, Treasurer to the Commissioners, being examined, said. That the said Sum of £. 14,000 was borrowed, and now remains due, and has been applied by the Commissioners, together with the Surplus of the said Taxes, after keeping down the Interest, to the Works directed by the said Act, and in executing divers other necessary and expensive Works for the Improvement of the Wisbech River, pursuant to another Act, made in the Thirteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, An Act for draining and preserving certain Lands and Grounds in the Pari (lies of Tid Saint Giles and Newton, in the " Isle of Ely, and County of Cambridge, and Tid Saint " Mary, in the County of Lincoln," which directs the said Works to be maintained by the said Commissioners, out of the Rates and Taxes afielTed upon the said North Level.

Then'another Act, made in the Twenty-ninth Year of the Reign of his said late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, "An Act for establishing a Fund " for Payment of the Bonds of the Governor, Bailiffs,

" and Commonalty, of the Company of Conservators " of the Great Level of the Fens, called Bedford " Level; and for exchanging the present Bonds of the " said Corporation for other Bonds payable out of the Revenues of the Middle and South Levels, Part of " the said Great Level; and for enabling the said " Corporation to borrow further Sums for the Use of " the said Great Level,* was read; whereby it appeared, that the said Corporation was impowered to borrow upon Bonds £. 5,000, for the Use of the said North Level, to be charged on the Taxes, Rents, and Revenues, of the said Corporation, arising within the said North Level. And,

Mr. John Brown, Clerk to the Register of the Bedford Level Corporation, being examined, said, That the said Sum of £. 5,000 has been borrowed, and applied for the Use of the said North Level, and now remains due.

" enable the Governor, Bailiffs, and Commonalty, of *« the Company of Conservators of the Great Level of the Fens, called Bedford , to complete and maintain the principal Banks and Works necessary to " the well draining and preserving the North Level, " Part of the said Great Level; and for laying Taxes " upon the Lands within the said North Level, and divers Lands adjoining thereto, in the Manor of " Crowland" was read; which recites. That divers Breaches had happened in the North Bank of Moreton's Leame, and that the said £. 5,000 had been expended, and other Debts contracted, upon Account of the necessary Works of the said North Bank, and other Works belonging to the said Corporation, upon Account of the said North Level; and the said Act directs, that all the Lands within the said North Level, and the Lands called Portsand, except as therein excepted, should be taxed Yearly, in the following Manner; that is to say, All the Lands within the North Level, with a Tax of Sixpence an Acre, and the said Lands called Portsand, with Three Pence an Acre, payable to the said Corporation; and the said Corporation were thereby impowered to borrow further Money upon Bonds, to be charged on the said Taxes; and that the said Taxes, and Money to be borrowed thereon, together with the other Taxes and Revenues arising, and payable to the said Corporation from the said North Level, should be applied, but without Prejudice to the Payment of the said D*bt of £.5,000, in and towards the Charges of the several Banks and Works directed to be maintained by the said Act of the Twenty-seventh Year of his late Majesty King George the Second. And,

Mr. Brown, being again examined, said. That the

further Sum of f. 20,000 has been borrowed upon Bonds, for the Purposes of the said last mentioned Act, and now remains due. And,

Mr. Wing, being again examined, said. That the Surplus of the Taxes payable to the Commissioners, after keeping down the Interest of the Debt of £. 14,000, is inefficient to maintain the Works to which the same is applicable. And,

Mr. Wing and Mr. Brown further said. That the Taxes, Rents, and Revenues, payable to the said Corporation from the North Level, after discharging the Interest of the said Debts of £. 5,000 and £. 20,000, and paying certain Salaries to their Officers, are inefficient to maintain the several Works to which they are applicable. Then,

Mr. Wing, Mr. Thomas Hare fine, and Mr. Emerson Harrifin, informed your Committee, That without further Aids, the several Banks for preserving the said North Level, will be in Danger of breaking in Times of high Floods, whereby the said Lands may be drowned, to the great Loss of the Proprietors, and to the Prejudice' of the Public. 1

And Mr. Wing added. That if Power was granted to raise further Taxes', for a limited Time, for discharging the said Debt of f. 14,000, and for the further Support and Maintenance of the said Works, it would be very beneficial to the several Persons interested.

Mr. Chaytor reported from the Committee, to whom

the Petition of the several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and'he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table:, Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Lewis Crinfoz, being examined, said. That he is an Exi-

' porter of Printed. Linen and Cotton Cloths; that if a Manufactory for making the said Cloths was established, upon a more extensive Plan than has hitherto been prac-tiled, it would be of Benefit to the Kingdom, and increase the Excile Revenues arising from the Duties laid thereon; but that such Manufactory cannot be established, and compleatly carried into execution, without it very large Capital, or Joint Stock, raised for that Purpose.

That the Witness knows several Persons who are ready to subscribe considerable Sums of Money for establishing and carrying on this Manufactory, if they could be put in such a Situation, as only to be icfponfi-b!e for such Sums as they shall respectively iubfcrtbe; but that they are intimidated, from the Fear of having Commissions of Bankruptcy issued against them as Traders.

That Companies are now established in and other Places Abroad, for carrying on such Manufactories, where they are no otherwise answerable than for the Sums they subscribe; by which Means their Capitals are so greatly extended, that they carry on the said Manufactories to a greater Extent and Perfection, and are enabled to give more Credit, than can be done, by any Individual here; that it requires many Trials before Things can be brought 10 Perfection, which are very expensive; and that Individuals here suffer from die Establishment of such Companies Abroad, there not being so many Goods exported from hence as for. merly, on Account of those Companies supplying the Markets.

Mr. Robert Allan (a Manufacturer of Printed Linen and Cotton Cloths) confirmed the Evidcncef o Mr. Crinjoz.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for establishing a Manufactory for making and printing Cotton and Linen Cloths within that Part of Great Britain called England, and for effectually supporting and conducting the same: And that Mr. Mr.

Dundas, and Mr. Turner, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Admiral Keppel being come to the Hopfe, Mr. Speaker acquainted him, That the House had, on the 12th Instant, ordered that the Thanks of this House be given to him, for his distinguished Courage, Con-dust, and Ability, in defending this Kingdom in the Course of the last Summer, effectually protecting its Trade, and more particularly for his having gloriously upheld the Honour of the British Flag on the 27th and 28th of July last: And Mr. Speaker gave him the Thanks of the House accordingly, as followeth; viz.

Admiral Keppel,

This House have done you the distinguished Honour of ordering their Thanks to be given to you, an Honour never conferred but upon extraordinary Merit; which Thanks it is my Duty to communicate to you in your Place.

After having fat so long in this Chair, I hope it is unnecessary to declare, that I have been always happy to obey the Orders of the House; and I have now a particular Satisfaction in that Obedience. Indeed, every generous Mind must feel Satisfaction, when the Day of honourable Acquittal succeeds to the Day of levere Trial; and this Pleasure was, I believe, never more general, nor more sincere, than upon the present' Occasion.

You, Sir, was called by your Sovereign, with the Approbation of all Descriptions of Men, particularly those of your own Profession, to a Station of the ut-

mod Difficulty, and of die highest Importance. The Safety of this Country, and the Honour of the Flag, were trusted in your Hands, when the Enemy was expected upon odr Coast; and, notwithstanding the most able Discharge of this great and momentous Trud, you was occufed of Misconduct and Neglect of Duty. But, after a very long and foil Investigation, by Men in every respect the belt qualified to jOdge, that Charge appeared to be ill-grounded and malicious; and your Judges have unanimously and honourably acquitted you; and have further added, that your Conduct on the 27th And 28th Days of lad was that t>f a judicious, brave-, and experienced Officer. Surely then it cannot be Matter of Surprise, that extraordinary Marks of Respect and Edeem are shewn to such a Cha-radter. We now know, frith Certainty, that our Confidence in you was not misplaced; and we entertain a well-grounded Hope that there dill-remain amongst the Naval Officers, Talents and Abilities fully equal to this dangerous Crisis.

Amidd this general Joy, t cannot help repeating the singular Pleasure which I feel in giving you the Thanks of this House, which I now do, for your distinguished Courage, Conduct, and Ability, in defending this Kingdom in the Course of the lad Summer, effectually protecting its Trade, and more particularly for your having gloriously Upheld the Honour of the British Flag on the 27th and 28th of July lad.

Upon which. Admiral said;

Mr. Speaker,

AJmihl It is impossible, by any Expressions I edn use, to do Keppel’* Justice to my Feelings of Gratitude to the House, for Auimi-. ^e {-fonour they have done me by their Approbation of tny Conduct.

The good Opinion of my Fellow Citizens, expressed by the Representatives of the Nation, cannot but be received by me as a most acceptable Addition to the Satisfaction 1 felt in the recent Sentence, to which you , have been pleased to allude, of a Court Martial; the Result of a full and deliberate Inquiry, expressive of their Sentiments of the Subject referred to their Examination, in Terms equally honourable to themselves, and to me.

The Pkafure 1 feel at this Moment is not a little heightened by the unavoidable Rccolleftion of the very different Emotions I felt when I was last in this House, and in this Place.

I should be guilty of great Injustice, if, on an Occasion like the present, I negtefted to inform this House, that my Efforts far the public Service, in the Indances in which the House has been pleased to distinguish them, were most zealously seconded by many as gallant and able Officers as the Navy of England ever produced; to whose Attention and Spirit, next to the Divine Providence, the Success of these Efforts ought to be in a great Measure ascribed.

I cannot fit down without returning to you, Sir, personally, my particular Thanks, for the very, very obliging Terms in which you have executed the Commands of the House.

15a 190 Februarii. A. 1779.

Petition A Petition of the Grocers, and Dealers in Teas, eomptaning Coffee, and Chocolate, residing in the Cities of Smuggling. &nd Bath, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That within about Seven or Eight Years past, the Smugglers have almost deprived the Petitioners of their laid Trades, and have been, as the Petitioners are informed, also extremely detrimental to the Revenue arising from the Spirit Trade, inso much that, unless a speedy Stop be put to such illicit Pra&Ices, the Petitioners, on their Parts, rather than, under such a Discouragement, fub-mit to the Inconveniency of the Revenue and Excise Officers, mud give up their laid Branches of Trade, as the Quantity of each Article they now vend is not sufficient to pay them for their Trouble; and that the Smugglers have a regular established Mode for disposing of their Goods through these Parts, and will in a short Time, if not speedily prevented, in a very great Degree, destroy the Whole fair Trade; and that the Vessels, employed to transport these smuggled Goods, are mostly manned by Twenty or Thirty resolute Fellows, and carry from Ten to Twenty Guns each, are fast Sailers, and very numerous on the Coalt, whereby the present Revenue Cutters are found insufficient to prevent the carrying on of such illicit Practices; and that the Mailers of these smuggling Vessels have regular Attendants on Shore to receive the Cargoes, who make Signals in the Night to inform the Crews when the Coast is clear; and that these Cargoes are fold, after they are safely landed, to the Smugglers on Shore, for which they pay in Specie, thereby draining this Country of a great Quantity of the Current Coin, which they carry to our natural Enemies, and enrich them at our Expence; and that these Smugglers on Shore form themselves into large Bodies, from Thirty to Eighty Men, well mounted and armed, their Horses carrying from about One hundred and Fifty to Two hundred Pounds-Wfigbi_oL.Teai__Spirits, and other Articles, each; and they daringly ride through the Towns, in Defiance of the King’s Officers, and the Dragoons,' who. ate sent to alfift them; and that, after having thus secured their smuggled Teas, Coffee, and Chocolate, from an established Correspondence which they have in almost every City, Town, and Village, throughout the Kingdom, where they have unentered Houses, in which they lodge such Goods, they dispose of the same to' Duffers, qj Hawkers, whose Business it is to make up the- Teas in Parcels, from One Ounce to One Pound, or any larger Quantity, and carry the same to almost every private Family in their respective Tow As and Neighbourhoods, and fell them at very low Prices; and that these Duffers or Hawkers also foil Spirituous Liquors, with every other Sort of smuggled Goods, mostly from Fifty to Seventy Pounds per Cent, lower than the fair Trader can afford; and that, by Reason of the great Difference in the above Prices, the Duty paid by the fair Trader on these Articles being so high, it is so, tempting, that there are great Numbers of Families induced to purchase of the Smugglers, almost constantly, instead of the fair Trader, to the great Lois of the Revenue; and that another great Grievance to the fair Trader is, the Captains and Crews of the East India Company’s Ships diipole of their private Adventures, at different Places in the English Channel, before they arrive at their Moorings in the ‘Thames, at Prices much lower than even those of the Smugglers: And Hating to the House, an Account of the Quantities and Values of Teas, Coffee, Chocolate, Spirits, &c. fold in the Year 1769, by the fair Traders in and about the Cities of Bristol and Bath, and some Parts adjacent; and also, an Account of the Consumption of the like Commodities therein, and therefrom, for the Year 1777, by which it appears, that the Duties for the Year 1769 amount to £.132,287. i$s. 5\d. and for the Year 1777 to £.64,778. os. fs\d.-, and that the Advantages, which should accrue to the Revenue, the East India Company, and the Petitioners, by the great Difference between the Two Years Consumption as above mentioned, are reaped by the Smugglers, and the natural Enemies of this Country: And therefore praying the House will take these Affairs under mature Confederation, and to the Hopping these Evils pass a Lav/, with such Regulations as to them shall seem meet, to effectually detect Smugglers in general, and inflict such Punishments and Penalties on them as will for ever prevent their being guilty of the like Practices, so injurious and detrimental to the Commerce and Revenue of this Kingdom.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Moyjey reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the President and Governors of the Hospital or Infirmary at Bath, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, "An Act for establishing and well governing an Hospital " or Infirmary, in the City of Bath," was read; by which it appeared, that the several Persons therein named were appointed a Body Politic and Corporate, for regulating and governing the said Hospital, with Power to receive and possess all such Sums of Money as then had been, or should then after be, contributed, given, deviled, or bequeathed, for the Purposes of the said Act, and with a further Power to them and their Successors, to purchase, take, and receive, at any Time then after, without Licence, in Mortmain, any Lands, Tenements, or Hereditaments, or any Eftats or Intcreii arising or derived out of the fame, so that such Estates or Interests did not, and should not, exceed the Annual Value of £. 1,000 in the Whole.

And it further appeared by the said Act, That all Persons resident in or belonging to Great Britain or Ireland, whole Circumstances were such that they were not able to have the Benefit of the medicinal Waters at Bath, without charitable Relief, should be entitled to the Relief of the said Hospital. Then,

Daniel Danvers, Esquire, bei ng examined, said, That in pursuance of the Powers and Directions of the said Act, the said Hospital was completed and opened many years ago, and great Numbers of poor Persons,

-The Lords desire leave for a Member to attend them*

Bonnevaux’s

Nat.

Bvh

HospiuL

ip Geo. III. 24*

Tons, who lived at various Distances from and from the Indigence of their Circumstances were incapable of using the medicinal Waters there, have been admitted Patients into the said Hospital for the Trial of the said Waters, many of whom have been completely cured of their Disorders, or greatly relieved thereby; that the said Hospital hath not as yet realized more than an Estate of £. 240 Annum above Reprizes, which, with the iaterest of 10,675, ’n the public Funds, amounting together to about £. 560. 51. per Annum, forms the Whole of the Income of the said Hospital, exclusive of voluntary Contributions and pecuniary Donations, which are very uncertain, and wholly contingent, so that, although the said Hospital is large enough to receive 113 Patients at a Time, the Income thereof is very inadequate to the Support of such a Number.

And being further examined, he said, That many Persons who have been desirous of promoting the charitable Ends of the said Act, were unacquainted with the Ceremonies and Requisites prescribed by the Statute of Mortmain, with respect to Conveyances or Bequests of Lands for charitable Uses, by which Means their good intentions have been wholly frustrated, to the Loss of the Hospital, and Disadvantage of the Public. And be concluded with saying, That if all Persons, who may hereafter be inclined to be benefactors to the said Hospital, were enabled to give or bequeath Lands, Tenements, or Hereditaments, or any Interest arising therefrom, to the Amount of the Sum limited by the said Act, and the Governors of the said Hospital were impowered to receive the same, without any greater or other Form, Ceremony, or Re-quilition, in the Will, Deed, or Conveyance of any Benefactor, than are required for devising or conveying. any Real Estate from one natural Person to another, the completing of the permanent Income of the Hospital to the annual Sum of £. 1000, as limited by the said Act would be accelerated; and a Charity, which extends to the Kingdom in general, the City of Bath excepted, the Inhabitants of which are expressly excluded from it, "would be greatly promoted.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, more effectually to enable the President and Governors of the Hospital or Infirmary at Bath, established by an Act, passed in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, "An Act for establishing and well-governing an Hospital " or Infirmary in the City of Bath" to take, or acquire and hold, any Lands, Tenements, or Hereditaments, or any Interest in Lands, Tenements, or Hereditaments, and any Money or Personal Property to be laid out in Lands, Tenements, or Hereditaments, pur-luant to any Will, or otherwise, to the Amount limited in the said Act: And that Mr. and Sir

To prove the Allegations of the First-mentioned Petition, Mr. Jeremiah Osborne, being examined, said, That the Road from the Ship at Alvestone, through the Town of Thornbury, to Stone, which is in Extent about Three

Miles and an Hail’, is too narrow, and would be a Road of great public Utility, if properly widened and repaired.

In Support of the Second-mentioned Petition, Mr. Osborne being again examined, said, That it would be very convenient to the Inhabitants of the Parish of Clifton, and its Neighbourhood, and to all Persons resorting thereto, if a Road was made from a certain Branch called The White Ladies Road, to Gallows Acre Lane, in the said Parish of Clifton, which would be about 150 Yards in Length; and that Notice has been given to the Owners and Occupiers of the Grounds through which such new Road would pass, of the intended Application to Parliament for a Power to make the lame. And he added, That so much of a Lane leading from a House in the City of Bristol, called the Red Lodge, to Clifton, as lies between the Top of Park Street and the End next Bristol of the Road which is usually called The White Ladies Road, cannot be kept in Repair by the Laws in being; the Extent of which Road is about too Yards.

In Support of the Third-mentioned Petition, Mr. Osborne laid, That the Road leading from a Place near the Coach and Horses, in the Parish of to the

Cross Hands, at the Top of C/erken Coomb, in the said Parish, is much out of Repair, and in many Places too harrow; which Road is about Three Quarters of a Mile* in Length.

In Support of the Fourth-mentioned Petition, Mr. Osborne being again examined, said, That the Road from the Two Mile Stone on the Ashton Road to bam Passage, and from thence, over Leigh Down, to Pill, is about Three Miles and an Half in Extent, and from Pill to the Sign of the Blue Anchor, at Portishead, is also about Three Miles and a Half in Length; which Road is much out of Repair, too narrow in many Places, and might be made a very useful Road if properly widened and repaired.

And the Witness being further examined in Support of the last mentioned Petition, he said, That the Lane or Way leading from Brockham's Hill, in the Parish of Bitton, in the County of Gloucester, to Kynjltam B idge, and from thence to the Briflmgtun Road, is much out of Repair, and cannot be repaired by the Laws in being; which Road is about a Mile in Length.

Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolution which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; v

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Sum of £.7,000,000 be raised by Annuities, and the further Sum of £.490,000 by a Lottery, in Manner following; that is to say,

That every Contributor to the said £.7,000,000 shall, for every £. 100 contributed, be entitled to an Annuity after the Rate of £.3 per Centum per Annum, redeemable by Parliament; and also to a further Annuity of £.3. 15*. per Centum per Annum, to continue for a certain Term of Twenty-nine Years, and then to cease; the said Annuity of £. 3 per Centum, and o £.3. 15s. per Centum. to commence from the 5th Day ot January 1779, and to be payable and transferable at the Bank of England and to be paid Half Yearly on the 5th Day of July and the 5th Day of January in every Year, and shall be charged and chargeable upon, and payable out of, a Fund to be established in this Session of Parliament for Payment thereof, and for which the Sinking Fund shall be a collateral Security:

Set ring forth, That the Petitioners, sensibly affected with the continual and most alarming Decline in the Deina d f u trie aici Commodity, feel themselves ne-Cellitr.cd ro request the I iterposition of the Legislature, to prevent their Ruin, and the total Destrudtiort of numherlels poor Artificers, whole Support for many Years past has been drawn from the said Manufacture, in which they have been reputably and industriously employed to public Advantage; and that this distressing Circumstance is occasioned, in a great Measure, by the itv.mense Quantities of Foreign Thread Bone Laces smuggled into this Kingdom, and His Majesty’s other Dominions, which are publicly fold under the Sanction or having paid Duty, a fallacious Pretence that succeeds with uncommon Impunity, through the Want of an Act to prevent the Importation of low-priced Laces, it being almost impartible, as the Law now stands, to convict any Lace Dealer of possessing un-li enfed Goods; and that the Evil stops not here, for if, by any Mismanagement, some small Packets of Laces, that cannot for Sale bear the Duty of 16 Yard, should be brought to the Custom House, through Mistake, they are ealily re-entered for Exportation, and a Drawback of 14 d. Yard being recoverable, the only Loss sustained is 2 in the Yard; and the Petitioners have great Realbn to believe, that the Dealers in contraband Goods, well' acquainted with this Business, carry it still farther, and re-land the Laces before they quit the Fiver Thames-, by which iniquitous Deceptions the most effectual Destruction overwhelms the fair Trader, while the industrious Artifice; peiilhes through extreme Want; and that, for these Six Years past, t ie Petitioners have been much affected with the Complaints and Distresses of this numerous Body of Artists, whom they have relieved, and have provided them with Materials, and taken their Work without a Hope of vending near the Quantity they made; and the Petitioners apprehend, that the only effectual Remedy against the Progress of these Calamities would be totally prohibiting the Importation of all foreign Thread or Silk Laces, commonly Called Bone Laces, the original or first Price of which is Six or even Five Shillings per Yard and under, an additional Duty of Eight Pence per Yard being laid &t the same Time on ail Laces from that Price to Ten Shillings, and a still higher Duty from Ten Shillings upwards; for an Act of this Nature would give such Vigour to the Petitioners Exertions, and so rapid a Progress to their Improvements, as would quickly enable them to increase the Reputation of this Commodity. The Revenue, in Consequonce of the increased Importation of the Thread and Silk used in this Manufacture, would receive an Addition so considerable as to render the Duties, loft by the Prohibition, a Matter of no Consideration, particularly if it be adverted to, that a very small Part of the I aces, under Five Shillings per Yard, are ever entered at all, or, if they should be entered, it is only to afford an Opportunity for carrying on an illicit Trade with greater Security; and that the Petitioners are well aware of the Objections that may arile against a Prohibition on the Importation of German Bone Lace, but apprehend that such Objections would be founded in Misinformation, as few low-priced Laces are ever entered; and that for One Yard of German Lace imported into this Country, and paying Duty, there are Ten thousand Yards of prohibited French Laces fraudulently introduced by the French Lace Merchants, and others, under that Denomination, through the Inability of the King’s Officers to distinguUh the one from the other, and they consequently fear to make a Seizure under hazardous Circumstances; and that the Notoriety of these Grievances is unquestionable, dif-trefling at they are, they contain but faint Outlines of the numerous Oppressions under which the British Lace Manufacturers have long struggled; and with ihc

utmost Deference the Petitioners submit the proposed Prohibitions to the Consideration of the House, humbly conceiving, if they were parted into an Act, it would prevent the destructive Practice of Lace smug-gling, and alleviate the Miseries arid Anxiety under which Thousands of the reduced Artificers now labour.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Dealers in Tea and Spirits, residing in the Town of Buckinghdm, and adjacent Villages, in the County of Bucks, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That within these Six Years past the daily Increase of Smuggling has almost deprived the Petitioners of their Tea and Spirit Trade, inlbmuch that without the speedy Interference of Parliament the Revenue arising from the Duties on these Articles will be daily decrealing; and that, from an established Correspondence which the Smugglers have in almost very Town and Village throughout the Country, where they have unentered Houses, in which they lodge their Goods, they dispose of the same to Hawkers and Duffers, who seldom carry more than Four or Six Pounds of Tea with them, and that made up in small Quantities, which they fell to private Families; the great Difference in the Prices (the Duty paid on this Article being lo high) is so great Temptation, that many Families are induced to purchase of the Smugglers almost their whole Consumption: And therefore praying the House will take the Aiffair under Consideration, and effectua'ly to flop the increasing Evil, pass a I aw with such Regulations as to them shall seem meet, to detect Smugglers, and inflict such Punishments and Penalties on them as will for ever prevent their being guilty of the like Practices, lo injurious and detrimental to the Commerce and Revenue of this Kingdom,

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

And a Member having proposed to examine Admiral Keppel (a Member) in his Place, with respect to the State of the English and French Fleets in June last; and

A Motion was made, and the Question was proposed. That the Questions proposed to, and Answers made by. Admiral Keppel, be taken down at the Table as Evidence.

And an Amendment being proposed to be made to the Question, by inserting after the Word " That," the Words, no Enquiry having been instituted by the House;"

The House was moved. That the Entry in the Journal of the House, of the 21st Day of October 1667, of the Proceedings of the House, on entering into Debate of the Matter of Miscarriages in the late War, might be read._

And the same was read accordingly.

And the same was read accordingly.

Then the Question being put, That the Words, " no " Enquiry having been instituted by the House," be inserted in the said proposed Question;

The House divided.

tures which the Captains and Crews of the Company’s Ships dispose of at different Places in the English Channel, and also in the River Thames, before they can be cleared at the Custom House; and that from Dunkirk and Fluffing the y smuggie Teas into the South and Ea(l Counties, from Guernsey and Jersey into the Wellern Counties, and from Gottenburgh into Scotland, and the Northern Counties; and that the Cutters and Vessels employed in this illicit Trade are fall Sailers, carrying from Fifteen to Thirty Guns each, and frequently import Ten to Fifteen Tons of Tea; enclusive of other uncustomed Goods, the Mailers whereof have regular Attendants on Shore to receive the Cargoes, who make Signals in the Night to inform the Crew when the Coall is clear; and that the Cargoes being landed, are paid for in Specie, or bartered for Wool, which they carry to our natural Enemies, to the great Detriment of our Manufactories; and that the Smugglers on Shore form themselves into large Bodies, from Thirty to Eighty Men, well mounted and armed, their Horses carrying from One hundred and Fifty to Two hundred Pounds cf Tea each, anil daringly ride through the Towns in Defiance of the King’s Officers, and the Dragoons who are lent to afilfl them, some of whom have lost their Lives in fruitless Attempts to flop their Progress; and, having secured their Goods, from a Correspondence which they have established, not only in the said Cities but throughout the Kingdom (where they have unentered Houses in which they lodge these Goods) the same are di(poled of to Duffers or Hawkers, whole Business it is to make up the Tea in Parcels, which they carry and fell to private Families, at the following Prices;

Petition* Hs; and that another Grievance, which calls aloud for eomplaming Redrgfs, is, the Commissioners of Customs and Ex-Smuggling cife, a°d Justices of the Peace, mitigating the Fines from perhaps £. ioo to £. 5 Sterling, when Tea Dealers have been detected by the Excile Officers, and convitfted on the clearest Evidence; and that the Petitioners have Reason to believe, that the Cutters and Vessels employed in this illicit Trade, after being seized, are restored to the Matters by the Officers of the Revenue Cutters, and immediately return to the same Service, going back to , or some other

Foreign Sea Port, in order to procure more contraband Goods, to import to this Country; and, in case they are intercepted by any of the Custom House Cutters, produce a Clearance from such Sea Port, by which Means they obtain their Discharge; and that the Petitioners have also Reason to believe, that the Custom House Cutters go alongside the smuggling Vessels and take only Part of their Cargo, and afterwards set them at Liberty, by which Means they give the Vessels an Opportunity of getting off with the Remainder of the Cargo, which they land at some small Distance, and set Sail for more; and that these Practices are carried on to such a Degree, that they are not only highly detrimental to the Trade and Commerce of this Kingdom, and the East India Company in particular, but also occasion a Lois to the Revenue of no less than £.600,000 per Annum; and that the Revenue also suffers great Lois by the injurious Practice of entered Dealers buying low Teas at the different Sea Port Custom House Sales, which they vend by Duffer tsV. at a triffing Loss wthout Permit; and, by virtue of tire Permit they receive from the Customs, bring , into their Stock fine Teas, which they fell at a considerable Profit into the inland Parts of the Kingdom; and that there are many Thousands of Sailors employed in Smuggling, few of whom ever serve on Board the Royal Navy, for, if they happen to be impelled, they generally find Friends sufficient to obtain their Discharge; but, if that Trade was flopped, they would in all Probability become Fishers, whereby our Sea Coasts would be greatly enriched, and our Ports be able to furnifti both Ships and Men in case of Necessity; and that there are many Thousands of Silk Weavers and Lace Manufacturers out of Employ, owing in a great Measure to the Smuggling of Silks, Callicoes, and'Laces, from France: And therefore praying the House will take the Affair into Consideration, and, effectually to stop the increasing Evil, pass a Law, with such Resolutions as to them thall teem meet, to detest Smugglers, and inllict such Punishments and Penalties as will for ever prevent their being guilty of the like Practices, so injurious and detrimental to the Commerce and Revenue of this Kingdom.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, made in the Thirteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for dividing and inclosing certain Moors, Commons, or Tracts of Waste Land, within the Parish and Manor of in the County

Palatine of Durham, was read; whereby it appeared, that the Commissioners appointed by the said Act are directed to set out and allot a Quantity, not exceeding Five hundred nor leis than Three hundred Acres, of the said Moors or Commons, to the Justices of the Peace for the County of Durham; and that the Money arising by the Rents and Profits thereof, are to be applied in making Satisfaction to Persons who should thereafter sustain any Damage by or on Account of searching for, winning, or working, any Mines or Quarries within their Allotments, by the Lord of the said Manor; and that, if, after satisfying all such Damages as aforesaid, there should be any Overplus, the same is directed to be laid out in repairing the Highways, Causeways, and other Ways, which should be made over the said Moors or Commons. And the said Commissioners are also directed to cauie the said Allotment to be inclosed with fufilicient Outfences, and to be subdivided into Fields or Closes by Quickset or other Hedges or Fences, or Walls, and to crest a convenient Farm House, with a Barn, Byer, Stable, Stack Yard, and Fold Yard, and other necessary Buildings or Conveniences, upon such Part oi the said Allotment as they should think fit.

Then Mr. Thomas Rippon being examined, informed your Committee, That the Commissioners have set out a Plot of Ground, containing Three hundred Acres# to His Majesty’s Justices of the Peace for the County of Durham, for the Purposes aforesaid, and have caused the same to be in Part ring-fenced, and certain Buildings to be erected thereon; but the same is not completed lb as to be fit to let to a Tenant; and that the compleiing the Ring-fence, and erecting the said Buildings, agreeable to the Directions of the Act, will be very expen live.

That he apprehends the Out-fence will cost, over and above what is.heady expended thereon, the Sum of One hundred and Forty-two Pounds, or thereabouts; and that proper Buildings, and other Conveniences, will cost about Forty Pounds more, exclusive of the Subdivision Fences necessary to be made, which he apprehends will cost about Two hundred and Forty Pounds. And he added. That the Commissioners have not yet executed their General Award.

And being asked, Whether* if the Land let out as aforesaid was properly fenced, and the Buildings and Conveniences completed, it might not be let to a Tenant at a Rent sufficient to answer the Expence of finishing the Fences, and erecting the necessary Buildings? he laid, He thought not} lor that near One Hall is an ordinary Sand, and not fit for the Purpose of Husbandry. And being asked, If he was a competent Judge of the Nature and Value of that Land? he said. He was; and that he had been brought up in the Farming Bufinel's in that Neighbourhood, where he now lives, and rents a Farm.

That about One hundred and Forty Acres of the Land is not fit to grow Corn, as it is a loofie Sand, and being situated on the North Side of a Hill, the Corn would not ripen if sown; that the rest of the Land might be made fit to grow Corn, but it would be attended with a great Expence, as some of it is very poor Land.

Being asked, What Quantity of Lime would be ne-cdTary to lay upon an Acre of this Land, in order to make it fa for Corn? he laid. It is customary in that Part of the Country to ule 1 hree Loads of Lime to an Acre; and that Lime there colls about Half a Guinea a Load.

Trade of a Baker, although- they shall hot have been brought up as Apprentices therein, upon an Allegation in the said Bill, that it may tend;tb reduce the present high Price of Bread; and that" the > Pertioners appre*." hend the Price of Bread has of late, and is at present,; much lower than in general it has Been for n^any Years past; and that the'Bakers have it not in their Power at any Time to increase the Price thereof, the^atue wholly depends, in'all Places were an Afflzd is' ict, upon the Price of Corn and Flour, and the- Allbw.tAce of lire Magistrates to the Baker for his Profit arid Expenses, which Allowance in London is the tone now as it ever has been, notwithstanding the ’ very great Increase of the Expences of their Trade, exclusive of those- Burthens which the Calamity of the Times inflicts on thefri in common with the rest of their Fellow Submits; and that the Number of Bakers in and about the Metropolis being considerably increased of late Years, the Quantity of Bread made and fold is not Co great'as it u’let for* merly to-be, most of them being capable of making, with the- same Hands more Bread than thTy now do, if there was a Demand for it; and that the''Trade of a Baker being principally carried bn with the Afliftar.ee of pdor Apprentices, the Petitioners conceive', that, should the said Bill pats'into a Law, it would be extremely prejudicial to the Bakers, particularly to those, in Corporate Towns, as Apprentices Would be thereby discouraged from coming into a Trade which was open to all Persons to exercise, and the M iller. Bakers con-., sequently be obliged, at a great Increase of Expence, to employ, for Want of Apprentices, J Urneymen who.' are free of such Corporate Towns, and who arp not at all Times to be got; and that, there being ah Art Or . Mystery in making Bread, and more elpccially- large ' Baches of that Sort of Bread which i5 f >r Sale, and in general required, ih great Cities or Towns, the Petitioners conceive, that the enabling Persons to cxeir-cife the Trade, who have not served an Apprenticeship thereto, may tend to introduce bad Bread, and pi event the Public from having so good a Commodity as it i$ in general allowed they now have: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, or such Parts thereof as affect the Petitioners, or that the House will afford them such other Relief as shall seem meet.

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for defraying the Charge of the Pay and Cloathing of the Militia, in that Part of Great Britain called England, for One Year, beginning the Twenty-fifth Day of March One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-nine i without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing and inclosing the Open Fields, Meadows, Furze, Leys, Stinted Common Pastures, and Waste Grounds, in the Parish of Willingham, in the County of Lincoln; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for continuing the Term, and varying the Powers, of Two Acts, made in the Twenty-sixth and Twenty-ninth Years of the Reign of his late Majesty, for repairing and widening the Road from the Top of White Sheet Hill, in the Parish of Donhead Saint Andrew, in the County of Wilts, and several other Roads therein mentioned, in the Counties of Dor jet, Somerset, and Wilts; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act more effectually to enable the President and Governors of the Hospital or Infirmary at established

" An Act for establishing and well-governing an Hospital or Infirmary in the City of Bath, " to take, or acquire, and hold, any Lands, Tenements, or Hereditaments, or any Interestin Lands, Tenements, or Hereditaments, and any Money or Personal Property to be laid out in Lands, Tenements, or Hereditaments, pursuant to any Will or ot'nerwife, to the Amount limited in the said Act; without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act for Sale of the Settled Estates of Henry Scourfield, Esquire, situate in the County of Brecon, and for purchasing other Estates in the County of Pembroke, to be settled in lieu thereof, to the same Uses; to which the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House: And also.

A Petition of several of his Majesty’s Roman Catholic Subjects of North Britain being offered to be presented to the House,

The Lord North, by His Majesty's Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth That we, your Petitioners, the Roman Catholics residing in the Cities of and

gozo, beg Leave, with the mcfl profound Respect and Deference, to lay before this honourable House the Treatment wc have lately met with from the Fury of a miiguided Populace, and to implore that Redress and Protection which we are persuaded this honourable House will think that our Wrongs require, and which the known Justice and Humanity of the Legifla-

ture give us Ground to expect: We, and the rest of our Brethren in Scotland, have, for a long Series of Years, endeavoured, by our inoffer.five and dutiful Conduct, to approve ourselves harmld's and useful Subjects of the British Empire; and were ready to embrace,

with Pleasure, every Opportunity of serving our County though at the Expense of our Lives and Fortunes: Encouraged by the Spirit of Humanity and Toleration, which we had Kealon to believe distinguished an cn-lightened and liberal Age, and having immediately in our View the late Relaxation of the Penal Laws against our Fellow Subjects (lie Roman Catholics of England, we ventured to hope that the same Indulgence might at lead, in home Respect, be shewn to us; and we flattered ourselves, that our loyal and submissive Behavior upon that Occasion, and our Willingness to have our Relief postponed, when the Bill was brought in for the Relief of the Roman Catholics of England, did, in feme Degree, entitle us to it: Conscious of the Justice of our Hopes, and of the Innocence of our Conduct, we beheld with Concern, that the very Circumstance of our Humility and Duty in postponing our Relief, in-ftcad of reconciling the Minds of tome mistaken Persons to us, was made use of to exasperate the lower People into Dispositions of great Violence: The public Papers were filled with the mofl virulent and inflammatory Advertisements; Pamphlets were published and dispersed every where among the Populace, representing us, in tire most unjust and odious Colours, as Enemies to Society, and unworthy of being allowed an Ex-iflence; Invitations were sent throughout all Scotland, encouraging the People to join all their Intcrell and Purles to oppose all attempts to allow us the smallest Part of the Rights of Subjects: The Consequences of all this were i'uch as might be expeCled; the Common People were every where stirred up to the utmost Rage and Fury against us, and the Public Papers were daily filled with llesolutions of Boroughs, Incorporations, Societies, Paddies, tdc. from several Parts of Scotland, drenuously to oppose any Attempt that might be made in Parliament to do any Thing in our Favour: YVe, on our Part, considering the Spirit which had by such unjustifiable Arts been raffed against us, and the seditious Tendency of many of those Means which had been used to inflame the people, and dreading the Consequences of their en-thufiaftic Fury, if raised to a certain Point, did, of Vol. 37.

our own accord, chearfully give up every Thought of applying to Parliament while that Ferment laded, choosing rather to podpone our own Ease to some mpre quiet Time, than to endanger the Peace of our Country; and this our Resolution was, immediately, in the most dutiful Manner, signified to the proper Officer of State: We hoped, that this convincing Proof, the greated that could be given of our Submission to Government, and our peaceable Disposition, if it did not reconcile the Peop’e to us, would at lead put an End to those Animosities which their groundless Apprehensions had raised against us; but in this we were greatly midaken: The enthusiadic Fury which had been excited in their Minds was got to such a Height, that they fecnied to be but the more obdinately bent on our Ded ruction; the Minds of the Populace in Edinburgh and Glasgow continuing irritated against us, and this Irritation being kept up by Art, a most violent Tumult arole; the Multitude, notwithstanding the Endeavours of the Magistrates of both these Cities, proceeded to the greated Extremeties, plundered our Effects, burned and destroyed our Houses, insulted our Persons, and even threatened the Lives of several, had they fallen into their Hands: We do not vvifh to exaggerate any Part of their Disorders, or of our Sufferings, or even to expose at large to this honourable House what wc wish we could with Safety to ourselves bury in eternal Oblivion. In these distressing Circumstances, to whom can we fly for Relief and Protection, but to the Justice and Humanity of Parliament ? By the Severity of the Laws against us, we are in a great Measure precluded from all legal Redress, and on that Account inferior Courts have it not in their Power to help us; it is the Legislature alone that can proiect us, and it is from their Goodneis alone that we expect to be protected: But, while we throw ourselves with Confidence upon the Mercy of Parliament, we beg Leave, with the most profound Submission, to make the Nature of our Requed fully known to this most respectable Body: In the first Place, we are far, very far, from entertaining a Resentmer.t against any one whatsoever, or from desiring that any l’crfon shoukl be called to Account, much lei’s should be punished, for the Injury done to us: We forgive from the Bottom of our Hearts; and, should any Perfort be taken into Cudody, orproiecuted upon our Account, it wc were worthy to be heard, we should presume to petition in the most earned Manner for his Pardon: This we declare, not from a Conscious-ness of having done any Thing that could dcierve the cruel Treatment we have met with, our Conscience is perfectly clear as to that, our Behaviour has been blame-lcfs both as Subjects and Citizens, and we challenge our greated Enemies, even those who have burned our 1 loufes and attempted our Lives, to prove any Breach of Duty against us in either respect; but we do it because it is the real Disposition of our Minds, dictated by Reason, and enjoined by our Religion: In the second Place, we chearfully lay alide all Thoughts of asking any Relaxation of the severe Laws against us at this Time: Indeed we cannot help thinking it very hard, that we alone should be wholly denied that Relief which has been in some Degree granted to our Brethren in all other Parts of his Majesty’s Dominions: Our Claim to such Relief is no Id's founded in Justice than theirs; but wc are sensible that, considering the present Flame which is raised against us, it might disturb the Peace of our Country to infid upon it, and on that Account alone we abstain, in the present Circumstances from defiling it, proteding always to this honourable House, and to the World, that our Conlctence acquits us of any Offence, either in Opinions or Actions, which can render us deserving of those Laws of extreme Rigour to which we submit; and that we are perfectly ready to give the most effectual Pro fs which the Wisdom of the Legislature can lugged, of our Fidelity to His Majesty, and Attachment to the Consti-

tution

tution of our Country; but though we abandon wholly our Refcntments, and even dutifully suspend our Petitions for thofj Rights of Subjects to which we conceive in all Humility that we are entitled, the Duty of Self-preservation will not suffer us to renounce all Claim to every fort of Protection; nor will the Narrowneis of our private Circumstances, and the Justice which several of us owe to our unhappy Families now utterly ruined, permit us to relinquish our humble Endeavours for Compensation for our heavy Losses from the Equity and Humanity of the Public: Had the severe Penal Laws 'been regularly put in Execution against us, had we been legally tried and condemned to suffer forieiVing Almighty God as our Conscience dictates, from the profound Respect we bear to the Laws of our Country, we lboukl have borne our hard Lot with Patience, as we already have often done without Complaint or Murmur;but we cannot help thinking it extremely hard to be exposed to the Fur)' of a lawless Multitude, without the lmalleft Provocation on our Parts, and to be so cruelly and inhumanly treated by them, without any Form of Trial, without being heard, examined, and legally condemned. What therefore we most humbly, and with the most profound Submission, venture to request is, That this honourable House, taking ourCafe into Confederation, would be graciously pieaied, in such a Manner as they fee fit, to find Means of Compensation to Persons utterly unable to bear them for the heavy Losses we have so unjustly fuf-tained-, and, seeing that we must still be exposed to the same barbarous Treatment from the desperate and mif-guided Zeal of the same furious People, if some effectual Protection be not given to us, that this honourable House would further be plealed to provide, for our future Safety, that, until the Laws can be coolly reconsidered, our Persons and Property may have (bme Security from such lawless Outrages for the time to come, by taking such Measures as they shall judge most adequate to that End. We most humbly beg Leave to assure this honourable House, that this our earnest Request for Protection is not made without the strongest Reason; for the same unprovoked Enemies, who have hitherto persecuted us in so cruel a Manner, far from being farisfied with their late Success, have made it a Ground for further Violence; those who have never threatened us, without executing their Menaces, have publishecj and dispersed a Sort of Manifcfto, calling upon all Orders of People strictly to enforce the Execution of the most sanguinary Laws upon us, denying the Authority of Parliament to repeal those Laws, or any other Laws made before the Union, threatening the Magistrates with the same Violence which they have employed against your Petioners, if they do not cause them to be executed; representing those Means of banishing and putting to Death your Petitioners, as their Rights and Privileges, and proposing Associations against buj ing or felling, borrowing or lending, or having any of the ordinary Intercourse of Society with those of our Religion, and threatening to proceed against all who shall refuse to join them in those Measures, as if they were Papists; and they have, in their late violent Attempts against some of the most respectable Characters in the established Church of ',shewn

how far they are capable of acting against such as discover any Degree of Moderation in their Sentiments: In a Word, nothing can be more deplorable, and (without the effectual Aid of the Legislature) more hopelef*, than our Condition. We humbly presume that this our Request will appear neither diifelpeft-ful nor unreasonable to this honourable House; and we hope the Justice and Humanity of that respectable Body, whole favourite and noblest Prerogative is to be the Protestors of the injured, and the Defenders of the Rights of that People whom they represent, will be graciously pleased to take us into their Protection, who have nothing more at Heart than to *7

demean ourfdves as dutiful Subjects, and good Citizens, and who by our Loyalty to our Prince, and by our innocent and Submissive Behaviour, will make it our constant Endeavour to merit their Favour and Approbation.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put. That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for preserving the Navigation of the River Lee, in the Counties of Hertford, Essex, and Middl and for Relief of the . Creditors under Two Acts of Parliament, of the Twelfth Year of his late Majesty, and of the Seventh Year of His present Majesty, relating to the Navigation of the said River;

The House divided.

The Yeas went forth.

Tdlm for the Yeas.j Lif }

Tellers for the No«,j Xlderman' Oliver:} 12'

So it was resolved in the Affirmative.

Ordered, That Mr. Plumer, Mr. Calvert, and Mr. Haljey, do prepare, and bring in, the said Bill.

Mtflage The Lord North acquainted the House, That he had

King* a Message from His Majesty to this House, signed by His Majesty; and he presented the same to the House: And it was read by Mr. Speaker (all the Members of the House being uncovered) and is as followerh j viz.

GEORGE R.

mentj His Majesty having received Information from the Earl of Buckingemshire, His Lieutenant General and

Governor General of His Kingdom of Ireland, That the Revenues of that Kingdom have, of late, proved greatly deficient, and inadequate to the Purposes for which they were granted; and His Majesty, moved with Concern and Compassion for the Distresses of His loyal and faithful Subjects of that Kingdom, and being anxious that some immediate and effectual Relief should be afforded to them, thinks it necessary to recommend to the Consideration of this House, whether it may not be proper, in the present Circumstances of Ireland, that the whole Charge of the Regiments on the Irish Establishment, now serving out of that Kingdom, should be paid by Great Britain. G. R.

Ordered, That His Majesty’s said Most gracious Message be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

The Lord North presented to the House, by His Majesty’s Command,

Estimate of the Charge of the Difference of Pay be- Regiment*, tween the Britishand Irish Establishment of One Regiment of Light Dragoons, and Six Regiments of Foot, serving in North America, as paid by Ireland, for the Year 1779.

And the Title of the said Estimate was read.

The said Estimate is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petitions, Mr. Richard Clitheroxv being examined, said, That within the Towns, Villages, Hamlets, and Places, of the said Soake, and Wapentakes, and Hundred, in the Petitions mentioned, there are carried on several extensive Branches of Trade and Business, and that many ill-disposed persons therein do contract Small Debts, and although able, refuse to Pay the fame, presuming that the Creditors lie under great Inconvenience in the Recovery thereof by the present Forms of Law, and on Account of the great Expences and Delays in the County Court, which lies upwards of Thirty Miles Distance from most of the Places, and from some of them near Forty Miles: and that if any easy and more effectual Method of Recovering Small Debts within the said Towns, Villages, Hamlets, and Places, was established, the same would greatly contribute to promote Industry and Trade, and be of Public Utility. And being further examined, he said. That it is proposed by the intended Bill to establish Seven Courts for the Recovery of Small Debts, at the following Places; viz. Horncastle, Wragby, , Louth,

Sal feet, and Freiston; and that if the same shoukl be established (the greatest Part of the Inhabitants living in and near the said Places) it will render the Recovery of Small Debts speedy and easy; and that the general Distance, upon an Average, from the Courts intended to be established will not be above Three or Four Miles.

A Petition of the Matter, Wardens, and Company, of Bake is, within the City of Bnjiol, was prdented to the HoulV, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill to enable Persons to exercise the Trades of Bakeis and Butchers, although they shall not have been brought up as Apprentices in the said Trades, and Setting forth. That, if the same should pals into a Law, it will be of great Prejudice "to the Public in general, as well as to the Petitioners in particular, and' an Innovation of the established Law of the Land, as in few or any Cafes whatever, Trades are suffered to be carried on without the Trader first having served a regular Apprenticeship thereto, in order that a just Infight may be acquired in such intended Trade or Calling, raid the Party thereby enabled to manufacture and vend a good and marketable Article; and that the Petitioners (at a considerable Premium as Apprentice Fees, and a Servitude of Seven Years) are become entitled to carry on their Trade, and the intended Bill would, in a particular )VIanner> prejudice them, by giving a general Right without any Inch Fee or Service; and, as all public Bakers are under the strict Regulation of the Magi ft rates, no Fraud, or unfair Practice, can pals with Impunity; and, in the Petitioners'present Situation, the Inspectors appointed, by them have hitherto taken the necessary Care that due R g.ird be paid to the Assize and Quality of the Bread wimin their Distpft, which Regulation, as to the Petitioners, of Conrfe would ceale, if the said Bill should pals into a Law; and that, as all Persons have at present a Right to manufacture and bake Bread for their Family, or as Clifts to the Poor, the said Bill can only tend to give a Right to unskilfui Persons to carry on the said Trades, to the immediate Prejudice of the Public, and of the Petitioners: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not be fullered to pais into a Law.

A Petition of the Wardens of the Butchers in the Town of Nottingham, anti of the several other Butchers of the Town of Nottingham, whole Hands are there-

unto let and subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and the rest of the said Trade, was also prdented to the House, and read; likewise taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, That, if the same should pads, it would be a very partial Law, and greatly prejudicial to the Petitioners, by depriving them of the Benefit they now are entitled to have by Law, in Exclusion of Inch who have not feryed regular Apprenticeships; and that the Petitioners neccttaviiy fuller great Lottes, from the* perishable Nature of the Co n. modi tv they deal in, which other Trades are free from, and apprehend, should such Bill pal’s into a Law, the same would be of no real Service (o this Kingdom: And therefore praying* That the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

A Petition of the Wardens of the Bakers in the

Town of Nottingham, and of the several other Bakers of the Town of Nottingham, whose Hands are there*

unto set and subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and the rest of the Trade, was also presented to the House, and read; likewise taking Notice of the find Bill; and Setting forth, That, should the same pass into a Law, it would be of no real Benefit to this Kingdom, yet, in its Consequences, would be greatly prejudicial to the Petitioners, by depriving them of the Benefit tnev are now by Law entitled to have, in Exclusion of others who have not served regular Apprenticeships; and that the Petitioners Trade is now already under the Regulation of an Assize, on which Account the Petitioners, notwithstanding the many Lottes they sustain in the Course of their Trade, can only have such Profits as the Magistrates think proper to allow them, which is not the same in any other Trade in this Kingdom: And there* fore praying. That the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

And ti:e said Petition was read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have perused a Bill, depending in the House, for preserving the Navigation of the River Lee, in the Counties of Hertford, Essex, and , and for Belief of the Creditors under Two Acts of Parliament, of tive Twelfth Year of his late Majesty, and of the Seventh. Year of His on sent Majesty, relating to the Navigation of the said River; and that, by the said last mentioned Act of the Seventh Year of His present Majesty, the Trustees, appointed to execute the Powers therein granted, were authorized to raise Money by Annuities upon the Rates and Duties therein mentioned, on the natural Life of every Contributor, or the Nominee of fitch Contributor, so as not to exceed the Rate of Eight Pounds per Centum per; yet the Petitioners

have been informed, and doubt not they shall be able to prow, that many Thousand Pounds have been borrowed, by the Trustees, at a much higher Rate than allowed by the said Act, and part thereof at not less than Eleven Pounds per Cent-, and that a very considerable Sum of Money has been raised by Annuities, without any Warrant or Order first obtained from a proper Number of Trustees for that Purpose; and that, notwithstanding the Trustees were restricted to Eight Cent. on a Angle Life, Annuities at that Rate on Two Lives have been granted; and that it appears to the Petitioners, that great Part of the Works relative to the said Navigation have been improperly executed, and various Sums of Money unnecessarily expended; and they conceive, that, if the Trust had been properly conducted, and due Attention paid to the regular Collection of the Tolls, the same would have been sufficient to have answered the Purposes intended by the said Acts; and that great Quantities of Corn, Malt, and other necessary Commodities and Articles of Life, are conveyed, by Means of the River Lee, from the County of Hertford, and other adjoining Counties, to the Cities of London and Westminster; and that, if the additional Tolls pro-

posed by the Bill should take Place, every additional Toll so created will be an additional Tax and Burthen imposed upon Trade and Industry, in order to supply a

Deficiency that has arisen from Irregularity and Miscon-dust in the Trustees who have hitherto executed the said Acts; and that, as to any Loss or Injury which the Creditors may fuftaiti by the improper and illegal Proceedings of the Trustees, under whole Sanction they have advanced their several Loans of Money, the Petitioners submit' it to the Consideration of the House, whether Kedrefe, in respect of such Loss or Injury, be not more property cognizable by the Courts in Westminster Hall than by the Legislature; and that the Imposition of an additional Toll upon the Public, and to be under the Confrool of the fa ne Trustees, is, in the Opinion of the Petitioners, under the Circumstances of tire present Application, a Matter highly deferring the Consideration of the Legislature: And therefore praying, ‘That they may be heard, by their Counfe!, before the Committee to whom the Bill stands committed; and that they may have such Rebel-in the Premifts as to the House shall seem meet.-

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the -said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Inftvuftion to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said. Petition.

A Petition or the Chancellor, Masters, and Scholars, of the University of Oxford, was presented to the House, and read; taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, That the same does not provide that such Ministers and School-Mailers shall make any Profession whatever of their Belief in the fundamental Doctrines of Christianity, or even the Authority of the Holy Scriptures, as containing a Revelation of the Will of God; and that, without iome such Provision, Distenting Ministers, and School-Masters, of all Denominations, will be at Liberty toprea.h any Doctrines, and instil into young Minds any Principles, how repugnant loever to the Christian Faith: The Petitioners, therefore, entrusted, by the very Nature of their Institutbn, with the Education of Youth in the Principles of True Religion, Friends at the same Time to Toleration, so far as the same may be confident with the Interests of Christianity, and the Security of our happy Establishment in Church and State, pray, that fuc;: Bill, which they cannot but regard as injurious and dangerous to both, may not be permitted to pals into a Law, under the unlimited Form in which it is now proposed.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to thi Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed.

A Petition of John SilveJIer, Esquire, Barrister at Law, Steward, and John Mors , Esquire, Barrister at Law, Deputy Steward, of the King’s Court of Record, within the Manors of Stepney and , in

the County of Middlesex, and of the Liberties of the fame, on Behalf of themselves, and others interested in the said Court, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth; That, in the Nineteenth Year of King Charles the Second, Letters Patent were granted for establishing a Court of Record within the said Manors of Stepney and Hackney, for the Determination of all Personal Actions under Five Pounds, the foie and exclusive Right to which Patent is now veiled in Ann King, Widow of John , Esquire, deceased; and that the Petitioners have perused a Bill, depending in the House, for explaining, amending, and rendering more effectual, an Act, passed in the Twenty-third Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, for the more easy and speedy Recovery of Small Debts within the Tower , wherein there

are certain Clauses, which, if palfed into a Law, will be very prejudicial to the Petitioners Interest, which is Freehold, and highly rated to the Land Tax, and of-preffive on the Inhabitants within the said Liberties, particularly those Clauses which are meant to give the Commifllioners under the said Act Power to take Cognizance of Debt for Rent under Forty Shillings, due from Persons residing within the Jurisdiction of the Court established by the said Act, which Jurisdiction is precileiy of the same Extent as that included in the above-mentioned Patent; and that the Petitioners conceive no Benefit could accrue to the Public by extending the Powers of the said Act to Debts for Rent, in settling which Questions, great Intricacy and Nicety in Law frequently arile, on which the Commissioners, by whom they must be tried, would probably be wholly incapable to determine: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against such Parts of the said Bill as may affect them, and that the same may not pass as it now stands

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves or Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Ordered, That all have Voices, who come to the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed.

The Lord Midltlon, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the allowing a Bounty on the Importation of Hemp into Great Britain from Ireland, the Resolution which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where (he same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Bounty be granted upon the Importation into Great Britain of Hemp of the Growth of the Kingdom of Ireland, for the Term of Twenty-one Years; namely, of Eight Pounds per Ton for the First Seven Years, of Six Pounds per Ton for the next Seven Years, and of Four Pounds per Ton for the last Seven Years.

The said Resolution being read a Second Time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.
