the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Tabic: Where the same was read, and is as followeth; viz.

In order to bring the Subject into Tome Method, your Committee will give,

First, An abridged State of such Evidence as they have received, respecting the Maintenance and Employment of Criminals under Sentence in various Prisons, within the City of London, and in the Counties within the Home Circuit, viz. MEJfex Kent, Herts, Surrey, Sussex, and some other Parts of England.

In the Second Place, Such Information as they have been able to collect, relative to the Execution and Efte&s of the Act of Parliament, which authorizes the Confinement and Hard Labour of Transportable Of- fenders aboard Vessels in the River Thames', and such Plans for the good Conduct and Management of Convids, who may be sentenced to Hard Labour, as have been suggested by several Persons, whom your Committee have examined.

Thirdly, A short Account of the Acts relating to Transportation, and of the Proposals which have been dated to your Committee, for recurring in some Degree to that Mode of Punishment.

And, Lastly, The Observations of your Committee, on these several Materials, and the Resolutions which they have formed thereon.

It appeared by the Returns referred to the Consideration of your Committee, as follows:

The City of London.

In the Gaol of Newgate there were 84 convicted Prisoners, 15 of whom were under imprisonment for Three Years, 4 for Five Years, and for Seven Years, besides several who were sentenced to work on the River Thames i that there was no Employment for them; and the Allowance for each Prisoner was One Penny Loaf per Day, and Once a Week, Four Stone of Beef was sent by the Sheriffs, which was distributed amongst those who were committed by Sentence of Fine and imprisonment.

Middlesex.

In Clerkenwell Bridewell there were 114 Convids, 70

of whom were Females, and 42 of them imprisoned for Three Years; that they were employed in beating Hemp, and picking of Oakum, and were allowed Three Pence per Day in Provisions.

In New Ptifon, Clerkenvjell, there were 10 Convids,

One of whom was imprisoned for Five Years, and had no Employment; and were allowed Two Pence per Day.

In Tothill Fields Bridewell there were 2 G»nvids; who had no Employment, and were allowed One Penny per Day in Bread.

In Wood Street Compter there were 3 Prisoners; who had no Employment, and were allowed One Penny per Day in Bread.

Essex.

In Halflead House of Correction there were 6 Convids; who were employed in spinning of Wool, and were allowed Three Pence per Day.

In Chelmsford House of Correction there were 6 Convids, One of whom was imprisoned for Six Years, and another for Three Years; who were employed in carding and spinning, and were allowed One Pound and an Half of Bread, and One Quart of Small Beer, per Day.

Kent.

In Maidstone House of Correction there were 9 Convids, 2 of whom were imprisoned for Three Years; the Men were employed in beating and sorting of Hemp, and the Women in spinning, and were allowed is. 6 d.per Week each for their Maintenance.

Herts.

In Hertford County Gaol there were 8 Convids, 6 of whom were sentenced to work on the River,

4 for Three Years, 1 for Four Years, and 1 fer Five Years; who were allowed 2*. 6 per Week; the other

Surrey.

In Southwark New Gaol there Were 2 Convids; One of whom was imprisoned for Three Years, and was employed in cleaning the Gaol, who was allowed a Three Half-penny Loaf per Day; and the other was imprisoned till he paid a Fine of £. 5, who had the same Allowance, and worked at his Trade as a Taylor.

In Southwark House of Correction there were 14 Convids; who were employed in beating of Hemp, and were allowed Three Half-penny worth of Bread per Day.

In Kimfton upon Thames House of Correction there were 3 Convids; Two of whom were employed in sewing of Sacks, and were allowed Three Halfpennyworth of B.ead per Day.

In the New Bridewell, Saint George's Fields, there were 14 Convids, amongst whom were 3 Women, sentenced to Ten Years Imprisonment; who were employed in beating of Hemp, and had an Allowance of Three Halfpenny-worth of Bread per Day.

In the County of Sussex.

There was no convicted Prisoner in any Gaol or House of Correction.

Your Committee then proceeded to examine Mr.

Richard Akerman, Keeper of Newgate; who being asked.

How the convicted Prisoners, mentioned in the Return, could fubfilt upon a Penny a Day each ? he answered.

Your Committee then called Doctor William Smith; who informed them. In pursuing this Enquiry, your Committee thought it their Duty to receive such Informations as they could obtain, respecting the Good Conduct and Employment of Convicts, who might be sentenced to Hard Labour, whether in Houses to be established for that Purpose on Shore, or the present Houses of Correction, or aboard Vessels in Navigable Rivers} and accordingly, John Howard, Esquire, informed your Committee, That at Baruth, in Franconia, the Men Convicts were employed in sawing and polishing of Marble; and he was told by the Governor it was a very profitable Employment. At Anfpach, he found the Conviefts worked at grinding of Glass for Spedtacles, an unhealthy Employment; and they were allowed a Sixth Part of their Labour. At Milan, there were between Two and Three hundred Male Convicts employed in manufacturing Cloth, who had small Chains on, and were so exceedingly well regulated, that he walked through their Apartments Two or Three different Days, and not One of them offered to leave their Work, or even to speak to him to ask Charity — That he was informed the Establishment was a very heavy Expence at first to Government, but that the Expence was continually decreasing. At Magdebourg, the Convicts were employed in the Re-

pairs of the Fortifications. At Leghorn, there were about 30 or 40 Convicts, who worked in the Lazeretto. — And the Witness further said, He was of Opinion that the Convicts in England might be profitably employed, in making coarse Canvas Bags, coarse Cloths for Soldiers, and Hop Bagging.

Mr. Benjamin Crook, who appeared to have made particular Enquiries on the Subject, recommended the making Cordage, as a very practicable and beneficial Species of Employment, for a considerable Number of Convicts. And he produced a Sketch of a Plan, to your Committee, recommending the making of Cordage, for the following Reasons:

That the Consumption of Cordage in the Royal Navy was so large, as to employ any Number of Convicts likely to be a Burthen to Government: Therefore,

No Expence or Loss could accrue, in procuring a Vent for the Commodity, when manufactured.

No private Individual would be injured, as Government manufactured their own Cordage in the Dock Yards.

The Mode of Work was such, that the Convicts might be easily and safely confined, and at the same Time would enjoy both Air and Exercise.

The greater Part was that Kind of manual Labour, which might be adapted to the different Degrees of Strength of Body and Constiturion of every Convict.

No mental Abilities, or any Kind of Education, were required.

The Commodity to be manufactured could not easily be wasted or spoiled by the Convicts.

No Tools or Implements, expensive or easily damaged, were required; nor any Tool or Implement employed, which could contribute to Escapes, or be dangerous.

No Evasion could be pleaded for Idleness or Neglect of Work, nor unnecessary Trouble given to Officers who were to oversee their Labour, or extraordinary Rigour requisite from them, as every Person could be regularly talked through the whole Process, and thereby

no Occasion could be given for Murmurs, as every one would know when his Labour was to cease.

As every Thing could be done by Task Work, little Rewards for Encouragement might be easily adapted so as to make Convicts go through their Labour chearfully.

One of the most hazardous Articles (viz. Hemp) would be removed thereby out of the Dock Yards.

It was suggested to your Committee, by the Chairman, Sir Charles Bunbury, who had conversed with Doctor Fothergill on this Subject, that the Convicts might be advantageously employed in (awing of Stone, in which Business about Three hundred Persons worked in London and the Environs, and earned from 7 to 30 Shillings per Man per Week — That no Appenticeship was necessary, as it might be learned in a Fortnight by a common Labourer — That the Occupation was healthy, and might be proportioned to the Strength of the Workman, as it was harder to work at a large Block, with a long Saw, than at a little Block with a small one — That the Materials could not be embezzled; and One Person might superintend many — That the Convicts might be employed in this Labour on the Side of Rivers, if thought eligible for them to lie on board Vessels, or they might be Rationed near the Quarries, by which Means Stone would be rendered much cheaper.

Your Committee next proceeded to take into their Consideration, the several Acts relating to the Transportation of Offenders to Foreign Parts.

And it appeared by the Act of the Eighteenth Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, that Persons convicted of certain Offences therein described, were made liable to be transported into any of His Majesty’s Dominions in America, there to remain and not to return; and by the Acts of the Twenty-second and of the Twenty-second and Twenty-third Years of the same Reign, certain other Offenders were made liable to be transported into any of His Majesty’s Plantations beyond the Seas, for the Term of Seven Years.

It also appeared by the Act of the Fourth Year of the Reign of King George the First, that Persons convicted of Offences within the Benefit of Clergy, were liable to be sent into any of his Majesty’s Dominions in America, for the Term of Seven Years; and Persons convicted of Capital Offences, and to whom his Majesty should be pleased to extend his Royal Mercy, and alfp Receivers of stolen Goods, might be transported for Fourteen Years; and Persons contracting for their Transportation, should have a Property in their Service.

And by the subsequent Acts of the Sixth Year of the Reign of King George the First, and the Sixteenth and Twentieth Years of the Reign of King George the Second, the Regulations in the said Act of the Fourth Year of the Reign of King George the First, were explained and enforced.

Upon this Head your Committee called Duncan Campbell, Esquire; who said he had been concerned Twenty Years in contracting for Felons sentenced to Transportation; Five Pounds per Man were allowed by Government till the last: Three Years, when, in Consequence of a Competition for the Contract, he agreed to take them without any Profit but that which accrued to him by disposing of their Servitude in the Colonies; that many Convicts who had Money bought off their Servitude, and their Punishment was only Banishment for the Term prescribed; he carried them only to the Provinces of Maryland and Virginia, and fold common Male Convicts, not Artificers, on an Average, for 10 Pounds apiece. Females at about Eight or Nine Pounds; those who were of nfefui Trades, such as Carpenters and Blacksmiths, from Fifteen to Twenty-five Pounds; the old and infirm he used to dispose of to those humane

19 Geo. III.

mane People who chose to take them, but with some he was obliged to give Premiums,

Being asked, Whether they could be disposed of in any other Colonies ? he said. He apprehended not in any considerable Number, which was the Reason he declined contracting for them upon the Revolt of the Colonies of Virginia and Maryland; and that he imagined about One hundred might be disposed of Annually in Georgia, and upon the Frontiers of ,but did not

think any could in Canada t that he transported, on an Average of Seven Years, 473 Convidls Annually; that he carried from One to Two hundred Persons in a Ship; that the ordinary Passage was about Two Months, during which Time, and in the Gaol, where they were confined frequently Two Months before their Embarkation, rather more than a Seventh Part of the Felons died, many of the Gaol Fever, but more of the Small Pox. He observed, that the Number of Women who died were only Half in Proportion to the Men, which he imputed to their Constitutions being less impaired, and to their Sobriety.

Your Committee thought proper, therefore, to examine how far, Transportation might be practicable to other Parts of the World: And,

Joseph Banks, Esquire, being requeued, in case it should be thought expedient to establish a Colony of convicted Felons in any distant Part of the Globe, from whence their escape might be difficult, and where, from the Fertility of the Soil, they might be enabled to maintain themselves, after the Fiift Year, with little or no Aid from the Mother Country, to give his Opinion What Place would be most eligible for such Settlement ? informed your Committee, That the Place which appeared to him bed adapted for such a Purpose, was Botany Bar, on the Coast of New Holland’, in the Indian Ocean, which was about Seven Months Voyage from;

that he apprehended there would be little Probability of any Opposition from the Natives, as, during his Stay there, in the Year 1770, he saw very few, and did not think there were above Fifty in all the Neighbourhood, and had Reason to believe the Country was very thinly peopled; those he saw were naked, treacherous, and armed with Lances, but extremely cowardly, and constantly retired from our People when they made the lead Appearance of Relidance: He was in this Bay in the End of April and beginning of May 1770, when the Weather was mild and moderate; that the Climate, he apprehended, was similar to that about , in the

South of France, having found the Southern Hemi-sphere colder than the Northern, in such Proportion, that any given Climate in the Southern answered to one in the Northern about Ten Degrees nearer to the Pole; the Proportion of rich Soil was small in Comparison to the barren, but sufficient to support a very large Number of People; there were no tame Animals, and he saw no wild Ones during his Sray of Ten Days, but he observed the Dung of what were called Kangourous, which were about the Size of a middling Sheep, but very swift, and difficult to catch; some of those Animals he law in another Part of the Bay, upon the same Continent; there were no Bealls of Prey, and he did not doubt but our Oxen and Sheep, if carried there, would thrive and increule; there was great Plenty of Fiffi, he took a large Quantity by hauling the Seine, and struck several Stingrays, a kind of Skate, all very large; one weighed 336 Pounds. The Grass was long and luxuriant, and there were some eatable Vegetables, particularly a Sort of Wild Spinage; the Country was well supplied with Water; there was Abundance of Timber and Fuel, sufficient for any Number of Buildings, which might be found necessary. Being asked, How a Colony of that Nature could be l'ublifted in the Beginning of their Establishment ? he answered. They mull certainly be furnished, at landing, with a full Year’s Allowance of Victuals, Raiment, and Drink } with all Kinds of Tools for labouring the Earth, and building Houses: with Vox.. 37.

311

Black Cattle, Sheep, Hogs, and Poultry j with Seeds of all Kinds of European Corn and Pulse; with Garden Seeds j with Arms and Ammunition for their Defence; and they should likewise have small Boats, Nets, and Fishing-tackle} all of which, except Arms and Ammunition, might be purchased at the Cape of Good Hopei and that afterwards, with a moderate Portion of industry, they might, undoubtedly, maintain themselves without any Assistance from England. He recommended fending a large Number of Persons, Two or Three hundred at lead; their Escape would be very difficult, as the Country was far distant from any Part of the Globe inhabited by Europeans. And being afleed. Whether be conceived the Mother Country was likely to reap any Benefit from a Colony established in Botany Bay ? he replied, ]f the People formed among themselves a Civil Government, they would necessarily in-Crease, and find Occasion for many European Commodities: and it was not to be doubted, that a Tratft of Land such as New Holland, which was larger than the Whole of Europe, would furnish Matter of advantageous Return.

John Roberts, Esquire, was next examined; who in formed your Committee, that he had been Governor of Cape Coast Castle, in Africa, and had the command of all the other Forts, about Nine Years; and being asked, Whether he thought a Colony of convicted Felons might be established in Africa ? he said. He thought there might, and the Place belt adapted for that Purpose, was called Yanimarew, situate about four 400 Miles from the Mouth of the River Gambia, where the Country was hilly, and far more healthy than the flat Parts near the Coast; the Soil was very fertile, and produced all Sorts of Vegetables and Fruits; it abounded in valuable Woods, Mahogany equal to that from Jamaica, Woods for dying, Gums, Balsam of Copivia, Castor Oil, Fig and Cotton Trees, Indigo, Tobacco, Rice, Sugar Cane, Orange, Lemon, and Lime Trees, Plantin, Banana, Yamb, Sweet Potatoe, Pumkin, and Meion, were Natives; the Vine, Coffee, Cocoa, Ginger, and Aloe, would no Doubt answer; the Native Grain was the Indian Corn, and Guinea Grain of various Sorts; the Ground or NegroeNut; Potash might be made; there were Plenty of Animals for Food, and excellent Filli in the River. He believed the King of Yanimarew would be very Glad to have any White People settled in his Country, though he even knew they were Felons, and would grant them Land at a moderate Price; he recommended to fend One hundred and fifty Men and Sixty Women, at first, to try the Experiment, and they should arrive there in the Months of November or December, being the proper Months for the Europeans, as the rainy Sealon would be over, and the Weather more temperate, and they would have the Seasoning Sickness, which all Europeans were subject to, on their Arrival in that Country, in a llighter Degree. Should a Company be established, to direct and manage the Commerce of Gambia River, the Convicts that may be hereafter sent out there, will be of no further Charge to the Public, from their Arrival in the said River.

Bring aflted, If, after the Second Year, they would be able ro maintain themselves without further Aid from this Country? he answered. Not only to maintain themselves, but to make very advantageous Returns to England; and by proper Management, they might be made most useful People, in finding out the Source of the River, and exploring that rich and populous Country of Africa, hitherto little known; that he did 'nor apprehend they could make their Escape from thence, as the Blacks would not let them pals through the Country.

Mr Thomas Perkins, who had resided Seven Years at Yanimate it’, as a Trader, supported the Evidence of Governor Roberts, and added, that he had been a Thou fa nd Miles up the River Gambia, in order to purclnfe Slaves, Gold, and Ivory; that was the moll eligible and healthy Spot; that there were about Five hundred Inhabitants in the Town; in the Year 1770 there were 25 Sail of Trading Ships in the River; e.ntlthat there were now about Two in a Year;

that he would advise the Conv'ufts should be lodged on a small Hill near the Town, about a Sixth Part of a Mile from the River; that a Fort should be built, and they must be allowed Arras, in order to be safe from the Negroes; that a sufficient Quantity of Land for 200 Convicts might be purchased for One hundred Pounds; that the Corn which it would produce might be loid at a great Advantage to the Shipping, and the Indigo and Cotton might be sent to England; that the Country was very plentiful and abounded in Cattle, Fowl, Fish, and Fruit; a Bullock of Two hundred Weight might be purchased for Twenty Shillings. Being asked, Whether the Seasoning Sickness would not probably be fatal to many ? he replied, He did not think above ao out of 200 would die, if they were lent at a proper Season.

Mr. Robert Stubbs, who had resided in Africa Four Years, confirmed the Evidence of Governor Roberts and Mr. Perkins, respecting Yanimarew He likewise informed your Committee, That there was a Place called Podore, Seventy Miles up the River Senegal, belonging to the Eng/ish, and where there formerly was a Fort, which was a very healthy and fruitful Spot, and he rather preferred it to Yanimarew for the Purpose of establishing a Colony of Convids, which he believed was very pradicable, and he knew a Person who was ready to engage in such an Undertaking, and give proper Security for the Performance; on their First Arrival the Climate would certainly be fatal to Numbers, but would be less so if they got there at the proper Season, which he advised to be in the Month of November.

Doctor Thomas Wallace acquainted your Committee, That he had resided Four Years in the River Gambia and Senegal; that Yanimarew and Podore were the Two

healthiest Spots on those Rivers; he thought the Convids should arrive there in the Month of January, that all Europeans upon their Arrival had a Fever, which was called a Seasoning Sickness; that out of 210 Convids, he did not apprehend above a Sixth Part would die of it; and those who recovered from that Disorder were usually very’healthy afterwards.

Richard Camplin, Esquire, delivered to your Committee a Paper, containing an Account of the Deaths of Ewopeansfent to Cape CoaCajlle, and the Out

Forts, in the Kingdom of Africa, from the Beginning of the Year 1755 to the Conclusion of 1776, by which it appeared, that out of 746 Persons lent, 334 had died, and 271 had been either discharged, or had deserted, and of many there was no Account; and that the Climate on that Part of the Coast was lb fatal, and the mortality had been so great, that the African Committee, during the last Three Years of the above-mentioned Period, had(sent only 7 Officers, and had manned their Garrisons with the Natives, and the Children of the European Soldiers born in that Country.

Colonel Charles O'Hara informed your Committee,

That he had resided some Years at Senegal, and that Podore was One of the healthiest Spots on the River; that the District of Podore belonged to that Tribe of Moors or Blacks which happened to be the strongest; that the ruling Party would probably fell a sufficient Quantity of Land for 200 Persons for One hundred Pounds, but that the Uncertainty of Possession, and Fluftuation of Power, was so great in that Country, that that Party would loon be driven oft’by a llronger, which likewise must soon give way to a Third, who would all make similar Demands, so that he could not name the Sum which would be sufficient to maintain an Establishment there; that the extreme Difficulty of defending it was the Reason the English abandoned the Fort they had at Podore; that he apprehened it would be equally difficult to support any similar Establishment on the River Gambia, the Moors and Blacks in Africa considering White Men as their Property, and taking every Opportunity of extorting Money front

them;

The Right honourable Sir John Irwin, a Member of the House, being asked his Opinion of the Propriety of employing Convicts on the Fortifications at Gibraltar ? he replied. If there were Hulks or Gallies for them to lie in, that they could be kept from mixing with the Soldiers, and from escaping into Spain, and were under strict Discipline, they would be of Lfe in doing the most laborious Works in the Repairs of that Garrison.

OBSERVATIONS.

U nder the Fi'fl: Head of Enquiry, which respects the Maintenance and Employment of Criminals sentenced to liuprilbninent in various Gaols, and Houses of Coirtdtion, throughout , your Committee

observe,

That the Allowance for the Support of these unhappy Persons varies in the different Counties, without a just or reasonable Caule, and in a Manner not Tcconciieable to any good System of Government, being in tome Places almost wholly precarious, or depending on the Charity of the Gaoler, and in many others, quite insufficienl for the buftananec of Life.

That the derm of imprisonment is, in many Instances, longer than can be useful either for Reformation or Example.

That the Means of Employment which should be provided for those who are sentenced to Hatd Labour are, if not altogether neg’ccled. generally unprofitable to the Public, anti in other Respects ill-chosen; the Accommodations for this Purpose being ini efficient in many of the Pi if ns, and it being quite impracticable to provide them in others.

That the good Effects both of fditary Confinement, and of conllrained Habits of Industry, have been proved to your Committee in many Infiances-, but that in fotne of the P:iions the Convicted are mixed with the A ecu fed, the Guilty with those who are to be presumed Innocent, the Ft Urns with tee Debtors, the Males with the Females; and the Convicted are often permitted to l’uffer long Imprilbnments in total Idle-ness.

In short, your Committee mud observe. That the whole Arrangement of the Prisons lb far as they are informed, is, at present, ill-iuited, either to the Oeco-rotny of the State, or the Morality of ti e People, and lccm> to be chiefly calculated fer the safe CuHotly of the Persons confined, without due Attention to the.r Health, Employment, or Reformation.

Under the Second Head of Enqu'ry, concerning the Execution and Effects of the Act of Parliament, which authorizes the Confinement and Hard Labour of transportable Offenders aboard Vessels in the River Thames, your Committee observe.

That the said Act, which was a temporary Expedient, intended only for the most daring and dangerous Offenders who n.ult otherwise have been crouded in Dungeons, or let looie again into Society, has been extended to several Criminals, who from their bodily Infirmities, from their extreme Youth, or their advanced Age, as also from the Nature of their Crimes, might have been more properly subjected to some other Mode of Punishment.

That the Mortality on Board the said Vessels may be attributed, in fume Degree, to the very disordered Conditutions to which the Profligacy of Criminals ex-poics them, and appears, in many Indances, to be occasioned bj an extreme Dej ection of Spirits, observable in all Prisons, bur more common and fatal in the Hulks, and most frequently afiefting Convicts from the Country; but chiefly arises from the epidemical Fevers, to which all Places, where the Freshness and

Vol. 37.

Aprilis. 313

Purity of the Air is destroyed by human Breath, are liable, and most especially Vessels indituted to collect the Refuse of the several Gaols of the Kingdom.

That the Mortality has been encreased by the Number of Convicts being too great for the Space allowed; by the Effluvia from the Sick; by the Contiguity of the Beds; by a Want of Cleanliness, which is extremely difficult to be enforced; and perhaps too by Ionic Circumstances in the Food, which might be better regulated.

That the Labour done appears to be of solid Advantage to the Public, and may be edimated at rathef more than One Third of the whole Annual Expence.

That the Execution of the said Aid appears to have received continual Improvements from its first Inditu-tion and that Farther beneficial Alterations may be made in it, in case it shall be thought proper to be prolonged as a Mode of Punishment; particularly, that it may be expedient, exclusive of providing against the Inconveniences to which your Committee have already alluded, to shorten the Term of Imprisonment, which is at present fora Period not exceeding Ten Years, nor less than Three Years, but which might better be. limited to a Term not exceeding Five Years, nor less than One.

That the Operaiions of this Aid should be redrided to Criminals convicted before the Judges of Gaol Delivery.

That it seems expedient to have fbme Place separate from the Vessels, to receive the Sick, in diflind and airy Cabins, or Apartments, if it should be thought adviseable to have the Hospital on Shore, according to the Nature and Degree of their Disease; and also to have a separate Veiled to lodge Felons on their first Arrival, in order to prevent their introducing the Gaol Didemper from the different Prisons.

That a large Piece of Ground should be inclosed for a Garden, by which the Health of many would be preserved, by a constant and ample Supply of fresh Vegetables; and in the Cultivation cf which, such Frions, who by Indisposition may be rendered incapable of severer Labour, may be profitably employee!, and in which those who are recovering from Sickness and from whom there is no Danger of Infection, and such others, as by their good and orderly Behaviour may be entitled to Indulgence, should at Times be permitted to walk.

That a Clergyman should attend to perform Divine Service on Sundays, and great Fedivals, and to bury the Dead.

That if it should be thought proper to continue the present Mode of executing this Law by Contract, it will be highly expedient that some Officer or Magistrate have Authority to visit and inspect the Hulks, and make a Report, from Time to Time, respecting the Management and Conduct of the Superintendant, and the due Execution of the Contract, to such Court or Person as may be appointed to receive it; and your Committee take this Occasion to observe, that such Inspector might be employed to Advantage in carefully examining oilier Places of Confinement.

That as the Separation of ill-disposed Persons, as far as is practicable, conduces both to Reformation end Health, and as it is expedient to avoid the Expence of very distant Removals, it seems adviseable to authorize the employing of Convicts in other navigable Rivers, and also in the Repairs of Sea Ports, in Embankments, in other public Works, and in Garrisons.

It further appears to your Committee, That the Clause in the said Act of Parliament, which directs the Justices of the Peace throughout to prepare

proper Places for the Reception of Offenders adjudged to Hard Labour, and to make due Provision for their Employment, Regulation, anil Government, has not engaged any competent Attention; and that in the mean Time there is a pressing Want of some adequate 4 L Provision

Provision for the Class of Convids heretofore liable to Transportation, and which, by very accurate Returns, may be estimated at near One thousand Annually.

That Iclitary Confinement, corporal Punishment, duly limited, and privately inflicted, Sobriety, well regulated Labour, and Instiudion, seem to be the belt Correctives for a considerable Part of the last-mcn-tioned Number, especially the Female Convicts, and such Males as from their Age, Infirmities, or the flight Nature of their Crimes are improper Objects for any severer Punishment.

That it may be expedient to make the Experiment, in the first Iuftance, by establishing Two Houses only, One for each Sex, within the Home Circuit, upon the Plan of a Bill, to this Purpose, though to a much greater Extent, submitted last Year to the Consideration of Parliament; in which House the Mode of Punishment may be proportioned to the Enormity of the Offence, and the Convicts may be properly lepa-rated and classed, according to their Crimes and Behaviour, in order to their being employed in such Labour as may be best luited to their respective Capacities, and most advantageous to the Public.

/hat Works and Manufactures should be cholen, in which a competent Knowledge may be acquired with little Application, and to which no Apprenticeship is necessary; in which many may be kept to Labour by the Supervision of few j and in which it is difficult to embezzle the Materials: such, for Example, as the sawing of Stone, the making of Cordage, or picking of Oakum; and, in order to induce such Convicts to work with Diligence and Alacrity, that it may be adviseable to allow them a certain Part of their Earnings for their own Use.

That although the immediate Advantages to be expected from such an Establishment will principally operate within the District where it is situated, your Committee hope that the Attention shewn by Parliament to this important ObjcCl of Police, and the alarming Evils with which the Community is threatened, from the Practice of crowding in incommodious Gaols great Numbers of filthy, idle; and abandoned Criminals, will raile a general Spirit of Reformation, and excite the Vigilance of Magistrates throughout the whole Kingdom, and that they will exert themselves in improving and enlarging their several Bridewells, for the Reception of infirm Convicts, and Females sentenced to Imprisonment and Labour; and to facilitate this Objcd, it will be expedient to give them further Powers to raise the Sums necessary, and make such Bye-Laws and Regulations, with the Content and Approbation of the Judges of Assize, as may be requisite for these faiu-tary Purposes.

And it being incumbent upon us to prevent, as much as possible, the spreading of that infectious and fatal Disorder, The Gaol Fever, which your Committee are

concerned to find has been communicated to the unhappy Persons on board the Hulks by Felons from various Gaols, it is expedient that a House be likewise provided in an airy Situation, to serve as a for the Reception of such ConviCls as may be discharged from the Vessels and Prisons, either by the Expiration of the Term of their Confinement, or conditionally, and may afterwards be inlisted in the Land or Sea Forces, in order that they may be properly cleanled and clothed, and the State of their Health examined, and ascertained by a Certificate from the in-speding Surgeon, before they are permitted to go to the Ship or Regiment in which they may be destined to serve.

That, as many very young Persons, by the Impulle of uncontrouled Passions, and from evil Habits, which naturally prevail where no Attention has been piid to th ir Education, are driven to the Commission of petty Offences, and as such unfortunate and defected Boys

seem peculiarly entitled to the Commiseration of Government, it is highly expedient, in order to reicue them from evil Communication and the contagious Society of Prisons, that a Power should be vetted in Two or more Magiftr?tes, to release any Youth under the Age of Fifteen, who may be brought before ti.^rn and accused of a Misdemeanor, or Petty Larceny j such Youth, with the Approbation of the Pr fecutor, having consented to serve in the Land Forces, in the East or (Vejl Indies, or in the Navy, for the Term of Three Years or upwards.

And, in order to prevent, as far as possible, those Convids, who may hereafter be discharged from the Vessels, and other Places of Confinement, from returning to their vicious Courses through the Want of Employment, it seems expedient, in Addition to the salutary Provision of Clothing, and Money, allowed by the present Act, to veil a Power in Two Magistrates, upon a Certificate of good Behaviour from the Superintendant of the respective Places of Confinement, to remit One Sixth Part of the Term of Imprisonment of any Convict, on Condition that a reputable Tradesman will agree to employ the Person so discharged, and give Security f>r his good Behaviour, for One Year; and those who may be f. i end lei's, should be entituled to the same Indulgence, provided that they will bind themselves for One Year to such Labour as shall be allotted to them, and comply with the Regulations prescribed.

Under the Third Head of Enquiry, which respects the Acts relative to Tranlbortation, and the Pradica-

k '

bility of recurring to that Mode of Punishment, your Committee observe,

That it is not in the Power of the executive Government at present to dispose of convicted Felons in North America, and that every other Plan of Transportation, hitherto suggested, appears to be attended with many Difficulties

That the fending atrocious Criminals to unhealthy Places, where their Labour may be used, and l heir Lives hazarded, in the Place of better Citizens, may in some Cafes be adviseable; and in the Instance of Capital Relpites is indifpmably just.

That the Plan of establishing a Colony or Colonies of young Convids in some dillant Part of the Globe, and in new-discovered Countries', where the Climate is healthy, and the Means of Support attainable, is equally agreeable to the D.daies of Humanity and (bund Policy, and might prove in the Refuk advantageous both to Navigation and Commerce.

That as the Laws respecting Transoortation are at present restrided, it is not in the Power of the executive Government to acLpt and pursue any new Syf-tem of Transportation.

Your Committee having thus gone through every Matter that was referred to their Considerati jn, came to the following Resolutions:

Refo/ved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That some Alteration should be made in the Li.vs receding the Maintenance and Employment of co i-vided Felons, confined by Sentence of Imprisonment, or by Sentence of Imprisonment and Hard Labour, in different Places within England.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it might be of Public Utility, if the Laws which now direct and authorize the Transportation ot certain Convids to His Majesty’s Colonies and Plantat oris in North America, were made to authorize the same to any other Part of the Globe that may be found expedient.

was Panted the House, and read; taking Notice of the Bill to enable Persons to exercise the Trades of Bakers and Butchers, although they shall not have been brought up as Apprentices in the said Trades; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners have served regular Apprenticeships to the Trade of a Baker for the Term of Seven Years, and have been at great Expence and Labour before they could receive any Benefit from their Trade, and there are now many Apprentices to the same Trade, who are obliged to lerve the respective Terms for which they are bound; and that it will be a very great Hardship upon the Petitioners, and all others who have served regular Apprenticeships, if Persons are allowed to exercise the Trade of a Baker without having first served regular Apprenticeships thereto; and that, there being an Art or Mystery in making Bread, the Petitioners conceive that the enabling Persons to exercise the Trade, who have not served an Apprenticeship thereto, may tend to introduce bad Bread, and prevent the Public from having so good a Commodity as is in general allowed they now have; and that B;ead is at prel'cnt the only Article in this Country on which the Dealer is not allowed to let his own Price, and to regulate the same according to the Expence and Trouble he is at in cirrying on his Bufi-nels; and the Petitioners apprehend, no Benefit can arii'e to the Public by passing the present B;ll, so far as it relates to Bikers: And therefore praying, that so much of the fit id Bill as relates to the Petitioners may not pals into a Law.

A Petition of several Persons, residing in and near the Towns of Hertford, fV and in the Counties of Hertford and Essex, interested in and using the Navigation of the River Lee, on behalf of them-fclres and others, residing in and near the said Towns, and using the said Navigation, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That a Bill is depending in the House for preserving the said Navigation, and for Relief of the Annuitants and other Creditors under Two Acts of Parliament, of the Twelfth Year of his late Majesty, and the Seventh Year of His present Majesty, for improving the Navigation of the said River, whereby it is proposed, that some additional Rates and Duties fhoaSd be laid upon all Goods conveyed upon the said River, for preserving the Navigation thereof, which additional Rates and Duties are to decrease in certain Proportions mentioned in the said Bill; and that the Petitioners find, that a Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, hath been presented to the House, wherein they object to any Increase of the present Rates and Duties; and allege, that, if the same had been regularly collected, the Navigation might have been earned on without any Increase thereof; and they charge the Trustees with Irregularity and Misconduct in the Execution^ their Trust, and submit to the Consideration of the House, whether, for the Realons given in their Petition the said Navigation ought to remain under the Controul of the same Trustees'; and that the Petitioners are much surprized at the Contents of the said Petition of the City of London, as the Lord Mayor, Court of Aldermen, and Recorder, of the said City, are, by the said Act of the Seventh Year of His present Majesty, appointed Trustees for the Care of the said Navigation; and the Petitioners apprehend, it was their Duty, as Trustees, to have attended the Meetings, and prevended any Misconduct and Mismanagement in the Proceedings of the Trustees, and which they might eafiiy have done, as full One Half of the Meetings of the said T. uftecs, fmee the passing of the said Act, where holden in or near the City of London; and that, at the Pune the said Act of the Seventh Year of His present Mijvfty was obtained, Engineers were employed to make Estimates of the Expence attending the 'making

and completing the said Navigation, and such Rate* and Duties were then laid as were tuppoled sufficient for carrying the Ad into Execution; but the Ex;>ence of completing the said Navigation hath greatly exceeded the said Estimates, and the present lutes and Duties have been found insufficient for the Purposts intended by the said Act; and that the Petitioners are very materially interested in the Preservation of the said Navigation, as they pay about Five Sixth Parts of the whole Rates and Duties collected upon the said Rive-; but, in order to preserve the said Navigation, and for the Relief of the present Annuitants and other Creditors, the Petitioners are willing to pay the proposed additional Rates and Duties, which, they apprehend, will occasion little or no Increase in the Price of Fr.ight, as the same will not exceed, on an Average, One Ha.foenny per Ton per Mile upon the G kkIs, Wares, and Merchandizes, conveyed upon the said River; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that the Charges made against the said Trustees by the City of London in their Petition, is done with a View to get the foie Cont roul and Management of the said Navigation into their own Hands; but the Petitioners hope that, as the Works are ah finished, and the Navigation completed, and found to be of great Benefit to the Country, the Controul and Management thereof will not be taken out of the Hands of the present Trustees, as they are all Gentlemen of considerable Property in the Counties through which the same pafles, and are equally interested with the Petitioners in the Prolperity of the Navigation: And the e-fore praying. That the said Bill may pass into a Law, and that such additional Rates and Duties may bev granted for preserving the said Navigation, and for Relief of the present Annuitants and other Creditors, as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be ref rred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the Bid for preserving the Navigation of the River Lee, in the Counties of Hertford, Essex, and Middlesex; and for Relief of the Creditors under Two Acts of Parliament. of the Twelfth Year of his late Majesty, and of the Seventh Year of His present Majesty, relating to the Navigation of the said River, is committed.

joaU to whom the Petition of several of His Majesty’s Justices of the Peace for the County of , and of several Freeholders and Inhabitants whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred;That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Tabic: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. I’/illiam Ford-Janies, Deputy Clerk of the Peace for the County of Pembroke, being examined, said, That the Common Goal belonging to the said County, situate at Haverford IVis too small, and very inconvenient for the Purposes intended; and that the same has of late Years become so ancient and ruinous, that it has been presented by the Justices of Assize, and Fines have been ordered to be levied upon the County, for Want of the same being put into a proper State — That the Situation of the present Goal is low and unhealthy, and the same is too confined; and that he thinks it is absolutely necessary that a new Goal and House of Correction should be built, in a more commodious and healthy Place, which will be of great Public Utility.

A Member present confirmed the above Evidence.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for building a new Goal and House of Correction for the County of Pembroke: And that Mr. Owen of Pembroke and Mr. Rice do prepare, and bring in the fame.

The Lord Midleton reported from the Committee, That they had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be now received.

The Lord Midleton accordingly reported from the said Committee, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That George Lord Pigot, a Member of this House, was, on the 24th day of August 1776, arrested by a Military Force and carried and confined, under a Military Force, at the House of Major Horne, at a Place called The Mount, about Nine Miles distant from the Town of Madrass and Fort St. George, of which he was Governor and Commander in Chief j and that the said George Lord Pigot continued in confinement under a Military Force for upwards of Eight Months, that is, from the 24th day of August 1776, until the 11th Day of May following, when he died.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That George Stratton, Henry Brooke, Charier Floyer, Archdale Palmer, Francis Jturdan, and George Mackay, Esquires, did, on the 23d Day of August 1776, form themselves into a Council, and did confer the Command of the Army and the Garrison of Fort Saint George on Colonel James Stuart, ordering him to arrest the Person of George Lord Pigot, their Governor and Commander in Chief, and to put the Fort, Garrison, and Fort House, under their Command.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Court of Directors of the East India Company have, by Letters of the 4th of July 1777, and of the 23d of December 1778, to their Presidency at Madrass, ordered, that Courts Martial should be held for the Trial of Colonel James Stuart, Colonel Edingtoun, Major Horne, and Captain Lsfaught, for having arrested and confined, under a Military Force, their Governor and Commander in Chief, George Lord Pigot.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an humble Address be pielented to His Majesty, praying His Majesty, that He would be graciously pleased to give Directions to His Attorney General, to prosecute George Stratton, Henry Erode, Charles Floyer, and George Mackay, Esquires, lor ordering their Governor and Commander in Chief, George Lord Pigot, to be arrested and confined under a Military Force; they being returned to England, and now within the Jurisdiction of His Majesty’s Courts of Hall.

The Three First Resolutions of the Committee being severalty read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by thf House.

The subsequent Resolution of the Committee, being

That the Petitioners apprehend, there are several Clauses and Provisions contained in the said Bill, which, if passed into a Law, will be very hurtful to them and others, and very injurious to their Property and Rights: And therefore praying. That they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against such Parts of the said Bill as may affect their Property, or that they may have such other Relief as to the House shall leeni meet.

A PETITION of the Bakers and Butchers of a, u

Prejloti, in the County of Lancajur, was pre- !

fented to the House, and read; taking Notice of the !

Bill to enable Persons to exercise the Trades of Bakers 1

and Butchers, although they shall not have been brought.

up as Apprentices in the said Trades; and Setting forth.

That the Petitioners think it incumbent on them to appeal a.gainst lb partial a Bill passing into a Law, which they conceive would be a very great Injury to the Bakers and Butchers in general; and that, as to the Bakers, they are already under the Regulations of an "

Assize, and can only have such Profits as the Magistrate thinks proper to allow them, which is not the same in any other Trade, and as the Butchers can have none but Lads of the Age of 13 or 14 Years, and their being bound for less than Seven Years, with the Expence of finding them Meat, Drink, Walbing, and Lodging, would greatly hurt their Trade, the Petitioners therefore hope the House will take their Calc into Consideration, and not fufier, a Bill, lb detrimental to their Trades, to pals into a Law. Ditto. =

A Petition of the several Persons whose Hands are thereunto let and subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and the rest of the Bakers within the City and Liberty of Wejminjrer, and Parts adjacent, was also presented to the House, and read; likewise taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, That, should the same pass.into a Law, the Petitioners apprehend it will be extremely prejudicial to the Bakers, and the Public in general, the Trade of a Baker being mostly carried on with the Assistance of Apprentices, and the Public deriving by that Means not only a great Benefit in the placing out of poor Apprentices, who might otherwise be destitute, but also in being supplied with so neceflury an Article as Bread upon more reaibo-able Terms than can be expected, should the Bakers be under the Necessity of employing Journeymen inliead of Apprentices; and that a very great Number of Apprentices are now taken in the Trade, who become Journeymen or Master Bakers at the Expiration of their Time, which makes the Trade very numerous, creates a Rivalfiiip among them, and tends to keep down the Price of Bread; but, should the said Bill pals into a ’

Law, the Petitioners fear that Apprentices will r.ot be induced to engage in the Trade; that the Expence to the Baker in employing Journeymen mull consequently be increased, and the Price of Bread raised; and as the Number of Hands in the Trade will gradually diminish for Want of a regular Supply by Apprentices, a Monopoly may in future take Place, to the great Inconvenience of the Public; and that the Profits of a Baker are less than almost in any other Trade, notwithstanding their being obliged to attend constantly to their Bufinds both Day and Night, and the Allowance of the Magistrate is the tame now as it has been for Years part, although y

the necessary F.xpences of their Trade are more than doubly increased, whereby the Bakers in general are become very poor and Indigent: And therefore praying the House will take their same into Consideration, and grant them such Relief, against those Parts of the Bill which affect the Petitioners, as to the House shall seem meet.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Lid Bill is committed.

the above Proceedings, it appeared, that in some of the Almanacks published by the Complainants, under such their pretended exclusive Authority, not only many ab-lurd, erroneous, but even many useless, immoral, and very indecent Pafidges, were introduced, which ought to be strictiy guarded against and avoided in every Work calculated for general Use and Knowledge; which Absurdities, Errors, and Indecencies, the said Complainants have fhemselves been more attentive to avoid since the Petitioner detested them by the afore-f*id Means; whereby the Petitioner has been greatly rnftrumental in rendering Almanacks in general more useful, by being more correct than they were heretofore, and, by exposing such Absurdities and Indecencies, will most likely be the Means of abolishing the fame, and of introducing in the room of it Matter of public Information and Utility; and that the Petitioner observes, by the Votes of the House, that a Bill is ordered to be brought in, to veil the foie Right of printing Almanacks, in that Part of Great Britain called England, in the Two Universities of Oxford and

Cambridge, and the Company of Stationers of the City of London, respectively; and that such Bill, if it should pass into a Law, will preclude the Petitioner from the Privilege which he has been so long, and at so great Expence contending for, and to which, by the aforesaid Determination, he is now entitled, and would tend to create a new Monopoly in the Two Universities, and the said Company of Stationers, destructive to the Object which the Petitioner has, with lb great Expence and Trouble, been labouring to effect, viz. the making Almanacks of more Utility than those formerly under the Monopoly of the Stationers Company, which cannot be otherwise than by leaving the Trade open, which will consequently create an Emulation in the different Publishers to attain the greatest Degree of Correftnels; whereas such Monopoly, being established, would tend, as formerly, to discourage Science, be a disgrace to Literature, and will moreover essentially injure and lessen the Revenue, by reducing the Number of Stamps, which will otherwise be required in a free Sale: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law; and that the Petitioner may be heard, by his Counsel, against the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill to veil the foie Right of printing Almanacks, in that Part of Great Britain called England, in the Two Universities of Oxford and Cambridge, and the Company of Stationers of the City of , respectively, be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioner be then heard, by his Counsel, against the said Bill, upon his Petition, if he thinks fit.

A Petition of Elizabeth , Widow, Grace , Widow, and William Jones and Mary his Wife, La*, dies and Lord of the Manor of Allerton, otherwise AL rington, in the County of Som and of several other Persons entitled to Right of Common on a certain Common, or Trade of Commonable Land, called, or known by the Name of Stone Allerton in the

Hamlet or Vill of Stone Allerton^ in the County of Somerset, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, was pre-fehted to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners have perused a Bill depending in the House for inclosing the said Common, in which it is alleged, that Katherine Yorke, Spinster, is Lady of the Manor of Weave, in the County of Somerset, and as such entitled to the driving, chacing, and other Royalties, of the said Moor, which the Petitioners, the said Elizabeth Gate, Grace Little, and William Jones and Mary his Wife, apprehend properly belong to them; and, exclusive of the Right belonging to which Manor, they are also possessed of Estates in the said Vill of Stone Allerton, to which Right of Common in the said Moor belongs; and that the said Bill appoints Five Commissioners for executing the feme; and, the said Common containing no more than about 95 Acres, the Petitioners are of Opinion, the Expences of the Inclosure, which are to be defrayed by a Sole of as much of the said Common as may be necessary, will be so great, that the Land remaining to be allotted to the Petitioners and others, after the Deduction for Roads, and Compenfetions for Manorial Rights, are made, will befo inconsiderable as to be by no Means a Recompence for the Right of Common they now enjoy on the said Moor; and the Petitioners apprehend no Benefit can arise to any of the Parties interested in the said Common by the Inclosure thereof: And therefore praying. That they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from tbr Committee, to whom the Bill for dividing and inclosing the Comj mon, or Tract of Commonable Land, called or known by the Name of Stone Allerton Moor, in the Hamlet or Vill of Stone Allerton, in the County of Somerset, is committed: And that the Petitioners be then heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

The other Order of the Day being read;

And the said Report was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petitions.

John Long being examined, said. That he is a Framework Knitter, and lives at That he has

been above Nineteen Years in the Business — That he is a good Workman — That Workmen could then earn, about Two Shillings and a Penny a Day; but that at this Time a good Workman cannot earn more than is. 7 d.out of which he has to pay Three Pence a Day for Frame Rent, and about Three Pence more for Winding, Seaming, Needles, and Candles — That Numbers of Workmen cannot earn so much, and that a Man must work from Six in the Morning till Ten at Night to earn 1 j. yd. — That Provisions are now incrcaled in Price full One Third — That the same Articles were manu-fastured 19 Years ago as now — That he thinks the Decrease of Workmen’s Wages to be owing to the Mailers refusing to give any more — That in the Course of the Time he has known the Trade, the Matters have in One Instance reduced the Price of Work is. a Dozen — The Value of a Frame is about Six or Seven Pounds, and he pays if. 6 d.a Week Rent for One, whether he has any work or not — That he has been obliged to pay Frame Rent although his.Master has not given him Work, and in Gale of illness he is obliged to pay Frame Rent — When Work is given, it takes up some Time to prepare the Materials for the Loom — That a Matter will not employ a Man who has a Frame of his own; they oblige the Persons they employ to hire a Frame of them, otherwise they will not employ them — That the Workmen are in a starving Condition, and are obliged to submit to the Matters Terms — That Framework Knitting is a difficult Manufacture, and cannot be thoroughly learnt in 20 Years — That several Hollers in Tewkesbury compel the Men to buy the Materials

Wright Hawley being examined, said, That he is a Framework Knitter; he lives at Nottingham, and has been in the Business about 35 Years — That he wotks in the Silk Way, and could not earn above is.a Day 20 Years ago, working from Seven in the Morning till Nine or Ten at Night, and that he can now earn about 18 or 2or/, a Day clear, working the same Hours — That the Price of Provi lions is increased One Third — That Journeymen j>ay 1/. 3d. per Week Frame Rent — That Silk Frames cost about £. 7 at this Time — That they pay Frame Rent for the Week, though they stand idle for Want of Stuff — That they pay Half Frame Rent the Three Holiday Weeks in the Year — That he has been out of Work a Week and some odd Days since , for

Want of Work from his Mailer, but was obliged to pay Frame Rent — That there are many Hollers at Nottingham who have Hinted their Men lrom making more than Three Pair of Hole per Week, at 2 per Pair, and some at 2J. tlVough the Men could have made Four Pair in a Week — That there are Silk Hose marked at 30 Silk, for which the Workman it only paid 28 Silk, which makes a Difference of is a Pair to the Workman — That the Masters exact from the Workmen, Work of a finer Quality, paying the Price for an inferior Quality — That about 600 Frames were unemployed at Nottingham about a Month or Six Weeks ago — Twenty Years ago they were all employed — That there has not been many Frames made within the last 13 Years.

John Rogers being examined, said. That he is a Framework Knitter, and lives in London; he has worked at Nottingham and Leicester, and has been in the Trade 23 Years — That Frame Rent is is. a Week in London, whether he works or not — That he has frequently been delayed in hi* Work Two or Three Hours at a Time, for Want of Stuff — That the Value of a Frame is about Seven or Eight Pounds; he has known Four Frames fold, within this Three Months, for 12. for. Two of which now let out at per Week — That it costs the Workman from $d. to 8 per Week, at the lead, for Needles, Candles, and Fire.

Mr. Edward Luck being examined, said. That he is a Framework Knitter, and lives at Godalming — That he has known the Trade ever since the Year 1725 — That the Prices for Work are not so high at present as when he first knew the Trade — In some Articles the Price is reduced Three Pence a Pair, and in the higher-jjriced Sort Sixpence — That a good Workman at Go-dalming cannot earn more than 6s. 6d. a Week clear, upon an Average; they Work 12 or 13 Hours a Day-Frame Rent is i$d.and some at is. per Week — That the Price of Provisions is in many Articles very near double — That a good Workman, who has Two Children, cannot live by the Trade, and many at Godalming receive Alms of the Parish, which he knows by transading the Parish Accounts — He has not worked at the Trade 14 or 15 Years, and he has known many good Hands leave the Trade because of the reduced Price of Work — That some have left the Trade for Want of Work, but more on Account of the reduced Prices.

John Clark being examined, laid, That he is a Framework Knitter, and lives at Derby — That he has known the Trade ever since the Year 1753 — That the Prices were then higher than now in some Articles, particularly in the finer Sorts; a good Workman can clear about 6s. 6 d.per Week — That he cannot earn more Umself, with working 13 Hours a Day — That they pay

That certain Rivers therein named, and all other Waters in the County of Lancaster, are put in Defence from Michaelmas Day to the Purification of our Lady; that is, from the 29th of September to the Second of February.

And all'o, an Act, made in the First Year of the Reign of King George the First, for the better Preservation of Salmon within several Rivers within that Part of this Kingdom called; whereby it appears, That no Person shall kill Salmon between the last Day of July and the rath of November in any Year, within the Counties of Southampton and;

and it also appears by the feme Act, that no Salmon shall be fallen or destroyed in the River Severn, and other Rivers therein particularly mentioned, between the last Day of July and the Twelfth Day of November.

And also, an Act, made in the Thirty-third Year of the Reign of his Majesty King George the Second, for pun idling Persons who shall take or fell any Spawn, Brood, or Fry of Fish, unfizable Fish, or Fish out of Season $ whereby it appears, That all Fish taken out of Season, may be seized by any Person or Persons; and on Proof made thereof before any Jiiftke of the Peace, the feme shall be forfeited, and delivered to the Person or Persons who shall seize the feme, and shall prosecute to Conviction any such Offender; and every such Offender shall besides forfeit and pay for every such Offence the Sum of Twenty Shillings,

Your Committee then proceeded to examine Edward Waters; who informed your Committee, That he lives at Tredunmck, and has been a Fisherman many Years — That he remembers the Fiftiery of the River Ujknear Fifty Years, in which he was constantly employed — That he always began to fiffi on Candlmas Day m every Year, and continued fishing till Saint Andrew’s Day j that is, from the Thirteenth of February to the Eleventh of December — That the Fish do not (pawn much in the U/h till the Month of January, and are in very good- Season till Saint Andrew’s Day — That he was never interrupted in fishing during that Time, and never heard of any Law to prohibit filking in that River according to such ancient Custom — That Salmon ought not to be killed in some Part of the Year; and he thinks the best Time to prevent Persons fishing, in order to preserve and increase the Breed of Fish, would be the Months of December, January, and Part of February — That the Salmon in that River are in as good Season, and as fit for Sale, in the Months of September, October, and November, as they are at any other Time of the Year; and that if any Restriction took Place to prevent killing of Salmon during those Months, it would be a great Lose to all the Owners of Fisheries in that River — That there are Three Fisheries in the River, which are private Property — and that there is One Weir, of about Two Yards in Height from the Bottom of the River, which he thinks does not hurt the River.

Richard Davis being then examined, informed your Committee, That he lives at , in Monmouth-

shire — That lie remembers the Salmon Fisheries in the River Ujk Thirty Years; and always understood trie Times and Seasons for taking Salmon there to have been such as is before mentioned by the former Witness« — That he thinks the Salmon in that River are in as good Season during the Months of September, October, and November, as they are at any other Time of the Year, and that they catch the greatest Quantity in the River Ujk at that Time; and he thinks that if there was any Restriction upon the taking Salmon during those Months, it would be extremely prejudicial to every Owner of the Fisheries in that River.

That the arbitrary Excrcilc of the Power of making honorary Freemen, vested in the Corporations of many Cities and Borough Towns, is a great Infringement of the Freedom of Election therein, and, if not prevented or retrained by the Interpolation of the Legislature, will, it is much to be feared, prove totally destructive of the lame; and that the Petitioners and their Ancestors have experienced the evil Effects of this Power in the Corporation of the said City, who, on Occasion of contested Elections, have grossly abused it; and that the said Act of the Third Year of His present Majesty appears not to be a sufficient Prevention of the Abuse of this Power, in as much as that the said Corporations, knowing the State and Number of Voters in their respective Cities and Boroughs, and ever making the Extension of their Influence the first Obj .‘ft of their Care, can and do continue to exercise this arbitrary Power with notorious Partiality, and for the direct Purpose of acquiring to , themselves a superior Interest at Elections, to the great Prejudice of the Citizens and Burgesses free of their respective Cities and Boroughs by Birth or Servitude, and in manifetl Violation of the Rights of Election, of which the House has shewn itself, on all Occasions, the firm Support: And therefore praying. That Provision may be made in the said Bill, for excluding all honorary Freemen, and others than such as are Free by Birth or Servitude, from voting at the Election of Members to serve in Parliament for Cities and Boroughs, and that the said Bill may pals into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the said Bill be read a Second Time.

Sir Herbert Mackworth reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of James Berkeithout, of Great Rufjel Street, in the County of *.v.Gentleman,

in Behalf of himself and of Thomas Clark, of the Town of Leeds, in the County of Dyer, was

A State of the Matter of Fast. contained in the said Petition is as follows:

Mr James Berkenhout being examined, laid, He had been between Five and Six Years employed in finding out and bringing to Perfection a Method of dying Linen and Cotton of Crimson and Scarlet Colours, and that for Two Years and an Half past he had been alfifted by Mr. Thomas Clark, of Leeds — That in prosecuting this Discovery, he had been at great Expences, arising from the high Price of Cochineal, the numerous Disappointments attending his various Experiments, and several Journies he had taken in the Prosecutioa of his Design. And, having produced to your Committee several Specimens of Linen and Cotton, dyed according to his Method,

Mr. David Davis, a ManchWarehouseman, was

called; who examined a Piece of Fustian produced by Mr. Berkenhout, and declared it to be a very good Scarlet, which Colour has never yet been known to succeed on that Article; he likewise examined some-Cotton Velvets of the same Colour, and, upon comparing those dyed according to Mr. s Me-

thod, with others also produced to your Committee, he said. He thought Mr. Berkenhout'% infinitely superior in Colour to any he ever law before — And being shewn Specimens of the same Goods dyed Green and Yellow, he declared them to be equally superior to any others he had seen.

Mr. Berkenhout then produced to your Committee, several Specimens of Cotton Yarn, and Linen, dyed Scarlet and Crimson. And,

Mr. William Chalontr, a Linen Draper, being examined, said, That Scarlet and Crimson are Colours in Linen hitherto unknown to the Trade — That he had examined the Specimens produced by Mr. and that they were in gcneial very good Colours.

Mr. Berkenhout then produced to your Committee, a Book published at Paris, under the Inspection of the Academy of Sciences there, in which it is said, that the Dying Materials which give a Scarlet Colour to Wool, do not give the same Colour‘to Silk, and none at all to Cotton.

Mr. Berkenhout also laid before your Committee, a Copy of a Memorial from the Board of . Trade to His Majesty (which is hereunto annexed) recommending his Discovery; and likewise a Certificate from the Committee of Trade at Manchester (also hereunto annexed) in its Favour; together with a Certificate from Two Chemists, Dr. William Saunders and Mr. Ambrcfe -frey (also hereunto annexed) which ftafes, that several Articles of Cotton, dyed Scarlet and Crimson, by Mr. Berkenhout, had undergone all the usual chemical Pro-

To the King's most Excellent Majesty.

May it please Your Majesty.

Wc have had under our Consideration the Memorial of Thomas Clark, of Leeds, Dyer, and James -

/tout, of Tottenham Street, Saint , Gentleman, Setting forth, That upon a general Idea of a considerable Premium having been offered by Government, for dying Scarlet on Cotton, they have applied them-(elves for several Years in order to obtain the said Premium; and after great labour and Study, and very considerable Expence, have not only accomplished the lame, but have produced a Crimson equal to that Colour on Silk; an Art long fought for in vain throughout Europe; and have likewise found out a superior

Method of dying Cotton in general; and therefore praying for Inch a Reward from the Public as the Importance of the Discovery shall seem to Merit: Whereupon we btg Leave humbly to rcpresent to your Majesty.

That we have been attended by Mr. Berken hout, who has exhibited to us Samples of Cotton Yarn, of a Scarlet and crimson Dye, accompanied with a Paper; Copy of which is hereunto annexed, signed by Seven of the Committee of Trade and Manufactures at

Chester, certifying the Advantage which may result to the Manufactures of this Kingdom from the above Discovery, if the said Colours will answer the Account given of them by the Memorialists; and upon our requiring some Proof of th- Permanency of the Colours thus produced, by a Process known only to the Memorialists, we have received the Certificates hereunto also annexed, signed by Dr. William , Teacher

of Chemistry, and, Mr. Ambrose , an eminent

Chcmift of this Cit\, purporting, tlat from the usual Experiments in the;e Calls, the Samples ot Cotton dyed in Scarier and Crimson, by the Method discovered by the Memorialists, appear to be true grained Colours. Under theil* Circumstances, we think, that as this Discovery may be of great Importance, by improving and extending the Manufacture of Cottons, the same is such as merits the public Attention; and we are therefore humbly of Opinion, that it would be adviieable to induce the Memorialists to communicate the said Discovciy, by such pecuniary Compensation from the Public as shall be judged adequate to its Merit.

.Which is most humbly submitted.

A Petition of the Bailiff, Aldermen, and Capital Burgesses, of the Borough of New Radnor, in Behalf of them leiVes and the rest of the Burgesses of the said Borough, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners observe by the Votes, that a Bill is intended to be brought into Parliament, to prevent the great Abuse which prevails in many Corporations, of making Honorary Freemen, for the corrupt and avowed Purpose of influencing the Election of Members to lerve in Parliament; and repre-lenting to the House, that the Petitioners (whole col-leftive Body consists of a Bailiff, Two Aldermen, and Twenty-five Capiral Burgesses, of which the Bailiff and Aldermen are Three) are, by their Charter, expressly confined, in the Choice of Common or Free Burgesses, to such Persons who are bona fide redding and inhabiting within the said Borough; and that there are Foup Contributary Boroughs belonging to the Capital Borough of New Radnor, the Burgesses of whom claim a Right of voting in the Election of a Ileprefcnta-tive for the salt! Borough; and that the Method of electing Burgesses belonging to the said Contributary Boroughs, is by a Presentment of the Jury at their Courts Leet; but that fuel) Preferments, instead of being confined to Persons residing within the said Boroughs, have been extended to a moll alarming Length, inso much that several Hundred Persons have been presented at One Court, the Majority of whom have not only never seen the Borough of which they have become Members, but very many not even residing within the County, or having any Connection with it; and that, previous to the late General Election, and with a View of entirely destroying the Rights and Privileges of the Petitioners, no Ids than upwards of Seven hundred Persons were, at different Courts Leet, presented by the Jury, as proper Persons to be sworn Burgesses of the Borough of Rayader, One of the aforesaid Contributary Boroughs; and that, in Consequence of such Presentments, upwards of Four hundred and Twenty-six Persons were sworn into their respective Offices, Seventeen only of whom appear to be lefident within, or to have any Connection with, the said Borough; and the Petitioners think it a Duty they owe to themselves, and the rest of their Fellow Butgeffes, to mention to the House, that another of the said Contributary Boroughs was purchased at a Public Auction, in Consequence of the following Advertisement, dated the 22d Day of September 1776:

" To be sold by Auction, on Friday the') Yearly Value " 17th Day of October 1776, the Borough and Lordship of Keveulleece,

" with a Court Leet, and a Right of) 000 " mak;ng Burgesses to vote at an " Election for a Burgess to serve in " Parliament for the Borough of Radnor-," A

the Petitioners therefore throw themselves for Redrels upon the Wisdom of the House, hoping that, as the Borough of New Radnor now is, the several Contributary ones in future may be, confined in the Election of their Burgesses to such Persons only who are resident within their several Boroughs, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Eames and Mr. Pechell:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for building a new Gaol and House ot Correction for the County of Pembroke; without any Amendment:

And also,

A Petition of the Burgesses and Freemen of the Bo- OccaConal rough of Derby, in the County of Derby, was presented Freemen, to the House, and Tead; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Bill is intended to be brought into Parliament, to prevent the great Abuse which prevails in many Corporations of making Honorary Freemen, for the corrupt and avowed Purpose of influencing the Election of Members to serve in Parliament; and for representing to the House. that great Numbers of Freemen of this Description have been lately made in the lard Borough, which the Petitioners conceive to be an Abuse of the Power exercised by the Corporation, and to be subversive of the Petitioners Rights and Privileges; and that the Petitioners do not wish, by this Application, to lessen the Number of Electorsj and they should be glad to see the Right of Election in tine Laid Borough as extensive as puffible, provided it was fairly done, and the Freedom of the Borough given to Persons residing in, and having a natural Connexion with, the Borough; but, if a Stop is not speedily put to the present Practice, the Election of Members to serve' in Parliament for the Borough of Derby, vyill be made by Persons who live at a Distance, and are total Strangers to the Place; the Petitioners therefore look up with great Deferrence to the collective Body of the liepresentatives of the People, as the natural and constitutional Guardians of the Rights of Election, and resort to them for Protection, hoping that the House will protect them in the Enjoyment of those Rights and Privileges which they pr their Ancestors have justly earned:

And therefore praying, That the intended Bill may pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill to explain, amend, and render more effectual, An Act, made in the Third-Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act to prevent occasional Freemen from voting at Elections of " Members to serve in Parliament for Cities and Boroughs," be read a Second Time.

of the ill Effects of the Power of making Honorary Freemen, vested in the Petitioners, and charging them with exercising that Power for the direct Purpose of acquiring a superior Interest at Elections, to the Prejudice of the Citizens, and in Violation of the Righc of Election; and that the Petitioners, finding themselves much injured by so unjust a Charge, beg Leave to repel the fame, and to allure the House, that, for ' upwards of Fifty Years pall, no Honorary Freemen have been made of the said City for the Occasional Purposes of Election, though many Election Contests have happened during that Time; but the Petitioners apprehending that a Right of cleding Freemen being vested in them by Charter, they admit, that the Mayor' of the said City hath, Annually, at going out of his.
