Mr. Ord, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty; the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an additional Stamp Duty of Twenty Shillings be laid upon every Skin or Piece of Vellum, or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which any Probate of a Will, or Letters of Administration, for any Estate, of or above the Value of One hundred Pounds, shall be ingrafted, written, or printed, and a further additional Duty of Twenty Shillings where the Estate is of or above the Value of Three hundred Pounds, over and above all other Duties now charged thereon.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an additional Stamp Duty of one Penny be paid for every Skin or Piece of Vellum, or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which is ingrossed or written the Copy of any Will.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an additional Stamp Duty of Six Pence be paid for every Skin or Piece of Vellum, or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which is ingrossed or written any Libel, Alligation, Deposition, or Inventory, exhibited in any Ecclesiastical Court, the Courts of Admiralty, and Cinque Ports, and Copies thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an additional Stamp Duty of Five Shillings be laid upon every Piece of Vellum, cr Parchment, upon which any Writ of Covenant for levying Fines shall be ingrossed or written.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an additional Stamp Duty of Five Shillings be laid upon every Piece of Vellum, or Parchment, upon which any Writ of Entry for suffering a Common Recovery shall be ingrossed or written.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an additional Stamp Duty of Five Shillings be paid for every Skin of Vellum, or Parchment, upon which is ingrossed or written any Exemplification, of what Nature soever, that shall pass the Seal of any Court what foe ver.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an additional Stamp Duty of Forty Shillings be laid upon every Skin or Piece of Vellum, or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which any Presentation or Donation which shall pass the Great Seal, or upon which any Collation to be made by any Archbishop, or other Bishop, or any Presentation or Donation to be made by any Patron whatsoever, of or to any Benefice, Dignity, or Spiritual or Ecclesiastical Promotion whatsoever, shall be ingrossed or written, provided such Benefice, Dignity, or Promotion, shall be of the Yearly Value of Ten Pounds, or above, in the King’s Books.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an additional Stamp Duty of Forty Shillings be laid upon every Skin or Piece of Vellum, or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which any Dispensation to hold Two Ecclesiastical Dignities or Benefices, or both a Dignity and a Benefice, or any other Dispensation or Faculty, from the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, or the Master of the Faculties for the Time being, shall be ingrossed or written.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Additional Stamp Duty of Eight Pence be laid upon every Skin or Piece of Vellum, or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which shall be ingrossed, written, or printed, any Certificate or Debenture, for drawing back any Customs or Duties, or any

GEORGE R.

His Majesty, rdying on the experienced Zeal and Affection of His faithful Commons, and considering that, in this critical Conjuncture, Emergencies may arise, which may be of the utmost Importance, and be attended with the most dangerous Consequences, if proper Means should not be immediately applied to prevent or defeat them, is desirous, that this House will enable Him to defray any extraordinary Expences incurred, or to be incurred, on Account of Military Services, for the Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-nine, and to take all such Measures as the Exigency of Affairs may require.

A Petition of John Mors Ellis, Esquire, One of the Four Counsel of the ancient Court of the Marshalsea, and of the Palace Court, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner purchased his said Office for a considerable Sum of Money, and has a Freehold in his Office, which is highly rated to the Land Tax, inso much that the Petitioner has paid thereto almost the Fifth Part of his Annual Fees; and for his said Freehold is intituled to a Vote for Represen-tatives in Parliament for the County of Surrey -, and that the Petitioner has peruled a Bill depending in the House to explain and amend an Act to prevent frivolous and vexatious Arrests, which, if passed into a Law, will take from the Petitioner his laid Freehold; and that the Petitioner held his said Office with a Confidence in Parliament as an additional Security, because those Acts of Parliament, which diminished the Coun-fel’s Fees in the Petitioner’s Court, gave them a specific Satisfaction for the Injury received; and that, if the House shall determine it is for the Benefit of the Public that the said Bill should pass into a Law, the Petitioner trusts they will not take his laid Freehold, or any Part thereof, from him, without giving him a Consideration for the fame, or making him Satisfaction to the Extent of the Injury received: And therefore praying, That he may be heard, by himself or Coun-fel, against the said Bill’s passing into a Law.

the House, and read; Setting forth. That, by ancient and immemorial Wage, confirmed by various Charters of His Majesty's Predecessors, there have been held within the City of London Courts, called the Sheriff’s Courts, wherein the Citizens and Inhabitants of the said City may have their Causes determined, at a small Expence, by Juries of their Fellow Citizens, which Courts are held Four Days in the Week for that Purpose; and that it is the Practice of the said Courts to issue Bailable Processes in all Causes where the Demand is above Forty Shillings, from which easy and expeditious Mode of Trial great Advantages have arilen to the Citizens and Inhabitants of the said City, in the Recovering of Small Debts; and that the Petitioners hold Offices in the said Courts, which they have purchased for large Sums of Money, the Emoluments of which are uncertain, and arile wholly from the established Fees of the said Courts, the Petitioners having no Salaries; and that the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Bill is depending, to explain and amend an Act, passed in the Twelfth Year of King George the First, intituled, "An " Act to prevent frivolous and vexatious Arrests," and, by such Amendment, to restrain Arrests in any inferior Court for any Sum under £.; and the Petitioners are well convinced, that, if the said Bill should pass into a I.aw, it will subject the Trading Part of the City of London in general to many Delays and Inconveniences in the Recovery of Small Debts, as well as diminish the Credit indispensably necessary to great Numbers of the inferior Class of People, and will also occasion a grievous Loss to the Petitioners and others, by diminishing, if not annihilating, the long established and moderate Fees of their Offices: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant them such Relief as may appear just and reasonable, and that they may be heard, by themselves dr Counsel, against the said Bill, so far as the same may affect the Rights and Jurisdictions of the City of don, or the several Courts of Law therein established.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered. to lie upon the Table, until the Bill to explain and amend an Act, made in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of King George the First, intituled, "An Act to prevent frivolous and vexatious Arrests," be read the Third Time; and the Petitioners are to be then heard, by themselves, or Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petitions, if they think fit.

Ordered, That the said Bill be read the Third Time Tomorrow Morning, if the said Bill shall be then ingrossed.

Sir Herbert Mackworthreported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of John Dawes of Canonbury-House, in the County of , Esquire, on

Behalf ofhimself and others, Owners, Proprietors, and Lessees, of Copper and Lead Mines, in the Isle of glfey, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Thomas Williams being examined, said, That there are several considerable Mines of Copper and Lead in the Isle of Anglesey, the Ore of which is in general, near the

Surface; and that about Forty thousand Tons have been taken up within the last Two Years — That the Mines are cli(covered to a great Extent, and appear at present almost inexhaustible ;but that there is no Coal, or other Fuel, in the Ille, proper for the Purpose of ftnelting the Ores — That Coats brought into the Ille pay a Duty of Five Shillings -per Chaldron besides Custom-House Vol. 37.

Jump 431

Fees, which amount to near Two Shillings and Six Pence a Chaldron more, exclusive of Freight.

That no Ore is smelted in the Isle, but is obliged to be carried to Bristol, Swansea, N, Warrington, and

Liverpool; and that above Ten thousand Tons have been smelted at the above Places, the Expence of which exceededj£. 3,000.

That the Freight of the Ore to Swansea, and

Neath, is Ten Shillings and Ten Shillings and Six Pence a Ton, and to the other Places about Five Shillings.

That above Fifteen thousand Tons remain on the'

Banks of the Mines unfmelted; and that the Ore is of an inferior Quality, and contains a great Quantity of Sulphur and Dross, which consequently increases the Expence of Carriage.

That a much greater Quantity of Ore might be linelted upon the Spot, if Coals could be had free from Duty; but that it would not be worth the Proprietors while to pay the Duty on Coals for ftnelting the Ore at the Mines;

and that none has been smelted there, nor any Duty paid at the Custom House on Coals used for that Pur* pose.

And the Witness further said, That if a Drawback of the Duties was allowed on Coals used for smelting Ore in the Me of Anglesey, great Quantities cotild be smelted there, which would be of great Advantage to the Proprietors, contribute to the Employment of the Poor Anglesey, and prove beneficial to the Public in general.

Then an Act, made in the Ninth Year of the Reign of her Majesty Queen Ann, intituled, "An Act for " reviving, continuing, and appropriating, certain Du-

ties upon several Commodities to be exported, and " certain Duties upon Coals to be waterborne and canried Coastwise; and for granting further Duties upon " Candles, for Thirty-two Years; to raise Fifteen hundred thousand Pounds, by way of a Lottery, for the " Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and " Eleven, and for suppreiEng such unlawful Lotteries,

" and such Insurance Offices, as are therein mentioned," was read; by which it appeared, that a Drawback of the Duties was allowed on Coals used for smelting Copper and Tin Ores in the Counties of Cornwall, and Devon.

Then an Act, made in the Fourteenth Year of the Reign of His late Majesty King George, the Second, intituled, "An Act for granting to His Majesty the Sum " of One Million out of the Sinking Fund, and for applying other Sums therein mentioned, for the Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and " Forty one; and for allowing a Drawback of the Duties upon Coals used in Fire Engines for draining " Tin and Copper Mines in the county of;

" and for appropriating the Supplies granted in this " Session of Parliament; and for making forth Duplicates of Exchequer Bills, Lottery Tickets, and Orders,

" loft, burnt, or otherwise destroyed; and for giving " further Time for the Payment of Duties omitted to be " paid for the Indentures and Contrafts of Clerks and " Apprentices," was read; by which it also appeared, that a Drawback was allowed on all Coals used in Fire Engines, for draining the Tin and Copper Mines in the County of Cornwall,

W«y» Mr. Ord, according to Order, reported from the and Committee of the whole House, to whom it was re-Mcani. ferre<j> to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty; the Resolutions which the Committee bad directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followed); viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards ruling the Supply granted to His Majesty, there be issued and applied the Sum of Two million Seventy-one thousand Eight hundred and Fifty-four Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Eight Pence Halfpenny, out of such Monies as have arisen, or shall or may arise, of the Surplusses, Excesses, or Overplus Monies, and other Revenues, compoGng the Fund commonly called The Sinking Fund.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Sum of One million Five hundred thousand Pounds be raised by Loans or Exchequer Bills, to be charged upon the First Aids to be granted in the next Session of Parliament; and such Exchequer Bills, if not discharged, with Interest thereupon, on or before the Fifth Day of April One thousand Seven hundred and Eighty, to be exchanged and received in Payment in such Manner as Exchequer Bills have usually been exchanged and received in Payment.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards railing the Supply granted to His Majesty, the further Sum of One million Nine hundred thousand Pounds be raised by Loans or Exchequer Bills, to be charged upon the First Aids to be granted in the next Session of Parliament; and such Exchequer Bills, if not discharged, with Interest thereupon, on or before the Fifth Day of April One thousand Seven hundred and Eighty, to be exchanged and received in Payment in such Manner as Exchequer Bills have usually been exchanged and received in Payment.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards railing the Supply granted to His Majesty, there be applied the Sum of Two thousand Seven hundred Sixty-three Pounds and One Shilling, remaining in the Receipt of the Exchequer on the Fifth Day of April One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-nine, subject to the Disposition of Parliament, exdu-iive of the Surplus Monies then remaining of the Sinking Fund.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That such of the Monies as shall be paid into the Receipt of the Exchequer, after the Fifth Day of April One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-nine, and on or before the Fifth Day of April One thousand Seven hundred and Eighty, of the Produce of the Duties charged by Two Acts, made in the Fifth and Fourteenth Years of His present Majesty's Reign, upon the Importation and Exportation of Gum Senega and Gum Arabic, be applied towards making good the Supply granted to His Majesty.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Vexation* A Petition of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, Trades-Arre.ls. men, Householders, and Shopkeepers, residing in the several Parishes within the City and Liberties of West-mn/ier, and in the several Parishes in the Counties of Midd'.ejex, Effete, Surrey, Kent, and Hertford, within the Didrift and Jurisdiction of the inferior Courts of Record, within the said Counties, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, from Motives of Neccfiity and Humanity, are induced to give Credit to Manufactures, and the lower Kind of Tradesmen, and their Families, in order to fuwiifh those, who cannot possibly have Ready Money at all Times, with the common Necessaries of Life, and without which Credit such Persons muff either starve with their Families, or become burthensome to the Parishes to which they belong; and that the Petitioners have been induced to give such Credit, not altogether upon a Confidence of the good Principles of the Debtor, but upon the Security which Credit in general receives from the established Laws of this Country; and that the Debts in general contrafted with the Petitioners, are in Sums amounting to Forty Shillings and upwards, and seldom to /. 10, for Lodgings, Cloaihs and Victuals, Medicines, Attendances in Sickness, and all other common Necessaries; and that the Petitioners have always been faci-1.tated and greatly secured in their. Demands, by the bailable Process of the inferior Courts of Record, by the cheap and expeditious Manner in which they proceed in thDie Courts for Creditors who are compelled to take such Methods to obtain Payment of their Demands; but the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Bill is depending, to explain and amend an Act, passed in the Twelfth Year of King George the First, intituled, "An Act to prevent frivolous and vexatious " Arrclls," and, by such Amendments, to restrain Arrests in any inferior Court, for any Sum under /. 10, which, if passed into a Law, will be very injurious to the Petitioners, and totally destroy the Credit to Persons of the Descriptions already mentioned, who are exceedingly numerous, and (land in need of Credit, and such Persons can easily evade the common Process of inferior Courts, whose Jurisdictions are limited, by removing themselves out of the Jurisdiction of such Courts after Judgment, in which same no Execution of such Court can be executed; and the Petitioners have many of them fatally experienced, that the Process of the superior Courts is so expensive, that a Creditor cannot obtain Judgment and Execution for a Debt under/. 10,

without being the greatest Part of the Money out of Pocket: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, and that such Amendments may be made thereto, as may effectually fee u re Public Credit, or that the Petitioners may be relieved, in respect of the said Bill, in such a Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie unon the *

Table, until the Bill to explain and amend an. Act made in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of King George the First, intituled, "An Act; to prevent frivolous and " vexatious Arrests,’* be read the Third Time.

449

That in the Progress of their Enquiry, much important Matter has appeared respecting the deliberative and the executive Conduct of the War; that the Part of the Examination immediately before them promises Discoveries into many other Objects that it may be highly essential to lay before His Majesty, in order to enable His Majesty to form a just Judgment upon past Measures, and to assist His future Councils:

That an Interruption in their Proceeding, at the present Crisis, would not only defeat these great and necessary Purposes, but also would be subversive of the Justice due to Characters of Persons in great Office among His Majesty’s confidential Servants, and others of High Rank in His Army, which (land at present committed by contradictory Evidence in Matter of Opinion, and by obscure, because imperfect. Evidence, in Matter of Fact;

For these Reasons, and others, that are but too dif-jjoftly pointed out by the Exigencies of the Time, they humbly implore His Majesty, not to prorogue the Parliament before the present Enquiry shall be finished; and they beg leave to assure His Majesty, that they will chearfully forego all Consideration of the private Benefits and Comforts of a Recess, to prosecute a Duty highly conducive to the public Satisfaction, and in the Course of which Lights may be received of the utenoft Importance to the Policy, if not to the Salvation, of the State:

GEORGE

Papers

ref;*ft:ng the War with Spain*

1.9 Geq. III. 170 453

GEORG £ R,

The Ambassador of the King of Spain having delivered a Paper to Lord Viscount and signi-

fied that be has received Orders from his Court immediately to withdraw from this Country; His Majesty has judged »t necessary to direct a Copy of that Paper to be laid before the House of Commons, as a Matter of the highest Importance to His Crown and People» and His Majesty acquaints them, at the same Time, that He has found Himself obliged, in Consequence of this hostile. Declaration* to recall His Ambassador from frjadrid.

His Majesty declares, in the most solemn Manner, that His Ddire to preserve and to cultivate Peace and friendly Intercourse with the Court of Spain, has been uniform and sincere; and that His Conduct toward? that Power has been guided by no other Motives or Principles than those of good Faith, Honour, and Justice: And His Majesty lees, with the greater Surprize, the Pretences on which this Declaration is grounded, as tome of the Grievances enumerated in that Paper have never come to the Knowledge of His Majesty, either by Reprdentation on the Part of the Catholic King, or by Intelligence from any other Quarter; and, in all those Cafes where Applications have been received, the Matter of Complaint has been treated with the utmost Attention, and put into a Course of Enquiry and Re-dress.

His Majesty has the firmest Confidence* that His faithful Commons will, with that Zeal and public Spirit whiduHe has so often experienced, support His Majesty ni His Resolutiou to exert all the Power and all the Resources of the Nation to refill: and repel any hostile Attempts of the Court of and that, by the Bkffing of God on the Rectitude of His Intentions and the Equity of His Cause, His Majesty will be able to withstand and to defeat the unjust and dangerous En-terprizes of His Enemies against the Honour of His Crown, and the Commerce, the Rights, and the Common Interests of all His Subjects.

Copy of a Paper delivered to Lord Viscount Weymouth, by Marquis d' Almodovar, the 16th 1779; and Transiation.

And the Titles of the said Copy and Transiation were read.

And the find Transiation was a!so read.

The laid Copy is preferred amongst the other Papers of tins SifTion; and the said Transiation is as followeth; viz.

All the World has been Witness to the noble Impartially of the King, in the Midst of the Disputes of the Court of London with its American Colonies and with France. Ik Tides which. His Majesty having learned that His powerful Mediation was detired, generously made an Offer of it, which was accepted by the Belligerent Powers; and for this Motive only, a ship of War was lent on the Part of His Britannic Majesty to one of the Ports of Spain. The King has taken the most energetic Steps, and such as ought to have produced the most EtFecft, to bring these Powers to an Accommodation, equally honourable to both Parties; proposing for this End, wife Expedients for smoothing Difficulties, and preventing the Calamities of War: But, although His Majesty’s Propolltions and particularly tho'e of his matum, have been conformable to those which at other Times the Court of London it Tell bad appeared to judge proper for an Accommodation, and which were also quite as moderate, they have been rejected in a Manner that fully proves the little Desire which the Ca-

binet has to restore Peace to Eand to preserve the King’s Friendship. In Effect, the Conduct of that Ca-

Vol. 37.

binet, with regard to His Majesty, during the whole Course of tire Negociation, has had for its Object to prolong it for more than Eight Months, either by vain Pretences, or by Anftvers, which could not be more in?-conclusive; whilst in this Interval the Insults on the Spanish Flag, and the Violation of the King’s Territories, were carried on to an incredible Excels. — -Prizes have been made. Ships have been searched and plundered, a great Number of them have been fired upon, which have beeq obliged to defend themselves; the Registers have been opened and torn in Pieces, and even the Packets of the Court found on board the King’s Packet Boats,

The Dominions of the Crown in America have been threatened, and they have gone to the dreadful Extremity of railing the Indian Nations, called the , Che-

roquies, and Chicacbas, against the innocent Inhabitants of Louisiana; who would have been the Victims of the

Rage of thele Barbarians, if the Chatcas themselves had not repented, and revealed all that the Seduction of the EngHJh had planned. — The Sovereignty of His Majesty in the Province of Darien3 and on the Coast of St. Bias, has been usurped; the Governor of Jamaica having granted to a Rebel Indian, the Commission of Captain General of those Provinces. — In short, the Territory of the Bay of Honduras; has been recently violated, by exercising Acts of Hostility, and other Excesses, against the Spaniards;who have been imprisoned; and

whole Houses have been invaded: Besides which, the Court of Londont has hitherto neglected to accomplish, what the 16th Article of the laftTreaty of Paris ftipu-lated, relative to that Coast.

Grievances so numerous, so weighiy, and recent, have been at different Times the Object of Complaints, made in the King’s Name, and ilated in Memorials which were delivered, either to the British Ministers at London, or transmitted to them through the Channel of the EngHJh Am ballad or at Madrid; But although the Answers which were received have been friendly, His Majesty has hitherto obtained no other Satisfaction, than to see the Insults repeated; which lately have amounted to the Number of One hundred.

The King, proceeding with the Sincerity and Candour which characterize him, has formally declared to the Court of London, from the Commencement of its Disputes with France, that the Conduct of England should be the Rule of that which Spain would hold.

His Majesty likewise declared to that Court, that at the Time their Differences with that of Paris might be accommodated, it would be absolutely necessary to regulate those which had arisen, or might still arile, with Spain iand in the Plan of Mediation which was sent to

the underwritten Ambassador the 28th of last September, and which was by him delivered to the British Mini-ftry in the Beginning of October (a Plan of which Lord

Grantham was apprized, and of which he received a Copy)

His Majesty declared, in positive Terms, to the Belligerent Powers, that, in Consideration of the Insults which his fuhjects and Dominions had suffered, and likewise of the attempts levelled against His Rights,

He should be under the Necessity of taking His Party, in case either the Negociation, instead of being continued with Sincerity, should be broken off*, or should produce no EffeCf.

The Causes of Complaint given by the Court of London not having ceased, and that Court shewing no Disposition to give Reparation for them, the King has resolved, and orders His Ambassador to declare, that the Honour of His Crown, the Protection which He owes to His Subjects, and His own personal Dignity, do not permit Him to fuller their Infufts to continue, and to neglect any longer the Reparation of those already received; and that, in this View, notwithstanding the pacific Dispositions of His Majesty, and even the particular Inclination He has always had and expressed for cultivating the Friendship of His Britannic Majesty,

5 Z He

454

He finds Himself in the disagreeable Necessity of Making use of all the Means which the Almighty has intruded him with, to obtain that Justice which He has solicited by so many Ways without being able to acquire. In confiding on the Justice of His Cause, His Majesty hopes, that the Consequences of this Resolution will not be imputed to Him, before God or Man; and that other Nations will form a Suitable Idea of this Resolution, by comparing it to the Conduct which they themselves have experienced on the Part of the British Ministry.

London, 16 June 1779.

The King’s Speech.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

The many great and’ essential Services you have rendered to Me and to your Country, during the Course of your long Attendance in Parliament, demand My most . cordial Thanks.

I have seen with entire Approbation the Zeal you1 have manifested for the Support and Prosecution of the just, and necessary War in which I am engaged* nor am I less sensible of your Attention to the present State of My Kingdom of Ireland, My paternal Affection for all My People makes Me sincerely anxious for the Happiness and Prosperity of every Part of My Dominions.

Hitherto the Events of War have afforded the Court of France no Reason to triumph on the Consequences of their Injustice and Breach of public Faith; and I trust that by a spirited and prosperous Exertion of the Force you have put into My Hands; that ambitious Power may be brought td wifti that they had hot, with- ' out Provocation, or Cause of Complaint, insulted the Honour and invaded the Rights of My Crown.

I have already acquainted you with the hostile Step which has been , lately taken by the Court of Spain. Whatever Colour may be attempted to be put upon that unjust Proceeding, I am conscious that I have nothing to reproach myself with: It has been followed by the clearest Demonfttations of the Loyalty arid Affection of My Parliament to My Person add Government, for which I repeat to you My Warm eft Thanks; and I consider it as a happy Omen of the SifcCefs of My Arms, that the Encrease of Difficulties serves only toaugrhent . the Courage and Constancy of the Nation, and to’animate and unite My People in: the Defence of their Country, and of every Thing that is dear to them.

The advanced Sealon or the Year requires that I-should afford' yOu feme Recess'from public Business; and I do it with the less Reluctance.'as, by the Powers vested in Me by Law,’ I can have the Aid of your Advice and Assistance within Fourteen Days, should any Emergency'make‘it necessary for Me to convene you before the usual Time. ‘ " '

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I meet you in Parliament at a Time when we are called upon by every Principle of Duty, and every Consideration of imereft, to exert Our united Efforts in the Support and Defence of Our Country, attacked by an unjust and unprovoked War, and contending with one of die most dangerous Confederacies that ever was formed against the Crown and People'of Great Britain..... .7 *- .

'"iThe Designs and" Attempts of our Enemies to invade this Kingdom, have, by the Blessing of Providence, been hitherto frustrated and disappointed. They stili menace Us with great Armaments and Preparations; but We are, I trust, on our Part, well prepared to meet every'Attack, an3 to repel every Insult. I know the Clutafter of My brave People: The Menaces of their Enemies, and the Approach of Danger, have no other effect on their Minds, but to animate their Courage, and to call forth that National Spirit, which has so often checked, and defeated, the Projects of Ambition and Injustice, and enabled the Fleets and

Armies to protect their own Country, to vindicate their pwn Rights, and at the same Time to uphold, and pre-lerve, the Liberties of Europe, from the restless and encroaching Power of the House of Bourbon.

In the Mid ft of My Care and Solicitude for the Safety and Welfare of this Country, I have not been inattentive to the State of My loyal and faithful Kingdom of Ireland. 1 have, in Consequence of your Addresses, presented to Me in the last Session, ordered such Papers to be collected and laid before you, as may assist your Deliberations on this important Business; and I recommend it to you to cOrtfider what further Benefits and Advantages may be extended to that Kingdom, by such Regulations, and such Methods, as may, most effectually, promote the Com most Strength, Wealth, and Interests of all my Dominions.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

The proper Estimates shall, in due Time, be laid before you. I fee, with extreme Concern, that the necessary Establishments of My Naval and Military Forces, and the various Services and Operations of the ensuing Year, mud inevitably be attended with great and heavy Expences; but I rely on your Wilclom and public Spirit, ‘for such Supplies as the Circumstances and Exigencies of Our Affairs shall be found to require.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I have great Satisfaction in renewing the Assurances of My entire Approbation of the good Conduct and Difeipline of the Militia, and of their Heady Perle-verance in their Duty; and I return My cordial Thanks to all Ranks of My Loyal Subjects who have Hood forth in this arduous Conjuncture, and, by their Zeal, their Influence, and their Personal Service, hath given Confidence 'as well as Strength to the National Defence. Trolling in the Divine Providence, and in the Justice of My Cause, I am firmly resolved to prosecute the War with Vigour, and to make every Exertion in order to compel Our Enemies to listen to equitable Terms of Peace and Accommodation.

To allure His Majesty, that we are truly sensible that, in the present arduous Situation of Affairs, we are called upon by every Principle and every Sentiment of Duty to His Majesty, and to those we represent, to exert, and to unite, our utmost Efforts in the Support and Defence of our Country against: a most unjust War, and one of the most dangerous Confederacies that was ever formed against: the Crown and People of Great Britain:

’That we fee and revere the Goodness of Divine Providence, in fruftraiing and disappointing the Designs of ©ur Enemies to invade this Kingdom; and whenever they attempt to carry their Menaces into Execution, we. trust.that their Attacks will be repelled, and their Enterprizfc defeated, by the Blessing of the same Provi-ao

Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That, where this House shall judge any Petition touching Elections to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person had procured himself to be elected or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person,

Resolved, That, it shall appear that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence, the same is declared to be a High Crime and Misdemeanor; and this Houfo will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Perfoti hath given false Evidence, in any Case, before this Houfo, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

appointed Yesterday to draw up an Address to be presented to His Majesty, That the Committee had drawn up an Address accordingly j which they had directed Aim to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read, and is as followeth; viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, Your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects. the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament a!Tembled> beg Leave to return Your Majesty the Thanks of this House, for Your most Gracious Speech from the Throne.

Wc are truly sensible that, in the present arduous Situation of Affairs, we are called upon by every Principle and every Sentiment of Duty to Your Majesty, and to those we represent, to exert, and to unite, our utmost Efforts in the Support and Defence of our Country against a moll unjull War, and one of the

mod dangerous Confederacies that was ever formed against the Crown and People of Great Britain.

We fee and revere the Goodness of Divine Providence, in frustrating and dilappointing the peligns of our Enemies to invade this Kingdom; and whenever they attempt to cany their Menaces into Execution, we trull that their Attacks will be repelled, and their Ln-terprize defeated, by the Blessing of the same Providence on the Valour and Intrepidity of Your Majesty’s Fleets and Armies; and that Your Majesty’s gracious and endearing Declaration, of Your Confidence in the Character and Courage of Your People, will be jollified by the most convincing Proofs that they are still animated by the same Ardour, and the fume Spirit, that have in former Times carried this Nation through so many Difficulties and Dangers, and have so often enabled their Ancellors to profest their Country and all its Dominions, and to save not only their own Rights, but the Liberties of other Free States, from the restless Ambition and encroaching Power of the House of Bourbon.

We acknowledge, with Thankfulnefe, Your Majesty’s Goodness and Attention to the Address of this House, respecting Your loyal and faithful Kingdom of Ireland, in being pleased to order such Papers to be communicated to this House, as may alii ft our Deliberations on this important Business: And we beg Leave to allure Your Majesty, that we will not fail to take into out Consideration, what further Benefits and Advantages may be extended to that Kingdom, by such Regulations, and such Methods, as may most effectually promote the common Strength, Wealth, and Imcrcils of all Your Dominions.

Permit us, Sir, to return our humble Thanks to Your Majesty, for the gracious Manner in which Your Majesty renews and confirms Your intire Approbation of the good Couduft and Heady Discipline of the National Militia; and to allure Your Majesty, that we concur most sincerely with Your Majesty, in acknowledging and applauding the meritorious Zeal and Services of those loyal Subjects who flood forth in the Hour of Danger, and who have added Confluence as well as Strength to the National Defence.

Your Majesty’s faithful Commons receive with Gratitude, and take a sincere Part in Your Majesty’s paternal Expressions of Concern, that the various and extensive Services and Operations of the entuing Year mud unavoidably be attended with great and heavy Expences: Yet, when it is considered how much the Commerce, the Prosperity, and the Safety, of Great Britain depend on the Issue of this Contest, we doubt not that such powerful Confederations and Motives will induce all Your Majesty’s Subjects to sustain, with Chearfulness and Magnanimity, whatever Burthens shall be found necessary for railing such Supplies as may enable Your Majesty to prosecute the War with Vigour and Effefl, and to make every Exertion in order to compel Your Enemies to listen to equitable Terms of Peace and Accommodation.

The said Address being read a Second Time;

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Committee in the said .-vdJrefs, to be presented to His Majesty.

Gentlemen,

I receive with the greatest and most cordial Satisfaction, this very loyal and affectionate Address; and I return you My particular Thanks for it.

The Spirit and Firmness you shew, the Zeal you so seasonably express in this arduous State of Public Affairs, and the Assurances of your Attention to the important Objects I have recommended to your Deliberation, cannot fail of having the bed Effects both at Home and Abroad.

The House, according to Order, resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill for removing the ensuing Election for a Knight of the Shire for the County of Southampton, from the usual Place of polling.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Ord took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Ordered, That the deport be now received.

The Amendments following were severally proposed to be made to the Bill; viz.

Pr. 2. 1. 10. After " Southampton'* to insert " and if not otherwise provided for, will be held,"

1. 30. After " at " to insert " the Town " of New."

1. 37. After ot " to insert " New."

1. 38. After " aforesaid" to insert " and " the Adjournment of the said " County Court, if any such has " been made, and is now de-" pending, to the said City of " Winchester, or any other Place,

" shall be deemed and taken to " be legally made to the said " Town of New Alresford."

Pr. 3. 1. 4. After " of " to insert " New."

And the said Amendments were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House; and the Bill was amended at the Table accordingly.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title be, An Act for holding the ensuing Election of a Knight of the Shire for the County of Southampton, at the Town of New Alresford, in the said County.

Ordered, That Mr. Secretary at War do carry the Bill to the Lords, and desire their Concurrence.

County of Northampton, was presented to the House, Income, and read; Setting forth. A Petition of W'dliam Smith, of Lower Brook

in the County of Middlesex, Doctor of Physic, being offered to be presented to the House;

The Lord North, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth. That in consequence of a Medical Publication of the Petitioner, containing some Observations for the better Regulation of Gaols, Application was made to him by Sir Charles , Chairman of the

Westminster Committee, by Order of that Committee, to visit the Gaols and Prisons in London, Westminster, and Southwark, in order to administer proper Relief to the Sick Prisoners therein; and that the Petitioner, in consequence of such Application, attended the said Gaols and Prisons, from the 25th of March 1776, to the 10th of November 1779, with great Afiiduity, by Means whereof the Lives of many Persons have been preserved that had no other Means to procure Medical Assistance; and that the Number of Sick in the different Gaols in London, Westminster, and Southwark, that have been under the Petitioner’s Care from the 25th of March 1776 to the loth of November 1779, amounts to 1051; and that the Petitioner from Time to Time made Reports of the State of the Sick, and the Expences for Medicines, to Sir Charles Whitworth, who, highly approving of such a humane and charitable Undertaking, and of the public Utility thereof, requested the Petitioner to continue his Attention to the same till legal Relief could be procured; and at the same Time, gave the Petitioner Assurance of being indemnified, and appointed Inspecting Physician to the Gaols in London, Westminster, Southwark, and the Home Circuit, an Appointment considered by Sir Charles Whitworth, and many others, of great public Utility, and they made no Doubt, of meeting with the Approbation of the House, when the Matter was laid before the House; and that the Petitioner, in consequence of such Assurance, has accordingly ventured, at a great Expence and Loss of Time, to continue to visit the said Gaols, and administer proper Relief to sick Persons confined therein, by Means whereof an Expence has accrued to him of ,£.566. ij. for Medicines, over and above many other very considerable Expences he has been at in the Prosecution of this Business, and the Loss of Time therein; and that the Petitioner has not received any Advantage whatever, directly or in-iireftly, on a'ccount of his attending the Sick in Gaol j And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant him such Relief therein as to them shall seem meet.

A Petition of John Henderson, Esquire, eldest Son of Sir Robert Henderson, Baronet, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, at the Election for the County of Fife, held on Friday the ad Day of July, in the present Year 1779, Major General Skene and the Petitioner were the only Candidates; and that General Skene was returned, as being the Candidate elected by a Majority of the Freeholders; but the Petitioner is advised, that General Skene is, by the Statute of the Sixth of Queen Anne, Chapter the Seventh, ineligible to Parliament, because he is in Possession of an Office, or Place of Profit, under the Crown, which has been created or erected since the 85th Day of 1705; particularly, because he is in Possession of the Office of Baggage Mailer to the Forces, and of the Office, or Place of Profit, of Inspector of Roads in North Britain, for which he receives a Salary, or An-

nual Allowance, paid by Warrants from the Treasury; which Offices, or at least that of Inspector of the Roads, did not exist till many Years after the said Statute of Queen Anne-, and that, at the Meeting for Election, the Petitioner, before the Vote was put for the Choice of Member of Parliament, did publicly apprize the Freeholders present, that General Skene was ineligible for the Reasons Hated above, aikl that any Vote given to him would be thrown away; and, after the Votes had been call up, the Petitioner did enter a Protest in the Minutes of Election, that the Votes given for Major General Skene should be held to be of no avail, and that the Petitioner should be held to be duly elected, and should be returned accordingly: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to find that the Petitioner was duly elected Member for the County of Fife, and to cause £e Return to be amended accordingly.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into; Consideration upon Tuesday the ill Day of February next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

Sir Herbert Maekworth reported from the Committee; Dr. \v. Smith’s to whom the Petition of William Smith, of Lower Brook Attendance Street, in the County of Middlesex, Doctor of Physio, London

was referred; That the Committee had examined the Gaol*. Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition; and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read thC Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

A State of the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition, is as follows:

Mr. John Ridout being examined, informed your Committee, That, as an Assistant to Mr. John Cofens, an Apothecary, he had attended the several Gaols in the Cities of London and Westminster, and Borough of Southwark; and he delivered in an Account, hereunto annexed, shewing the Number of Patients in each Gaol, together with the Expence of the Medicines that had been administered to them. And added, That all these Medicines were administered under the Prescriptions, and by the Directions* of the Petitioner, Dr. Smith, and only sent to such Patients as could not afford to pay for such Medicines.

And he produced to your Committee, a Book in which the above-mentioned Prescriptions were entered; by which it appeared, that the Attendance given by the Doctor to the several Gaols, was daily. — And the Witness said, That the making up and carrying the Medicines, was his whole Employment from the 26th of March 1776, when it began, to this Time.

And he also produced to your Committee, a Book of Charges for the Medicines made up in Consequence of Dr. Smith's Prescriptions; by which it appeared, that the Expence thereof was £. 566, or thereabouts, as stated in the annexed Account.

And he further informed your Committee, That the Prices at which the Articles are charged, are the same as those charged to all Paupers; — that there were sometimes Persons relieved who were deemed capable of paying for themselves, and who having promised lo to do, their Medicines are not charged in the said Book; but that since their Release from Confinement, only One of the whole Number has paid his Bill, and that was a very inconsiderable one; — that many Persons being discharged from Confinement before their Cures were completed, had afterwards been under the Doctor’s Care, and relieved, for which also no Charge is made in the above Account; — that in some few Instances the Medicines were sent without the Doctor’s Prescription, but it was either in Cafes of extreme Danger, or when the Hour for shutting up the Gaols was near; — that at the Time when he began this Attendance, the Gaols were full, and the Prisoners very sickly, but that by the Skill, Management, and Attention of the Doctor, the Number of Patients is now much reduced- that many Chirurgical Cafes occurred, for which no Charge is made; and that Mr. Cofens has received in Discharge of Part of his Bill, only £. 50, which was paid by the Chairman of the Westminster Committee. And he concluded with saying. That the Doctor gave daily Attendance to the above Gaols, and sometimes went Twice a Day in dangerous Cafes; — that the Doctor never was sent for that he did not go; and that lie was well assured, that Dr. Smith had never received any Gratification whatever for his Trouble.

Your Committee then called the Petitioner, Doctor-Smith; who said. That in Consequence of the Publication of his Book, intituled, " A Sure Guide in Sick-

The Lord North, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up; and read; Setting forth. That in the Second Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, the said Trustees represented to Parliament, that the Sum allowed them for the Establishment and Support of the said Museum, was reduced to a Capital of /. 30,000 Reduced Bank Annuities, the Dividend of which, amounting to £. 900, was, notwithstanding their utmost Attention to the forming their Establishmenl with Frugality, greatly insufficient for that Purpose; upon which Representation they have, at sundry Times, obtained from this House, various Sums to supply the Deficiencyof their Income; which Sums, together with the Salary allotted to the King’s Librarian, yearly amounting to about £.250, have proved inefficient to defray the necessary Expences of the said Museum, and what now remains in the Hands of the Trustees, is not sufficient to defray the Expences of the current Year: And therefore praying the House to grant the Petitioners such Support, towards enabling them to carry on the Execution of the Trust reposed in them by Parliament, for the general Benefit of Learning and useful Knowledge, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Member* A Petition of thq Freeholders of the County of eligible Middlesex, was presented to the House, and read; Set-

to lerve ting forth, That your Petitioners, in Justice to them-

or Place! W selves and the Electors of Great Britain, are con-

strained to lay before this House, their Complaint of an Injury which has been offered to one of their most essential and undoubted Rights — The Minister affect* ing a Regard for the Peace and quiet of this County, on the Death of our late worthy Representative (a Pretence in which his former Conduct, in more than one Instance, had flatly contradicted) by the secret Promise of a Nominal Place to one of the Members of this House, for the Purpose of vacating his feat in Parliament, brought forward a Candidate, in direct Oppofi-tion to our declared Willies; and, by an open and avowed Refufid of the same Privilege to the Person whom we were known to have preferred, has robbed us of the Means effectually of preserving that Peace. — The Event of the Contest hath clearly shewn to Whom *5

the Credit of promoting that desirable Object is really due, and who, with Views not the most justifiabie, must truly be considered as the Enemy of our Peace, Honour, and Independence. If we have so far acqui-efeed in this Injury, as not to press our Preference to the utmost, by returning to this House the first Object of our Choice, under these Circumstances of reputed Ineligibility, it is not that we admit the Justice of his Exclusion, or the Legality of a Proceeding so conduct ed; but because Experience hath taught us not to risque the Decision of a substantial Right on a Question collaterally arising from the Subject of our Complaint; and we conceived it to be more becoming the Dignity of our Cafe, as well as more respectful to this House, to prefer a direct and formal Charge against the Minister himself. Lord North, for a wanton and arbitrary Abuse of Powers, which, if not wholly usurped, have, in this, and many other Instances of the like Nature, been exercised, to the utter Subversion of all free Election. As if the Wrong which we have sustained were not sufficient, Insult has been added to Injury; and Mr. Tuffnell, whose offer of Services to us, by his own Mode of Reasoning, could be supported only on the absolute Resignation of his former Seat, is still, and has constantly continued the legal and unimpeached Member for Beverley. By this pretended Vacancy, thus clandestinely attempted, confefiedly incompleat, and therefore not notified to the Electors in any useful Form, we have been deprived of the Exercise of a most valuable Franchise; and have been raved from becoming the Dupes of this unwarrantable Combination only by the Spirit of the Freeholders, and the Difinterestedness of the worthy Gentleman whom we have returned. In complaining of this complicated Greviance, we presume not to dispute any Prerogative which the Crown may justly exercise j but we cannot, without the highest Indignation, fee a Minister avowedly assume to himself a Right of discharging from the Service of his Constituents, any Member whom he may please to favour, and of deciding who shall offer themselves to the Electors for their Choice. It is unnecessary to observ© that the Act of the Sixth of Queen Anne was passed by Men jealous of the Power of the Crown, to preserve the Fidelity of the Representative to his Constituents; and that it is from an Abuse and Perversion of that Act, that the Power claimed by the Minister to vacate Seats in Parliament is derived. The Invasion of our Rights is direct, the Consequence arising from it plain and indisputable; if any Power on Earth can dictate to our Choice, and prescribe who shall, and who shall not, become Candidates to represent us in Parliament, we may talk of our Rights, and take a Pride in our Freedom, but, in Fact, we have none. To this Evil, at all Times intolerable, Circumstances of extreme Aggravation, in the present Instance, have been added. It is not necessary to refer to other Evidence than to the Journals of this House, to {hew the calamitous Situation to which this Country is reduced; and it requires little Proof that the Wiklom of a Parliament alone, freely chosen, and acting without Influence, can relieve us from that Situation. But so miserable is our Condition, and {o contemptuously have we been treated, that the same Person in whose Administration we have suffered Losses the most unparalleled, by preventing the Operation of this only Remedy which, under Heaven, can lave us from utter Ruin, has contributed to increai’e and perpetuate our Distress. To this House, therefore, which claims the exclusive Cognizance of all Matters affecting the Rights of the Electors of Great Britain, we appeal for Justice; and most earnestly pray and expect, that some permanent Law may be provided for the effectual Security of those Rights; that some known, certain, and equal Rule may be established, for vacating the Seats of Members chosen to represent the People in Parliament; and that an immediate and thorough Inquiry may be

instituted

ao Geo. III. io8 — 130 Decembris. 5°7

instituted into the true Cause of those Misfortunes which have reduced this once powerful and flourishing Empire to a State which Words cannot describe, and of which History affords no Example.

The House was moved, That the Resolution of this House, of the 26th Day of November last, "That it " is a high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any " Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any " County, to concern themselves in Elections of " Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament," might be read.

And the same being read accordingly;

Resolved, That it is highly criminal in any Minister or Ministers, or other Servants under the Crown of Great Britain, directly or indirectly, to use the Powers of Office in the Election of Representatives to serve in Parliament; and an Attempt at such influence will at all Times be resented by this House, as aimed at its own Honour, Dignity, and Independency, as an In-Vol. 37.

The Earl of Drogheda, according to Order, reported Trade ol from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it Ireland, was referred to take into Consideration the several Papers which were presented to the House by the Lord North, upon the lit and 8th Days of this Instant December, relating to the Trade of Ireland, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table; Where the same were read; and are as followeth;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That it is expedient to repeal so much of any of the Laws passed in Great Britain, as prohibit the Exportation from the Kingdom of Ireland, of all Woollen Manufactures whatsoever, or Manufactures made up, or mixed with, Wool or Wool Flocks.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That it is expedient to repeal so much of an Act, made in the Nineteenth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, as relates to the Exportation ol Glass, Giats Bottles, or Glass of any Denomination whatsoever, from the Kingdom of Ireland.

A Petition of several of the Commissioners appointed to put in Execution Two Afb of the Tenth and Eleventh Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, for better supplying the City of Worcester with Water, and for the better paving and lighting the said City, and for removing and preventing all Obstructions and Annoyances therein, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have proceeded to put the said Acts into Execution, but find, that, owing to the Insufficiency of the Rates which the Petitioners were impowered to collect, they have incurred a Debt of £. 9,000 and upwards, in completing the Waterworks only, so that the other good Purposes intended by the said Acts, cannot be carried into Execution, owing to such Deficiency in the Rates; and that some further Powers and Regulations are wanting, in order effectually to complete the Whole of the useful PLn of Improvement intended by the said Acts: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring' in a Bill to amend and render more effectual the said Acts, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Sixteenth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, to continue and render more effectual several Acts of Parliament for repairing the Highways leading to Highgate Gatehouse and Hampstead, and other Roads in the said Acts mentioned, in the County of Middlesex; and also to continue and render more effectual an Act to enable the respective Trustees of the Turnpike Roads leading to High-gate Gatehouse and Hampstead, and from Saint Giles's Poiatd to Kilburne, to make a new Road from the

Great Northern Road at ljlington, to the Edgeware Road near Paddington, so far as the same is by the said Act directed to be under the Care and Management of the Trustees of the said first-rnentioned Acts, and for making a Road from the said new Road, near Queen's Row, to Bagnigge; and for watching, lighting, and watering the said Roads, was read.

And your Committee having inspected the Books of Accounts and Proceedings of the said Trust, it appeared to them, that the Trustees under the said Act had granted a Lease of the Tolls to arise from the several Gates at Tottenham Court, Battle Bridge, Saint John's Street, Goswell Street, Cold Bath Fields, Holloway, Balls

Pond, the East Gate on the New Road, and the West Gate on the New Road, to John Evans, for the Term of Three Years from Michaelmas 1777, at the clear Yearly Rent of £.5,410. — And it further appeared, that at the General Monthly Meeting of the Trustees in November following, and only Six Weeks and Two Days after the Commencement of the said Lease, Mr. Winter, on Behalf of the Lessee, applied to the Trustees prefect, for a Gate at Gray's Inn Lane — -That in Consequence of this Application, the Trustees, in December, ordered that a Gate should be erected across the Road near the End of Gray's Inn Lane, and directed Tolls to be taken thereat.

And it appeared to your Committee, from the Accounts of Receipts of the said Trust, That, for Seven-, teen Weeks and Two Days preceding the Commencement of the said Lease to John Evans, that on a Medium, the Sums received at the said Cold Bath Fields Gate, amounted to £.3. 7 s.a Week; and that there was but a very trifling Variation in the Sum so received Weekly, the whole Amount of what was taken in the Four frit Weeks being £.13- antl *n the four last£. 13. is. 6 d.

Peter Swinton, Esquxre, being examined, said, That from Calculations he has made, and from the best

' 5*

Evidence he has been able to collect, several Hundred Pounds per Annum have been received at the Gate erected in Gray's Inn Lane, no Part of which hath been applied by the Trustees, either in paying off any Part of their Debt, or in repairing the Roads under tbtir Care, the Whole being given to the Lessee, although that Gate was neither erected nor had in Contemplation by the Trustees at the Time of executing the said Lease; and for which Gate the said Lessee hath not paid any additional Rent, or other Consideration whatever.

That the Gate at Cold Bath , which, on account of a pretended Diminution of the Tolls collected-there, was made the Plea, when the Lessee applied for Relief, as mentioned in the Trustees Books, was never of such Importance as to affect in any great Degree, the Value of a Lease of the whole Tolls, for, when the Receipts were at the highest, the Charges of collecting amounted to very near the Whale of the Money taken there, which had induced the Trustees for many Years to desist from employing any Collector there.

A Petition of John Batten, William John

Woodlands, and William How, was presented to the House, and read , Setting forth, That the Election of a Member to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Downton, in the County of Wilts, in the room of Thomas Duncombe, Esquire, deceased, came on the Seventeenth Day of December last, when Robert Shajto, Esquire, and the honourable Bartholomew were

the only Candidates; and that the Petitioners are Freeholders of ancient Burgages in the said Borough, and are in Right thereof entitled to vote in the Choice of Members to serve in Parliament for the said Borough; and that there was a great Majority of legal Votes in Favour of the said Robert Shajto, who was therefore duly elected, and ought as such to have been returned; but that Henry Dench, who a died as Deputy to Edward Poore, Esquire, the Returning Officer of the said Borough, behaved unfairly and partially in the Execution of his Office; and though he admitted on his Poll the Names of those who voted for the said Robe)t Shajto, yet, contrary to the Duty of his Office, he put Queries on the greatell Part of the Votes he so received, and, notwithstanding such Majority in Favour of the said Robert Shajto, thought proper, at the Clole of the Poll, to declare the said Bartholomew Bouverie duly defied, and has accordingly returned him to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, in Prejudice as well of the Petitioners as of the said Robert And there-

fore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant them such Reliei as shall upon Examination appear to be just.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Tuesday the 15 th Day of February nexr, at the same Time that the Petition of Robert Shajto, Esquire, is ordered to be taken into Consideration.

Memorandum:

In pursuance of Two Acts, made in the 10th and nth Years of His present Majesty’s Reign, to regulate the Trials of controverted Elections, or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament, the like Notices, as in the former Cafes, were lent to the Parties -, accompanied with Orders for their Attendance, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, at the Time on which the said Petitions were ordered to be taken into Consideration.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant, or Wariants, for such Persons, Papers, and Records, as shall be thought necessary by the several Parties, on the Hearing of Lhe Matter of the said Petition.

Complaint being made to the House, That the Duke of Bolton, a Peer of Parliament, had written a Letter with his own Hand, respecting the late Election of a Knight of the Shire for the County of Southampton, previous to the said Election, thereby concerning himself in the said Election, in Breach of the Privilege of this House, and in Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain;

Ordered, That it be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges, to examine the Matter of the Cud Complaint; and to report the lame, with their

- Opinion thereupon, to the House.

A Petition of several of the Trustees for putting in Execution Two several Acts of Parliament, One made in the Twency-seventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, for repairing the Road from Warwick to Halford Bridge, and from Warwick to Stratford upon Avon, in the County of Warwick, and other Roads therein mentioned; and the other made in the Twenty-eighth Year of the Reign of his said late Majesty, for repairing the Road from Stow in the Wold to Ha Bridge aforesaid, and

other Roads therein mentioned; was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, with other Trustees in the said Act named, have proceeded in the Execution of the said Acts, and have borrowed considerable Sums of Money on the Credit of the Tolls authorized to be coileded on several Parts of the said Roads, Part of which still remains due j and that the Tolls coileded upon the said Roads from Warwick to Halford Bridge, and from Warwick to Stratford upon Avon, and so much of the said Road from Stow in the Wold to Halford Bridge aforesaid, as lies between the said Halford Bridge and Paddle Brook, in the Parish of Stretton upon , in the said County, together with the Money borrowed on the Credit thereof, have been applied towards the Repairs of such Roads respectively, and great Progress hath been made therein but the said Roads cannot be effectually amended and kept in good Repair, and the Money borrowed repaid, unless the Terms of the said Acts, so far as they relate to the several last mentioned Roads, be further continued, and same additional Powers granted to the Trustees for those Purposes; and that the Petitioners apprehend the several last mentioned Roads might be better amended and kept in Repair, if the same were made a separate District, and put under the Care of separate Trustees, and if the several Clauses and Provisions necessary for repairing such Roads were reduced into and made One Act of Parliament: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for effecting the several Purposes aforesaid, by such Ways and Means, and in such Manner, as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Sir Thomas Skipwith, Sir Charles Holte, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber;

SI R John Thorold reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, and several of the Trustees appointed to put in Execution an Act, made in the Tenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for repairing and widening several " Roads leading from the Town , in the County of Lincoln," was referred j That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, of the lyrh of April 1774, relative to Turnpike Bills, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act was read: And,

Mr. Thomas Phillips, Treasurer to the Trustees for putting the said Act in Execution, produced to your Committee, a State of their Debt, to the Amount of the Sum of £.4,684; Part of which, he said, the Trustees have borrowed on the Credit ^of the Tolls and Duties by the said Act granted, and Part arises from the Interest: Money which has become due thereon being made Principal: That the First Year that the Subscribers received any Interest, they were paid only Three per Cent, and since that, no more than Two and an Half* and he has at present only £.11 in his Vot. $7.

Hands. He further said, That since the first of gufl last, the Trustees had laid out upwards of £. 200 on the Roads; and had only received for TclU£. 164:’

That the Money 1 borrowed has been applied towards repairing the said Roads, shod the several Tolls authorized to be taken, have been received and applied for the said Purpose, and keeping down the lmereft of the said Money borrowed; but there still remains a great Sum of Money due ano owing, the present Tolls and Duties being inlufhcient to pay the Principal Money and Interest, and to keep the fipd Roads in Repair.

That the great Inconveniences and Defers which occasion such Deficiency in the Tolls, arise from Two Restrictions in the said Act; the one, preventing the Trustees from erecting -any Gate within the Parish of Louth, except within One hundred Feet from the North-east End of Stanmore Hill Lane, in consequence of which Restriction, all Persons travelling from the Country, South and , South West of Louth, and who travel to the Canal, go almost Two Miles on the Road Toll-free. Which Space of Road, Mr.

Robert Hall, the Surveyor of the Roads, informed your Committee, was the most expensive Part of the Road, and cost near £. 200 a Mile making. Then;

Mr. Phillips being examined, laid, That the other Restriction is, that the Trustees have not a P-wvcr of letting up a Turnpike Gate nearer the Town of -cajile than at the North End of the Town of West Ajiiby.

And he added, That People travel Fifteen Miles -on tlus Road, paying only One Toll. And Mr. ing again examined, said. That the Materials upon many Parts of the Road were very expensive, and of a perillruble Nature, and the Advantage aiding by the Statute Duty was very ttrail. T en,

Mr. Phillips further said. That if the above-mentioned Restrictions writ- taken off, a {mail additional Toll granted, and the Term of the said Act further continued, it would add to the Security of the Creditors on the said Tolls, and the Trustees would be enabled more effectually to complete the Repair Of the said Roads, a:to the Country in general would be thereby benefited.

Sir James Douglas informed your Committee, That the Trustees appointed by the said Act, have proceeded in the Execution thereof, and have cauled the said Duty to be regularly collected; but although the same has been expended with the utmost Frugality, the Whole thereof (together with a considerable Sum of Money which has been borrowed, and dill remains due, upon the Credit of the said Act) has been applied in finishing and compleating the said Bridge only, and the Trustees have net yet been able to proceed in any of the other Works directed by the said Act to be performed; which Works would be of great Advantage to the said Town, and of public Utility; but the same cannot be done, and the Money due as aforesaid be repaid, unless the Term and Powers of the said Act be continued, there being no other Revenue belonging to the said Town.

And the Witness produced to your Committee, a Certificate of the Overseers appointed by the said Act to audit the Accounts of the Trustees; by which it appeared, that they had considered the Receipts and Disbursements vouched by the Books and Accounts of the Trustees, and the Building of the Bridge, and found that the Money had been applied as directed by the said Act, and there had been no Misapplication or Embezzlement thereof.

Committee of Privileges, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the several Complaints made to the House, upon the Tenth and Seventeenth Days of December last (that the Duke of Chandos, a Peer of Parliament, and Lord Lieutenant of the County of Southampton, had ligned several Letters with his own Hand respecting the then ensuing Election for the said County, thereby concerning himself in the said Election, in Breach of the Privilege of this House, and in Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain) together with the Refactions of the Committee thereupon; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as folio wet h; viz.

To prove what is alleged in the said Complaints, the Seven Letters mentioned therein, were delivered in to your Committee; and Five of them being shewn to the Persons to whom they were addressed (the other Two not attending the Committee) Four of the said Persons said they had received them by the Poll, and the other Person laid* he had received a Letter to that Purpose; but could not say that was it, as it had been out of his Custody, but he believed it was.

The said Five Letters were traced by your Committee from the Hands of the Persons to whom they were addressed, into the Hands of the Member who delivered them in to your Committee. Then,

Mr. William Lawless being called before your Committee, and the several Letters mentioned in the Complaints, being shewn him, said, That he wrote them all himself, and saw the Duke of Chandos sign them; and that he had written 3 or 400 such Letters, moll of which were ligned in his Pretence.

Mr. Coulfton, Inspector of the Bye Days at the General Poll Office, being examined, laid. He had never seen the Duke write. — Being shewn the Super-feriptions of the Letters, said, he believed, from the Number he had seen, they were the Duke’s Hand Writing; that he had passed them as franked; and that when he law any which he suspected, he charged them.

Then Five of the said Letters were read, and appeared to relate to the said Election. — And the Resolution of the House, upon the 26th Day of November last, " That it is a high Infringement of the " Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord " Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves " in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament," was also read.

Upon the Whole, your Committee came to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That James Bridges, Duke of Chandos, a Peer of Parliament, and Lord Lieutenant of the County of Southampton, has concerned himself in the late Election of a Knight of the Shire for the said County.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Comnflt-tee. That James Bridges, Duke of Chandos, a Peer of Parliament, and Lord Lieutenant of the County of Southampton, has been guilty of a Breach of the Privilege of this House, and an Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Britain.

Thair.e* Petition of Michael Dicker Sanders, of the City of bridge. Exeter, Esquire, was presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth, That the Petitioner’s Uncle Samuel Dicker, of Walton upon Thames, in the County of Surrey, Esquire, was, by virtue of an Act, made in the Twentieth Year of the Reign of King George the Second, enabled to build a Bridge cross the River Thames, from the Parish of Walton upon Thames, in the County of Surrey, to Shepperton, in the County of Middlesex; and, in pursuance of the Powers granted by the said Act, did build and complete such Bridge, which has been passable for several Years; but the said Bridge hath, from various Accidents, become ruinous and in a dangerous Condition, in-so much that it has become necessary to support the same by Props from the Bed of the River; and that the Petitioner is now foie Proprietor of the said Bridge; and it has been found, from Experience, that the Tolls payable by the said Act are inadequate to anliver the Expence of building and maintaining the said Bridge, and the Reparation thereof will be attended with a very considerable Expence: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to brine in a Bill to enable him to repair or rebuild the said Bridge, and to collect such new and additional Tolls as shall be thought reasonable, and adequate to the very large Expence that will attend effectually fijpporting the said Bridge.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

within the said Counties of Suffolk and Essex, having atl Estate in Land of the Yearly Value of £. 150 at the lead, or a Personal Estate of J. 3,000, in the Place of him or them so dying or refusing, which said n<_w Commissioner or Courniissioners should from thenceforth have like Power and Authority in all Things relating to the said Navigation, as if he or they had been expressly named in the said Act; and that all the several Persons nominated and appointed Commissioners by the said Act, are deceased, and there are now only remaining, of Persons appointed Commissioners under the Powers of the said Act, William Jennens, of Aden, in the County of Suffolk, and Charles Grey, of in the County of Essex, Esquires, who are not a sufficient Number to do any Act for continuing and effecting the Purposes of the said Navigation, and for appointing new Commissioners; and that the Powers and Authorities given to the said Commissioners by the said Act, have, in some Respects, been found defective and ineffectual for the Purposes thereby intended: And therefore praying.
