The Lord North, by His Majesty’s Command, ac- Stow'* quainted the House, That His Majesty, having been Portable informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recom- Telescope. mends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up and read;

Setting forth. That the Petitioner hath, by particular Study and Attention, and after a great Number of Experiments, and at much Expence, made great Improvements in Optical Instruments in general; and that he hath lately invented a Portable Telescope, which, on account of the Smallness of the Size, its great magnifying Powers, the Largeness of the Field of View and Distinctnels of Vision, and the Facility of adjusting the magnifying Power to the Size of the Object and State of the Atmosphere, and other Qualities, will be of great Utility to the Public in general, and particularly with respect to Navigation, as it may be used at the Mast-head of a Ship, whereby an Elevation is gained to deserv Objects at a Distance, far beyond the Power of any Telescope now in Ule, and remarkably excels all others in exhibiting Objects more clearly in a hazy At-mosphere, and will likewise be of great Advantage to the Officers of the Army both in the Field and in Garrison; and that the said Telescope may also be applied to the most minute Microlcopic Discoveries, with the particular Advantage of exhibiting to the Eye opake as well as pellucid Objects, and by Candle Light as well as by Day Light; and that it is also peculiarly adapted for making Astronomical Observations, which last mentioned Quality the Petitioner doubts not may be so improved as that thereby, together with the Means now in Use for the ascertaining the Longitude at Sea, that valuable Discovery may be completely obtained; and that, for the bringing the said Telescope to a Degree of Perfcftion adequate to the last mentioned Purposes, fume further Experiments will be required, which he is desirous and ready to make in case some Provision be made towards enabling him to defray the necessary Expences that may attend the Prosecution thereof: And therefore praying the House, to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant him such Reward, and so to enable him to prosecute his Experiments, as to them may appear reasonable and proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the' Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the lame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Penton, Sir Gilbert Elliot,

&cc.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and all who come to the Committee are to have Voices.

Expenditure A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and Freehold-of ers of the County of York, was presented to the House,

PoM* Moiiejk antj rcatj. setting forth, That this Nation hath been engaged for several Years in a most expensive and unfortunate War; that many of our valuable Colonies, having actually declared themselves independent, have formed a ftritft Confederacy with France and the dangerous and inveterate Enemies of Great Britain; that the Consequence of those combined Misfortunes , bath been a large Addition to the National Debt, a heavy Accumulation of Taxes, a rapid Decline of the Trade, Manufactures, and Land Rents of the Kingdom: Alarmed at the diminished Resources and growing Burthens of this Country, and convinced that rigid Frugality is now indil'penfably necessary in every Department of the State, your Petitioners observe, with Grief, that, notwithstanding the calamitous and impoverished Condition of the Nation, much public Money has been improvidently Iquandered; and that many Individuals enjoy sinecure Places, efficient Places with exorbitant Emoluments, and Pensions unmerited by Public Service, to a large and still increasing Amount, w'hence the Crown has acquired a great and unconditional Influence, which, if not checked, may soon prove fatal to the Liberties of this Country: Your Petitioners, conceiving that the true End of every legitimate Government is not the Emolument of any Individual, bur the Welfare of the Community, and considering that, by the Constitution of this Realm, the National Purse is intruded in a peculiar Manner to the Custody of this honourable House, beg Leave farther to represent, that, until effectual Measures be taken to redress the oppressive Grievances herein Rated, the Grant of any additional Sum of Public

Vol. 37.

Money, beyond the Produce of the present Taxes, will be injurious to the Rights and Property of the People, and derogatory from the Honour and Dignity of Parliament: Your Petitioners, therefore, appealing to the Justice of this honourable House, do most earnestly request, That, before any new Burthens are laid upon this Country, effoctual Measures may be taken by this House, to enquire into and corredf, the Grols Abuses in the Expenditure of Public Money, to reduce all exorbitant Emoluments, to refeind and abolish all sinecure Places and unmerited Pensions, and to appropriate the Produce to the Necessities of the State, in such Manner as to the Wisdom of Parliament shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, Sheriffs, Expenditure and Commons of the City of York, in Common Coun- of

cil assembled, was also presented to the House, and Publ‘c Mon*r‘ read: Containing the same Allegations and Request as the last preceding Petition.

A Petition of the Mayor, Burgesses, and Common- ,to* alty, of the City of Bristol, in Common Council assembled, was also presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth. That the unhappy and destrutftive Contest so long subsisting between this Country and the American Colonies, having first annihilated a large Proportion of the National Commerce, has at last plunged this Kingdom into a most expensive War with the combined Powers of France and Spain, by which Means, while it has been the Occasion of increasing the Public Burthens to a Degree beyond Example, it has greatly diminished the Ability of supporting them, and the gre<* Increase of Taxes is so heavily felt, that many of the Manufactures and Branches of Commerce which are still retained, mud fink under the Preshire of any additional Weight; in Order to prevent such ex-tenlive Ruin, your Petitioners humbly submit to this honourable House, the Necessity there is that no Part of the Public Revenue, drained from the Industrious and Laborious, be diverted from the Purposes for which it was granted, and that Public CEconomy supply the Place of New Taxes; the Abolition of Pensions unmerited by Public Services, and of Places which are Sinecures, the Reduction of exorbitant Emoluments of Office, and a ftrid Attention to CEconomy in making Public Contrafts, would furnish, on Occasion of the present Emergency, some of the most safe and leasonable Resources, would introduce a Spirit of Frugality, the Want of which has been long lamented, and reduce the Influence of the Crown within those Bounds to which our wife Ancestors deemed it expedient, for the Safety of the Constitution, that it should be limited; by such a Zeal for the Public Good, a Confidence in Public Measures would be restored, and the Inhabitants of thele Kingdoms again become a great, an happy, and united People: Your Petitioners therefore humbly pray. That this just and necessary Reformation in the Public Expenditure, may be adopted, and the Savings accruing therefrom be faithfully applied to the National Service, in such Manner as to the Wisdom of Parliament shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Mayor and Burgesses of the Ditto. Town and County of the Town of Nottingham, in Common Council assembled, was also presented to the House, and read: Setting forth. At the Height of National Calamity, we. the Mayor and Burgesses of the Town and County of the Town of Nottingham, in the Common Hall assembled, approach a British House of Commons with that Respect which is due to the appointed Guardians of our Rights, and with that Hope which it becomes us to entertain from those who are honoured with so great a Trust. The growing and almost insupportable Distrcfles of this injured and degraded Country, summon us into your Presence, that you may know our Scnfe of these

71 Distresses,

5 o a 3° Februdrii. A. 178 o.

Expenditure Distresses, of their Cause, and of their Remedy, and Public°Monej-. ^n<^’ *n l*ie Wishes of the People, the heft Encourage;

inent to an immediate and effectual Interposition for their Rescue. Whether by Crime, or by Misfortune, or both^ One great Member of the Empire' be

gone, yet, with such a Diminution of Wealth and Power, to be engaged in the most complicated and formidable War, surely alks for the most rigid CEconomy in every Department of the State: But with Grief and Shame we observe, that a Wasteful Prodigality has CUffipated our remaining Strength, and by enfeebling our Efforts, disgraced our Arms, and multiplied our L"ffes, while this very Prodigality becomes the Source of increased Demands, aggravates the Burthens under which every Rank and Description of the People bow, arid threatens in its Progress a general Ruin: We look vp to your honourable House for a Period to this dreadful Progress, and that, with the Integrity and Firmness of the Commons of Britain, you will make a.levere Enquiry into the Expenditure of that immense Treasure, which a Liberality unknown in the most flourishing Period has drawn from an almost exhausted Nation. The Magnanimity of a Free People can give the last Shilling in the Cause of their Country, but in no other Cause; and this Confidence, which shall dispose them to the last Exertions, can only be derived from your Inquisition into those Abuses, which may render such Exertions necessary; they expect to know that successive Grants shall not find them less prepared to meet an elated Foe, and facilitate the most awful of all Calamities, the Ruin of their Liberties. In this reduced and humble State of the Nation, it is a further Pain to observe the enoimous Sums which are diverted to no public Good, the exorbitant Emoluments annexed to real, and much more to nominal Offices, with indiscriminate unmerited Pensions, which devour the public Treasure, defeat the National Efforts, degrade the Spirit, of EngliJJimcn into a sordid Avarice, subvert the Independence of Parliament, and aft with a malignant Influence on all that is dear to our Country. Under the Impression of these awful Truths, we beg Leave to represent, that the Redrels of these ruinous Abuses is the Right of Britons, and the only Source from which Hope can again be brought baeje to their Country; and that, till foine wife and vi-goicus Measures for tire effecting this Purpose be adopted, no Addition can, with Wisdom, Honour, or Safety, he made to the Pecuniary Burthens of . these Kingdoms; we would respecttully observe, that such a Conduct, in Times of Danger, Distress, and Apprehension, has been the distinguishing Character of your honourable House, that, by which the very Being of your House, and the Being of our Constitution, has been preserved; and that in no. Period has Distress and Apprehension more summoned the Representatives of Britain to the Exertion of their proper Character, to the fulfilling every Hope of their anxious Constituents: With these Abuses, in all their Magnitude, in all their Operation before you, every Grant beyond the Produce of the present Taxes will be to wanton with the Rights and Property of the People, and betray the Faith and Dignity of Parliament: It js our Prayer, therefore, to this honourable House, That all extravagant Emoluments be reduced, all superdu-ous and nominal Offices;be abolifiled, all unmerited Pensions be resumed, and that the Produce be appropriated to the Nca.(Titles of the State; and that till this wife and necessary Reform be adopted, and till \ effectual Means be applied to enquire into, and cor-

red the Abuses in the Expenditure of the Public Money, whereby the Fears and Jealousics of the People may be appeased, and a well-grounded confidence dif" filled through the Community, you wi.ll, with that Justice and Patriot ilin which wepromise ourselves from your honourable House, wituhojd.. all Grants of php

Public Money beyond the-Produce of the present Tuxes; trusting that this our just and interesting Petition will meet with all favourable Reception, we ever pray,

A Petition' of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and ’Freeholders, of the County of , was presented to

the House, and read; Setting forth, That this Nation hath been engaged for several Years in a most expensive and unfortunate War; that many of our valuable Colonies, having actually declared themselves Independent, have formed a strict Confederacy with France and Spain, tire inveterate Enemies of Great Britain; that the Consequencfe of those combined Misfortunes hath been a large Addition to tire National Debt, a heavy Accumulation of Taxes, a rapid Decline of the Trade, Manufactures, and Land Rents, of the Kingdom: Alarmed at the diminished Resources and growing Burthens of this Country, and convinced that rigid Frugality is now indispensably necessary in every Department of the State, your Petitioners observe, with Grief, that, notwithstanding the calamitous and impoverished Condition of the Nation, much Public Money has been improvidently squandered, and that many Individuals enjoy finccure Places, efficient Places with exorbitant Emoluments, and Pensions unmerited by Public Service, to a large and still increasing Amount, whence the Crown has acquired a great and unconstitutional Influence, which, if not checked, must soon prove fatal to the Liberties of this Country: Your Petitioners, conceiving that the true End of every legitimate Government is not the Emolument 6f any Individual, but the Welfare of the Community, beg Leave further to represent, that, until effectual Mcalures be taken to redress the oppressive Grievances herein stated, the Grant of any additional Sum of Public Money, beyond the Produce of the present Taxes, will be injurious to the Rights and Property of the People, and derogatory from the Honour and Dignity of Parliament: Your Petitioners, therefore, do most earnestly request, That, before any new Burthens are laid upon this Country, effectual Measures may be taken to enquire into and correct the gross Abuses in the Expenditure of Public Money, to reduce all exorbitant Emoluments, to rescind and abolish all fmecure Places and unmerited Pensions, and to appropriate the Produce to the Necessities of the State, in such Manner as to the Wisdom of Parliament shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Freeholders, and others, of the County of Southampton, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Situation of this Country is so very alarming, that we think it our Duty ho longer to remain silent and inactive at lb dangerous a Crilis; that, involved as we arc in a most expensive War with the combined Forces of France and Spain, and our revolted Colonies in Ame-

rica, who have acceded to that formidable Alliance,

and conceiving that our Navy, in its present State, is not adequate to the Magnitude of that Danger which threatens the immediate and total Rum of this Country; and feeling that our Revenue is diminished by the Loss of l’ome of our Islands in the West Indies, and by the Danger and Distress of others, and by a general Decay of Trade and Commerce; we, your Petitioners, do pray. That this honourable House will make an immediate and feriouS Enquiry into the Causes of these Dangers and Misfortunes, which we apprehend could not have happened, but from the Misconduct of Ministers, and from the Want of an early and proper Information having been laid before this honourable House; under all these calamitous Circumstances, opprested by the Burthen of a vast Public Debt, and of accumulated Taxes, we implore this honourable House to take such Measures, for alleviating the Distresses of the People, as in its Wisdom shall seem proper; and we humbly conceive, that a Correction of the Abuses in the Expenditure of Public Money, a Reduction of all exorbitant Emoluments, and an Abolition of all linecure Places and unmerited Pensions, will greatly tend to so necessary and desirable an Object.

A Representation and Petition of the Planters, Merchants, and other Persons interested in the Island of Jamaica, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That your Petitioners, in all Duty and Humility, beg Leave to lay before this honourable House, several Circumstances which they presume it is important for the House to know, and to which they are certain it is of the utmost Importance to them that a due Attention should be paid: Your Petitioners represent to this honourable House, that the Island of Jamaica has not been protedled; they represent, that the Temporary Safety which it has enjoyed, has been owing to the Di-redtion of the Enemy’s Force towards other Objects, and not to any intrinsic Means of Defence provided for that Island by His Majesty’s Ministers; they conceive, that the Safety of such a Possession as Jamaica ought not to have been left to Chance; they represent, that the Island of Jamaica is inferior in Value to none of the Dependencies of Great , that great Part

even of what appears to be the interior Wealth of Great Britain itself, is, in Reality, the Wealth of Jamaica, which is so intimately interwoven with the internal Intere 11 of this Kingdom, that it is not eal’y to distinguish them; that a great Part of the Trade and Navigation, a large Proportion of the Revenue, and very much of the Mercantile and the National Credit, and the Value of the Landed Interest, depend immediately on its Preservation, that its Defence is therefore 14

an Object as important to Great Britain as any Part of Great Britain itself, and that it is an Object to be provided for with still greater Care and Forelight, because its natural Means of Home Defence are infinitely less considerable; they solemnly declare, that, conscious of their invariable Loyalty to the Crown of Great Britain, their unbounded Attachment to the Prosperity of the whole Empire, they are not able to conjecture for what Offence, real or pretended, they have so long been put under this Proscription} if your Petitioners had been active by factious Clamours, or delusive Representations, by concealing true or suggesting false Information, in betraying their Sovereign and their Country into War, they might have the lets Reason to complain of the Neglect by which they have suffered so many Dif-trelfes, and have been exposed to so many Dangers; it is in the Recollection of this honourable House, that, at an early Pencil of the present unhappy Troubles, the Body of the West India Planters and Merchants did humbly Hate their Apprehensions to Parliament, and deprecated the unhappy Measures which were then taken; it is the Misfortune of the Public, as well as theirs, that no Attention was paid to their humble Prayers, and that their most dutiful and faithful Representations were totally neglected; they affirm, that they have not deserved to be thus abandoned, from a Want of having purchased for a valuable Consideration the Protection of the State; the Planters have seen, not only with Acquiescence but Pleasure, their Trade almost wholly confined to the Mother Country, the Place of Residence of the greater Part, and the Object of the tenderest Affection to all of them; bath Planters and Merchants have had the Produce of their Estates as largely taxed in Great Britain, to the Common Support, as any others; the Assembly of the Island of Jamaica has, beyond any former Example of Liberality, and far beyond their Abilities, laid destructive Impositions on their Estates and Properties within the Island; vast Personal Services, burthensome in the Extreme, and nearly ruinous to the present Value of all they

possess, have been chtarfully given; they have borne patiently, the heavy Losses and Burthens, the fatal* though not unforeteen Consequences of their Separation from North America; after all these Impositions and Taxes in England, these Taxes and Personal Services in "Jamaica, and after Sufferings of every Kind in this War, on Suggefiion from Friends of Government, they have had Resort in their individual Characters to their almost exhausted Purses, and made a large private Subscription for their own Defence; they represent, that they have been credibly informed, that at the Time when Administration declined to provide the necessary Forces, either by Sea or Land, for their Defence, that His Majesty’s Secretary at War publicly declared, that His Majesty did then command more numerous Forces, by Sea and Land, than the most formidable Monarch of the World had under his Orders, when his Power alarmed all Europe; and they are informed, that large Additions to His Majesty’s Forces were made some Time after; they now also feel, that they are amongst those who are taxed for the Maintenance of an Army of upwards of Seventy thousand Men employed in North America; and they prelume, that tee Suppression of no Rebellion whatever can be a more near and urgent Concern of any Government, than the Protection of its loyal and useful Subjects; they represent, that they have not been wanting to themselves, by every Representation in their Power, and every Soli* citation, to call upon His Majesty’s Ministers for the necessary Protection; for though, from the Duty of their Station, and their high Trust, His Majesty’s Mi-nifters ought to have shewn an anxious and provident Care of all His Majesty’s Dominions, even if Individuals, through Ignorance, or Want of Forefight had neglected their own private Interest in them; yet they humbly inform the House, that many ftror.g Remonstrances were made on this Subject to His Majesty’s Ministers by your Petitioners, beginning so early as 1773, and continued to the 8th of December 1779; and that Add relies on the same were made to His Majesty by the Assembly of Jamaica, as also a Representation of the Want of Men, Ships, Stores, Arms, Ammunition, and of every other Means for their Defence, yet they never did, at any Time, receive from the said Ministers any Answers, other than Excuses on Account of the Number of Ships employed on' the American and Home Service, and certain loose, general Assurances, from which they received little Comfort, and have reaped no Advantage; and that even the positive Assurances of the Governor to the Assembly of the Island, of His Majesty’s gracious Intention thac the Squadron on that Station should be considerably reinforced, have not been fulfilled: Your Petitioners most humbly request the Attention of this House to their past and present Situation, pledging themselves to prove, beyond a Doubt; the Truth of their Allegations: In the mean Time, your Petitioners acquaint this honourable House, that unless a strong regular Force be permanently efbbhlhed in Jamaica during the War, and a considerable Fleet stationed there, they cannot think that Island in a State of Security; this they conceive themselves as bound to lay before the Representatives of the People of Great Britain, humbly claiming Protection as their undoubted Right; and looking back with Horror at the Dangers from which (by the foie Disposition of the Divine Providence) they have escaped, whilst lundry of their Fellow Subjects are now obliged to prostrate themselves at the Foot of the Throne of the French King, to implore the Mercy of that Munarch, instead of the Protection of their natural Sovereign.

Ordered, That the said Representation and Petition do lie upon the Tabic.

A Petition of the Noblemen, Gentlemen, Clergy, Expeoditm Freeholders, and other Inhabitants of the County of Sussex, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That your Petitioners cannot view the rapid Decline of the British Empire, without calling upon this honourable House, by every Tie of Honour, Interest, and Religion, to avert the Ruin that menaces this lately prosperous and happy Nation, by a timely Exertion of those Powers, with which, by the Constitution, this honourable House is in veiled; that among the many Causes which have contributed to produce our present calamitous Situation (all of which we trust this honourable House will speedily investigate anil redress) your Petitioners beg Leave to point out the Neglect of public (Economy, as a Grievance which is capable of receiving, and stands in need of, immediate Remedy; that your Petitioners conceive the Syftein of Finance, as at present established, to be of most ruinous Tendency, the National Debt beirg thereby so greatly augmented during War, and so little reduced during Peace, that it encreases without End, and cannot therefore be supported by any finite, much leis by diminished Resources; that your Petitioners are alarmed, by the Practice of Government in laying filfe Estimates before Parliament, by those Estimates being con-

your Petitioners, therefore, lament the Disuse of the ancient Practice of appointing Commissioners of Accounts, from Time to Time, for the Examination of the Public Expenditure, which might have prevented the Growth of these Evils; that your Petitioners believe, that the undue Influence of the Crown, deriving its greatest Support from the uncontrouled Possession of the Public Purse, is a principal Cause of our present Calamities, and is highly dangerous to Liberty; that your Petitioners think it their Duty to acquaint this honourable House with the Distresses which your Petitioners feel, from the Loss of Trade, the Decay of Manufactures, the diminished Value of Land, the high Price of Money, and the Increase of Taxes; they are so univerlal and (o heavy, that, unless the utmost Frugality be exerted to keep our Burthens within the shift Limits of Necessity, it will be impossible for the 'Teople to support those extraordinary Exertions, which a vigorous Prosecution of the War against France and Spain may require: Your Petitioners, therefore, humbly pray, and firmly expect, That this honourable House, in discharge of the High Trust reposed in them, will take effectual Measures, that Money supplied with lo much Difficulty from the private Fortune or Industry of the Subject, may be faithfully and frugally applied for the Purposes for which it is granted; that such Regulations may be established as shall bring the Public Expenditure to a speedy and strict Account; and that some Plan, for the Reduction of all exorbitant Emoluments of Office, and the Abolition of all sinecure Places, and unmerited Pensions, be adopted, that by thele Means the dangerous and unconstitutional Influence of the Crown may be diminished, and the Burthens of the People aeleviated; and your Petitioners further pray, that no fresh Supplies may be granted, or new Taxes laid on the Subject, until these their just Grievances are redreflfed, in such Manner as to the Wisdom and Justice of this honourable House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the principal Merchants and Inhabitants of the Town and Parish of , in the County of Devon, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners have received Information from their Correspondents abroad, that, if the Import Duties on Linens and Laces, and Lace Thread, imported from the Imperial Dominions in the Low Countries into this Kingdom, are not lessened, a Duty of Sixteen Pence a Yard will soon be imposed on all British Woollen Manufactures imported into that Country, which will be equal to a Prohibition on all Woollen Goods manufactured in this Part of the Kingdom; and the Petitioners apprehend and believe, that, if the present Duties on the Importation of such Foreign Linens and Laces, and Lace Thread, into this Kingdom, could be lessened, it would greatly promote and increase the Woollen Manufactures of this Country, which have been declining for several Years past, while those of Prance have increased: The Petitioners therefore hope

I the House will give them such Relief and Assistance

as the Wisdom of Parliament shall deem proper on this Occassion.

A Petition of the Merchants, Mariners, and Trades-men of Liverpool, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, Was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the general Importance of the Island of Jamaica, from the great Value of its Produce, which is chiefly expended on the Manufactures and Productions of Great Britain, is rendered still more consequential to this Town and Neighbourhood, through the weighty Connections produced by our Trade to as well as by an immediate Export and Import; that the Loss of this invaluable Settlement would certainly prove exceedingly prejudicial, not only to the Manufactures, Commerce, and Navigation, of this Country, but, from the Numbers who would thereby be involved in certain Ruin, might give a fatal Blow to our National Credit, and endanger our Existence as a great Maritime Power; that this Island is, from its Situation, particularly ex poled to the1 joint Attacks of the common Enemy, and ought therefore to be in a constant State of Defence; the Track of its homeward-bound TVade is along the French and Settlements, and

nfcctffarily require! strong Convoys; these Circumstances render it a very proper Station from whence to alarm and distress the Enemy; if a Force Was constantly maintained there, adequate to all these important Purposes: Your Petitioners therefore pray. That; through the Mediation of this honourable House, such Measures may be pursued as may probably tend to remove the Danger to which the Island of Jamaica has too long remained exposed; and that the Establishments there, both Military and Naval, may be augmented in such a Manner as the Safety of lb valuable a Possession, the Security of its Commerce, and the Annoyance of the Enemy, shall appear to require.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and Free- Expenditure holders, of the County of Dorset, was presented to the of House, and read; Setting forth. That this Nation hath Pub)ic Monty' been engaged for several Years in a most expensive and unfortunate War; that many of our valuable Colonies, having actually declared themselves independent, have formed a strict Confederacy with France and Spain, the dangerous and inveterate Enemies of Great;

that the Consequence of those combined Misfortunes, hath been a large Addition to the National Debt, a heavy Accumulation of Taxes, a rapid Decline of the Trade. Manufactures, and Land Rents of the Kingdom: Alarmed at the diminished Resources and growing Burthens of this Country, and convinced that rigid Frugality is now indispensably necessary in every Department of the State, your Petitioners observe, with Grief, that, notvvichftancling the calamitous and impoverished Condition of the Nation, much Public Money has been improvidently squandered, and that many Individuals enjoy finccure Places, efficient Places with exorbitant Emoluments, and Penfrons unmerited by Public Service, to a large and still increasing Amount:

Your Petitioners, conceiving that the true End of every legitimate Government, is not the Emolument of any Individual, but the Welfare of the Community; and lonffilerng that, by the Constitution of this Realm, the National Purse is entrusted, in a peculiar Manner, to the Cull oily of this honourable House, beg Leave further to represent, that, until effectual Measures be taken to redress the oppressive Grievances herein stated, the Grant of any additional Sum of Public Money, beyond the Produce of the present Taxes, will be injurious to the Rights and Property of the People, and derogatory

Expenditure A Petition of the Nobility, Gentlemen, Clergy, pnbi °M Freeholders, and others, of the County of Berks, was lc on*y alii) presented to the House, and read; Settipg forth. That this Nation hath been engaged for several Years in a mol): expensive and unfortunate War; that many of our Valuable Colonies, having actually declared themselves independent, have formed a strict Confederacy with France and Spain, the dangerous and inveterate Enemies of Great; that the Consequence of those combined Misfortunes, hath been a large Addition to t)ic National Debt, a heavy Accumulation of Taxes, a rapid Decline of the Trade, Manufactures, and Land Rents of the Kingdom: Alarmed at the di-niinished ‘Resourcesand growing Burthens of this, Country, and convinced that rigid Frugality is now indif-penfably necessary in every Department of the State, your Petitioners observe, with Grief, that, notwithstand,-ing the calamitous and impoverished Condition of the Nation^ mucfr public Money has been improvidcntly squandered, and that many Individuals enjoy sinecure Places, efficient Places with exorbitant Emoluments, and Pensions unmerited by Public Service, to a large and frill increasing Amount, whence tire Crown Las acquired a great and unconstitutional Influence; which, if not checked, may soon prove fatal to the Liberties of this Country: Ypur Petitioners, conceiving tjiat the true End of every legitimate Government, is not the Emolument of any Individual, but the Welfare of the Community; and consider? ing that, by the Constitution of this Realm, the National Purle is entrusted in a peculiar Manner to the Custody of this honourable House, beg Leave further to R-present, that, until effectual Measures be taken to redress the oppressive Grievances herein Rated, the Grant of any additional Sum of Public Money, beyond the Produce of the present Taxes, will be injurious to the Rights and Property of the People, and derogatory from the Honour and Dignity of Parliament: Your Petitioners, therefore, appealing to the Justice of this honourable House, do most earnestly request, That before’ any new Burthens are laid upon this Country, effectual Measures may be taken by this House, to enquire into and correct the gross Abuses in the Expenditure of Public Money, to reduce all exorbitant Emoluments, to refeind and ab ildh all sinecure Places and unmerited Pensions, and to appropriate the Produce to the Necessities of the State, in such Manner as to the Wilciom of Parliament ILall f'ecm meet.

and if Relief be not given to the Petitioners, the Enemy will, from Ransoms of their Ships, receive large Sums of Money, Part of which otherwise would come to the Officers and Crews of Ships which might have retaken them, had they not been ransomed; and, to shew the great Hardship the Petitioners labour under from the said Law, they pray Reference to the Colls attending the Adjudication in the Court of Admiralty on the Re-capture of such of their Vessels as have been retaken; A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Sheriffs, and Expenditure Common Council, of the City of Gloucester, in Com- of mon Council assembled, was presented 10 the House, u 1C M<mtT and read; Setting forth. That this Nation hath been engaged for several Years in a most expensive and unfortunate Contest with many of her Colonies; and that France and Spain, the dangerous and inveterate Enemies of Great Britain, have taken Advantage of these Circumstances, and proceeded to unjust and unprovoked Hostilities; that the Consequences of these combined Misfortunes, have been a large Addition to the National Debt, a heavy Accumulation of Taxes, a rapid Decline of the Trade, Manufactures, and Land Rents of the Kingdom: Alarmed at the diminished Resources and growing Burthens of this Country, and convinced that rigid Frugality is now indispensably necessary in every Department of the State, your Petitioners observe, with Grief, that, not with (landing the Calamities and impoverished Condition of the Nation, much Public Money has been improvidently squandered, and that many Individuals enjoy sinecure Places, efficient Places with exorbitant Emoluments, and Pensions unmerited by Public Service, to a large and Hill increasing Amount, whence the Crown has acquired a great and unconstitutional Influence, which, if not checked, may soon prove fatal to the Liberties of this Country: Your Petitioners, conceiving that the true End of every legi timate Government is not the Emolument of Individuals, but the Welfare of the Community, and considering that, by the Constitution of his Realm, the National Purie is entrusted in a peculiar Manner to the custody of this honourable House, beg Leave further to represent, that, until effectual Measures be taken to red rest

the oppressive Grievances herein dated > the Grant of any additional Sum of Public Money beyond the Produce of the present Taxes, will be injurious to the Rights and Property of the People, and derogatory from the Honour and Dignity of Parliament: Your Petitioners, therefore, appealing to the Justice of this honourable House, do most earnestly request, That, before any new-Burthens are laid upon this Country, such Measures may be taken by this House, as will tend effectually to enquire into and correct the gross Abuses in the Expenditure of Public Money, to reduce all exorbitant Emoluments, to refeind and abolish all sinecure Places and unmerited Pensions, and to appropriate the Produce to the Necessities of the State, in such Manner as to the Wisdom of Parliament shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Electors of the Borough of Reading was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That your Petitioners, considering the vast Sums of Money that have beea expended in the present raoft unfortunate War, sensibly affected themselves by the heavy Taxes already laid upon the Subjects of this Kingdom, and alarmed at the Idea that others may be shortly imposed, humbly request your honound>ie House, to turn their most serious Attention to the di-tninished Resources and growing Burthens of this Country; your Petitioners conceive, that, in this Time of general Diflrels, it will be necessary to alleviate the Public Burthen, by abolishing sinecure and useless Places, curtailing the exorbitant Salaries and Perquisites annexed to others, and resuming many unmerited Pensions, the Disposal of which not only oocafions a great Waite of Public Treafute, but gives an unconstitutional Power to the Mi aiders of the Crown, sub-, verts the Independence of Parliament, and operates with an undue Influence on, all that is dear, to our Country; your Petitioners humbly conceive, that the Interposition of your honourable House in these Points, and its diligent Attention to a just and (economical Expenditure of the Public Revenue by Persons entrusted with it, may be productive of great National Good, and enable this Country, by properly directing and combining its Relburces, to prevail over its most powerful Enemies. They therefore presume thus to add refs their Petition to your honourable House, alluring them that it does not in any wise originate from a Spirit of Party, but is dictated by the cleared Conviction, that the present Situation of Affairs requires the Attention of every Man, and his honed and (peedy Exertion of all possible Means to promote and defend the Public Weal.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Merchants and others interested in America* the Trade to North America, was presented to the Trade. House, and read; Setting forth, Thar, by the Operation of the Prohibitory Act of Parliament, passed in the Sixteenth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, tha Petitioners are not permitted to export any Articles of Clothing or Merchandize to the Colonies therein mentioned; and that a considerable Number of His Majesty’s Subjects in America have thrown themselves under the Protection of His Majesty’s Army at New York, and other Places; and in consequence of the Prohibition contained in the said Act, they, as well as the other Inhabitants of those Places, are deprived of that Support and Advantage which they had promised themselves under such Protection; and that many of the Petitioners have received Orders from their different Correspondents in New York, and other Places, for a considerable Quantity of Clothing, Stores, and other Articles of British Manufacture and Merchandize, which are effectially necessary for the Use of the Inhabitants; and representing to the House, that it requires very large Quantities of the Manufacture* of this Countiy to answer the necessary Confiimption of such Places as are already in the Possession of His Majesty’s Forces, and the Inhabitants must, if deprived of their expected Supplies, be subjected to much Hardship and Inconvenience, and His Majesty’s Service may, as the Petitioners conceive, be thereby greatly injured; whereas, if Permission was given to export Merchandize to New York, and all other Places which are and may be in the Possession of the King’s Troops, it would greatly tend to the Benefit of the Inhabitants of such Places, and to encourage the Trade and Ma-nufeftures of Great Britain: And therefore praying the House to take the same into Consideration, and to grant them such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will. Tomorrow Morning, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Petition.

County of Norfolk, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That your Petitioners, alarmed at the still growing Burthens of this Country, notwithstanding the annual Diminution of its Rel’ources, feeling that the strictest (Economy must be adopted in every Rank of private Life, must hive loft every Power of lle-fleftion, not to difeern that the most rigid Frugality is indispensibly necessary in every Public Department of the State; to this honourable House then, your Petitioners look up for Succour and Protection; to you they apply, as more peculiarly entrusted with the Controul of the National Purle; and, with all that Solicitude which the Pressure of Private Distrcls and the Dread of Public Ruin, can excite, earnestly request, that this House would be pleased to make no Grant of Public Money without the most palpable Evidence of its Necessity 1 and that you would be pleased farther to provide, by all the Means with which the Constitution furnishes, and with all that Vigour and Resolution with which Zeal for that Constitution can inspire you, that none of the Public Money, when granted, be improperly applied, or improvidently squandered: Thus roused by Effects to the Investigation of their Causes, suffer your Petitioners still farther to represent, that the Time is now arrived, when it is become absolutely re-quisite that all fi nocure Places, and Pensions unmerited by Public Service, should be abolished, and that the exorbitant Emoluments even of efficient Places should be reduced, that such Expenditures may no longer continue to incrcale the calamitous and impoverished Condition of the Nation, and to add a great and unconstitutional Influence to the Crown, an Accession of Influence, which the bell informed in the Laws, the sincerest Friends of Government, and the most loyal and faithful Subjects to the King, have, in the Hour of calm Reflection, unwarped by Interest, unbiafi'ed by Party, not only deplored as inimical to the Liberties of this Country, but as tending to effect, what it loon may, the entire Subversion of the whole Fabric of the Constitution. Your Petitioners, therefore, appealing to the Justice of this honourable House, and confiding in your Fidelity to the Principles of your delegated Trull, do now moll earnestly request, That effectual Measures may be taken towards redressing the oppressive Grievances herein Hated, before any new Burthens be laid upon this arflifted Country; but beg Leave likewise firmly to represent, that unless such Measures be lo taken, the Grant of any Public Money, beyond the Produce of the present Taxes, will be injurious to the Rights and Property of the People, and consequently . Vot. 37.

derogatory from the Honour and Dignity of Parlia* meat.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Merchants and Manufacturers of the Importation Town of Wellington, in the County of Somerset, was of

presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That Lace!

the Petitioners are alarmed at receiving Information from their Correspondents in Flanders, importing, that in Consequence of a Clause in an Act passed the last Session of Parliament, intended to prevent the pernicious Practice of Smuggling Foreign Lace, but operating materially to affect the Importation of that Article from The Low Countries, the Imperial Court is about to lay a Duty of Sixteen Pence per Yard on all Woollens imported into their Dominions in the Low Countries, which will amount to a Prohibition of all Woollen Goods manufactured in this Part of the Kingdom, prove highly injurious to the Nation at large, to the Petitioners more particularly, and greatly distress the numerous Poor employed in such Manufactories: And therefore praying, That such Regulations may be adopted, respecting the Importation of Flanders Lace, as the Wisdom of the House may fee meet, for preventing the Iiupofts threatened by the Imperial Court, and promoting the declining Staple Manufactories of this Kingdom.

Macclesfield A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are Read. thereunto subscribed, on the Behalf of themselves and others, Consumers of Lime, in the Towns of Macclesfield and Kmitsford, and Parts adjacent, in the County of Chester, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That all the Lime used by the Petitioners, and others the Inhabitants of the Towns and Parts above described, is brought to them from certain Kilns situate at Grin, in the Parish of Hartington, in the County of Derby; and that the Price of the above very necessary Article hath of late been greatly increased, by reason of certain Tolls taken for the Passage of Coal and Lime, on the Turnpike Road from Buxton to Leek, from which Road the Petitioners do not reap the least Benefit, it being only necessary to crofi the fame, in order to go to the Coal Pits and Lime Kilns used by the Petitioners, and to which they had, before the making Vol 37.

of such Road, a free Passage from the Turnpike Road leading between Broken Cross in Macclesfield, and Bux* ion-, and that the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that Application is making for a Bill to enlarge the Term and Powers of an Act, passed in the Thirty-second Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, for repairing and widening the Road from The Cross at Broken Cross, in Macclesfield, in the County of Chester, 4

through Macclesfield Forest, to the present Turnpike Road at the South End of Buxton, in the said County of Derby, and for Power to make a certain Branch from the said Turnpike Road, to the Coal Pits at Thatch March and Gait, and thence to rejoin the same Turnpike at Thatch Marsh; and allb one other Branch from the same Turnpike Road near The Gofiing Bar, to the said Lime Kilns at Grin: and that the making of such Branches of Road will be much to the Advantage and Relief of the Petitioners, and all Consumers

of Lime in the above-mentioned Towns, and Parts ad- j

jacent, by reducing the Price to what it was before the Trustees for the said Leek Road unjustly subjected it to the Payment of Toll, and by facilitating the Carriage thereof: And therefore praying, That the Bill prayed for by the said Macclesfield Road Trustees, may be passed into a Law, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

the House, and read; betring forth, lhat this Nation has been engaged for several Years in a moll expensive and unfortunate Contest with its Colonies; that many of the moil valuable of them have declared them (elves independent; that France and Spain, the inveterate Enemies of Great Britain, have taken Advantage of these Circumstances; that the Consequences of these >

combined Misfortunes, have been a large Addition to the National Debt, a heavy Accumulation of Taxes, a rapid Decline of the Trade, Manufactures, and Land Rents of the Kingdom: Alarmed at the diminished Re-lources and growing Burthens of this Country, and convinced that rigid Frugality is now indispensably necessary in every' Department of the State, your Petitioners observe, with Grief, that, notwithstanding the calamitous and impoverished Condition of the Nation, much Public Money has been improvidently squandered, and that many Individuals enjoy sinecure Places, efficient Places with exorbitant Emoluments, and Pensions unmerited by Public Services, to a large and still increasing Amount, wheuce the Crown has acquired a great and unconstitutional Influence, which, if not checked, may soon prove fatal to the Liberties of this Country: Your Petitioners, conceiving that the true End of every legitimate Government is not the Emolument of any Individual, but the Welfare of the Community, and considering that, by the Constitution of this Realm, the National Purle is entrusted, in a Peculiar Manner, to the Custody of this honourable House; beg Leave further to represent.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Fifth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, "An Act for reviving an Act, made in the Fifth Year of " the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First,

T.o prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, made in the Twentieth Year of the Reign of his Miljeliy, King George the Second, for building a Bridge crois the River Thames from, Walton to Shepperton, was read; And, . , ‘

James Paine, Esquire, an Architefl, being examined, laid, That the Bridge.crols the River Thames at IB alum, hath been passable for Passengers several Years — That he has lately surveyed the lame, and finds, that from various Accidents it is become ruinous, and in a dangerous Condition, insomuch that it has become necessary to support the same by Props from the Bed of the i River — That the Timbers are in an actual State of De-

cay, and if the Props were to be taken away the Bridge would tumble down. And the Witness further said,

7

That it will be necessufy to take down the Three Arches over the River as low as the Piers, in order to rebuild or repair the said Bridge, so as to be safe for Passengers. — Then,

Mr. William Nichols, Agent to the Petitioner, being examined, confirmed the Evidence of Mr.; and produced to your Committee, an Account of the Produce of the Tolls at the Bridge for the last Ten Years; by which it appears, that the same on an Average have produced £.302 17*. annually, and that the Disbursements on an Average for the same Time, for collect -ing the Tolls, Repairs, and other incidental Charges, amounted to £. 82 18 s. 2dannually, which reduces the neat Annual Produce to £. 219. 19*. iorf. — And the Witness being further examined, laid. That he was employed as a Carpenter in the Building of the said Bridge, which was begun in the Year 1747, and finished in 1751; That he has heard and believes the Building of the Bridge, and other Works appurtenant thereto, and the making the Roads and other incidental Expences, cost upwards of £. 12,000. Then,

Mr. Paine being again examined, said. That he has made Two different Plans for the rebuilding of the said Bridge; one of which is a Stone Bridge, which, by using the present Stone Piers, and dividing the great Arch into Two, lie estimates at about £.6,500; and the other is to rebuild it with Timber, dividing the great Arch into Two, upon a Stone Pier, and using the present Piers, which he estimates at about £. 2,800. — That he has sub-

mitted these Plans to the Consideration of the Petitioner the Proprietor; who believing that the Tolls necessary to be raised to carry the Plan for rebuilding the Bridge with Stone into Execution, will be too burthensome for the neighbourhood has it now in Contemplation; to carry the Plan for rebuilding the Bridge with Wood into Execution. And he further added, That if the Bridge was to be entirely rebuilt upon the last mentioned Plan, without the Assistance of the present Works, it would cost upwards of £. 6,000.

Then Mr. David Barclay being examined, said, That it is proposed to reduce the Tolls in some respects, and to increase them in others, and to make them payable for every Time of passing the Bridge, instead of Once a Day, as authorized by the Act; and that it is intended to make the Tolls confident with the Tulls levied upon the different Bridges on the River. And he further said.

That the Tolls now taken at the Bridge, are not equal

10 the Tolls taken at Hampton Co, ,or

Bridges.

Mr. James Potts being examined, said, That the said Road leading from the Flint Turnpike Road at or near Ty maen, in the Parish of Whitford, through the Towns of Newmarket and Rhuddlan, over Rhuddlan Marsh, to Abergeley, is in a ruinous Condition, and in some Parts narrow, and totally impassable for Carriages, and cannot be effectually 1 mended and kept in Repair by the ordinary Course of Law.

And the Witness added. That the repairing the said Road will be of public Utility, and of great Benefit

29

and Advantage to all Persons travelling from London to Holyhead, through Chester, as it will be a considerable Saving, both in Expence and Time, being a much leveller Road than the present Turnpike Road from London to Holyhead, and shorter by 13 Miles than by any other Route; and would also open a Communication to several Collieries in the County of Flint, which would be a great Benefit to the Inhabitants of the Town and Neighbourhood of Abergeley.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

he or they paying, for and in lieu of Salvage, One Eighth Part of the true Value of the Ship to be restored, such Salvage to be paid and divided as therein diteded; which Clause the Petitioners conceive to be very' detrimental to the Owners of such Ships of small Value as may be taken and retaken, as well on Acfcount of the Length of Time the Property is withheld from the Owners, before a Decree for Restitution can be obtained in the Court of Admiralty, as also of the great Expence attending Adjudications in that Court, the Owners’ Proportion whereof being Seven Eighths, generally amounts to double the Salvage due to the Recaptors, which induces the Petitioners to believe, that the Owners of Ships of l’mall Value will find it more beneficial to ranlbm their Ships wheft taken by an Enemy, than to futter them to be retaken (if a Chance offered) by any of His Majesty’s Ships, or any private Ships of War, as the Owners, by ransoming, will have the immediate Possession of their Property, and often at a less Expence than what the Salvage and Expences of Adjudication amount to; but as the ransoming of Ships taken by the Enemy is depriving the Officers and Crews of Ships of War of considerable Sums of Money, and veiling the same in His Majesty’s Enemies, the Petitioners prelume the Salvage may be ealily and speedily settled between the Owners or Mailers of rc-taken Ships, and the Commanders or Agents of Ships of War, which will be a Saving to their Officers and Crews of at lead One Eighth Part of the Expeifce attending Adjudications in the Admiralty Court: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that all Ships, employed in the Coal and Coasting Trade, may be exempt from Adjudications in the Admiralty Court, and that such other Relief may be given to the Owners of Ships as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill to amend an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for the Encouragement of Seamen, and the more speedy and " effectual Manning His Majesty's Navy," and for making further Provisions foT those Purposes, is committed.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and tree- Expenditure holders, of the County of Gloucester, whole Names are the thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and jPu '* °n* read; Setting forth, That this Nation hath been engaged for several Years in a most expensive and unfortunate Contest with many of her Colonies; and that France and Spain, the dangerous and inveterate Enemies of Great Britain, have taken Advantage of these Circumstances, and proceeded to unjust and unprovoked Hostilities; that the Consequences of tfiefe combined Misfortunes, have been a large Addition to the National Debt, a heavy Accumulation of Taxes, a rapid Decline of the Trade, Manufactures; and Land Rents of the Kingdom: Alarmed at thedi-miniftied Resources and growing Burthens of this Country, and convinced that rigid Frugality is now indispen-sably necessary in every Department of the State, your Petitioners observe, with Grief, that, notwithstanding the Calamities and impoverishecj Condition of the Nation, much Public Money has been improvidently squandered, and that many Individuals enjoy sinecure Places, efficient Places with exorbitant Emoluments* and Pensions unmerited by Public Service, to a large and (till increasing Amount: whence the Crown has acquired a great and unconllitotional Influence, which if not checked, may soon prove fatal to the Liberties of this Country: Your Petitioners, conceiving that the true End of every legitimate Government, is not the Emolument of Individuals, but the Welfare of the Community; and considering that, by the Constitucion of this^Realm, the National Purse is entrusted, in a peculiar Manner, to the Custody of this honourable House, beg Leave further to represent, that, until effectual Measures be taken to redress the oppressive Grievances herein Hated, the Grant of any additional Sum of Public Money, beyond the Produce of the present Taxes, will be injurious to the Rights and Property of the People, and derogatory from the Honour and Dignity, or Parliament: Your Petitioners, therefore, appealing to the Justice of this honourable House, do mostear-neftly request, That, before any new Burthens are laid upon this Country, such Measures may be taken by this House, as will tend effectually to enquire into and correct the gross Abuses in the Expenditure of Public Money, to reduce all exorbitant Emoluments, to refeind and abol lh all sinecure Places and unmerited Pensions, and to appropriate the Produce to the Necessities of the State, in such Manner as to the Wisdom of Parliament shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Citizens, of E>p:mfite the City of Hereford, in Common Council assembled, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, " 01

That your Petitioners, considering the vast Sums of Public Money which have been lavished in a m >ft unfortunate and unlucceCsful War, sensibly affected thein-selves by the heavy and accumulated Taxes already laid upon the Subjects of this Kingdom (which are at prc-lent more fenlibly felt on Account of the Decline of Trade and Scarcity of money) and alarmed at the Idea that others may be shortly imposed, humbly request this honourable House to turn their most serious Attention to the diminished Resources and growing Burthens of these Kingdoms, by setting on Foot a Parliamentary Enquiry, whether, m these Times of general Dill rets a very large Sum may not be annually saved, by abolishing many useless Places and Sinecures, the Disposal of

which.

20 Geo. III. 8° — JMartii. 703

which, not only (as wc apprehend) occasions a great Waste of Public Treasure, but gives an unconftitu-tional Influence to the Ministers of the Crown throughout the Kingdom* anti whether the Salaries and Perquisites annexed to other Places (many of which are enor-mously great, and far exceeding an adequate Compensation for the Services performed) may not be most beneficially reduced; your Petitioners humbly conceive, that the Inrerposition of this honourable House in these Points, and its diligent Attention to a just and economical Expenditure of the Public Revenue, by Persons entrusted with it, may be productive of great National Good, and enable this Country, by properly directing and combining its Resources, to prevail over its most powerful Enemies; they therefore presume thus to address their Petition to this honourable House, assuring them that it does not in anywise originate from a Spirit of Party, but is dictated by the cleared Conviction that the present Situation of Affairs requires the Attention of every Man, and his honest and I'peedy Exertion of all possible Means to promote and defend the Public Weal.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Merchants and Traders of the City of London, trading to, and interested in, the Commerce carried on between Great Britain and the Imperial Dominions of the House of was presented

to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, in confer quence of an Act lately paired, against the pernicious Practice of Smuggling, there is a Clause inserted, which, affecting the Importation of low-priced Lace from Flanders, hath cauled the Court of to en-

quire into the Duties Flanders lace pays on its Entrance into Great Britain, which they finding to be 1 Sterling per Yard, in consequence, the Petitioners are informed, that the Imperial Court are meditating an heavy Duty on all the Manufactures of Great Britain, imported into the Imperial Dominions of the House of Austria-, and the Petitioners are also informed, that such an Alteration may be made in the said Law, as would be of great Advantage to the Revenue, a general Benefit to Trade, and destroy the pernicious Practice of smuggling that Article, and at the same Time be the Means of preventing the apprehended Evils from the Imperial Arrets, for the laying heavy Duties on the tish Manufactures: And therefore praying, That such Alterations may be made in the said Law, consistent with the general Interest of Great Britain, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Merchants and Manufacturers of the Town and Neighbourhood of Manchester, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners have received lundry Advices, that, in consequence of a late Act passed, against the pernicious Practice of Smuggling, there is a Clause which materially affects the Importation of low-priced Flanders Lace, the chief Article of Remittance to this Country in Return for the many Staple Articles exported hence; and representing to the House, that, if the said Law should continue in Force, it would prove very injurious to this and the adjacent Manufactures, on account of its Dependance on the great Trade carried on with the Dominions of the House of Austria: And therefore praying. That such Regulation in the Laws respecting Flanders Lace, may be made, as may be consistent with the Interest of this Country in general, and coincide with that of the Court of Brussels.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petitions, an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for the more effectually preventing the pernicious Practices of Smuggling in this Kingdom; and for indemnifying Persons who have been guilty of " Offences against the Laws of the Customs and Excise, upon the Terms therein mentioned," was read: And,

Edward Hague, Esquire, informed your Committee, That by the Laws now in Force, a Duty of Sixteen Pence per Yard is laid upon the Importation into this Kingdom of Foreign Thread Lace, of all Qualities, which, by the said recited Act, has been enforced — That the said Duty amounts to a Prohibition of the lower Sort of such Lace, being more than its real Value — That before the passing the said Act, this Duty upon Importation was evaded; the lower Sort of such Lac# has chiefly been consumed in England, being brought iu clandestinely; but by the Clauses in the said Act, that Practice cannot be continued — That the better Sort of such Lace could afford and did pay the Duty, or the Portage, which was equal to the Duty.

That the British Minister at Brussels has confirmed the Advices received by the Merchants concerned in the Flanders Trade, that the Imperial Court had premeditated a heavy Duty on all English Manufactures imported into their Dominions — That the British Exports of different Kinds imported into the Low Countries, amounts in Value to about per Annum;

and that the Value of the Importation of Foreign Thread Lace into this Kingdom, does not amount to Jt, 50,000 per Annum.

A Member present produced to your Committee, Letters from Court ray and G; stating thar the Imperial Ambassador had apprised the British Minister of the Determination of the Imperial Court, to lay a Duty of Sixteen Pence per Yard on all British Woollen Manufactures imported into the Low Countries, unless the Duty of Sixteen Pence per Yard upon Foreign Thread Lace imported into this Kingdom, be reduced. And,

Mr. Hague being again called, was of Opinion, That, if instead of the present Duties upon Foreign Thread Lace imported into this Kingdom, a Duty of Ten per Cent, ad valorem was laid, according to the different Species of Lace, the same would give a sufficient Security to the British Manufacturers, and would likewise give Satisfaction to the Imperial Court.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Electors, and other Inhabitants, paying 'Faxes to Government, reli-dent in the City and Liberty of Westminster, was prefer) ted to the House, and read; Setting forth, 'I hat this Nation hath been engaged for leve-ral Years in a most expensive and unfortunate War; that many of our valuable Colonies having actually declared themselves independent, have formed a llrict Confederacy with France and Spain, the dangerous and inveterate Enemies of Great Britain-, that the Consequence of those combined Misfortunes hath been a large Addition to the National Debt, a heavy Accumulation of Taxes, a rapid Decline of the Trade, Manufacture-, and Lands Rents of the Kingdom: Alarmed at tie diminished Resources and growing Burthens of this Country, and convinced that rigid Frugality is now inciif-penfably necessary irf every Department of the State, your Petitionersoblerve, with Grief, that, notwithstanding the calamitous and impoverished Condition of the Nation, much Public Money has been improvidcntly squandered, and that many individuals enjoy sinecure Places, efficient Places with exorbitant Emoluments, and Pensions unmerited by Public Service to a large, and (till increasing Amount, whence the Crown has acquired a great and unconstitutional Influence, which, if not checked, may soon prove fatal to the Liberties of this Country: Y©ur Petitioners, conceiving that the true End of every legitimate Government is not the Emolument of any Individual* but the Welfare of the Coril-munity, and considering that, by the Constitution of this Realm, the National Purse is entrusted in a peculiar Manner to the Custody of this honourable House, beg Leave further to represent that until effectual Measures be taken to redress the oppressive Grievances herein stated, the Grant of any additional Sum of Public Money, beyond the Produce of the present Taxes, will be injurious to the Rights and Property of the People, and derogatory from the Honour and Dignity of Parliament: Your Petitioners, therefore, appealing to the Justice of this honourable House, do most earnestly request, That, before any new Burthens are laid upon this Country, effectual Measures may be taken, by this lloule, to enquire into and correct, the gross Abuses in the Expenditure of Public Money, to reduce all exorbitant Emoluments; to refeind and abolish all sinecure Places and unmerited Pensions; and to appropriate the Produce to the Necessities of the State, in such Manner as to the Wifdotn of Parliament thall fcefli meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Prasfefes of Eighty-five Societies in Roman Glasgow, reprelcnting above Twelve thousand of His Catholic* Majesty’s loyal and well-affected Protestant Subjects, united in a Correspondence for the Defence of the Protestant Religion, was presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth, That the Petitioners, truly sensible of the many distinguished Blessings and Privileges which they as Protestants have enjoyed, since our happy and glorious Resolution, when thele Nations were freed frorp the Tyranny, Slavery, Arbitrary Power, and Perfection of the preceding Reigns, cannot but be deeply affected with any Attempt to infringe these Privilege? and Liberties so vvilely and firmly secured to us by the Laws of the Realm; and that the Petitioners were greatly alarmed at the Act lately passed in Favour of the Papists in England, by repealing certain Parts of the Penal Statutes, made in the Reign of King William ths Third, for preventing the Growth of Popery; and the more l'o, as they were certainly informed, and had the greatest Reason to fear, the same Indulgence was to be extended to Papilts in Scotland-, and that the Petitioners are convinced, that the Genius of Popery is still the fame, and that Papists only want Power put in their Hands 10 evince it; their Principle? jure pproicious,

their

Expenditure

of

\'>Mk Money.

724' 150 Martii. 1780.

their PraChce intolerant; and to grant them more Power in these Kingdoms than they formerly had by Law, is, the Petitioners apprehend, an Attempt to undermine our Protestant Constitution, to invade our Religious Liberties and Privileges, as Protestant Subjects, and may in the Issue be productive of the most direful Consequences to the Subjects, to the State, and even to His Majesty himself, in regard His Majesty’s Predecessors alcended the Throne of Britain in virtue of their being the nearest Heir of the Protestant Line, and He Himlelf sways the Sceptre merely on the Footing of His being a Protestant, and maintaining and defending the Protestant Religion, which He Hands engaged to do by his Coronation Oath; and that, though the Petitioners have Reason to be thankful that the Repeal of the Penal Statutes against Papists, have not extended to Scotland, yet they cannot but feel for their Protestant Brethren in England, who have already begun to experience the disagreeable Effects of their being repealed amongst them, as they have let forth in their Petition to this honourable House; and if the lnfolence of Papists, already begun to let up its Head, is hot timeously, checked, there is Ground to fear more dismal Scenes will yet open; and that the Petitioners are certain many of the People in Scotland, though they had official Assurance last Session of Parliament, that no Law was then to be made in Favour of Popery in that Kingdom, are not without their Fears, that, while the Law in Favour of Papists Hands unrepealed in some

future Period may be taken to grant an Indulgence to them in Scotland also, which if it should take Place, may be productive of introducing those bloody Scenes which were formerly exhibited amongst them: Wherefore, to disappoint their Fears, to prevent all those disagreeable Effects, to preserv our established Christian Liberties as Protestants, and to tecure the regal Succef-. fion in the illustrious Hanoverian Line, the Petitioners cordially join with their Protestant Brethren in England, in humbly praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to repeal the Act passed in the Eighteenth Year of His present Majesty, in Favour of the Roman Catholics in England.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and Freeholders, together with others paying Duties and Taxes, being Inhabitants of the County of Essex, Was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That 20

this Nation hath been engaged for several Years in a most expensive and unfortunate War; that many of our valuable Colonies, having actually declared thern-selves independent, have formed a ft rid Confederacy with France and Spain, the dangerous and inveterate Enemies of Great Britain; that the Consequence ofthofe combined Misfortunes hath been a large Addition to the National Debt, a heavy Accumulation of Taxes, a rapid Decline of the Trade, Manufactures, and Land Rents of the Kingdom: Alarmed at the diminished Resources and growing Burthens of this Country, and convinced that rigid Frugality is now indispensably necessary in every Department of the State, your Petitioners ob-. serve, with Grief, that, notwithstanding the calamitous and impoverished Condition of the Nation, much Public Money has been itnprovidently squandered, and that many Individuals enjoy finccure Places, efficient Places with exorbitant Emoluments, and Pensions unmerited by Public Service, to a large and ft ill increanng Amount, whence the Crown has acquired a great and unconditional Influence, which, if not checked, may soon prove fatal to the Liberties of this Country: Your Petitioners, conceiving that the true End of every legitimate Government is not the Emolument of Individuals, but the Welfare of the Community, and considering that, by the Constitution of this Realm, the National Purse is entrusted, in a pecuiiar Manner, to the Custody of this honourable House, beg Leave further to represent, that, until effectual Measures be taken to remove the oppressive Grievances herein dated, every Addition to' the present Taxes, will be injurious to the Rights and Property of the People, and derogatory from the Honour and Dignity of Parliament: Your Petitioners, therefore, appealing to the Justice of this honourable House, do most earnestly request, That towards lessening the Burthens laid upon this Country, effectual Measures may be taken by this House, to enquire into and correct any gross Abuses in the Expenditure of Public Money, to reduce all exorbitant Emoluments, to refeind and abolish all sinecure Places and unmerited Pensions, and to appropriate the Produce *0 the Ncceffities of the State, in such Manner as to the Wisdom of Parliament shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and Freeholders, of the County of was also presented to

the House, and read; Setting forth, That the many Burthens under which your Petitioners labour would be cheerfully borne, wrere they not attended with the Mortifying Reflection, that they are frequently misapplied, and enormously increased by a Multitude of extravagant Salaries, ufeicls Places, Sinecures, and Pensions, which serve at once to lessen the Respecc and Independence of Parliament, and take from Government a considerable Share of the Powers of carrying on the War against France and Spain with Decenary Vigour: Your Petitioners, therefore, humbly pray, and firmly hope, That this honourable House, in Discharge of the high Trust reposed in them, will take e fie dual Measures that the Supplies granted by Parliament may be faithfully and truly applied to the National Advantage, and to such Purposes only for which they were granted; that such Regulations may take Place as shall bring the Public Expenditures, and all unreasonable Contracts, to a speedy and ftrid Account; and that some Plan be adopted for the Reduction of all exorbitant Emoluments of Office, and the Abolition of all sinecure Places and unmerited Pensions, and thereby take away from present and future Ministers the Means of knpro*

?er Influence, detrimental to the Interests of the ’cople.

A Petition of the Commissioners acting under the Imprisonment Authority of a certain Act of Parliament, made and °^D^S passed in the Twenty-third Year of the Reign of his pCbtsUum. late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, "An Act for the more ealy and speedy Recovery of Spiall " Debts, within the Tower Hamlets," was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill to exempt from Imprisonment the Bodies of Defendants, liable to be imprisoned by Precepts, or other Process, issuing out of Courts erected by Acts of Parliament, for the more easy and speedy Recovery of Small Debts; and Setting forth. That, if the same should pass into a Law, the Petitioners apprehend the Court established by the said Act, will be rendered almolv useless, by reason, that the Creditor will be without Remedy, if no Goods belonging to the Debtor can be found, and by the fraudulent Practices that will consequently prevail to defeat Executions against the Goods, many Concealments, pretended Sales, and Protections from Landlords, under the Claim of a Year’s Rent; and that the small Credit of Forty Shillings, which the Petitioners apprehend the Legislature intended poor People by these Courts, will be totally destroyed, by reason of the Losses that Tradesmen must sustain, for want of an adequate Remedy for the Recovery of their Debts; and that Labourers and Artificers will be reduced to the great«ft Inconveniences and Hardships, for Want of a small Credit; and such of them as shall happen to fall lick, or be out of Employment, must starve, unless they obtain Parochial Relief, or are enabled to raise Money by the destructive Practice of Pawning; and that the Petitioners have observed, that the sober and industrious Poor are always able to pay their Debts, under the Indulgences granted by these Courts of Payment by Instalments, which are frequently limited to One Shilling a Month, and leldom exceed Five Shillings, according to the Abilities of the Debtor; and very few go to Prison, in comparison to the Number of Executions issued; and that, under the Powers vested in the Petitioners, by an Act passed in the Nineteenth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, they have taken up the Sum of f.yco, and intend to take up the further Sum of 800, which the said Act hath authorized them to raise for the Purposes therein mentioncdr

20 Geo. III. io°

upon the Grant cf Annuities for Lives, charged upon certain additional Fees of the said Court, established by the said Act, which Fees are found to produce no more Money than what is sufficient to secure the Payment of the said Annuities $ the Petitioners, therefore, apprehend, that if the said Bill palfes into a Law, the said Fees will be so reduced, that the said Annuitants will be nearly deprived of their Annuities: And therefore praying. That so much of the said Bill, as intends to exempt the Bodies of Debtors from being taken in Execution by the Process of the said Court, may not pat's into a Law; and that the Suitors of the said Court may continue to have the same Remedy for the Recovery of their Debts, as by Law they are now entitled.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time.
