A Petition, purporting to be a Memorial of His Majesty’s Justices assigned to keep tte Peace in the County of M'uidlesex, was presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth, That the said Justices observe, by the Votes, that a Petition hath been presented by William Smith, Doctor of Physic, Hating that Application having bce.i made to him, by Sir Charles Whitworth, to visit the Gaols and Prisons in London, Westminster, and Southwark, in order to administer Relief to the lick Pri-loners therein, in consequence thereof, he attended the said Gaols and Prisons from the 25th of March 1776 to the 10th of November 1779, with great Assiduity, by Means whereof the Lives of many Persons had been preserved that had no other Means to procure Medical Assistance; and that the Number of Sick in the Gaols aforesaid, under the Care of the said Wilfiam Smith, during the Period abovementioned, amounts to 1,051, and that, besides his Lot's of Time in visiting the said Gaols, and administering Relief to the lick Persons confined therein, an Expence has accrued to him of/. 566. ir. 3 d.for Medicines, over and above other contiderable Expences; and that it appears to the said Justices, by a Copy of a Report of a Committee of the House, that a Person named John Ridout had delivered in to the said Committee, an Account shewing the Number of Patients in each Gaol, together with the Expence of the Medicines administered to them by the Directions of the said William , amounting to /. 566, or thereabouts, adding, that the said William Smith attended the said several Gaols, daily, and sometimes Twice a Day, and, by his Skill and Management, the said Gaols, which were very full, the Number of sickly Prisoners therein was reduced, all which Particulars,' with others of less Importance, are stated in the Report abovementioned, and to which the said Justices crave Leave to refer; and that it also appears, by the Votes, that a Sutn, not exceeding One thousand Two hundred Pounds hath been granted to the said William Smith, in Recompence for his Attendance upon lick and diseased Prisoners in the several Goals aforesaid, for near Four Years last past, and for repaying to him the several Sums of Money by him expended in Medicines for such lick and diseased Persons; and further setting forth, that the said Justices have under their Government Two Prisons, namely, Newand Clerkeitwell Bridewell, and there are also others within the said County, which arc either Prisons or Franchises, or under l’ubordinatc Jurisdictions; that, with respect to the latter, they have examined the Keepers thereof, by whom they are informed, that the Pretensions of the said William Smith, respecting the fame, are groundless and fallacious, and more particularly and flagrantly so in the same of Whitechapel Prison, which the said William Smith pretends to have attended and sent Medicines to in like Manner with the other Gaols by him enumerated, for that the said Justices have been credibly informed that the said Prison, being situated nearly opposite to the London Hospital, the Keeper thereof, as often as any of the Prisoners confined therein have been sick or diseased, has applied to the said Hospital, and always had Assistance and Medicines from the same; and as to New Prison and Clerkenwell, they are constantly and duly attended by a skilful Surgeon and Apothecary, appointed under the late Act of Parliament, to whom the said Justices pay an ample Salary and Recompence for his Attendance on, and for Medicines administered to, the lick and diseased Prisoners confined therein; and that the said Justices are prepared to lay before the House such Evidence respecting the Prisons within this County, and of the State and Condition of the Persons confined therein during the Period abovementioned, as also of the Means uied by the said William Smith, to mislead the Public into an Opinion, that, by the Exertion of himself, great Benefits have resulted to the Prisoners

1780.

aforesaid, as cannot fail to convince the Members thereof, that the little Attendance he ever gave to any of the Prisons aforesaid, was needless and officious; that the Relief by him administered to those confined therein, if any, was very small and inconsiderable, and that his Pretentions to a Reward or Recompence for the lame, or a Satisfaction for Monies expended by him in Medicines, have scarce any Foundation in Truth and Justice.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Wood, ?clr. Alderman Wilkes, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records; and all, who come to the Committee, are to have Voices.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petitions, an Atfl, passed in the Seventeenth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for the more cafy and speedy Recovery of Small Debts within the Parishes of Halifax, Bradford, Right ex, and other Places therein-mentioned, in the County of York, was read: And,

William Lee being examined, said, That he was Gaoler of the Prison belonging to the Court of Requests at Halifax, for Eighteen Months, in the Year 1777 anc* lll8 — That Fifty-four Persons were committed in that Time, all of whom were committed for Three Months — That some of the Debts were as low as 3 s. 8 d. — That in Six of the Warrants of Commitments, there were Orders not to let the Prisoners have any Work in the Gaol — That lie applied to one of the Commissioners respecting the Order, but could not obtain Red refs — That he then applied to the Friends of the Prisoners, and to the Towns to which they belonged, for Relief for the Prisoners, but could not obtain any; he then applied to a Justice of the Peace, and finding he could not get any Relief, he was at length obliged to supply them with Provisions himself, otherwise they would have been llarved — That he had Orders to keep the Prisoners close locked up — That he expended about Eleven Pounds in the Relief of the Prisoners, which has never been repaid to him — That the Men becoming riotous, a Pair of Handcuffs and the Key of the Hole was lent to him — That when the Men had Work they behaved well — That One of the Prisoners, who was a lickly Man, and had a Wile and Two Children, being upwards ot Seven Weeks out of Work, was al-1110ft starved, to prevent which, he lent him Money to buy Provisions, which were bought for him at the Town — That he was advised to summon the Man to the Court for the Amount of the Money he had so advanced him, which he did; and represented to the Commissioners the Circumstances of the Cafe, and extreme Poverty and Distress of the Man and his Family, upon which the Commissioners made an Order for Payment of the Money by Instalments.

"That a Woman of upwards of 80 Years of Age, being committed for a Debt of 135. 3 d. besides 5^. io d. Colls, after buffering an Imprisonment of Three Months, was ordered to be discharged upon Payment of 5;. for Gaol Fees, which being paid, 1 s. 8 cl. was

Then

Silas Hainsworth being examined, said, That he was

committed a Prisoner in Execution at Bradford, for a Debt of £. 1. 19 s. n d. That he remained in Prison from the 16th January 1779 to 16th April following, when he was discharged upon paying his Gaol Fees — That he is a Clothier by Trade — That he w-as put into a Room under Ground, called The Breaking School — That it was a nasty (linking Hole, without Glass to the Window's — That they put all the Prisoners there at first, in order to fee if they will pay the Debts. — That he was locked up in that Room for Three Week', without being suffered to go out — That there was a Closet in the Room, which was used as a Necessary, and which was Six Weeks all but Two Days without being once cleansed — That he found himself much affected by the Smell, and complained daily — That Four other Persons were confined with him, One of whom (James Smith) died; that he found him dead by him — That the Water they were supplied with was nasty and (linking, notwithstanding which they were obliged to pay Eight Pence per Week (or it — That there is no Fire allowed — That they had a wooden Bed, but no Bed Cloaths — That about Ten or Twelve, and sometimes 15 or 16 Persons, were confined in Prison at a Time while he was there — That he has a Wife and Five Children, which he supported without any Aflifiance before he was sent to Prison — That after his Commitment, his Family had an Allowance of 6j.a Mont!) from the Parish — That he had $s. towards his W ife’s Lying-in, but has had nothing since — That he has known many Families reduced in the like Manner — That the Prisoners were in general unhealthy while he was in Prison — That Three young Women were committed for Three Months, for a joint Debt of 5 6d.;

and when they were discharged they were obliged to leave a Pair of Stays for the Gaol Fees.

William Sutcliffe being then examined, said, That he was committed to Prison for a Debt of 9 r. on tlle 19th July 1779, and was discharged on the 19th October — That about Fourteen or Fifteen Persons were in general in Prison while he was there — That he remembers a Person who was committed for Three Months for a Debt of 1 s. 6 d. — That there were 16 Persons in Prison at one Time, who were the Parents of 68 Children, and whole Debts, altogether, amounted to about £. 15 — That there were at another Period 15 Persons confined in Prison, who were the Parents of 73 Children, and whole Debts amounted to 17. — That the

Prison is unhealthy, and the Prisoners frequently fub-ject to Fevers; and that he had one himself whilst he was there.

That there is no Fund for providing a Gaol, in case Imprisonment shall be allowed; nor is there any Fund for supporting tire Sick, or such as shall be unable to maintain themselves when confined.

That in calc of an Elcape the Plaintiff has no Remedy.

That in case the Goods are taken and fold upon Execution, the Charges are in no respect limited; nor is the Return of the Overplus to the Party, or the Con-dud of the Officers thereupon, sufficiently provided and guarded against.

That the Conirwissioners have no Power to reduce the Fees*, which are, in fume Cafes, very exorbitant and oppressive, and frequently exceed the original Debt.

That the Clerk is not chosen annually, but appointed to hold his Onice during good Behaviour; and in case of his Removal, there is no Power to compel him to give up the Books, or pay over the Money remaining in his Hands.

That the Qualification of the Commissioners is much too low.

That if the Powers of the Court did not extend to Debts contracted at Alehouses, it might be a Means of preventing Drunkenness and Dissipation.

That Persons rclident within the Jurisdiction of the Court, are obliged to attend on Subpoenas, under a Penalty, although their Expences are not tendered to them — That Witnesses are frequently obliged to travel i 5 or i 6 Miles.

That there is no Power in the Commissioners to charge the Plaintiff with Costs, when improper Credit has been given, or on any other Account.

Pengturc The Petition of the Mayor, Burgesses, principal In-Montyl<* habitants, and Freeholders, of the Town and County of Sezvcqflie upon Tyne, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That this Nation has been engaged for several Years in a most expensive and unfor-tunare War; that many of our valuable Colonies have actually declared themselves independent, have formed a drift Confederacy with France and Spain, the dangerous and inveterate Enemies of Great Britain; that the VOL. 37.

Consequence of these combined Misfortunes hath been a large Addition to the National Debt, a heavy Accumulation of Taxes, a rapid Decline of the Trade, Manufactures, and Land Rents of the Kingdom: Alarmed at the diminished Resources and growing Burthens of this Country, and convinced that rigid Frugality is now indispensably necessary in every Department of the State, your Petitioners observe, with Grief, that, notwithstanding the Calamities, and impoverished Condition, of the Nation, much Public Money has been improvidently squandered, and that many Individuals enjoy sinecure Places, efficient Places with exorbitant Emoluments, and Pensions unmerited by Public Service, to a large and still increasing Amount; Your Petitioners, therefore, appealing to the Justice of this honourable House, do moll earnestly request. That speedy and effectual Measures may be taken, by this House, to enquire into, and correct, the gross Abuses in the Expenditure of Public Money, to reduce all exorbitant Emoluments, to refeind and abolish all sinecure Places and unmerited Pensions, and to appropriate the Produce to the Necessities of the State, in such Manner as to this honourable House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and Freeholders, of the County of Y, and several other Petitions, are referred.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards railing the Supply granted to His Majesty, an Additional Duty ot Three Pence per Bushel be charged upon all Malt which shall be brought tro:n Scotland into England, Wales, or the Town of Berwick upon Tweed, and so in Proportion for any greater oriel’s Quantity.

Yearly, Monthly, or at any other Interval of Time, exceeding One Week, over and above all other Rates and Duties now imposed thereon, there be charged an additional Duty of Six Pence.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

Thar, for every Skin, or Piece of Vellum or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which any Receipt, or other Discharge, for any Legacy, left by any Will, or other Testamentary Instrument, or for any Share or Part of a Personal Estate, divided by Force of the Statute of Distributions, or the Custom of any Province or Place, shall be ingrossed, written, or printed, the Amount whereof shall not exceed the Value of Twenty Pounds, a Stamp Duty ot Two Shillings and Six Pence; and where the Amount thereof shall be of the Value of Twenty Pounds, and not amounting to One hundred Pounds, a Stamp Duty of Five Shillings, and where the Amount thereof 111 all be of the Value ot One hundred Pounds, and upwards, a Stamp Duty of Twenty Shillings, be charged thereon.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, there shall be raised, levied, and paid, by all and every Person and Persons dealing in, or vending. Coffee,

Tea, and Chocolate, or either of them, throughout the Kingdom of Great Britain, for a Licence to be taken out by each and every such Person or Persons, Annually, the Sum of Five Shillings.

The laid llesolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill, or Bills, be brought in, upon the said Resolutions: And that Mr. Ord, the Lord North, the Lord Beauchamps Mr. Cornwall, the Lord Wefcote, the Lord Palmerfion, Mr. Attorney General,

Mr. Solicitor General, Sir Grey Cooper, and Mr. Rob inf on, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Expenditure A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and Frec-Mone>*'C holders, of the County of Denbigh, whose Names are thereunderwritten, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth: We think it our Duty as Britons, and in Compliance with the general Sense of the whole Kingdom, to petition the honourable House of Commons, to enquire with all Diligence and Fidelity into the Disposal of those enormous Sums which, in virtue of the Trulls reposed in them by the People, they have lately granted, or shall grr.nt in future, to Government: The universal Calamines, which not only affect the Public, but find their Way into esrery private Family, even at this Distance from the Seat of Government, are a Proof how little we are able to support the Weight of Ministerial Profusion, which every Year grows heavier, and is more severely felt: We therefore moll llrongly make it our Request and Petition to this honourable House, as to the upright Reptefentatives of their Fellow Citizens, to abolish all Sinecures, to retrench all unmerited Pensions, to link all unnecessary Places, and to reduce all exorbitant Salaries and Perquisites, that, in our State of National Poverty, what is left of, the Public Revenue, may be frugally managed. We own, too, we have a Motive in this Petition, beyond the Views of CEconomy; we wish to lessen, by all possible Means, those Funds of Corruption, which good Mi-nifters never want, and which only make bad Men more worthless and dangerous: We wish that our Represen-tativ’es may secure to themselves the Confidence of the People, by having no interest separate from theirs; and we flatter ourselves, that our Petition has a just Title to the Approbation of this honourable House, since, by granting it, they will vindicate their own Integrity, and qualify themselves for those great disinterested Views and Measures which may possibly become necessary to lave our Country.

of the County of Cumberland, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That this Nation hath been engaged for several Years in a most expensive and . unfortunate War; that many of our valuable Colonies,

having actually declared themselves independent, have formed a ftriift Confederacy with France and Spain, the dangerous and inveterate Enemies of Great Britain; that the Consequence of these combined Misfortunes hath been a large Addition to the National Debt, a heavy Accumulation of Taxes, a rapid Decline of the Trade, Manufactures, and Land Rents of the Kingdom: Alarmed at thediminished Resources and growing Burthens of this Country, and convinced, that rigid Frugality is now indispensably necessary in every Department of the State, your Petitioners observe, with Grief, that, notwithstanding the Calamities, and impoverished Condition of the Nation, much Public Money has been improvidently squandered, and that many Individuals enjoy sinecure Places, efficient Places VoL. 37.

with exorbitant Emoluments, and Pensions unmerited by Public Service, to a large and Hill increasing Amount: Your Petitioners, therefore, appealing to the Justice of this honourable House, do most earnestly request, That foeedy and effectual Measures may be taken by this House, to enquire into and correct the gross Abuses in the Expenditure of Public Money, to reduce all exorbitant Emoluments, to refeind and abo-liiffi all sinecure Places and unmerited Pensions, and to appropriate the Produce to the Necessities of the State, in such Manner as to the Wisdom of Parliament shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Nobility, Gentry, Clergy, and Expenditure Freeholders, of the County of Buckingham, was also of Public presented to the House, and read ;. Setting forth. That this Nation hath been engaged for several Years in a most expensive and unfortunate War; that many of our valuable Colonies, having actually declared themselves independent, have formed a Uriel Confederacy with France and Spain, the dangerous and inveterate Enemies of Great Britain; that the Consequence of these combined Misfortunes hath been a large Addition to the National Debt, a heavy Accumulation of Taxes, a rapid Decline of the Trade, Manufactures, and Land Rents, of the Kingdom: Alarmed at the diminished Resources and growing Burthens of this Country, and convinced that rigid Frugality is now indispensably necessary in every Department of the State, your Petitioners observe, with Grief, that, notwithstanding the calamitous and impoverished Condition of the Nation, much Public Money has been improvidently squandered, and that many Individuals enjoy sinecure Places, efficient Places with exorbitant Emoluments, and Pensions unmerited by Public Service,: to a large and still increasing Amount, whence the Crown has acquired a great and Influence, which, if not checked, may soon prove fatal to the Liberties of this Country: Your Petitioners, conceiving that the true End of every legitimate Government is not the Emolument of any Individual, but the Welfare of the Community, and considering that by the Constitution of this Realm, the National Purle is intruded, in a peculiar Manner, to the Custody of this honourable House, beg Leave further to represent, that, until effectual Measures be taken to redress the oppressive Grievances herein dated, the Grant of any additional Sum of Public Money, beyond the Produce of the present Taxes, will be injurious to the Rights and Property of the People, and derogatory from the Honour and Dignity of Parliament: Your Petitioners, therefore, appealing to the Justice of this honourable House, do most earnestly request. That, before any new Burthens are laid upon this Country, effectual Measures may be taken by this House, to enquire into and correct the gross Abuses in the Expenditure of Public Money, to reduce all exorbitant Emoluments, to refeind and abolish all sinecure Places and unmerited Pensions, and to appropriate the Produce to the Necessities of the State, in such Manner as to the Wisdom of Parliament shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Tradesmcn and Manufacturers reading in the Hundreds of Blackheath, of Bromley and Beckenham, of Ruxley, and Little and in the County of Kent, and of the Hundred of Wallington, in the County of Surrey, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Court established by the Acts of the Fifth and Sixth Years of His present Majesty’s Reign, for the more easy and speedy Recovery of Small Debts in the said Hundreds, has been of great Utility to Artificers and Labourers, as well as to the Tradelincn and Manufacturers residing within the said Difhifts, the former being protected from the excessive Expences to which they were subject by Suits for Small Debts in the Superior Courts, and the Danger of perpetual Imprisonment for the fame, and the latter relieved from the many Lodes they formerly sustained for Want of an adequate Remedy for the Recovery of fuel) Debts; and taking Notice of the Bill to exempt from Imprisonment the Bodies of Defendants, liable to be im-prisoned by Precepts, or other Process, ilfuing out of Courts erected by Acts of Parliament, for the more easy and speedy Recovery of Small Debts; and alledging, that, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, the Petitioners apprehend the intended good Purposes of the said Court will be, in great Measur, prevented from taking Effect, by real'on the Creditor will be without a Remedy where no Goods belonging to the Debtor can be found, which is most frequently the Cafe, and where any are found they are claimed by the Landlord, or, if taken away by either of such Means, the unhappy Defendant and Family are frequently left without a Bed, whereas the Terror of a Gaol being held out to them, they most commonly submit to the Direction of the Court to pay their Debts by Instalments, which are always proportioned by the Court to the Debtor’s Civeum-stances and weekly Earnings, which Indulgence enables the Sober and Industrious Poor to avoid an Execution, and those who are willing, and by their Industry endeavour 10 maintain their Familes, and pay their Debts, are neither subjad to Imprisonment, or any other Hard-ship under the Process of the said Courts; and that the Poorer Sort of People cannot always support themselves VOL. 37.

and Families without the Assistance of a small weekly Credit, particularly in Cafes of Sickness or Want of Employment: And therefore praying, That the said Bill, for exempting the Bodies of Defendants from being taken in Execution, upon Process issuing out of the Court of Requests, may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed.

Expenditure A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and Free-of. holders, of the County of Brecknock, whose Names are Money thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read j Setting forth. That your Petitioners considering the very great Sums of Public Money lavished in a truly unfortunate and unsuccessful War, sensibly affected themselves by the heavy and accumulated Taxes already laid upon the Subjects of this Kingdom (now grievously felt by the Decline of Trade, Fall of Rents, and Scarcity of Money) and alarmed at the Idea that others may be shortly imposed, humbly request this honourable House to turn its most serious Attention to the diminished Resources and growing Burthens of these Kingdoms, by setting on Foot a Parliamentary Enquiry, whether (in thel'e Times of general Distress) a very large Sum may not be annually saved by abolishing many useless Places and Sinecures, the Disposal whereof (as we apprehend) not only occasions great Waste of Public Treasure, but also gives an unconstitutional Influence to the Ministers of the Crown throughout the Kingdom; and whether the Salaries of efficient Places, many of which are enormously great, and far exceeding an adequate Compensation for the Services performed, may not be beneficially reduced: Your Petitioners humbly conceive, that the Intcrposition of this honourable House in these Points, and its diligent Attention to a just and (Economical Expenditure of the Publie Revenue by Persons intrusted with it, will be productive of National Good, and, by properly combining and directing its Resources, enable this Country to prevail over its most powerful Enemies: They, therefore, thus humbly address themselves to this honourable House, with the most solemn Assurance that they are in no Degree actuated by a Spirit of Party, but by the clearest Con-3

viction of their Minds, that the present Situation of Affairs requires the Attention of every Man, and his honest and speedy Exertion of all possible Means to promote the Public Weal.

Setting forth. That your Petitioners considering the vast Sums of Money which have been expended, as well as the great Increase of the National Debt, occasioned by the present most unfortunate War, and being sensibly affected by the heavy Load of Taxes already laid on the Subjects of this Kingdom, and apprehensive that others must soon be imposed, humbly request this honourable House seriously to turn their Attention to the diminiffied Resources and growing Burthens of this Country: Your Petitioners conceive, that, in this Time of National Distress, it will be necessary, as much as possible, to alleviate the Public Burthens, by abolishing sinecure and useless Places, and reducing the exorbitant Salaries and Perquisites annexed to others, the Disposal of which not only occasions a great Waste of Public Treasure, but gives an unconstitutional Power to the Ministers of the Crown: Your Petitioners humbly conceive, that the Interposition of this honourable House in these Points, and a diligent Annual Examination into the Expenditure of the Public Money, must be productive of great National Good, and enable this Country, by properly directing and combining its Resources, to prevail over its most powerful Enemies: They esteem it their Duty, therefore, to address this honourable House, hoping, that the reasonable Request of this Petition will be taken into their most serious Consideration.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and Freeholders of the County of Derby, was also presented to the House, and read; Setring forth, That the many Burthens under which your Petitioners and the Kingdom in general now labour, would be less grievous were they not attended with the mortifying Reflection that the Grants of Parliament are shamefully misapplied, and have been enormously increased by extravagant and unmerited Pensions, Sinecures, and inefficient Places, which serve to no Purpose but to lessen the llespect and Independence of Parliament, and to deprive Government, in a considerable Degree, of the Powers of carrying on tire War against our natural Enemies with the necessary Vigour: The Decrease of our Commerce, the Fall of Rents, the Distress of our Manufacturers, are Evils which every Individual must feel, who is not loft to all Sense of his own Situation, and to all Feeling of the common Calamity; and these Evils, we apprehend, can only be remedied by a careful Attention to the Public Treasure: Your Petitioners, therefore, appealing to the Justice of this honourable House, do most earnestly request (both for the Relief of the Subject, and the Security of the Constitution) That such Measures may be taken, that the Supplies granted by Parliament may be faithfully applied to the National Advantage, and to such Purposes only for which they were granted; that such Regulations may take place as shall bring the Public Expenditures, and all unreasonable Contracts, to a fipeedy and Uriel Account; and that an effectual Plan may be adopted, for the Reduction of all exorbitant Emoluments, and the Abolition of all sinecure Places, and unmerited Pensions; that the present and alt future' Ministers may, by such Means, be deprived of tlje Power of improper Influence, fatally detrimental to the Interests of the People.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and Freeholders of the County of Cambridge, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That your Petitioners do thus publicly profess their entire and zealous Approbation of the Legislature of this Country, as placed in the free and independent Concurrence of King, Lords, and Commons, in Preference to every other Mode of Civil Government; that they anxiously wish the Blessing of this Form of Legislation to be continued to their latest Posterity, in its constitutional Purity; that they seriously apprehend this Form of Legislation will be essentially vitiated, if not virtually changed, whenever the Treasure and Offices of the Community shall be successfully employed to bring the Representatives of the People under the Influence of the Executive Power; that they conceive a strong Tendency to this Change is at present, and has been formerly, too notorious to admit of Doubt, or to require Proof; that they consider any System of public Administration, carried on by Means of Parliamentary Corruption, however fane-tified by Time, Precedent, or Authority, to be absolutely unjustifiable on every Principle of good Sense and found Policy, to be as dishonourable to the upright Intentions of the Crown, as it is burthensome to the Property and dangerous to the Liberty of the People: Your Petitioners do therefore most solemnly apply themselves to the Wisdom, the Justice, the Integrity of this honourable House, praying, That effectual Measures may be taken by this House, to enquire into and correct any gross Abuses in the Expenditure of Public Money, to reduce ail exorbitant Emoluments of Office, to refeind and abolish all sinecure Places and unmerited Pensions, and to use all such other constitutional Means as may tend toestablish the Independency of Parliament on the most Lifting Foundation: And your Petitioners are the more earned in this their Prayer, because they are of Opinion, that no other Expedient can equally tend to heal our internal Divisions, to unite the whole Nation in the warmed Support of His Majesty’s Per Ion and Government, against the unprovoked Hostilities of the House of Bourbon, and to put a final Period to that primary Source of National Distress, the American War. j A Petition of the Nobility, Gentlemen, Clergy, Freeholders, and Land Owners, of the County of Suffolk, was also presented to the House, and read; A Petition of the Gentlemen, Tradesmen, Manufac- Imprison-turers, and Artificers, whose Names arc thereunto sub- ,

feribed, residing within the City and Liberty of Westminster, and that Part of the Duchy of which Courts,

adjoineth thereto, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Court established by an Act of the Twenty-third Year of King George the Second, for the more easy and speedy Recovery of Small Debts within the City and Liberty of Westminster, and that Part of the Dutchy of Lancaster which adjoineth thereto, has been found by Experience to be of the greatest Utility to all Persons, Debtors as well as Creditors, for small Sums, residing within the Jurisdiction thereof; and by the said A Cl no Person can be im-prisoned, upon an Execution, for a longer Space than Forty Days; and that Credit for small Sums is in general exceedingly necessary, more especially to those of the lower Clals of People, who, from occasional Want of Employment, Sickness, or other Accidents, would not, unless by such Credit, be able to supporf. themselves and Families, but niuft of Necessity become burthenlbme to their Parishes; and that the good EffeCls of Credit for small Sums, in Trade, by far overbalance any bad Consequences which arise therefrom; and that, if the Bill, now depending, to exempt from Imprisonment the Bodies of Defendants, liable to be imprisoned by Precepts, or other Process, issuing out of Courts erected by Acts of Parliament, for the more easy and speedy Recovery of Small Debts, should pass into a Law, the Petitioners apprehend a total Stop will be put to ffich Credit for small Sums, Trade will be thereby very much decreased, and the poorer Peojfle will experience very great Hardships for Want thereof: And therefore praying. That the said Bill may not be passed into a Law, and that the Petitioners may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill.

A Petition of the several Manufacturers, Tradesmen, Shopkeepers, and Dealers, within the Town and Borough of Southwark, and adjoining Parishes, was pre-

fented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill to exempt from Imprisonment the Bodies of Defendants, liable to be imprisoned by Precepts, or other Process, issuing out of Courts erected by Acts of Parliament, for the more easy and speedy Recovery of Small Debts; and Setting forth, That Two Acts passed in the Twenty-second and Thirty-fecood Years of the Reign of King George the Second, for the more easy and speedy Recovery of Small Debts, in the Borough of,

and several Parishes and Places therein mentioned, the Commissioners for executing which Acts are chosen annually, by the Vestries of the several Parishes and Places, out of the most respedable of their Inhabitants; and that the said Acts have been of great Use, by promoting and encouraging useful Credit amongst the lower ClaTs of People, who otherwise could by no Means provide properly for themselves and Families; and that the Power of imprisoning is not made an ill Use of, very few having been imprisoned under the said Acts, and the Petitioners have always considered the Power of committing, to be a Punishment, held out to deter Persons from endeavouring to avoid paying their Debts, rather than to be executed upon them, and apprehend it may fairly be concluded to have had that Effect, from the very small Number of Persons annually committed; and that the Petitioners apprehend, the taking away the Terrors of a Gaol, will, in great Measure, if not totally, defeat the good Intention of the Legislature, in passing the said Acts of the Twenty-second and Thirty-second Years of his said late Majesty: And therefore praying. That the District of Parishes and Places included in the said Acts, may be exempted from the Provisions of the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Coelideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Traders, am! other Inhabitants of the Borough o{ K Lynn and the Liber-' ties thereof, in ttie County of was presented to

the House, and read; Also taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, That an Act passed in the Tenth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for the more easy and speedy Recovery of Small Debts, within the Borough of King's Lynx and the Liberties thereof; the Execution whereof hath been found to produce all the salutary Effects that were intended by it, by supporting Credit amongst (lie lower Sort of Traders and Inhabitants, and by providing an effectual Remedy for the Recovery of Small Debts; and that the Petitioners do not know of any instance of the Powers given to the Commissioners of the said Court having been perverted, or made subservient to the Purposes of Injustice or Oppression; and that the Number of Persons who have been committed in Execution under the said Act, is very final! in Proportion to the Number of Persons who have paid the Debts which have been adjudged to be due from them by Decrees of the said Court, there not having been more than Six Persons imprisoned under the said Act since the Commencement thereof, and there have been One thousand Four hundred and Sixty-six Cauies heard and determined by the Commissioners, who very feLdom make Orders for poor Persons to pay then Debts at a higher Rate than Six Pence or One Shilling per Week, and often for Three Pence or Four Pence; and seldom award Execution against the Bodies of the Defendants, except in Cafes where it is alledged by rite Plaintiff that the Defendants hare no Goods, or have removed them to avoid their being taken in Execution; and the said Coramifliorers have not Power under the said Act* to commit for any longer Time, than Three Months; and that the Petitioners are apprehend-

*7

five, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, that tl»e Provisions made by the said Act of the Tenth Year of His present Majesty, would be rendered very ineffectual for the Purposes for which it was made, the Fear of Ira-prisonment having produced a greater Reform than the Seizure of Goods, which is the greatest Distress to Families: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, or that they may have such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Tradesmen, and Manufactures, residing in the Tower Hamlets, was also presented to the House, and read; likewise taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth. That the Court established by an Act, made in the Twenty-third Year of the Reign of King George the Second, for the more easy and speedy Recovery of Small Debts in the Tower Hamlets, commonly called The Court of Requests, has been found of the greatest Utility to Artificers and Labourers, as well as to the Tradesmen residing in the said District, the former being thereby protested from the excessive Expences to which they were subject by Suits for small Debts in the superior Courts, and the Danger of an unlimited Imprisonment for the fame, and the lattev relieved from the many Losses they formerly luf-tained, for Want of an adequate Remedy for the Recovery of such Debts; and that, if the said Bill palfes into a Law', the Petitioners apprehend the said Court would be rendered ahnoft useless, by reason the Creditor would be without Remedy, where no Goods belonging to the Debtor can be found, which would generally be the Cafe, through the fraudulent Practice that mult confe* questly prevail, of Concealments, pretended Sales, and Protections from Landlords for a Year’s Rent, so that the useful Credit which Tradesmen give poor People under Confidence of the Remedy in this Court, for the Recovery of their Debts, would be totally destroyed; and that Artificers and Labourers cannot support themselves and Families without the Assistance of a small Credit, particularly when lick, or in Want of Employment, so that if they arc stripped of Credit, they most consequently become burthensome to the Pariftj after their little Property is exhausted by the destructive Practice of Pawning; and that the great Moderation, practised in the said Court of Requests, by indulging the Debtors with Time to pay their Debts by Install meats, in very Itxiall Sums, according to their Abilities, enables the sober and industrious Poor to avoid the Coercion of an Execution, so that the Power of taking the Body in Execution under the Process of this Court, only affects the idle and dissolute Part of the People, and becomes a Punishment for those Faults which are the foie Cause of their Neglects: And therefore praying. That the fold Bill may not pass into a Law, and that the Suitors of the said Court may continue to have the tame Remedy for the Recovery of their Debts, as by Law they are now entitled.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Tradesmen, Manufacturers, and Artificers, within the Borough of Derby, in the County of Derby, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That by an Act, passed in the Sixth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for the more easy and speedy Recovery of Small Debts, within the Borough of Derby, and the Liberties thereof, the Petitioners, and other Inhabitants witliih the said Borough, have reaped great Advantages, by being able, at a small Expence, to recover Debts under Forty Shillings and that, previous to the obtaining of the said Act, great Numbers of People, employed in Throwing of Silk, Wool-combing, and Framework-knitting, frequently contrafted Debts under Forty Shillings in the said Borough, which in the Whole amounted Yearly to a large Sum of Money, and although well able to pay the feme, yet they refused, prduming on the

A Petition of the Mayor, Sheriffs, Citizens, and Commonalty, of the City of Norwich, in Common Council assembled, and also of the Governor, Deputy Governor, Assistants, and Guardiaps of the Poor in the said City and County of Norwich, and Liberties of the fame, was all'o presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That a very considerable and extensive Manufactory is carried on in the said City, in which many Thousand Poor are employed; and that, for the Eal'e of the lower Set of People, necessarily requiring Credit to be given them, as well in Times of Sickness as during a Scarcity of Employment, an Act was obtained in the Twelfth and Thirteenth of King William the Third, for Recovery of Small Debts within the said City, which has been attended with great Advantage, as well to the Poor as to the Persons giving them Credit during the Times of such Sickness or Want of Employment; and the Petitioners conceive, that, if the Bill, now depending before the House, should pals into a Law, by which the Power given by the said Act of imprisoning the Persons of Debtors for Small Debts, shall be absolutely taken away, it will be attended with great Dilad vantage to the labouring Poor of the City of Norwich, by putting an End to the Credit usually given to them in such Times of Sickness or Want of Employment, and will inercafe the Poor Rates of the said City (already very burthensome) to a Degree which the middling Ranks of Tradesmen will be totally unable tosupport; And therefore praying, That the Bill now depending in the House, to eXenipt from Imprisonment the Bodies of Defendants liable to be imprisoned by Precepts, or other Process, idling out of Courts erected by Acts of Parliament, for the more easy and speedy Recovery of Small Debts,’may not pass into a Law.

- Icribed, for and cn Behalf of themselves and other Merchants and Traders of the said City, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill to explain and amend an Act, passed in the Thirty-second-Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, "An Act for Relief of Debtors, with

- ", rei pc ft to the Impril'onment of their Persons; and " to ohlicre Debtors, who shall continue in Execution in Prison beyond a certain Time, and for Sums not exceeding what arc mentioned in the Ad, to make Discovery of, and deliver upon Oath, their Estates for " their Creditors Benefit;" And letting forth. That it appears to the Petitioners, that the Objects of the said Bill, as well as the Provi lions thereof, are of the most dangerous and pernicious Tendency, not only to the Ln-terest of the Petitioners and other Individuals, but will also greatly lessen. the Confidence and Security of Creditors, increase their LoiTes, multiply Frauds in Debtors, give unjust Preferences, and cauiett great Stagnation to all inland Trade, to the Distress and lluin of many innocent and industrious Families j and in particular the Clause contained in the said- Bill, which impowers the Court, or Judges, or JuRices, to dilebarge any Prisoner; confined in Execution for Debt, notwithstanding the.

Creditor fliull infill on Lia being detained in Piiidn, and shall be ready to make the Allowance mentioned in the Bill; and the Clause, by virtue of which any Prisoner confined for Debt for Want of Bail, is to be discharged from Imprisonment upon making Affidavit of his not being worth Five Pounds, ur.leis the Creditor agrees to support him in Prilcn, will be highly injurious to the fair Trader, and, the Petitioners apprehend, destructive of the internal Commerce and Credit of the Kingdom: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, or, at least, that such Parts of the said Bill, which empower the Court, or Judges, or Justices, to dilebarge any Prisoner confined in Execution for Debt, notwithstanding the Creditor shall infill on his being detained in Prison, and shall be ready to make the Allowance mentioned in the Bill, and under which any Prisoner Confined lor Debt for Want of Bail, is to be discharged from Imprisonment upon making Affidavit of his not being worth Five Pounds, may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report which was made from the Committee, to whom the said Bill was committed, be taken into further Confederation.

A Petition of the Prisoners confined for Debt in The King sBench, Fleet, Poultry Compter, and Borough

Compter, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners find themselves bound by the Ties of Gratitude, to exert their utmost Endeavours to wipe off the unjust Odium that has been throum on Doctor William Smith, by a Memorial presented from the Justices of the Peace for the County of;

and that the Petitioners are actuated by Motives of Justice to declare, that Doctor Smith, for Four Years part, has paid unremitted Attention to all unfortunate People in Confinement, who have been affhded with Sickness, in the most dangerous Complaints, great Numbers of whom must inevitably have perished, had they not been humanely and regularly attended by him and his Assistant, and furnished with all Medical Necessaries; and not only those now labouring under Imprisonment, but some Hundreds discharged, would have been exposed to great Misery, without his Profellior.al Skill and singular Care; and that the Petitioners venture to aver, no Medical Person whatever has attended them in their various illnesses but Doctor nor have they had

any other Relource when such AfHidions have befallen them, and on all such Occasions he hasheen applied to, and punctually attended; and that-the Petitioners are fully convinced, he must have expended considerable Sums of Money in Medicines for great Numbers he has attended in lingering Disorders, who have been daily supplied for a long Time together; and that the Petitioners sincerely lament such invidious Steps have been taken to deprive them of Doctor Smith's Advice and Assistance, as it might prevent him in future from rendering them thele Services in the Hour of their Calamity: And that, as the Petitioners are deprived of those Benefits which Society and Freedom would entitle them unto, and as great Numbers afflicted with Disease consequeiuly must perish without Physical Aid, they humbly hope so valuable and humane a Benefactor as Doctor Smith, through ill-founded Prejudices and Mif-representations, will not be discontinued to them.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition, purporting to be a Memorial of His Majesty’s Justices assigned to keep the Peace in the County of Middlesex, is referred: And that they do examine the Matter of this Petition; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

That the Petitioners conceive, that the Mode of opening the Ports of this Kingdom, for the Importation and Exportation of Grain, as prescribed and regulated by the Laws now in being, is liable to much Abuse, whereby the Prices of Grain, in some Instances, are unnecessarily depressed, to the Discouragement of Agriculture, and in others unnecessarily advanced, to the Injury of Manufactures and Oppression of the Poor, and that the Temptation to such Abuse has been considerably increated by the Provisions of an Act, passed in the Thirteenth Year of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act to regulate the Importation and Exportation of Corn," and may, as the Petitioners apprehend, be prevented or restrained by proper Amendments of the said Act: And therefore praying. That the House will grant such Relief in the Premises, as the Nature of the Cale may require, and to the House shall seem proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of several Gentlemen, Merchants, Manu- Halifax, fasturers, Traders, Landowners, and others, Inhabitants &c. of Halifax, Bradford, Kigh/ey, Bingley, and other Parishes Small and Places within the West Riding of the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That an Act was passed in the Seventeenth Ye.r of His present Majesty’s Reign, for the more easy and speedy Recovery of Small Debts, within the Parishes of Halifax, Bradford, Kighley, Bingley, and other Places within the said West Riding; and that the said Act, so far as relates to the Court of Requests thereby authorized to be holden, has been put in Execution in a very arbitrary if not illegal Manner, and several Persons, becoming the Objects of it, have had many Acts of Severity and Oppression exercised upon them; and that the Petitioners conceive, that the said Act, so far as' relates to the said Court of pequests, should be very materially altered arid amended, to make it in any Degree answer the Intention of the Legislature in passing it, which the Petitioners presume was for promoting Industry, and encouraging useful Credit within its Limits, instead whereof, it has beeh found to be very injurious; and submitting to the House, that in case the said Act, so far as relates to the said Court of Requests, cannot be altered and amended, so as to make it conducive to the good Ends thereby intended, whether the same ought not to be repealed; and the Petitioners are informed, that Application has been made to the House on the above Subject: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to give such Relief therein as shall appear reasonable and proper.

Expenditure A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Burgesses, Com-of monalty, and other Inhabitants, of the Borough of IVal-Public Money. ling ford, in the County of Berks, was pretented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That this Nation hath been engaged for several Years in a most expensive and unfortunate War; that many of our valuable Colonies having actually declared themselves independent, have formed a thrift Confederacy with France and Spain, the dangerous and inveterate Enemies of Great Britain; that the Consequence of those combined Misfortunes hath been a large Addition to the National Debt, a heavy Accumulation of Taxes, a rapid Decline of Trade, Manufactures, and Land Rents of the Kingdom: Alarmed at the diminithed Resources and growing Burthens of this Country, and convinced that rigid Frugality is now indispensably necessary in every Department of the State, your Petitioners observe, with Grief, that, notwithstanding the calamitous and impoverished Condition of the Nation, much Public Money has been improvidently Iquandered, and that many Individuals enjoy finecurc Places, efficient Places with exorbitant Emoluments, and Pensions unmerited by Public Service, to a large and ltill increasing Amount, whence the Crown has acquired a great and unconstitutional Influence, which, if not checked, may loon prove fatal to the Liberties of this Country; Your Petitioners, conceiving that the true End of every legitimate Government is not the Emolument of any Individual, but the Welfare of the Community, and considering that, by the Constitution of this Realm, the National Purle is intruded, in a peculiar Manner, to the Custody of this honourable House, beg Leave further to represent, that, until effectua) Mcalures be taken to redress the oppressive Grievances herein stated, the Grant of any additional Sum of Public Money, beyond the Produce of the present Taxes, will be injurious to the Rights and Property of the People, and derogatory from the Honour and Dignity of Parliament: Your Petitioners, therefore, appealing to the Justice of this honourable House, do moll earnestly rc-quest. That before any new Burthens are laid upon this Country, effectual Measures may be taken, by this House, to enquire into, and correct, the grot's Abuses 1 in the Expenditure of Public Money, to reduce all

| exorbitant Emoluments, to rescind and abolish all fine-

I cure Places and unmerited Pensions, and to appropriate

' the Produce to the Necessities of the State, in such

Manner as to the Wisdom of Parliament shall feein meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and Freeholders, of the County of York, and several other Petitions, are referred.

A Petition of the Tradesmen and Manufacturers re- - -siding in the Western Division of the Hundred of Brix-ton, in the County of Surrey, was presented to the by House, and read , Setting forth. That the Court efta- blished by an Act, made in the Thirty-first Year of the a‘ Reign of King George the Second, for the more easy and speedy Recovery of Small Debts in the said Wei-tern Division of the Hundred of has been of

great Utility to Artificers and Labourers, as well as to the Tradesmen and Manufacturers residing within the said Division, the former being protested from the excessive Expences to which they were subject by Suit* for Small Debts in the Superior Courts, and the Danger of perpetual Imprisonment for the fame, and the latter relieved from the many LoffeS they formerly sustained for Want of an adequate Remedy for the Recovery of such Debts; and taking Notice of the Bill to exempt from Imprisonment the Bodies of Defendants^ liable to be imprisoned, by Precepts, or other Process,1 issuing out of Courts etefted by Acts of Parliament, for the more easy and speedy Recovery of Small Debts) and alleging, that, if the said Bill should pass into a l^aw, the Petitioners apprehend the intended good Purposes of the said Court will be in great Measure prevented from taking Effect, by reason the Creditor will be without a Remedy, where no Goods belonging to the Debtor can be found, which is most frequently the Cafe, and where any are found they are claimed by the Landlord, or if taken away by either of such Meansj the unhappy Defendant and Family are frequently left without a Bed, whertas the Terror of a Gaol being held out to them, they most commonly submit to the Direction of the Court to pay their Debts by Instalments, which are always proportioned to the Debtor’s Circumstances and Weekly Earnings, which Indulgence enables the sober and induttrious Poor to avoid an Execution,-and those who are willing, and, by their Industry, endeavour to maintain their Families, and pay their Debts, are neither subject to Imprisonment, or any other Hard-ship, under the Process of the said Court, and that the poorer Sort of People cannot always support themselves and Families without the Assistance of a small Weekly;

Credit, particularly in Cafes of Sickness, or Want of Employment: And therefore praying. That the said Bill for exempting the Bodies of Defendants from, being taken in Execution upon Process Issuing out of the Court of Itequests, may not pals into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed.

The said Accounts are as followeth;

An ACCOUNT of the Money which has arisen from the Sale of Ely , with it’s Application.

Ely House, after having been advertised and offered to Sale more than a Twelvemonth, was at length

Iiurchafed by Mr. Cole, a Builder, for fs. 10,600, in September 1776, and in December the same Year, 3,000, ’art of the rurchafe Money, were, by Order of Treasury, paid into my Hands, to be applied towards carrying on the New Buildings at Somerset House; the remaining £s. 7,600, which, by Agreement, should have been paid: in November 1778, are not yet paid; for the Purchaser having, on the stipulated Day of Payment, declared his Incapacity, the Lords of the Treasury agreed to his Request, which was, that instead of paying the whole /r. 7,600, he might be permitted to pay only/r. 1,600 then, and the Remainder by Instalments of 1,000, at the Distance of Six Months, with Interest thereon from the Date the Whole was due.

No Article, however, of this Second Arrangement has yet been fulfilled on the Part of the Purchaser, so that the whole Sum of ^r. 7,600, together with the Interest thereupon, from November 1778, remain still due.

William Chambers.

Roman A Petition of His Majesty’s Loyal ProtcAant Sub-Catkolics. jecfcs of the Town of Fol, in the County of Kent, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners, sensible of the many Blessings which as Protestants and Britons they enjoy, cannot but be alarmed at an Act, passed tn the Eighteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, repealing certain: Penalties and Disabilities imposed on the Papilb,. by a Statute enacted in the Eleventh and Twelfth. Years of William the Third, for further preventing the Growth . of Popery j and that it is with thedeepeft Concern they petition the House against a Law which has already . received the Royal Assent; but as this Act was so suddenly introduced, and so hastily passed, before the Sense of the Nation at large could be obtained, or any Opposition formed against it, they are encouraged to hope that this, together with many other Applications, will not prove too late for Red refs.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Halifax, A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Merchants, &c. Manufacturers, Traders, and other Inhabitants, of the Small Debts. Parishes of Halifax, Bradford, , Bing ley,

Ca her ley, Batley, Birfiall, Mirfield, cum >

Almondbury, Kirkheaton, Kirkburton, and Huddersfield, and the Lordshipor Liberty of Tong, in the West Riding of the County of York, whose Names are thereto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read j Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed, a Bill is depending to repeal so much of an Act, passed in the Seventeenth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, as relates to the more easy and speedy Recovery of Small Debts, within the Parishes and Lordship aforesaid, and for granting other Powers for those Purposes; which, if passed into a Law, the Petitioners are advised that the Power of awarding Execution against the Bodies of Debtors, as authorized by the said Act, will be totally annulled, and the Fees to be taken will be entirely at the Discretion of the Commissioners, thereby inverting them with a Power of charging the same with Annuities for Life, and of creating additional Fees to answer Deficiencies, proposing at the same Time to create a new Office (very unnecessary, in the Petitioners Opinion) and which mull of course enhance the Expence of executing such new proposed Law, and render the same leis beneficial, as well as the Practice of the Courts more uncertain; and- that the said Act, in its present State, hath been found to be of great Utility in the populous trading Part over which it gives JurilHiftion, as it thereby promotes Industry, and encourages useful Credit, particularly amongst the lower Class, chiefly employed in the Woollen Manufacture of the Country; but that if the Power of Imprisonment, in consequence of Judgment and Execution, was taken away, the good Ends intended by the Act, and which have manifestly appeared in the Execution of it, would be totally frustrated, and if altered, as proposed by the Bill, would be rendered in a great Measure useless, as such new proposed Powers might become rather injurious than advantageous to the Creditors seeking Relief under it: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law; on the contrary, that the aforesaid Act may remain in its present State without any Repeal or Alteration.

A Petition and Representation of the several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Prisoners confined for Debt in His Majesty’s Prison of the King’s Bench, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That a Petition hath been presented, from certain of their Fellow Prisoners, complaining against the Marshal and his Officers; and that the Petitioners conceive themselves bound in Justice to represent to the House, that they are not sensible of the Injuries complained of in the said Petition, and verily believe they do not exist, for that every reasonable Request and Indulgence which can be expected by Men in their Situation is readily granted by the said Marshal and his Officers, and, in Cafes of Illness and extreme Poverty, the Marshal has always given them every necessary Assistance *, and that the Petitioners are strongly impressed with Hopes, that Parliament will relieve them from their real Distresses, by granting them an Act of Insolvency, according to the Prayer of their former Petition.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Prisoners of the King’s Bench Prison, confined for Debt within the Walls of the feme, is referred: And that they do examine the Matter of this Petition; and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

That the Objects and Provisions of the said Bill, appear to the Petitioners to be of the most alarming and dangerous Tendency, and, if pa fled into a Law, will be of the most injurious and fatal Consequences, as well to the Interests of the Petitioners, as of all the other great commercial Cities and Towns in the Kingdom, and will be highly prejudicial and destructive to Trade and Public Credit in general: And therefore praying,

That the said Bill may not be carried into a Law.

Vicinities employed many Thousands of Men, Women, and Children, but that of late those Manufactures have very much dccrcafed, and Thousands of industrious Poor have become destitute of Employment, and reduced to extreme Distress; and that the subsequent War with Spain, the Prohibition of the Importation of Cotton Manufactures into that extensive Kingdom and its Dependencies, the Collation of the African Commerce, the Abridgement of it to The IVIndies, with the Exclu-fion of British Ships from the Mediterranean Ports, have precipitated the Decline of Trade and Manufactures; and that, in Addition to this casual Diminution of Commerce, and the consequential Sufferings of the Petitioners, a Domestic Evil of very great Magnitude, has l'prung up within these few Years, and increased to such an Extent as threatens the total Lois of Employment to this very numerous Body of industrious Individuals; and that the Evil in Question is the Introduction of Patent Machines anil Engines, of various Descriptions, which have luperfeded Manual Labour to such a 'fatal and alarming Degree, that, with the Decrease of the Manufactures proceeding from the Event already recited, and several other incidental Caules, many Thou land industrious and worthy Members of the Community are at this Moment, with their Families, pining for want ot

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Owners and Mailers of Ships and Vessels, and others concerned in the Commercial interclls of this Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have often experienced very considerable Damages, Delays, and Distress, by the present Mode of Manning the Royal Navy, to which they have patientiy submitted, as no Svflern hath hitherto been found proper to remedy thele Lvils; and that the Petitioners have seen, and maturely considered, a Maritime Syllem, composed by Mr. John Green, which they (being experienced in Maritime Affairs) are fully persuaded will, with such Alterations and Amendments as the House may think proper to make, l'peedily and effectually man the Royal Navy, without the Practice of Imprelling, so soon as Mariners can be made sensible of the general Encouragement which those in the Fellowship of Seamen (holding themselves ready to serve the State) will be entitled to, and it will also be attended with great Advantages to the Commercial Interests of this Kingdom, which it will effectually relieve from the many Hardships it has hitherto laboured under: And therefore praying the House to take the said Plan into their Consideration, and pal's the Whole, or such Part of it, into a Law', as may appear useful and necessary for the Good of the State in general.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Edward Hague, Esquire, informed your Committee, That by the Laws now in force, a Duty of Sixteen Pence per Yard is laid upon the Importation into this Kingdom of Foreign Thread Lace, of all Qualities, which by the said recited Act has been enforced — That the said Duty amounts to a Prohibition of the lower Sort of such Lace, being more than'its real V alue — That before the passing of the said Act, this Duty upon1 Importation was evaded; the lower Sort of such Lice has chiefly been consumed in England, being brought in clandeffinely; but by

th’e Clauses in the fai'd Ad, that Pradiee cannot be continued — That the better Sort of fetch Lace could afford, and did pay, the Duty, cV the Postage, which was equal to the Duty.

That the British Minister at has confirmed

the Advices received by the Merchants concerned in the Flanders Trade, that the Imperial Court had premeditated a heavy Duty on all Manufactures

imported into their Dominions — That he believes the British Exports, of different Kinds, imported into the Low Countries, amounts in Value to about 800,000 per Annum-, and that the Value of the Importation of Foreign Thread Lace into this Kingdom, does not amount to £ .50,000 per Annum: Then

A Member present produced to your Committee, Letters from Courtray and Ghent; (fating, that the Imperial Ambassador had apprized the Minister of the Determination of the Imperial Court, to lay a Duty of Sixteen Pence per Yard on all Woollen

Manufactures imported into the Low Countries, unless the Duty of Sixteen Pence per Yard, upon Foreign Thread Lace imported into this Kingdom, be reduced: And

Mr. Hague being again called, was of Opinion, That if instead of the present Duties upon Foreign Thread Lace imported into this Kingdom; a Duty of Ten Cent. ad Valorem, was laid, according to the different

Species of Lace, the same would give a fuflident Security to the British Manufacturers, and would likewise give Satisfaction to the Imperial Court: Then

A Member present produced to your Committee a Letter from Samuel Unwin, Junior, of Sutton, near Mansfield; inclosing Copy of a Letter from his Correspondents in Flanders, — Copies of which are hereunto annexed, N* 1 and 1.

Mr. Samuel Wor thing ton produced a Letter from Jonas Vander Straeton, his Correspondent at dated nth January 1780; and also a Letter from Green, dated Leeds, 8th April 1780. — Copies of which Letters are also hereunto annexed, N* 3 and 4.

And being examined, he laid, He was an Exporter of Woollen Goods to Flandas, and lived in Jeffrey Square, Saint Mary Axe.

That he had heard his Predecessor say, that about 30 or 40 Years ago the Woollen Goods exported on Commission from his House amounted to from 30 to £.40,000 a Year — That ever since that Time the Trade has been exceedingly declining in , owing

to the Manufacturers going abroad to Flanders; when they found the Merchants would not give them Orders, they applied to the Shopkeepers, who, willing to become Merchants, gave the Manufacturers Orders, and by that Means the People abroad correspond with the Manufacturers.

That the Returns made to him to the Exports are good Bills of Exchange, or Orders to draw upon Jlerdam; and sometimes they make Returns in Guineas: Then

Mr. Josiah Jowett (Partner with in

Capel Court, London) being examined, said, He is concerned in the Export of Goods by Commission to Flanders from London; at present to not more than £. 20,000 per Annum — That there are not many Woollen Goods lent from London; they are chiefly from the Country — That the Exports consist at present of Lead, Tin, Sugar, and Prize Goods, of all Sorts —

That the Proportion of Exports from London, is about £. i,oooo; from Shrezvfimyto the Amount of 6,000; and from Manchester from 30 to £. 40,000 a Year; the chief Article lent from thence is Printed Cotton — That the Value of Woollens exported from different Parts, amounts to between 30 and 40/000 a Year; and the Returns to those Exports are chiefly Bills upon People in London and some Returns are made rn Gold — That 6-yths are in Bills of Exchange and Money — That the greatest Part of the Foreign Lace is smuggled into this Country: Then

Mr. Edward Bridgen, of Paternofier Row, an Im* porter of Foreign Thread Lace, being examined, said. He had been in the Business between 30 and 40 Years — That there is a great Demand for Common Lace — That he deals chiefly in fine Lace — That the Lace imported into this Country amounts to about 150,000 a Year; he grounded his Opinion from the Quantity fold.

That before the Act of last Session, he kas received several Letters from Flanders, offering to Lnfure Lace into his House for £. 10 per Cent. — That they import Thread for the Buckinghamshire Manufactory, perhaps

to the Amount of £. 30,000 or £. 40,000 a Year, which all comes to London — That he imports perhaps £. 2,000 a Year; and if such Thread should be denied coming, the Lace Manufactory in Buckinghamshire would drop — That it is smuggled out of French Flanders into the Austrian Dominions, bleached in Flanders, and imported into Great Britain — That he mentioned this Circumstance of the Thread, because it is in the Power of the Imperial Court to prohibit it, to the Ruin of the Manufactory here: Then

Mr. Abraham Benjamin, of Saint Mary Axe, was examined, who said, He is an Exporter of Woollen Goods of all Sorts from hence to Flanders, and has been about 30 Years in England — That he makes l'ome Returns in Lace from Flanders, and has a House established there — That some Years he has exported Goods to the Amount of from 20 to £. 30,000 a Year — That he does not lay out above 3 or £. 4,boo a Year in Lace; he receives the rest in Money and Bills of Exchange — That the Duty upon Goods imported

into Flanders does not amount to more than£.10 per Cent, upon an Average.

That about 7 or 8 Years ago, a Calculation was made (taken from the Custom House Books in Flanders) of the Exports from this Country to Flanders, which he law; they amounted to about 1,500,000 a Year — That the Proportion of Woollen Goods is more than Half a Million a Year — That there is nothing wore in general in that Country, but Eng/ish Manufactures — That he supposes the Lace imported into this Country amounts to from too to £.100,000 per Annum — That he believes the Determination of the Court of , is to lay a Duty of Sixteen Pence a Yard upon Woollen Goods — That he has received Letters withina Fortnight from that Country; stating, that if the Duty on the Importation of Lace is not lowered, the Duty upon Woollen Goods will take place — That the Woollen Goods which are not consumed in the Austrian Dominions are sent to Germany. — And the Witness added. That he exports upon his own Account all the Goods he fends.

My Lord,

Presuming that a Bill either is, or shortly will be brought into Parliament, to regulate the Duty imposed on Foreign Thread Lace, I take the Liberty of transmitting your Lordship the inclosed relating thereto, which I have received from some Correspondents in the Austrian Dominions; to which I beg Leave to add, that such Regulation as is therein pointed out, appears to me very necessary to be made, otherwise the Sale

2* Ma.

20 Geo. III. 2° Mali. 8ic

of the Staple Manufactufes of this Kingdom, particularly those of Wool, mud bs materially injured, by heavy Duties being imposed on all such as may be exported to, orpafs through, the Dominions, for

other Parts, as a Retaliation for exorbitant Duties laid on the Lace of that Country, on Importation into this Kingdom.

I believe it is unnecessary to explain to your Lordship how much many of the Fanners now i'uffer, on Account of the very reduced Price of Wool; and that the Landed Interest must in some Measure be affected thereby. — It never can be good Policy to endeavour to establish the Lace Manufactory in this Kingdom, to the Prejudice of the Woollen Manufactories, which are by far the bed adapted to this Country; whilst that of Lace can never have any great Stability here, because the Manufacturers are obliged to other Countries for the Materials which they work upon, and have to contend with those who have Labour at a much cheaper Rate; consequently more real Benefit to this Kingdom must arise by an Exchange of Commodities between the Two Countries, than from any other Plan interfering with our Woollen Trade which can be adopted. If your Lordship shall concur in this opinion, I doubt not you will give the Bill which I have mentioned, such Countenance and Support, when the Matter shall come before the House, as may seem necessary.

I have the Honour to be, my Lord,

Your Lordship’s moll obedient Servant,

An Affair of the utmost Importance to the Commerce ol G’Vi:/ Britain in general, and to the Interest of the manufacturing Towns in particular, will apologize for my addrelung you on the following Occasion.

An Act to prevent Smuggling having past the Parliament during the lad; Sessions, containing a Clause which enaCls, That all Foreign Thread Lace that shall in future be imported into Great Britain, shall be marked and sealed at both Ends of each Piece; and if any such Foreign Thread Lace shall be hereafter found in any Shop or Warehouse, without such Mark and Seal, the same to be seized; and very severe Penalties (specified in the said Clause) are incuireJ by the Offender.

Be pleated to observe, that previous to the passing of the above-mentioned Act of Parliament, all Foreign Thread Lace imported into Great Britain were lub-jedted to the Payment of a Duty of Sixteen Pence per Yard, without making any Distinction of Value, so that a Yard of Lace, worth only Six Pence, paid a Duty equal to a Yard of Lace of the value of Five Pounds, an Imposition io unequal and unjust in its Principles, joined with the Facility of running Goods of this Kind, could not fail to produce a 5warm of Smugglers; and it may be reasonably presumed, that not Five Yards In a Thousand paid the Duty, and consequently the Revenue was very little benefited by such an Itnpost.

This Duty however was not in any Manner prejudicial to the Lace Manufacturers of this Country, as it was a Matter of Indifference to them whether their Lace was purchased by the Smugglers or fair Trader, provided they could find a sufficient Vent for their Manufactures; but the carrying into Execution the above-mentioned Clause, withrel'pest to the low-priced Laces, must operate as an absolute Prohibition, the exorbitant Duty of Sixteen Pence per Yard on Lace of Vol. 37.

fnull Value present their Importation by the fair Trader, as the felling Price can never support the Duty; and with respect to Smugglers, the Efteft will be the fame, the heavy Penalties inflicted upon the Offender, must deter them from carrying on a Trade attended with so great a Risque; so that in both Cafes the Lace Manufacturers of this Country, foreseefiig that the said Clause must crush their ancient and ilaple Commerce with Great Britain, has spread a general Alarm amongst the Traders interested in this Branch; they have in consequence presented a Petition to this Government, in order to endeavour to obtain from the British Legislature an Act of Parliament, to permit the Importation of Thread Lace from this Country, ort the Payment of a Duty of £.10 per Cent, on the Value, in same Manner as almost all the British Ma-nufadures are taxed in this Country; should this rea-(onable Request meet with a Refusal on the Part of the British Government, the Petitioners humbly hope that her Imperial Majesty will be pleased to impose such Duties on the British Manufactures imported into her Dominions, as may be equivalent to a Prohibition — In consequence of this Petition, Government here, having thoroughly examined the Nature of the Trade carried on between this Country and Great Britain, find that various Articles, of the different Kind of Manufactures, freight near 150 Vessels from the different Ports of Great Britain to the Port of OJiend, all of which are fully freighted with different Articles of British Produce; and that most of these Vessels return to England in Batlaft; they also find that Thread Lace is the only and foie Manufacture imported into England from this Country, consequently a considerable Bal ance of Trade refu!ts to England from this Country, of which the constant high Price of Exchange in Favour of England is a convincing Proof: This Government is therefore clearly of Opinion, that it is highly unjust that the foie Manufacture of this Country imported into Great Britain, should be loaded with a Duty equivalent to a Prohibition. Instructions have in consequence been transmitted to the Imperial Am-ballad or at the Court of London, for him to endeavour to obtain Red refs; and in case of Refusal, to declare that equivalent Duties will be laid on the Manufactures of Great Britain imported into the dnftrian Dominions, which will operate equal to a Prohibition.

It is needless to enlarge on this Point; the pernicious Consequence of such an Imposition may prove fatal to the Trade of many thousand British Manufacturers, and deprive the Nation of a very beneficial Branch of Commerce.

It highly regards therefore your Interest, Sir, as well as that of every Well-wisher to the British Trade, to second the Efforts of the Imperial Arnbaffador, to obtain the Permission to import Laces into Great Britain, paying io per Cent. on the Value, as the only Means ot rc-establishing a good Understanding between the Two Countries, increasing the British Revenue, and preventing entirely the smuggling of this Article in future, to the great Benefit of the British Nation in general.

In order to obtain theie Benefits, I beg Leave to recommend a Meeting of the Parties interested in your Neighbourhood, to consult on the most proper and effectual Means t6 prevent this threatening Evil, by instructing your Representative in Parliament to use his utmost Endeavours to have the above-mentioned Clause repealed } and to obtain an Act of Parliament, that the Laces of this Country may be admitted to enter,- on paying the above-mentioned Duty.

The only plausible Objection that can be produced against this deiirable Act of Parliament (as far as I can suggest) is, that the Lace Manufacturer in England will be prejudiced *, in Answer to which I beg Leave to remark, that if the English Manufacturer cannot bring his Commodity to Market on equal Terms with the
