The Progress made in the new Works at Somerset House would be better Teen and understood by Inspection upon the Spot, than by Descriptions, or even Designs, upon Paper; in Obedience, nevertheless, to the Order received, the following Account is humbly presented.

THE Building which faces the Strand is now almost completely finished; it extends in Front 135 Feet, is 61 Feet deep, and has Two Wings each 46 Feet Wide, and 42 Feet in Depth; the whole being Seven Story high, is faced with Portland Stone, built with Hard Greyflock Bricks, RussianTimber, and (he belt Materials of all Kinds, and is covered Part with Copper, Part with Lead or Westmorland Slate.

All the Fronts of this Structure are decorated with a rustic Arcade Basement, a Corinthian Order of Columns and Pilaflers, enriched Windows, Balluftrades, Statues, Malks, Medallions, and various other Ornamental Works, necesfury to distinguish this principal and most conspicuous Part of the Design; which being in itself trifling when compared with the Whole, required not only particular Forms and Proportions, but likewise some Profusion of Ornaments, to mark its Superiority: Decorations too have been more freely employed in the Veftibuleof Entrance, and in all the public Apartments of this Building, than will be necessary in the Remainder of the Work, because tire Vestibule, open to the moll frequented Street in London, is a general Passage to every Part of the whole Design; and the Apartments are intended for the Reception of useful Learning and polite Arts, where it is humbly presumed Specimens of Elegance shouldat least be attempted.

The Work just described, forms the upper Part of a large quadrangular Court, being in Width aio, and in Depth 296 Feet, which is to be surrounded with Buildings 54 Feet deep, and Six Story high, containing the Navy, the Navy Pay, the Victualling, and the Sick and Hurt Offices; the Ordnance Office, the Stamp, Salt, and Tax-Offices, the Surveyor General of Crown Lands, and the Offices of the Duchies of Lancaster and Cornwall\ also the Offices of the Two Auditors of Imprefts, and the Pipe, the Treasurer’s Remembrancer, the Clerk of the Estreats, and Comptroller of the Pipe, with various Apartments for Secretaries, and other Persons, whose Residence in their several Offices has been judged convenient for the Public Service. All these Buildings, surrounding the said Court, are now raised Two Story high (excepting at one Corner, where the old Palace, yet (landing, has prevented it) they have Two Floors laid on, and the Third Story carried up to a considerable Height on all the Part which forms the Bottom of the Court, and at the same Time makes a considerable Portion of the great River Front, which, when finished, is, according to the general Design, to extend 800 Feet.

This Work is likewise all faced with Stone, is built of the bed Materials, in the most substantial Manner polfi-b!e, and set on Brick Foundations, a great Part of them laid in the Bed of the River, with various expensive, but necessary, Precautions, and others funk through loose-made Ground 10, 12, and even 16 Feet deep.

The greated Part of the Vaults too, surrounding the Arreas of this large Quadrangle, are turned, as also a great Part of the Crol's Passage of Communication from the Areas on one Side to those on the other, which all aie built of hard Grcydocks, with Stone Plinths necefl'arily set in most Parts on very deep Brick Foundations.

Besides the Progress made in the extensive Works already mentioned, the Foundations are laid at a very considerable Expense in the River, for the Embankment, to the Extent of 438 Feet by a Width of 46 Feet, upon which is raised a rustic Granite Basement, 13 Feet 7 Inches high, with a Range of arched Stone Galleries, and Apartments built thereon, all to the same Extent, and at this Time raised, in some Parts, to the Height of 18 Feet 1 Inch, and in others to the Height of 28 Feet, having One Floor already on, and the Centers ready to set for turning the Arches, which are to support the Street of the Terrace:

The Building now ere<fling on the Scitc of Somerset House is of a very' uncommon Kind, unusually extensive, intricately complicated, and attended with many and great Difficulties in the Execution, whence it was at first, and is even yet, impossible to form an exact Estimate of the Expence; as far however as the Architect’s Judgment and Experience in Business can guide him, he thinks it will certainly not exceed the Sum of £. 250,000; which will be divided nearly in the following Manner:

A Petition of the Tradesmen, Manufacturers, and Halite, other Inhabitants of the Pariftics of Leeds, Wakefield, ire Bradford, Halifax, Huddersfield, Birjlall, S(ni11 Dfto.

verley and other Places in the West Riding of the County of York, whose NarrteS are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth,

That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Bill is depending, for laying an additional Duty of Six Pence 'per Bushel, and upwards, upon all Malt brewed by private Families; and that the Petitioners conceive such additional Duty will be a greater Hardship upon the People residing in this Part of the Country, and particularly upon the poof Manufacturer and Labourer, than upon other Places, for as much as there being no Common Brewers in the said West Riding, Wefhvards of the Town of Leeds, the Inhabitants have been accustomed in general, to brew their own Beer, and therefore will feel the full Weight of the proposed new Duty upon Malt, if the same shall be now laid on; and that the Article of Beer is so necessary a Nourishment and Support to the Manufacturer and Labourer, that it is scarce possible for them to carry on their Work, or undergo their Labour, without the Assistance of that Article; and, it being supposed that the poorest Manufacturer mud consume at least Two Quarters of Malt in a Year, for the necessary Support of himself and Family, the additional Burthen he will feel from that small Consumption, will be near Ten Shillings a Year; and that the Wages and Earnings of the Manufacturer and Labourer in these Parts, being in general small, their strictest Ckre and CEconomy is necessary to enable them to support themselves and Families; and, by the Addition of so heavy a Burthen as the proposed new Duty upon Malt, the Petitioners apprehend, many of them will be very much distressed and reduced: And therefore praying, That the said new Duty upon Malt may be laid and raised in some more convenient or equal Mode, and that the Petitioners may have such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall l'eem meet.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being proposed. That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for granting to His Majesty additional Duties upon Malt, and upon Low Wines and Spirits made for Home Consumption, and upon Foreign Spirits imported into Great Britain, and upon the Produce of the said several Duties; and for granting a Duty on Licences to be taken out by all Persons trading in, vending, or felling of Coffee, Tea, or Chocolate; is committed;

A Motion was made, and the Question being put,

That the other Orders of the Day be now read;

It passed in the Negative.

That it would also be a public Convenience, if the Street called Great Garden Street, leading from Whitechapel Road aforesaid into the said Hamlet, was properly paved, clsanfed, lighted, watched, and regulated.

Richard Vinfon confirmed the above Evidence.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Committee, to whom the Bill for the better Relief and Employment of the Poor of the Hamlet of Mile End New Town, in the Parish of Stepney, in the County of

Middlesex; for paving, cleansing, lighting, and watching, the Streets, and other Open PafiSges and Places within the said Hamlet, and removing Nuisances and Annoyances therefrom, and preventing the like for the future; and for consolidating the Highway Rates with the other Rates within the said Hamlet, is committed; That they have Power to make Provision in the said Bill, for making a Carriage Way through Baker's Row, leading from Whitechapel Road to the said Hamlet of Mile End New Town and for paving and regulating so much of such Carriage Way as lies within the said Hamlet, and also the Street called Great Garden Street.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

A Petition of the several Persons whole Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and the other Tallow-Chandlers in the Cities of London and Westminster, and Part? adjacent, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill to permit Goods, the Product or Manufacture of certain Places within The Levant or Mediterranean Seas, to be im-pbrted into Great Britain or Ireland, in British or Foreign Vessels, from any Place whatsoever, for a Time to be limited; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners are greatly alarmed at perceiving an Objection made to the said Bill extending to the Importation of Cotton Wool; for that the Wicks of Wax, Spermaceti, and Tallow Candles, are, and can only be, made of Cotton Yarn spurt from Cotton Wool, the Growth of the Places within the above Seas, commonly called Turkey Cotton, and no Cotton Wool of the Growth of the West India Islands can be used in making Wicks for Candles; and that there is annually consumed in this Kingdom, in making Tallow Candles only, above Five hundred thousand Pounds Weight of Turkey Cotton Wool and Yarn, and large Quantit.es arc also used in making Wax and Spermaceti Candles, and for Lamps; and that the Duty paid upon Tallow Candles is about Two hundred thousand Pounds a Year, and great Numbers of Persons are employed in this Country in (pinning Turkey Cotton Wool into Yarn, in order to make Candles, and for Lamps; and that Tin key Cotton is lately advanced to a very great Price, and there is none now at Market j; and that unless Turkey Cotton Wool can be imported, and sold at a reasonable Rate, the Price of Candles must be greatly increased, the Revenue materially injured, the Spihriers of Cotton unemployed, and the Tallow-Chandlers Trade very much diitrefied: And therefore praying the House tb take the Premises into Consideration, and grant them such Relief as to the House shall seem meet; and that they may be heard by themselves, or their Counsel, in Support of the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Corisideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed.

and that the Acid and Alkali contained in Sea Salt have never till now been found capable of being separated; and that the Petitioner is possessed of a Principle in Chymistry, hitherto unknown, by the ik.il-ful Application of which, such Separation is now actually made, and that in consequence of this Discovery new Sources of Commerce, and Industry are capable of being immediately opened, 'which will be of great Importance to the Trade and Manufactures of Great Britain, provided an Exemption is granted to the Petitioner from the Duties on Salt made Use of by him in extracting from thence his Marine Acid, and Foffil or Mineral Alkali, or by Bounties given, or other Allowances made, equal to those Duties, in such Manner as to the Wisdom of Parliament shall seem meet; and that during the last Three or Four Years the Bafillia of Spain has gradually risen up from Sixteen Pounds to Fifty-six Pounds per Ton and upwards, and the Value given for it and other Afttes is actually given to Enemies or Foreigners; that from Sea Water, Sea or Rock Salt, or Salt Springs, a great Annual Saving may be made to this Country and Ireland; and the Petitioner trusts the Opinion of the Lords Commissioners of Trade and Plantations, so recently given, and that after the most mature and compleat Investigation of the Matter, in consequence of a Reference from the Board of Treasury for that Purpose, will have feme Weight on a Subject which has ever been considered by the World of the greatest Moment; and that the obtaining the necessary Informations, and settling with the different Revenue Boards those Regulations which seemed proper to be first established, have till now prevented the Petitioner from presenting a Petition for the Permission of the House to have Leave to bring a Bill for an Exemption from the old Duty on Salt, and for a Drawback of the Whole, or of a Bounty equal to the new Duty, on that Quantity of Salt which he shall make and use in his said Manufacture for the aforesaid Purposes: And1 therefore praying. That, under the particular Circum-starrees above stated, he may have Leave to present his Petition for the Purposes aforesaid, notwithstanding the -Time limited by the House for receiving Petitions for private Bills hath elapsed.

Ordered, That, in Consideration of the particular Circumstances set forth in the said Petition, Leave be given to present a Petition, as desired by the said Alexander Fordyce.

Joseph Frederick IVallet , Esquire, pro*

duced to your Committee Four Volumes of Maps, published under the Directions of the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty; the First "ml Second Volumes containing Charts and Views of the Coalls and Harbours of Nova Scotia-, the Third comprehending the Coasts and Harbours of New New

Connefiicut, and other Places; and the Fourth Volume comprehending the Coasts and Harbours in the Gulph and River o {'Saint Lawrence, the Coast and Harbours

from New York to Cape Florida.

He then acquainted your Committee, That he was allowed, upon the Representation of the Board of Trade, 35 Guineas for each Plate compleated for Publication, and Twenty Shillings per Day, this Allowance being founded on the precedent of what had been thought reasonable for the former Part of this Work, published under the Direction of the Lords of the Admiralty — That he has already compleated 246 Plates — That in Consequence of this Assistance from the Public, he has found himself enabled to fell the Maps, Charts, and Views, taken from those Plates, at One Shilling per Sheet; which, had the Plates been so engraved at his own Risque and Expence, could not, upon an Average, have been sold at less than Five Siblings per Sheet — That he fells each Map, Chart, or View separate by which Means the Navigators may be supplied with such as they want oniy for their respective Dies without being burthened with the Purchase of the Whole.

That he has, under the former Parliamentary Grants, been paid for 414 Plates, according to the Allowance above mentioned — That the Estimate prefen ted to the House upon the 6th of March last, and referred to this Committee, includes the Witness s Demand for the remaining 32 Plates, which, at 35 Guineas per Plate, amounts to f. 1,176, and which Sum, together with the Sum of £*365, being his Allowance at 20 Shillings per Day, for One Year amounts to 1,541# the Sum charged in the said Estimate, being the Completion of the General Work.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Rates and Duties granted by an Act, nude in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act " for granting to His Majesty certain Duties on Licences, to be taken out by all Persons letting Horses " to hire for travelling, in the Manner therein mentioned; and certain Duties on all Horses let to hire for the Purposes of travelling Post, and by Time;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, for and in respect of every Horse hired by the Mile or Stage, to be used in travelling Post in the Kingdom of Great Britain, there be charged a Duty of one Penny for every Mile such Horse shall travel Post, such Duty to be paid by the Person or Persons by whom such Horse shall be so hired or uled.

A MESSAGE by Mr. Yeoman Usher

of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker.

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s Commission for declaring His Royal Assent to several Acts agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendance of this honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House, at the De-fire of the Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s Commission aforementioned, had been at the House of Pcersj where a Commission under the Great Seal was read} giving, declaring, and notifying, the Royal Af-sent to the several Public and Private Bills therein mentioned; and also impowering the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, the Lord High Chancetlor of Great Britain, the Lord President of the Council, the Lord Privy Seal, and several other Lords, to declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills j and that the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, and the Lord President of the Council and the Earl of Mansfield, named also in the said Commission, did accordingly declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills; which Bills are as followeth , viz.

An Act for granting to His Majesty additional Duties upon Malt, and upon Low Wines and Spirits made for Home Consumption, and upon Foreign Spirits imported into Great Britain, and upon the Produce of the said several Duties} and for granting a Duty on Licences to betaken out by all Persons trading in, vending, or felling of Coffee, Tea, or Chocolate:

An Act to continue, for a limited Time, so much of an Act. made in the last Session of Parliament, lot the more easy and better recruiting His Majesty’s Land Forces and Marines, as relates to the Encouragement of Volunteers:

An Act for obviating Doubts touching the binding and receiving of Poor Children Apprentices in pur-luance of several Acts of Parliament, made for the Relief of the Poor within particular incorporated Hundreds or Districts; and for ascertaining the Settlement of Bastard Children born in the Houses of Industry within such Hundreds or Districts:

A Petition of James Keir, was presented to the House and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioner observes, by the Vo'es, that a Petition hath been presented from Alexander Fordyce, Esquire; alledging, that he is possessed of a Principal in Chymistry hitherto unknown, by the skilful Application of which the Alkali and Acid contained in Sea Salt and Rock Salt arc separated, and that the Acid is found in many Cafes preferable to Vitriolic, and the Alkali superior in Value to the Barillia of Spain, and praying for Leave to bring in a Bill for an Exemption from the old Duty on Sait, and for a Drawback on the Whole, or a Bounty equal to the new Duty on such Salt as he shall use in the said Manufacture of Marine Acid, and fixed Foflil or Mineral Alkali; and representing to the House, that in the Year 1771 the Petitioner discovvered a new Method of obtaining the Mineral Alkali from common Salt, and did intend to establish a Manufacture for that Purpose, and to secure his Invention by Patent, and with that View entered a Caveat in the Patent Office, dated the 14th of February 1771, that no Person should obtain a Patent for an Invention, by which an Alkaline Salt may be extracted from common Salt, or from Sea Water, or from the Water of Salt Springs, without giving Notice to the Petitioner; but that he was prevented from executing his laid Intention of establishing a Manufacture of Alkali obtained from common Salt, principally by the high Price of Salt, occasioned by the Duty on that Commodity; and that the Petitioner has, since that Time, discovered other new Methods of extracting the said Alkali from common Salt, by which he could beneficially manufacture large Quantities of the said Alkali, provided he was exempted from the Duties on common Salt: And therefore praying, That he may be allowed the same Exemption and Drawback from the Duties upon Salt, as are prayed for by the said Alexander Fordyce, or that the said Exemption and Drawback may be allowed to all Persons concerned in the said Manufacture of obtaining Alkali from common Salt.

A Petition of His Majesty’s loyal Protestant Subjects of Soham, and the adjacent Villages, in the County of

Cambridge, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners, sensible of the many Blessings which, as Protestants and Britons, they enjoy, cannot hut be alarmed at an Act, passed in the Eighteenth Year of the Kcign of His present Majesty, repealing certain Penalties and Disabilities imposed on the Papists by a Statute, enacted in the Eleventh and Twelfth Years of William the Third, for further preventing the Growth of Popery; and that it is with the deepest Concern they petition the House against a Law which has already received the Royal Afl’ent: but as this Act was so suddenly introduced, and so hastily passed, before the Sense of the Nation at large could be obtained, or any Opposition formed against it, they are encouraged to hope that this Application will not prove too late for Redress: And

therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to repeal the Act lately passed in favour of the Papists.

(he Petition ot rlltxu ndcrF of Harley Street, VCndiJhSquare, Esquire, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and bad directed him to lej.ort the lame, as it appeared to them, to tie House; and he read the Report in his Place} and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was lead; and is as followed!; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, your Committee examined the following Witneife?: First,

Doctor George Fordyee, Physician to Hospital, Prctelfor and Lecturer of Cfymiftry; who informed your Committee, That he believes the Principle by which the Acid and Alkali contained in Sea Silt, are separated by Mr. Fordyee, is entirely new — That he has been acquainted with it about Three Years — That he has teen the Marine Acid procured by those Precedes, which is a pure Acid, and is employed in Preference to the Vitriolic Acid, in making, Tin Plates; and is alto preferable in bleaching Linen, and preparing it for printing, being lets apt to burn the Linen, Vofc. 37.

the Vitriolic being more corrosive, and consequently more apt to dissolve Vegetable or Animal Substances — That the Marine Acid evaporates with the Water in bleaching, but the Vitriolic remains so as to burn the Cloth when dry — That there are many lesser Manufactures to which it is applicable, but these are the Two greater ones — That he has seen some of the Alkali procured by Mr. Fordyee in consequence of his newly discovered Principle, which is a pure Foflil Alkali, at least worth double the Value of the best Barillia, and consequently worth a great deal more than double the Money, because it docs not require to be purified as the Barillia does — That it contains Twice the Alkaline Salt, and is already pure — That its Strength will be uniform, which that of the Barillia is not, and consequently a purer Ingredient — That it is as fit for the Purpose of bleaching as the Alkali of Barillia, which is generally used for that Purpose, and they are as like each other as Salt brought from different Salt Pits — That it will make line Glass — That in general the Mineral Alkali is capable of performing what the Vegetable Alkali performs, and particularly in all the great Manufactures — That they are both Substances of the same Class, but not of the same Species of Alkali; they agree, therefore, in many Properties; in all, he conceives, except in the making of Saltpetre, and some Species of Soap, meaning loft Soaps — That the Introduction of the Use of Mineral Alkali will not prevent Kelp being also used, because the Purposes for which Kelp is employed are not on account of the Alkali which ic contains, but on account of the Sea Salt, and other Properties — That Kelp is employed for some Purposes, because it contains a small Quantity of Alkali, but it is very little — That the Sale of British Kelp and Alkali will not at all interfere with each other as far as he can judge — That he has been enabled to form his Judgment upon the Subject by analyzing Kelp, and employing it ^Experiments madetd ascertain its Properties — That Kelp is employed in Green Glass, for the particular Purpose of uniting with the earthy Substances to form the Glass, for which Purpose Mr. Fordyee's Alkali will be too dear — And being asked, Whether it was not owing to its Alkaline Properties that it so unites the earthy Substances ? lie laid, There is not One-twentieth Part of the Kelp that is Alkali — That the Kelp enters into the Composition of the Glass; therefore it cannot be from its Alkali that it forms the Glass — That if the Alkali is taken away, it will (till form the Glass — That he has himself made Glass from Kelp after extracting the Alkali — That it is on account of the Alkaline Property in Kelp that it is used in making of AUum — That he is of Opinion, that the Alkali proposed to be made by Mr. Fotdyce, will not answer the same Purposes in the Manufacture of Allum, for which Kelp is at present used. — And being asked, If the Alkali was laid out of the Question, what Principle he attributes to the other Ingredients of Kelp, to make it useful in making Glass? he said, The Sea Weed, from whence Kelp is principally made, is a particular Class of Plants; called Alga:, whose Structure is loch as to render them able to imbibe more Salt than Plants of other Clalfes, so that when they are burnt, they forma Mals proper for producing Glass — That he has frequently tried, by various Processes, to extract Alkali from Sea Salt, of the same Nature as that now found out by Mr. Fordyee, but those Processes are all too expensive ever to come into common Use, though he thinks it can be dene by Mr. Fordyce'% Method at such an Expence as to make it so, provided the Salt can be made without Duty — That he did not know of the Discovery until it was communicated to him by Mr. Fordyee, nor had ever met with any Thing leading to the Principle in any Book of Chymistry — That Kelp, or some Substitute for it, is generally made use of in making the different Kinds of Soap, but not on account of its

Your Committee then called Mr. Samuel,

Chymist and Druggist in London; who laid, He was not acquainted with Mr. Fords Method of separating the Alkali and Acid contained in Sea Salt — Thac he believes it to be a new Discovery, which has not been communicated to him — That he has seen some of Mr. Fordyces Alkali separated from Acid — That he

has examined it; and it appears to him to be the purest and cleared Mineral Alkali he ever law — That he has compared it with the purified or refined Barillia, and it is infinitely stronger and better — That in all the Barillia he ever has seen, there has been a Mixture of the Vegetable Alkali with the Mineral Alkali; but the Mineral Alkali, procured by Mr. Fordyce, is pure and unmixed — That he thinks it is about One-half superior to the refined Barillia, but cannot say how much to the common Barillia — That he speaks in his Comparison according to Weight — That he conceives it will be of more Advantage to the Manufactures in the same Proportion (for the Reufons he has already given) than any Bariliia — That Mr. s Alkali will,

in every Cafe, be applicable in Preference to Barillia, where Barillia is uied; viz. Bleaching, making fine Glass, and Soap; and, he supposes, in scouring Woollen Clothes — That he has seen Mr. Marine

Acid made from Sea Salt, and examined it, and thinks it is preferable to the Vitriolic in many Instances (not being so corrosive) particularly in Bleaching, and that it is peculiarly adapted for uniting Iron and Tin in Plates, which no other Acid can do — That he cannot say he has ever compared Mr. Ford) ce's Marine Acid with any other Acids formerly made from Sea Salt; but recollecting Experiments made with Spirit of Sea Salt, he is enabled to say, the Spirit made by Mr. Fordyce is stronger and finer than any he ever saw — That he never knew the Spirit of Sea Salt had been employed in Bleaching, or preparing Linen for Printing, until very lately — That formerly the practical Chymistswere at aids how to dispose of their iMarine Acid — that he has fold large Quantities at a Penny a Pound, and has thrown a great deal down the Kennel.

Mr. ljaacHarman being examined, laid, That he

had been employed in the Management of a C'allico Printing Manufactory for Mr. Watson and Mr. Nnfh *5 Years — That they were both dead, and that, he was now engaged for Mr. s Executors — That

they have used, ever since he has been so employed. Oil of Vitriol for prepairing the Linens for Printing — That he has made an Experiment with Mr.

Marine Acid for the above Purpose, against Oil of Vitriol, of equal Weight, upon the same Piece of Cloth, printed with the same Colours, and boiled in the same Madder; and that which was prepared with the Marine Acid became white sooner than that which was prepared with Oil of Vitriol, and the Colours were much stronger — That he would certainly use it in Preference to the other in any Work of his own, from what he knew of both, even it die Prices were equal, as the Circumstance of the Cloth becoming white looner would favc the Expence of Wages — That he found no Difference in the Experiment he made, in regard to the Damage of the Clodi — That he does not know the present Price of Oil of Vitriol, having used none for 1'omeTime; that it was 4 a Pound; but the Person said, the next Parcel he had would be 5 [d. — That he does not know the Price of the Marine Acid.

Then the Witness produced to your Committee, a Piece of Cloth whereon the above Experiment was made.

And he further said, That he could not say how long it is since the Experiment was made, but thinks, it to be within the last Two Months.

Your Committee then called Doctor James Sims, Physician in London; who informed them, He had made Chymistry Parc of his Study — That lie has seen feme of Mr. Fordyce's Alkali — That he had made an Experiment, to discover whether it is better or worse than the Spanish Barillia: and that it appeared to him

to be much superior — That the Acid is superior to any he has seen lately, and believes it to be superior to any he ever has seen — That he has combined them, and from them procured very fine and pure Salt — That it is his Opinion, that the Acid will, in Bleaching, and preparing Linen for Printing, answer better than the Vitriolic, because the Marine Acid seems more powerfully to dissolve the Substances they take out of Cloth in Bleaching than any of the other Acids — That he has read moll of the approved Books of Chymistry, and has heard Lectures upon the Subject — That he believes the Principle by which Mr. Fordyce separates the Acid and Alkali in Sea Salt, is a new Discovery, and that no one before him has separated the Acid and Alkali in such a manner as they shall be marketable Articles — That he apprehends the Discovery will, in all Probability, prove a great national Advantage, and that it was for that Ueafon he made the Experiment upon it — That lie has bought no Quantity of it — That he does not know any Price it has been fold for at Market — That he apprehends the Marine Acid and the Oil of Vitriol, employed in preparing Linen for Printing, are both corrosive alike — That if they are not properly diluted, they will be both corrosive.

Not in London; in Ireland they ule a great deal; and in some Places in the Country they ule Wood Allies — That Kelp is not used in making of Yellow Soap, unless Barillia is very dear, and then it is made Ule of with other Allies — That it is not necessary at all in the Manufacture of courier Soap, when Barillia is to be got at a moderate Price — That the general Average Price of Barillia is £ .23. a Ton — That Kelp in moderate Times is from 3 to £.4. a Ton, but now it is not under £.10. — And being asked, What Proportion of Kelp in Quantity it requires to make the same Quantity of Soap as Barillia ? he laid, He could not answer, as they never used it alone in London, but mixed it with other Allies, as there is not a sufficient Quantity of Alkali in it; but is principally used for its Marine Salt. — And being asked, If Kelp alone would make a marketable Soap? he laid, In Ireland some Soap is made of Kelp alone; but it does not do here, because they cannot afford the Expence of long Carriage — That he believes Mr. Fordyce's Alkali is equally good for making all Sorts of Hard Soap — The particular Use of Kelp in making Soap in London, is for its binding Quality and for separating the Lye.

Mr. Alexander Brown, Sonpmaker in C/erkemvell, being examined, said, He chiefly used Barillia in the making of Soap, and gave a Preference to it — That he has iecn some of Mr. Fordyce's Alkali, and made several Experiments on it. — And being asked, What he could afford to pay him for his Alkali, provided Barillia was at £.50. a Ton? he said. That he had nude a final] Boil from his Alkali, which he found to be very much preferable to Barillia — That it at Icaft makes double the Quantity of Soap, and therefore he would give double the Price, as it laves Labour — That he used 1 cwt. 3 qr. 131b. in the Boil — That if there was no Difference in the Price of Barillia and this Alkali, and £.\oo. laid out in Barillia would produce as much Soap as the same Sum laid out in Mr. Fordyce* Alkali, he would in this same use Mr. Fordyce's Alkali, because Two Men will make more Soap than Four will with Barillia. — And being asked. If the Alkali made equally good Soap with the Barillia? he said, He did not know there was any Difference in the Quality; but if there was any, that made with the Alkali has the Preference — That he looks upon it, that if Mr. Fordyce can make a sufficient Quantity of Alkali, we shall not want any Barillia at all, because Von. 37.

it will always be used in Preference — That he has known the Price of Barillia as low as £.16. a Ton — That he has known it has high as £.60; that it is at this Time £.46. — And being asked, Whether he knew any Thing that would answer the same Purpose in Soap-making that Barillia does, equally with Mr. Fordyce's Alkali ? he said, He had never fecn any Thing to be compared to it — That he put 8 cwt. 2 qr. of Tallow to the 1 cwt. 3 qr. 131b. of Alkali.- — And being asked, Why he supposes the Labour will be less in making Mr. Fordyce's Alkali into Soap than Barillia ? he said, Because it saves pounding, and many other Operations Barillia mull undergo — That he puts 7 cwt. of Barillia to a Ton of Tallow — That what Barillia he ever used was not of so good a Quality as that of the Alkali — That he used Kelp in the making of YeKow Soap, but he never found it worth the Labour and Expence.

Mr. Alexander Duncan, Clerk to Mr. Fordyce, being then called, said, He had been employed in Mr. For-dyce's Affairs almost Two Years — That Mr. Fordyce had communicated to him the Principle by which he separates the Alkali and Acid, which are contained in Sea and Rock Salt — That from the Knowledge he has of the Matter it is his Opinion that Mr. Fordyce could not carry on his Manufactures of Marine Acid and FoUil Alkali in England, was he subject to the Duties on Salt — That Mr. Ford)ce can make any Quantity of Acid and Alkali — That he thinks it is probable that some Money may be drawn from Foreigners, by the Exportation *f these Articles, because he has been present at the Delivery of some Marine Acid, and was told, that the Person who bought it was to fend it to a Foreign Market — That he cannot tell exactly what Quantity it was, but that it was several Hundred Weight, and that there were many Orders from the same House for more — That this was about 8 or 9 Months ago — That he has been in the North of England; was there Six Months, and came away lately. — And being asked, Whether he had had Access to learn any Thing of a Mr. King, Glass-maker, at Newcastle, who is said to make Birillia? he said. He had heard he makes a Substitute for Kelp, which is used as a Flux for common Green Gla-k — That he law One House that he has for the Purpose of making this Substitute — That it is laid, his Baruiia is fold for A3, a Ton.

Mr. Duncan being again called, informed your Committee, That he had often applied the Principle by which Mr. Fordyce obtains his Alkali, and produced to your Committee /some Specimens of it in Two Vials, and in Two Boxes, all which he said he was Witness to the making of from Sea Salt upon Mr. Frodyce's Principle. — And being asked, Whether all the Specimens (having such different Appearances) have the same Properties, and are applicable for the same Purposes ? he said. The Two Specimens in the Vials, and that in One of the Boxes, are applicable to the same Purposes — That the Reason of their different Appearances is from the different Manner of making. — And being asked, Whether those Three Specimens were all applicable to the making of Soap ? he said, He never attended the making ot Soap — That he knew Alkali of the same Kind had been sent to a Soap Maker, who said he had made Soap of it. — And being asked. Whether they were applicable in the making of Glass ? he said, He was not a Glass Maker.* — And being asked, If he knew, by any Chymical Proof, whether those Three Alkalies were the same Quality, so that if the One was useful in any Manufactory, the others mull necessarily be the same ? he laid, He was not bred to Chymiltry. — And being asked. If he knew whether Soap Makers have had/any of the Alkaii in the Box N° 1. and made Soap of it ? he said, He did not know — That Mr. Fordvce has made a considerable Quantity of Alkali, and he knew some had been lent to Mr. George Rujjell — That

Your Committee understanding that a Reference had been made from the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury to the Lords Commissioners for Trade and Plantations, dated 26th Apr 80, for their Opinion on Mr. For dyce's Proportion, they called for a Copy of the Answer given to the said Reference, to be laid before them, which they hereunto subjoin.

Cony of a Letter from the Board of Trade, dated 6th May 1780, on Mr. s Petitions.

Whitehall, May 6th, 1780.

Sir,

1 have, in tire Abtence of Mr. ,laid be-

fore the Lords Commissioners for Trade and Plantations, your Letter to him the 26th of , toge-

ther with Two Petitions of Alexander Fordyce, Esquire, and the several Papers therewith transmitted; and their Lordships have taken the same into Confederation. I have it now in Command to acquaint you, for the Information of the Lords Commissioners of His Ma-joliy’s Treasury, That mv Lords having examined into the Facts Rated in the said Petitions and Papers, and having been attended by the Petitioner, and several Persons, Chymists, Manufacturers, and others, in Support of the fame, it appeared from their Evidence, as well as from the Letters adduced of others skilled in the Subject,

That the Marine Acid prepared by the Petitioner may be applied in many Instances, by the Manufacturers to Purposes for which the Vitriolic Acid is at present used and with Advantage to the Manufactures.

It appeared in like Manner, that the Mineral or toffil Alkali, prepared by the Petitioner from Sea Salt,

1 9

will be applicable in the Manufactures of these kingdoms to all the Purposes which Barillia, Pearl Affi, Pot Affi, Weed Affi, and Kelp have been used; of these Kelp alone is produced in any great Quantity in these Kingdoms; the others being chiefly imported from Foreign Parts. It appeared also, that the Petitioner’s Alkali is much superior in its Quality to the others, and in a State of Preparation more convenient to the Manufacturers.

Their Lordships think, therefore, that the Utility of the Undertaking is established; and if it could be carried into such general Effect, as to become a Substitute for the Articles above mentioned* it would not only employ a considerable Number of Hands in a Work perfectly new in this Kingdom* but would prove a National Saving, and an additional Source of Public Wealth; as the Foreign Alkali imported, appeared to their Lordships from the Custom House Books, to have amounted of late Years to near £.350,000. a Year} and that from these Considerations, the Expediency of giving every reasonable Encouragement to the Petitioner, seems evident. How that Encouragement is belt to be given; whether in the exclusive Mode, and to the full Extent proposed by the Petitioner, muit ultimately be decided by the Wisdom of Parliament. And their Lordships conceive, that though the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury will certainly take into their serious Regard that Part of the Report of the Commissioners of the Salt Duties, which proposes a Taxon the Petitioner’s Manufacture, proport ionably equivalent to the Produce of the Duties paid upon the Importation of Foreign Alkalies, and which Amount to about £.11,116. a Year; it should on the other Hand be considered, how far an infant Undertaking of great Extent can bear such a Charge* whether the Encouragement proposed to be given, would not thereby be defeated j and also how far the Defalcation from the Revenue above mentioned, will be made good to the Nation by various Advantages obtained to the different Manufactures. That with respect to the present Produce of the Salt Duties it is evident, that it will not suffer any Decrease by the Exemption prat ed for in the Petitions, as the Salt to be used by the Petitoner in his Undertaking, would not otherwise be made or consumed.

The Revenue, therefore, cannot be effected, except by Frauds* against which their Lordships apprehend sufficient Precautions may be provided, e:tlier by adapting some or all of the Proposals made by Mr.

Fordyce to the Commissioners of the Salt Duties, or by other Regulations to be ascertained and adopted to that End.

I am, Sir,

Your mofl obedient and

Most humble Servant, (Signed)

John Robh/on,

Esquire.

By the KING.

A PROCLAMATION.

GEORGE R.

Whereas it hath been represented to Us, That a great Number of Persons, in consequence of Advertisements or Hand Bills, inciting them thereto, did, on last the Second of this Instant >v,e, alienable in a riotcms and tumultuous Manner in Saint George's in the County of Surrey, from whence they proceeded in several Bodies to Palace Yard, surroundtd both Houses of Parliament, and pofi'efted themselves of the Avenues to the same (the said Houses of Parliament being then fitting) where they continued in a riotous and tumultuous Manner, committing great Outrages and Violence against several of Our Subjects, and feloniously taking Money from them; after which, in the Evening of the same Day, they insulted and attacked the Houses or some of the public Ministers of Foreign Princes and States, residing at Our Court, and broke into, spoiled, and let Fire to Chapels, which in every civilized Country are allowed to such Public Ministers far the free Exerciseof the Religion of their Country, to the great Scandal and Offence of all truly pious and good Protestants; We therefore, in Order that the Reproach of lo frantick and atrocious an Outrage against the Precepts of Religion, as well as the Obligations of all Laws, may not remain a Disgrace to our Kingdom, but may be confined to the Authors, Abettors, and Perpetrators of the said Outrage, and that they may be brought to speedy and condign Punishment, and that l'uch dangerous and wicked Practices may hereafter be prevented, have thought fit, by and with the Advice of Our Privy Council, to publish and declare Our Resolution to put the Laws in Force against Inch Offences: and We do hereby enjoin and require all Justices of the Peace, Sheriffs, Mayors, Bailiffs, Constables, and all other Our loving Subjects, to be aiding and assisting to the utmost of their Power in supprtffing such illegal and tumultuous Assemblies, and in detecting, apprehending, and bringing to Justice the Persons concerned in allcmbling or mitigating the fame, and guilty of any of the Violences above-mentioned: And for the better Detection of the Persons who were concerned in the Outrages committed at the Houses of the said Public Ministers, We are graciously pleased to promise, that if any Person shall discover any other Person or Persons who, directly or indirectly, were concerned in pulling down, or beginning to pull down, or in setting Fire to the Chapel of any Public Minister, lb as that t he Pertonor Persons discovered may be prosecuted for the lame, such Discoverer shall have and receive, as a Reward, upon Conviiftion of such Offender or Offenders, the Sum of Five hundred Pounds, and alfoOur Gracious Pardon for the said Offence in case the Person making such Discovery shall himself be liable to lac prosecuted for the lame, except the Person who first broke into, or began to pull down or let Fire to the said Chapels. And the Commissioners for executing the Office of Treasurer of Our Exchequer are hereby required to make Payment accordingly of the said Rewards.

Given at Our Court at St. James's, the Fifth Day of June, One Thousand Seven hundred and l'.ighty, in the Twentieth Year of Our Reign.

God save the King.

By the KIN G.

A PROCLAMATION.

GEORGE R.

W Jicrcas a great Number of disorderly Persons have afteinh'cd themselves together in a riotous and tumultu-

ous Manner, and have been guilty of many Acts ofTrea-lon and Rebellion, having made an AlFault on the Gaol of Newgate, set loose the Prisoners confined therein, and let Fire to and destroyed the said Priforr: And whereas Houses are now pulling down in several Parts of our Cities of London and H'ejlniiujler, and Liberties thereof, and Fires kindled for consuming the Materials and Furniture of the fame, whereby it is become absolutely necessary to ule the moil effectual Means to quiet such Disturbances, to preserve the Lives and Properties of Individuals and to restore the Peace of the Country: We therefore, taking the same into our moil serious Consideration, have thought fit, by and with the Advice of Our Privy Council, to ifi’ue this Our Pioyal Proclamation, hereby strictly charging and exhorting all Our loving Subjects to preserve the Peace, and to keep themselves, their Servants and Apprentices, quietly within their respective Dwellings, to the End that all well-disposed Persons may avoid those Mif-cliiefs which the Continuance of such riotous Proceedings may bring upon the Guilty: And as it is nccei-fary, from the Circumstances before-mentioned to employ the Military Force, with which we are by Law entrulled, for the immediate Suppression of such rebellious and traiterous Attempts, now making against the Peace and Dignity of Our Crown, and the Safety of the Lives and Projxuties of Our Subjects, We have therefore issued the most direct and effectual Orders to all Our Officers, by an immediate Exertion of their utmost Force to reprels the lame, of which all Pei ions are to take Notice.

Given at our Court at St. Jameses, the Seventh Day of June, One thousand Seven hundred and Eighty, in the Twentieth Year of Our Reign.

God save the King.

By the KING.

A PROCLAMATION.

GEORGE R.

Whereas a great Number of Dilbrderly Persons have for several Days past assembled themselves together, in a riotous and tumultuous Manner, and have been guilty of many Acts of Treason, Rebellion, and Felony, having formed Deilgns to break open and destroy the Gaols and Pnions, and ro set loolc the Prisoners confined therein, and having actually broke into and set on Fire the Gaol of Newgate, the King's Bench Prison, and the Prison of The Fleet, and released the Prisoners, anti made Attempts on other Gaols and Prisons in and about this Metropolis; and having set Fire to and pulled down the Dwelling Houses of divers of Our peaceable Subjects, and also set Fire to, burnt anu cie-stroyed, the Materials thereof, and the Furniture and other Effects found therein; and also taken Money from divers of Our Subjects: Wc therefore, taking the same into Our most serious Consideration, have thought fit, by and with the Advice of Our Privy Council, to publish and declare Our Resolution, That the Authors, Abettors, and Perpetrators of the said Offences be prosecuted asexpeditioully as may be, according to the due Course of Law; and We do hereby enjoin and require all Justices of the Peace, Sheriffs, Mayors, Bailiffs Constables and all other Our loving Subjects, to be aiding and assisting to the utmost of their Power in detecting, apprehending, and bringing to Justice, the said Offenders. Mr. Speaker also reported, That His Majesty was afterwards pleased to make a most Gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of Parliament; of which Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy; which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The Outrages committed by Bands of lawless and desperate Men, in various Parts of this Metropolis broke forth with such Violence into Acts of Felony and Treafbn, had so far overborne all Civil Authority, and threatened so directly the immediate Subversion of all legal Power, the Destruction of all Property, and the Consulion of every Order in the State, that I found Myself obliged, by every Tie of Duty and Affection to My People, to suppress, in every Part, those rebellious Insurrections, and to provide for the Public Safety, by the most effectual and immediate Application of the Force intruded to Me by Parliament.

I have directed Copies of the Proclamations issued upon that Occasion, to be laid before you.

Proper Orders have been given for bringing the Authors and Abettors of these Insurrections, and the Perpetrators of such criminal Acts, to speedy Trial, and to such condign PunUhrrsent as the Laws of their Country prescribe, and as the Vindication of Public Justice demands.

Though I trust it is not necessary, yet I think it right at this Time, to renew to you My solemn Assurances, that I have no other Object but to make the Laws of the Realm, and the Principles of our excellent Constitution, in Church and State, the Rule and Measure of My Conduit; and that I shall ever consider it as the first Duty of My Station, and the chief Glory of My Reign, to maintain and preserve the established Religion of My Kingdoms, and, as far as in Me lies, to secure and to perpetuate the Rights and Liberties of My People.

Resolved, Nernine Contradicente, That an humble Ad-

drefe be presented to His Majesty, to return His Majesty the humble Thanks of this House, for His most Gracious Speech from the Throne; and for the Communication which His Majesty has been pleased to make to this House, of the Proclamations issued during the late most dangerous and alarming Disturbances.

That we think it our indif'penlable Duty, to exprefe, in the strongest Terms, our Abhorrence of the Proceedings of those tumultuous Assemblies, and of the criminal Acts of Outrage and Violence committed by those desperate Bands of Men, and our highest Indignation against the Authors, Promoters, and Perpetrators of them; and to acknowledge, with the warmest Emotions of Gratitude, Duty, and Affection, His Majesty’s Paternal Care and Concern for the Protection of His Subjects, in the Measures which His Majesty, as the Father of His People, and the Guardian of the Public Safety, took, in the Hour of extreme and imminent Necessity, for the immediate and effectual Suppression of those rebellious Insurrections.

That we learn, with Satisfaction, that proper Orders have been given for bringing the Offenders to speedy Trial, and to such Punishment as, upon Conviction of their Crimes, the Laws prescribe, and the Vindication of Public Justice certainly demands.

That although the constant Tenor of His Majesty’s just and constitutional Government made a Renewal of His Majesty's Royal Assurances to His Parliament unnecessary, yet we cannot but receive, with great Thank-fulness, lb signal a Mark of His Majesty’s Gracious Attention; and we beg Leave, on our Part, to assure His Majesty, that this condefccnding and endearing Declaration cannot fail of securing to His Majesty, in the Hearts of His People, the most affectionate Returns of Confidence, Attachment, and Support.

And the said Petition was read; Setting forth, That, since the Act made in the Eleventh and Twelfth Years of the Reign of King William the Third, intituled,

" An Act for the further preventing the Growth of " Popery," the Papists have experienced no Perfecu-tion, and the State has enjoyed perfect Tranquillity; and that repealing Part of that Act, has occasioned much Discontent, and produced dangerous Tumults:

And therefore praying, That the Act of the Eighteenth of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for relieving His Majesty’s Subjects, professing the Popish " Religion, from certain Penalties and Disabilities itnposed on them by an Act, made in the Eleventh and " Twelfth Years of the Reign of King William the " Third, intituled, An Act for the further preventing " the Growth of Popery," may be repealed; that being, in the Petitioners Opinion, the most probable Means of immediately quieting the Minds of the People.

had considered the fever?.! Petitions to them referred: and had come to several Refutations; which th-y had directed him to report to the House; and had also directed him to make a Motion, when the House will please to receive the same.

Mr. Ellis accordingly reported from the said Committee, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followed!: viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Effect and Operation of the Act, passed in the Eighteenth Year of the Reign of His present Ma-jefey, intituled, "An Act for relieving His Majesty’s " Subjects, protcffing the Popish Religion, from certain '

" Penalties and Disabilities imposed on them by an " Act, made in the Eleventh and Twelfth Years of the " Reign of King William the Third, intituled, "An Act

Supply Bill j Exchequer Buis.

912 20°---- I'

" Act for the furlhet preventing the Growth of Popery," have been misrepresented and misunderstood.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Act, passed in the Eighteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, does not repeal or alter, or in any Manner invalidate or render ineffectual the several Statutes made to prohibit the Exercise of the Popish Religion, previous to the Statute of the Eleventh and Twelfth Years of King William the Third.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Ecclesiastical or Spiritual Jurisdiction or Authority is given, by the said Act of th® Eighteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, to the Pope or to the See of Rome.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That this House does, and ever will, watch over the Interests of the Protestant Religion with the most unremitted Attention; and that all Attempts to seduce the Youth of this Kingdom, from the Established Church to Popery, arc highly criminal, according to the Laws in force, and are a proper Subject of further Regulation.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Endeavours to difquict the Minds of the People, by misrepresenting the said Act of the Eighteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, as inconsistent with the Safety or irreconcileable to the Principles of the Protestant Religion, have a manifest Tendency to disturb the Public Peace, to break the Union necessary at this Time, to bring Dishonour on the National Character, to discredit the Protestant Religion in the Eyes of other Nations, and to furnish Occasion for the Renewal of the Persecution of our Protestant Brethren in other Countries.

The Three First Resolutions of the Committee, being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The Fourth Resolution of the Committee, being read a Second Time;

Resolved, Nemine Contradicente, That this House does and ever will, watch over the Interests of the Protestant Religion with the most unremitted Attention; and that all Attempts to seduce the Youth of this Kingdom, from the Establillied Church to Popery, are highly criminal, according to the Laws in force, and are a proper Subject of further Regulation.

The subsequent Resolution of the Committee, being read a Second Time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Mr. Ellis also acquainted the House, That he was directed by the Committee to move, that Leave be given to bring in a Bill to secure the Protestant Religion in Great Britain from any Encroachments of Popery, by more effectually restraining Papists, or Persons professing the Popish Religion, from teaching, or taking upon themselves the Education or Government of, the Children of Protestants.

And Mr. Ellis moved the House accordingly.

Ordered, Nemine Contradicente, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to secure the Protestant Religion in Great Britain from any Encroachments of Popery, by more effectually restraining Papists, or Persons pro-fefiing the Popish Religion, from teaching, or taking upon themselves the Education or Government of, the Children of Protestants: And that Sir George Savile, Mr. Ellis, Mr. Hartley, Mr. Burke, Mr. Recorder of

To prove the Allegations of the First-mentioned Petition, your Committee had, pursuant to their Order, a Copy of a Caveat, entered the 14th of February 1771, by Mr. James Keir, against any Person obtaining a Patent for an Invention by which Alkali may be extraded from Common Salt, from Sea Water, or from the Water of Salt Springs, laid before them; which is hereunto, annexed.

And in further Support of the said Petition, your Committee examined the following Witnesses: First,

Mr. John Whitehwfl \who being asked Whether he

was acquainted wdth the Method by which Mr. Keir obtains his Alkali ? said. He saw him make a Substance Yesterday, in Part from Sea Salt, which the Wit-nels delivered to Mr. Moore, Secretary to the Society of Arts and Sciences — That he saw the Process from the Beginning to the End. — And being asked, If he was Judge enough to say, whether the other Substances used. with the Sea Salt were such as now make Part of the Body of that Alkali, or whether they were only used in the Process as Solvents or Menstruums ? he said, They were used to make Part of it; there were no other Bodies in the Composition but the Sea Salt that could produce the Alkali — That he has heard, some Years ago, of Mr. Keir’s making Alkali, but he does not know it of his own Knowledge, as he never saw any Specimen of it — That he never heard or knew of his felling any Quantity of it some Years ago — That the Quantity made Yesterday was a small one — That he is not a sufficient Judge to know, whether the same Process wiil certainly succeed in making a large Quantity — That Mr. Blair was present at the above Process — That the Witness'knows what the Ingredients were, that were used in the Process.

Alexander Blair, Esquire, being examined, said, That he saw Mr. Keir obtain an Alkali Yesterday from Common Salt, which was delivered to Mr. Moore, Secretary to the Society of Arts and Sciences — -That he saw the whole Process from the Beginning to the End, and that no oilier Substances containing Alkali were used. — And being asked. Whether he was acquainted with the Substances that were used ? he said. He was, as far as his Reading and Knowledge in Chymistry went, and could say they contained no Alkaline Quality — And being asked. If he had made Chymistry his Study ? he said. Only generally; that he had once a Chymical Object in View with Doctor Irvine, who received a Premium from Parliament for making Salt Water fresh. — And being asked, Whether he could say, with Certainty, that the same Process will answer in a large Quantity ? he laid, It will certainly produce Alkali, and as Materials are cheap, at a reasonable Rate. — That the Apparatus used Yesterday in the above Process, were very impeded, therefore he cannot judge from thence, pre-cilely, at what Expence it can be made in large Quantities. — And being asked. Whether he knew that large Vessels can be procured, which will answer for the Process, without great Expence in breaking and losing the Materials? he said, Mr. Keir could procure every Thing necessary for his Process in large. — And being asked. Whether he had any llcafon to suppole, from what he saw, that the Alkali can be manufactured by 10 Z Mr.

Mr. Samuel Moore, Secretary to the Society of Arts and Sciences, being examined, said, That lie had examined the Alkali which Mr. Blair and Mr. Whitehw laid they law made by Mr. Keir from Common Salt, as far as the small Time allowed him, gave Permission for him to make Experiments with it. — And being asked, Whether he believed from the Trials he had made, th.it it was actually an Alkali, and applicable to the Purposes to Which other Alkalies are commonly applied? he laid, It Was brought to him in a State of Solution, and in that State it was strongly Alkaline, and believes was as applicable to the Pnrpoles for which Alkaline Salts are used, as any Solution of the same Strength would be — That he had not Time to compare it with BariUia — That the Manner in which he tried to ascertain its being a fixed Alkali, was by the Taste, by its dccompoling crude Sal Almoniac, Alum, and the common Epsom Salt; and by those Trials he was convinced the Liquor was strongly Alkaline.

Cotton Trade, and also several Weavers and Spinners; the Substance of whole Evidence is as follows; viz.

That there is at present, and was last Year, full Employment for Persons concerned in the Cotton Manufacture in many Parts of the County of Lancaster -r-T.iat the Wages of Spinners have varied of late Years — 'That last Year a Spinner by the single Spindle could only earn Three Pence or Four Pence a Day, who, by working upon a Jenney, can now get Two Shillings or 2J. 6 d.a Day — That a Fufban Weaver can earn from One Shilling to Two Shillings a Day, and that the Manufacturers in general are not distressed for Want of Employment.

- That the Cotton Manufacture in has in-

creased double within the last Ten Years; and a Cal-licoe Manufactory has been estab ished. and owes its Existence to the Use of the Machines — That the Price of Spinning Cotton Warps has been much reduced; which Reduction has occasioned the Introduction of the Callicoe Manufactory, and improved the Quilting — That the Linen Manufactory has very considerably decreased during the same Period; That the Cotton Manufactory has been supported, by the Use of the Machines, without which, that Manufactory must have funk as well as the Linen; and that the Demand for Cotton Goods could not have been fupnlied, if the Machines had not been made use of — That Cotton Goods were never made better than they have been within these Five Years; and that fewer Complaints of them have been made by their Correspondents abroad frnce the Introduction of the Patent Machines than before, and the Trade in general was never known to ilourish more than in the last Spring.

That if the Machines are supported, and Improvements in them encouraged, the Manufacture will be farther extended — That there are Three Times as many Looms employed now, as there were Ten Years ago; and that if there were many more Looms than there are at present, the Manufacturers would be glad to employ them — That if the Spinning Machines were, prevented from working, it would not be possible to supply the Weaver with Warp equal to the present Demand — That the Wages to the Weaver are higher now than they were Ten Years ago; and that Patent CottOn Warp would answsr as well as Linen in many other Articles besides those to which it is now applied, particularly in all Corded Dimities.

And one of the Witnesses being examined in relation to the Increase of the Poor Rates, acknowledged they were increased’of late Years; but that it was not owing to the Diflrrefs of the’ Manufacturers by the Introduction of the Machines, but to various other Causes.

Upon the whole Matter, your Committee came to the following Resolutions; j.'Refohed, That it appears to this Committee, That tire Cotton Manufactures in the county of,

have of late Years greatly increased.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Increase of the said Manufactures is owing to the Introduction of the Patent Machines, which are used in carding, roving, spinning, andtwilting Cotton; and that a very valuable Manufacture of Callicoes has been established in the said County, by the Use of the Patent Machines.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the great Demand for the Cotton Manufactures could not pofttbly have been supplied without the Ulc of the Patent Machines; and that there is no Want of Emp'oyment for the industrious Poor.

Resolved, Tint it is the Opinion of this Committee, That if the Manufacturers were deprived of the Use of the Patent Machines, it would be the Means of transfer- . ring those evident Advantages which we now reap from them, into the Hands, of Foreign Nation*, who are our *7

Rivals in the Cotton Trade, and would, in a great measure, be destructive of that valuable Branch of Commerce. .

The laid Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Quest on severally put thereupon, agreed to by the Hause Neniine Contradicente.

Ordered, That the said Report be printed.

A Petition of Thomas iVa, of , in the County Palatine of Lancaster, Merchant, on behalf of himself and the rest of the Proprietors of the Cotton Works at Birkacre, in the said County, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner, together with some other Persons his Partners, about Three Years ago contracted with Richard Arkwright, of Cromford, in the County of Derby, for a Number of Spindles and Spinning Machines, invented and - constructed by the said Richard,

and for the exclusive Ule whereof he obtained His Majesty’s Letters Patent; and that in order to reap the Benefit of such Cqntraft, and to carry on the Trade of Spinning Cotton, the Petitioner and his Partners, agreed with John Chadwick, late of Burgh within Cher ley, in the said County of , Gentleman,

since deceased, for an old Iron Forge, a Corn-Mill, and other Buildings, Lands, and Premisses, at Birkacre within Charley aforesaid, for a long Term of Years, at the Yearly Rent of One hundred and Eighty Pounds, and upwards; and that the said Machines are worked by Water, and require very strong and great Variety of large Wheels, Shafts, and other Geers and Implement, which are attended with heavy Expence, and that the' Petitioner and his said Partners erected and fixed upon the said Premisses at Birkacre proper Buildings, Wheels, and of her Machinery, and had got Part of the Number of Spindles so agreed fur at Work, which were likely to be attended with Advantage to tha Petitioner, as well as being, as he conceives, of g eat. Utility to the Public, by making Yarn or Thread of a superior Quality to any other now spun from Cotton; but that, upon the Fourth Day of October last, a most riotous and outrageous Mob assembled in the Neighbourhood, armed in a warlike Manner, and after breaking down the Doors of the Buildings, they entered the Rooms, destroyed most of the Machinery, and afterwards let fire to and consumed the whole Buildings, and every Thing therein contained; and that the Lol's sustained by the Proprietors On this Occasion, amounts to Four thousand Four hundred Pounds, and upwards, they having aft u ally expended more, than that Sum in the Premium or Price of the said Spindles, and the said Buildings, Wheels, and Machinery necessary for working the fame; and that, previous to the Destruction of the said Works, the Petitioner (who had been apprized of the Mob’s assembling) applied to the Civil Magistrates in the Neighbourhood, and also ta such Military Forces as were then within any reasonable Distance, and several of such Magistrates, and allb a linall Party of Invalids, which were all the Troops that could be got to the Place in Time, did attend, but were unable to relict the Number^ and Violence of the Rioters; and the Petitioner being advised that the Building* and Property destroyed, were not such as fall within the Description or Meaning of the Statutes, which give an Action to the Party injured to recover Damages against the Hundred wherein the Offence was committed, the Petitioner and the other Proprietors have not brought any such Action, or pursued any other Mode for obtaining Satisfaction for their Lois, nor have they received any Satisfaction or Compensation whatsoever for the lame: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and order that a Satisfaction be made to the Petitioner and the other Proprietors, for the great Injury they have suffered by this lawless Proceeding, in such Way as to Parliament shall seem expedient.

Sir, Whitehall, 12th June, 17 80.

I Lave received the Favour of your Letter of thi4-Date, with the several Papers inclosed.. If, in the printed Paper, with the Lord Mayor’s Name annexed, Firelocks are meant by the Words " with their " Arms," in the first Article in the Paper, I wholly disapprove of that Intention: No Persons can bear Arms in this Country, but under Officers having the King’s Commissions.

The Inhabitants of the Borough of Southwark, those of th.e Parish of Covent Garden, and of some other Parishes, have formed themfc.ves into1 very useful, arid at the same Time unexceptionable Associations; and it something of the same Kind Was adopted in the City, there is no doubt but much Uie artd great Security would arise therefrom but the using of Firs Arms is improper* unnecessary, and cannot be approved.

Sir, Whitehall, 14th June 1780.

I have had the Honour to receive your Letter of this Dai’s Date; and I have also seen Lieut. Colonel

Giinfield i cannot say more regarding the Proposal for putting Arms into the Hands of the Inhabitants of the Ci y. than is contained in my Letters to you of Monday's and Yesterday’s Date; and I fully approve of your Conduct upon the whole of this Business.

There can be no Doubt that the Aldermen, in pro* poling to arm their Wards, mean, by way of general Defence; but supposing that the assembling the Inhabitants under Arms was legal, the Inconveniences which you have dated to the Mayor, 13c. as likely to arise from the motley Appearance of the armed Inhabitants, in case of the Rioters assembling again, should, I think, be sufficient to induce the Magistrates of the City to drop the Intention.

In support of the Petition of the said John Col*

//Jon,

Samuel More, Esquire, Secretary to the Society for the Encouragement of Arts and Sciences, being examined, said, That Mr. Coliifon gave him some Alkali Salt; which he produced to your Committee, and which Mr. Coliifon informed him he had produced from Sea Salt — That he did not fee the Process, but that he is convinced that it is an Alkali of that Kind, commonly called the Foflil or Mineral Alkali — That he has tried the Properties of it by Experiment; and found, that when combined with the Vitriolic Acid, it made a very good Globar Salt; of which he produced to your Committee a Specimen; and lays, that lie believes it is equally as strong (from the Taste and Combination of Vitriolic Acid) as the Salt extracted from Barillia — That there is a great Difference in Ba-rillias as to Strength; and that it will go farther in Ule than the Barillia as imported, and is much the same as Mr. Fordyce's.

Mr. Coliifon then produced to your Committee, Three B >ttles of the Salts made by him; and fays, They are all fit for the Purposes to which that Kind of Alkaline Salt is applied: And,

Mr. More, being further examined, said, That he has tried the Salt in Two of the Bottles, and chat there is some Sea Salt in them — That he never met with any without tome — And that they are as pure as those Salts generally are.

Mr. Joseph Fry, being then examined, said, That he is acquainted with the Process in Chymistry by which Mr. Coliifon separates the Acid from the Sea Salt — That he has Lea and attended the Process — That he has made great Quantities himself — That ic is superior in Quality to the Barillia as it is sent over — That it is the same as Salt of Barillia, and is half as good again as Barillia; and will answer the Purpose of Barillia in making Soap and Glass — That he has made many Tons, aid converted it into Soap — That it can be made in any Quantity, at an Expence equal to Barillia at Twenty-five or Twenty-six Shillings per Hundred, if no Duty is paid for the Salt; but if it pays a Salt Duty it cannot be afforded at the Price of Barillia — That Mr. Coliifon s Process is precilely the same with

is a Merchant, and lives near — That he

knows of Dr. Black and Mr. Walt's having discovered a Method of extracting Mineral Alkali from Sea Salt many Years ago — That he has seen Mr. separate

James Black, Esquire, a Merchant in London, being also examined, laid. My Lords, and Gentlemen,

It gives Me great Satisfaction to find Myself able to determine this long Session of Parliament, that you may be at Liberty to return to your several Counties, and attend to your private Affairs, after so laborious a Discharge of your Duty in the Public Service; and I take this Occasion to express My sincere Acknowledgment for the fresh Proofs you have given Me of your affectionate Zeal for the Support of My Government, and of your just Estimation of the real and permanent Iff-terefts of your Country.

Your Magnanimity and Perseverance in the Profecu* tion of this just and necessary War have enabled Me to make such Exertions as will, I trust, by the Assistance of Divine Providence, dilappoint the violent and uri-just Deligns of My EnemTes, and bring them to listen to equitable and honourable Terms of Peace.

These Exertions have already been attended with Success by Sea and Lind; and the late important and prosperous Turn of Affairs 1:1 America, 1:7yc Is the

fairest Prospect of the returning Loyalty and A fleet ion of Mf Subjects in the Colonies, and of their happy Re-union with their Parent Country.
